Proof of Theorem 1. On x = 0 parity gives W1 = 0 and Theta_x = 0, so (P2) reads V T' = lambda T. Suppose
beta != 2. Since T(y)/y -> a0, T has the sign of a0 and no zero on some (0, delta); the axis equation then gives
V != 0 on (0, delta), so V has constant sign there by continuity. The mean value theorem gives a point of (0, delta)
where T' has the sign of a0, and there V = lambda T/T' has the sign of lambda; hence lambda/V > 0 on (0, delta).
Let y* > 0 be the smallest positive zero of V, if any. On (0, y*) the coefficient lambda/V is continuous and positive,
and the linear equation T' = (lambda/V) T gives T(y) = T(y0) exp(int_{y0}^y lambda/V) for y0 in (0, delta) and
y in [y0, y*). Hence |T| >= |T(y0)| > 0 on [y0, y*) and T(y*) != 0 by continuity. The equation at y* reads
0 = lambda T(y*), a contradiction. Hence V has no zero on (0, inf) and V has the sign of lambda there.
(a) If 0 < beta < 2 then V < 0 on (0, inf), i.e. U2(0, y) < -beta y for every y > 0; this contradicts U2(0, y) = o(y).
(b) If beta > 2 then V > 0, and T = T(y0) exp(int_{y0}^y lambda/V) is strictly increasing in modulus. Since
V(y) <= (beta + eps) y for y >= y_eps, int_{y_eps}^y lambda/V >= (lambda/(beta + eps)) log(y/y_eps).
(c) follows from (a) and (b).

Proof of Theorem 2. U = o(|X|) gives X.W >= |X|^2 for |X| >= R. Along a backward trajectory outside B_R,
d/ds |X(-s)|^2 <= -2 |X(-s)|^2, so every backward trajectory enters the closed ball B_R in finite time. W points
outward on dB_R, so the ball is backward invariant. Theta is constant along trajectories (lambda = 0), hence
|Theta(X)| <= max_{B_R} |Theta|.

Proof of Theorem 3 (outline; the complete proof is in Appendix A.4).
 Step 1 (nonresonant stagnation interval). By Lemma 3 below, V := W2(0, .) vanishes wherever Theta0' != 0. The
   function T' = Theta0' is continuous with T'(0) = a0 != 0. If T' took values only in the closed discrete set
   S = {0} u {lambda_k}, lambda_k = 4(m - 1)(4m - 7) (m odd >= 3) = 40, 208, 504, 928, ..., then T' would be
   constant, T affine and nonconstant, contradicting the boundedness of Theta (Theorem 2). Hence there is an open
   interval I of the positive y-axis on which T' != 0, T' avoids S, and V = 0.
 Step 2 (transverse flatness). Put phi = Psi + 2xy and eta = Theta - T(y). On I, induction over odd m >= 3 using
   (P1)-(P3) gives at the first possibly nonzero order 4(m - 1) eta_{m-1} + m T' phi_m = 0 and
   -m(m - 1)(4m - 7) phi_m = (m - 1) eta_{m-1}, so [T' - 4(m - 1)(4m - 7)] phi_m = 0 and phi_m = 0 on I. All products
   of perturbations enter at strictly higher order. Hence phi, eta and Omega are flat in x on compact subintervals.
 Step 3 (local flat rigidity). Straighten the flow by Theta-level coordinates; (P1) divided by W1 becomes a Volterra
   identity expressing Delta phi through phi and its first derivatives integrated from the interface. A Carleman
   estimate for the Laplacian with weight -log x (log b(z) - log r at a curved interface), the dilation bounds for the
   Volterra kernels and absorption for large weight parameter give phi = 0 in a one-sided neighbourhood.
 Step 4 (propagation). Unique continuation across regular interfaces transversal to W and a support-minimum argument
   for x + K (y - y0)^2 propagate phi = 0 to a half-strip (0, inf) x J. There U1 = 2x, contradicting U = o(|X|).
 Lemma 3 (used in Step 1): at beta = 2, V Theta0' = 0 on the y-axis by the axis equation of the proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Proposition 5. The flow phi_s of W is complete and has Jacobian e^(2 beta s). Then
int |Theta|^p = int |Theta(phi_s Y)|^p e^(2 beta s) dY = e^((lambda p + 2 beta) s) int |Theta|^p for every s, so
lambda p + 2 beta = 0, i.e. beta = 2p/(p + 2) < 2. At beta = 2 each superlevel set {|Theta| > eps} is invariant and
has area e^(4s) times its area; if Theta -> 0 at infinity it is bounded, hence of zero area, and being open it is
empty for every eps > 0, so Theta = 0.

Proof of Proposition 6. Write Psi = xy H, Omega = xy G with H, G smooth and even in each variable. Lift
h(p, q) = H(|p|, |q|), g(p, q) = G(|p|, |q|) to R^3 x R^3; then -Delta_{R^6} h = g. Sublinearity gives h -> 0 at
infinity: for |x| >= |y|, Psi(x, y) = -int_0^y U1(x, s) ds, so |H| <= sup |U1|/|x| -> 0, and symmetrically. If
Omega >= 0 on Q1 then g >= 0, h is superharmonic and tends to 0, so h >= 0 by the minimum principle. But
h(0) = Psi_xy(0) = c = -2.

Proof of Proposition 7. Outside a disc of radius R containing the support, (P1) gives Theta_x = 0. A horizontal
line may meet the exterior in two components; evenness in x identifies the two constants, so Theta(x, y) = F(y) for
|X| > R with F(y) := Theta(x0, y) for a fixed x0 > R, smooth and odd. For compactly supported vorticity the
convolution K * Omega is O(1/|X|) at infinity, and the subtracted constant int K(-Y) Omega(Y) dY vanishes by the
odd-odd parity, so the canonical velocity tends to 0 at infinity. Letting x -> inf in (P2) gives
beta y F'(y) = lambda F(y) for all y. On y > 0, F = C y^alpha with alpha = 1 - 2/beta < 1, and F is odd. If beta < 2,
continuity at 0 forces C = 0; if beta = 2, F is constant on each half-line with opposite constants, and continuity
forces both to vanish; if beta > 2, differentiability at 0 forces C = 0 since F(y)/y = C y^(alpha - 1). Hence Theta
has compact support and is nonzero by its jet, which Proposition 5 excludes (compact support gives both L^1 and
L^2, i.e. beta = 2/3 and beta = 1 simultaneously).

Proof of Proposition 8. Theta = y A(X) with A(X) = int_0^1 Theta_y(x, t y) dt and A(0) = a0 > 0, so Theta > 0 on
{y > 0} near 0. The x-axis is invariant, so trajectories starting in {y > 0} stay there. Every X in B with y > 0 enters
this neighbourhood backward in time, and Theta(phi_s X) = e^(lambda s) Theta(X) preserves the sign. If 0 is the only
equilibrium, X.W >= (beta/2)|X|^2 outside a ball keeps backward orbits bounded. A periodic orbit enclosing a region D
would give 0 = int_{dD} W.n = 2 beta |D| > 0, so there is none. The origin is a source (DW(0) = diag(beta + 2,
beta - 2)), so a backward limit set containing 0 forces convergence to 0; a compact backward limit set without
equilibria would be a periodic orbit by the Poincare-Bendixson theorem. Hence B = R^2.

Proof of Proposition 9. U = o(|X|) gives X.W >= (beta/2)|X|^2 for |X| >= R, so every backward orbit enters the
closed ball B_R in finite time and stays there (W points outward on its boundary); the backward half-orbit of X lies
in the closed ball of radius M_X = max(R, |X|). Along any orbit d/ds [e^s Omega(phi_s X)] = e^s Theta_x(phi_s X).
Integrating over [-S, 0] and letting S -> inf, e^(-S) Omega(phi_(-S) X) -> 0 and the integrand is bounded by
e^s max |Theta_x| over the ball of radius M_X.

Proof of Proposition 10. Differentiating (P2) in y on y = 0 gives w tau' = (w' - beta - 2) tau with w(x) = W1(x, 0),
tau(0) = a0, w = (beta + 2) x + O(x^3). On (0, x*), x* the first positive zero of w (or inf),
tau(x) = tau(x0) [w(x)/w(x0)] exp(-(beta + 2) int_{x0}^x ds/w(s)), so tau keeps the sign of a0; tau -> 0 as
x -> x* (if x* < inf because w -> 0 and the exponential is at most 1; if x* = inf because w(x)/x -> beta gives
log|tau|/log x -> -2/beta, i.e. |tau(x)| = x^(-2/beta + o(1))). The intermediate value theorem gives
tau(x_h) = a0/2; spatial scaling by l = 1/x_h places it at x = 1 and preserves a0.

Proof of Theorem 11 (outline; the complete proof is in Appendix A.12). Write D = W.grad,
M = DW and J(v1, v2) = (-v2, v1). Differentiating (P2) and using J M^T = (tr M) J - M J with tr M = 2 beta gives,
for h = J grad Theta, the exact identity D h = M h - (beta + 2) h. Outside a large circle W_r > 0, and
h = f W + (lambda Theta/W_r) e_phi with f = -Theta_phi/(r W_r); the radial component of the identity gives
D f + (beta + 2) f = lambda Theta (d_phi W_r)/(r W_r^2), in which the derivative of U is multiplied by Theta/r^2
rather than by grad Theta. Along outgoing trajectories r grows like e^((beta + o(1)) s). A local div-curl estimate
(cut off the vorticity on B(X, r/2), subtract its Biot-Savart field, and bound the harmonic remainder) gives
|DU(X)| <= C_N [r^(-1) sup_{B(X,r/2)} |U| + (1 + log r) sup_{B(X,r/2)} |Omega| + r^(-N)] for every fixed N > 0,
with a constant C_N, using the polynomial bound on grad Omega. The characteristic formula of Proposition 9 for Omega and the subtracted kernel
bound (Omega = O(r^(-a)) with 0 < a < 1 implies U = O(r^(1 - a))) close a finite iteration of exponents that ends
at (a). The limits in (b) come from the convergence of M_s = e^(-beta s) D(phi_s) along outgoing trajectories (the
coefficient DU is integrable in s; det M_s = 1). With a(Z) = lim e^(-beta s) phi_s Z for Z on a large circle Sigma,
beta a = M_inf W(Z), so det(beta a, a') = det(W(Z), Z') > 0 for a counterclockwise parametrization; the angular map
Z -> arg a(Z) has positive derivative and degree one, hence is a C^1 diffeomorphism. Holder continuity of A follows
by balancing the convergence rate |e^s Omega(phi_s Z) - b(Z)| <= C e^(-s) against the Lipschitz bound
C e^((1 + beta (m + 1)) s) of the finite-time expression, which gives the exponent 1/(beta (m + 1) + 2) (m >= 0). F(pi/2) has the sign of a0 because the positive y-axis is invariant with positive
speed (Theorem 1). V is identified by rescaling the subtracted Biot-Savart integral (dominated convergence) and the
homogeneous inverse of r^(-delta) A. (c) follows by integrating beta r d_r (r^(-gamma) Theta) = -r^(-gamma) U.grad Theta
from r to infinity. (d): on D = {1 < |X| < 2} put T_R(X) = R^(-gamma) Theta(RX), Z_R = R^(2 delta) Omega(RX),
W_R = beta X + R^(-1) U(RX). For eta in C_c^infinity(D), (P1) gives
int_D T_R eta_x = int_D Z_R [W_R.grad eta + (2 beta - 1) eta]. T_R -> T_inf := |X|^gamma F(arg X) uniformly, and there
is eta with int_D T_inf eta_x != 0: otherwise d_x T_inf = 0, so F = C_+ sin(phi)^gamma on 0 < phi < pi and
F = C_- |sin(phi)|^gamma on pi < phi < 2 pi, and C^1 regularity at phi = 0 with 0 < gamma < 1 forces C_+ = C_- = 0,
contradicting F != 0. Since W_R.grad eta + (2 beta - 1) eta is bounded, int_D |Z_R| >= c > 0 for large R, which is
the annular L^1 bound. For p >= 1 Holder gives int_{R<|X|<2R} |Omega|^p >= c_p R^(2 - 2 delta p), excluding
1 <= p <= beta (p = beta by summing disjoint dyadic annuli); for 0 < p < 1, |Omega| <= ||Omega||_inf^(1 - p) |Omega|^p
reduces to p = 1.

Proof of Proposition 13. Backward orbits of points of Q1 stay in Q1 (both axes are invariant), so Theta_x >= 0 on
Q1 gives Omega >= 0 on Q1 by Proposition 9, which Proposition 6 excludes. Suppose Theta_x <= 0 on Q1 and put
f = -Omega >= 0, g = -Theta_x >= 0. Along the forward flow, f(phi_t X) = e^(-t) f(X) + int_0^t e^(s - t) g(phi_s X) ds
>= e^(-t) f(X). The flow preserves Q1 and has Jacobian e^(2 beta t), so if M := int_{Q1} f^p is finite then
M = e^(2 beta t) int_{Q1} f(phi_t X)^p dX >= e^((2 beta - p) t) M for all t >= 0. For p < 2 beta this forces M = 0. At
p = 2 beta equality holds for almost every X, so g = 0 along a.e. forward orbit segment, hence g = 0 on Q1 by
continuity and then f = 0 by Proposition 9. M = 0 means Omega = 0 on Q1, hence on R^2 by parity; then U is harmonic
and sublinear, hence constant and by parity zero, contradicting c = -2.

Proof of Theorem 12 (outline). If A = 0, the forward characteristic integral for Omega from the observation time to
infinity, together with the limit of r^(2 delta) grad Theta, gives r^(2 delta) Omega -> -d_x[r^gamma F] r^(2 delta)
= B. If B were 0, then F = C_+ sin(phi)^gamma on 0 < phi < pi and F = C_- |sin(phi)|^gamma on pi < phi < 2 pi, which is
not C^1 at phi = 0 unless C_+ = C_- = 0, contradicting F(pi/2) != 0. In both branches the rescaled subtracted Biot-Savart integral converges to the homogeneous field with
curl -r^(-a) C_a (a = delta, C_a = A, or a = 2 delta, C_a = B); both fields have the same divergence and curl in distributions on the
whole plane (the boundary terms on a circle of radius eps are O(eps^(2 - a))), so their difference is an entire
harmonic field, homogeneous of degree 1 - a in (0, 1), hence zero; so the limit is the homogeneous inverse, which is nonzero because d H_a = 0 forces C_a = 0.
Continuity gives an angular interval on which |U| >= c r^h, which yields the annular bound. In branch (ii),
one-signed Theta_x on Q1 is excluded by Proposition 13, since Omega = O(r^(-2 delta)) lies in L^p(Q1) for every
beta < p <= 2 beta. For a0 > 0, B = sin(phi)^(gamma + 1)
d/dphi [F/sin(phi)^gamma] is positive somewhere, and the absolutely convergent strain identity
-2 = (4/pi) int_{Q1} x y |X|^(-4) Omega forces Omega < 0 somewhere.

Proof of Proposition 14. Since div W = 2 beta and W.grad Theta^2 = 2 lambda Theta^2, for X != 0
  div(Theta^2 W |X|^(-k)) = [beta (4 - k) - 4] Theta^2 |X|^(-k) - k Theta^2 (U.X) |X|^(-k-2),
  div(W |Omega|^m/m) + (1 - 2 beta/m) |Omega|^m = Theta_x Omega |Omega|^(m-2)   (m >= 2 beta > 4, so |Omega|^m is C^1).
Integrate over eps < |X| < R. Near 0, Theta, U and W are O(|X|), so the planar temperature integrands are
O(|X|^(2-k)) (radial densities O(r^(3-k))) and the inner flux is O(eps^(4-k)), which vanishes for k < 4. By the
odd-odd parity Omega = O(|X|^2), so the inner vorticity flux is O(eps^(2m+2)). At infinity Theorem 11(a) gives the radial integrands O(r^(2 gamma + 1 - k))
for I_k, O(r^(2 gamma + 1 - delta - k)) for J_k, O(r^(1 - m delta)) for the moment and O(r^(1 - (m + 1) delta)) for the
source, integrable for k > k_*, k > k_* - delta, m > 2 beta and m > 2 beta - 1 respectively. The outer fluxes are
int Theta^2 (beta R + U_r) R^(1-k) dphi and (1/m) int (beta R + U_r) |Omega|^m R dphi, which are O(R^(k_* - k)) and
O(R^(2 - m delta)); they vanish in (a) and (c), and by Theorem 11(b) and U_r = o(R) they tend to beta int F^2 at
k = k_* and to (beta/m) int |A|^m = (1/2) int |A|^(2 beta) at m = 2 beta, where the volume coefficients vanish
identically, which gives (b) and (d). In (a), a0 != 0 gives I_k > 0 and beta (4 - k) - 4 < 0 for k > k_*, so J_k < 0.
I_{k_*} = inf because int_0^{2 pi} Theta(R, phi)^2 dphi >= c R^(2 gamma) for large R (F != 0). In (c), Omega is not
identically zero by Theorem 11(d), so the moment is positive. At the critical exponents the identically zero
volume term is removed before R -> inf, so no product 0 times inf occurs.

Proof of Theorem 15 (outline). Put tau = T - t and omega = tau^(-1) Omega(z/tau^beta), theta = tau^(beta-2) Theta(z/tau^beta),
u = tau^(beta-1) U(z/tau^beta); then D_t omega = theta_x, D_t q = -(Du)^T q for q = grad theta, div u = 0 and curl u = -omega
(D_t = partial_t + u.grad). Theorem 11(a), the A1 parity and smoothness give, for 0 < tau <= 1 and z != 0, the bounds
|u| <= C|z|^(1 - delta), |theta| <= C|z|^gamma, |omega| <= C|z|^(-delta), |grad theta| <= C|z|^(-2 delta) (inside the
ball |z| <= tau^beta use |z|^delta <= tau). The polynomial bound on grad Omega in the hypotheses of Theorem 11, the decay of
Theorem 11(a) and a local logarithmic elliptic estimate give |DU(X)| <= C(1 + |X|)^(-delta) log(2 + |X|), hence
sup_K |Du(t)| <= C_K(1 + |log tau|) on every compact K not containing 0, which is integrable in t up to T. On a ball away
from 0, Du = T(chi omega) + h with T an order-zero Calderon-Zygmund matrix and h having all derivatives bounded by the
pointwise bounds alone (no high derivative of distant vorticity is used); the commutator [phi, T] partial_j is bounded on
L^p, 1 < p < inf. With the cutoff phi = chi((|z - z0| + M(t - t0))/R), chi nonincreasing, M a bound for |u| on the
ball, one has D_t phi <= 0, and the weighted L^p norms E of the m-th derivatives of omega and q satisfy
dE/dt <= C(1 + sup_ball |Du|)(1 + E): the only top-order terms besides transport are D^m q_1 and (D^m Du)^T q, controlled
by E through the commutator estimate, and the mixed products are controlled by the previous order in every finite L^p
and Holder's inequality. Gronwall gives uniform W^(m,p) bounds on compact sets away from 0 for all m, p, hence C^k
convergence to the homogeneous terminal fields r^(-delta) A, r^gamma F, r^(1 - delta) V; (a) and (b) follow by scaling
(tau = r^(-delta) at unit physical radius). Integrating partial_t omega and partial_t theta, which converge in every
local C^k norm, from T - tau to T gives the first corrections u_0.grad omega_0 - partial_x theta_0 = r^(-2 delta) B and
u_0.grad theta_0 = r^(gamma - delta) F_1. For the velocity, |(omega - omega_0)/tau| <= C|z|^(-2 delta) on the whole plane,
which is integrable against the subtracted Biot-Savart kernel near 0, near the target and at infinity because
0 < 2 delta < 1; dominated convergence identifies the limit of the velocity difference quotient, and localized W^(m,p)
estimates together with dominated convergence for the distant differentiated kernels upgrade the convergence to C^k on
compact sets away from 0. The limit is homogeneous of degree 1 - 2 delta, divergence free with curl -r^(-2 delta) B on the
whole plane; its difference from r^(1 - 2 delta) V_2 is an entire harmonic field of that non-integer degree and vanishes.

Proof of Theorem 16 (outline). For odd-odd sources the quadrant-folded kernel K_Q(X, Y) = sum eps1 eps2 K(X - Y_eps)
has vanishing constant and linear Taylor terms in Y and vanishes at X = 0, so the folded inverse converges for
sources bounded by |Y|^(-a), 0 < a < 4, gives velocities O(|X|^(1-a)), with symbol bounds provided the source also
satisfies |D^m f(Y)| <= C_m |Y|^(-a-m) for every finite m, coincides with the canonical inverse in the original class,
and has zero flux through circles about 0 (Fubini applied to the folded integral). For homogeneous odd-odd sources
r^(-a) A(phi) it gives the homogeneous field with stream function r^(2-a) H, -H'' - (2-a)^2 H = A, including a = 2.
With the physical fields of the proof of Theorem 15 and the symbol bounds of Theorem 15(a), the time derivatives
omega^[n], theta^[n], u^[n] obey the bounds r^(-(n+1) delta - k), r^(gamma - n delta - k), r^(1 - (n+1) delta - k) for
(n + 1) delta < 4, by induction on the equations for partial_t^(n+1) omega and partial_t^(n+1) theta and
u^[n] = B_Q omega^[n], and have C^infinity local terminal limits. After obtaining velocity derivatives and terminal
limits through order N, the transport equations give vorticity and temperature derivatives and terminal limits
through order N + 1, without inverting that extra vorticity derivative. One-sided Taylor expansion at t = T and
comparison of powers of tau give the coefficients, which are homogeneous by induction; at unit physical radius
tau = r^(-delta), and polar differentiation of the coefficient recursion gives the displayed relations.

Proof of Proposition 17 (outline). With lambda_x = beta + 2, lambda_y = beta - 2 the linear part of W is
(lambda_x x, lambda_y y). Writing Omega = sum g_ij x^(2i+1) y^(2j+1), Poisson inversion gives
g_ij = -(2i+3)(2i+2) h_(i+1,j) - (2j+3)(2j+2) h_(i,j+1). The coefficient of x^(2i) y^(2j+1) (i + j = n) in (P2) is
L_ij a_ij + (2i+1) a0 h_ij + P_ij = 0 with L_ij = 2i lambda_x + 2j lambda_y > 0 and P_ij a sum of products of strictly
lower blocks; the degree 1 row is a0 (c + 2) = 0, which forces c = -2 and does not fix a0. The coefficient of
x^(2i+1) y^(2j+1) (i + j = n - 1) in (P1) is M_ij g_ij - 2(i+1) a_(i+1,j) + Q_ij = 0 with
M_ij = (2i+1) lambda_x + (2j+1) lambda_y + 1 > 0, where Q_ij involves h of blocks at most n - 1 and g determined in
blocks at most n - 1. Eliminating a and g gives
h_(i,j+1) = -(A_i/B_j)[1 - a0/(L_(i+1,j) M_ij)] h_(i+1,j) + [Q_ij + 2(i+1) P_(i+1,j)/L_(i+1,j)]/(M_ij B_j),
A_i = (2i+3)(2i+2), B_j = (2j+3)(2j+2), with
L_(i+1,j) M_ij = [2n(beta-2) + 8i + 8][2n(beta-2) + 8i + 5] >= [2n(beta-2) + 8][2n(beta-2) + 5] >= D. Under the bound
every bracket is positive, the homogeneous response to h_(n,0) is (-1)^j k_j with k_0 = 1, k_j > 0, and the angular
projection C_(2n+2) = 2^(-2n-1) sum_j (-1)^j h_(n-j,j) has coefficient kappa_n = 2^(-2n-1) sum_j k_j > 0. At n = 1 the
lower sums vanish, h_01 = -(1 - a0/D) h_10 and C_4 = (2 - a0/D) h_10/8. For the moment formula, |U| = O(r^(1-delta))
gives Psi_m = o(r^m) for every m >= 2, which together with regularity at 0 selects the modal Green representation
Psi_m(r) = (1/(2m))[r^(-m) int_0^r rho^(m+1) Omega_m d rho + r^m int_r^inf rho^(1-m) Omega_m d rho]; Omega_m = O(r^m) at 0
and Omega = O(r^(-delta)) at infinity make the first term and the omitted interval O(r^(m+2)), which identifies C_m.

Proof of Proposition 18 (outline). (a) With s = (L/r)^delta one has rho^m E^(gamma/2) = (r/L)^gamma [1 + alpha (L/r)^2
+ O(r^(-4))], alpha = (gamma - m)/2 < 0, and z = s(1 + s^p)^(-delta/2). Theorem 16 with N = n - 1 (admissible since
n < 2 beta + 1 < 4 beta) gives the modal expansion Theta_m = r^gamma sum_{j<=n} F_(m,j) r^(-j delta) + o(r^(gamma - n delta)).
Writing r = L z^(-beta) (1 - z^p)^(1/2) and rho = (1 - z^p)^(1/2), this becomes
P_m(1 - 2z) = sum_{j<=n} B_j z^j (1 - z^p)^((gamma - m - j delta)/2) + o(z^n), B_j = L^(gamma - j delta) F_(m,j); since p + 1 > n
and 2p > n only j = 0 contributes a correction, P_m(1 - 2z) = sum_{j<=n} B_j z^j + (m - gamma) B_0 z^p/2 + o(z^n). A function
of class C^n from the left has an integer-power Taylor polynomial with remainder o(z^n), and n - 1 < p < n, so B_0 = 0,
contradicting F_m != 0. (b) The temperature monomials have relative exponents j delta + 2l; below 2 only l = 0 occurs and
at 2 only (j, l) = (0, 1), with angular coefficient S = (L^2/2) sum (gamma - m) F_m sin(m phi). Vorticity tails
c r^(-a) sin(m phi), a = (j + 1) delta + 2l < 2, have the canonical stream functions c r^(2-a) sin(m phi)/(m^2 - (2 - a)^2);
interior multipoles give velocities r^(-m-1) (a >= 4), and after subtracting the finitely many tails with a < 2 the rest
of the velocity is O(r^(1 - a_*)) with 2 < a_* < 4. Hence the nonlinear term contributes only exponents (j + k + 1) delta
through relative order 2, none equal to 2. Since [beta r d_r - (beta - 2)] r^(gamma - q) = -beta q r^(gamma - q), the
r^(-2) coefficient is C = -2 beta S. If F = 0 and j0 >= 1 is the first z-power with nonzero angular coefficient T0, then
R_Theta = -j0 r^(gamma - j0 delta) T0 + O(r^(gamma - (j0 + 1) delta)).

Proof of Proposition 19 (outline). Suppose both spectra are finite. Omega != 0, since Omega = 0 gives U = 0 and
Psi_xy(0) = 0, against c = -2. Let m (even) and n (odd) be the top modes of Omega and Theta; the top mode of Psi is m,
since an unforced stream mode A r^j + B r^(-j) is removed by regularity (B) and sublinearity (A, j >= 2). Write p, t for
the radial coefficients of Psi and Theta in these modes and g = -p'' - p'/r + m^2 p/r^2. With U_r = -(1/r) Psi_phi and
U_phi = Psi_r, the sin((m + n) phi) coefficient of (P2) gives m p t' = n p' t, and the coefficient of
sin(max(2m, n + 1) phi) in (P1) involves only m (p'g - p g')/(2r) (mode 2m of U.grad Omega) and (t' - n t/r)/2 (mode n + 1
of Theta_x). If n + 1 > 2m then t = C r^n, excluded by |Theta| = O(r^gamma). If n + 1 < 2m then p'g - p g' = 0, and
g = k p on (0, inf) (zeros of p at positive radii are simple and cannot accumulate). The radial Helmholtz solution then
vanishes: for k = 0, p = A r^m is excluded by sublinearity; for k != 0, p = k^(-N) L_m^N p with L_m = -d_r^2 - (1/r) d_r +
m^2/r^2 and the bounds of Theorem 15(a) give decay of p, p' faster than every power, after which the energy identity
int_0^R [r p'^2 + m^2 p^2/r - k r p^2] dr = R p(R) p'(R) settles k < 0, and the Liouville form v = sqrt(r) p with the
energy (v')^2 + Q v^2, Q = k - (m^2 - 1/4)/r^2, settles k > 0. If n = 2m - 1 then m (p'g - p g') = r t' - n t. On a
component where p != 0, t = C |p|^(n/m); C = 0 leads back to the Helmholtz case, and for C != 0 one finds
(g/p)' = a (r h^(-1/m))' with h = |p|, a = C n/m, hence h'' + h'/r - m^2 h/r^2 + k h + a r h^(1 - 1/m) = 0. A finite positive
endpoint of a component cannot be a flat zero (finite-interval interpolation between h and its derivative of order 2m,
evaluated at a maximum of h), and a nonflat zero has order exactly 2m (smoothness of t gives m | order, the balance of
h'' and a r h^(1 - 1/m) gives 2m), with C, a, k and the sign of p unchanged across it. So the equation holds on a half-line
with h = sign(p) p >= 0 smooth. Theorem 11(a) gives h <= C r^nu, nu = m gamma/(2m - 1) < 1, then |g| >= (|a|/2) r h^(1 - 1/m)
and h -> 0; at a maximum of h on [R, inf), half-line interpolation with |p^(2m)| <= C r^(2 - delta - 2m) (from Theorem
15(a), p' being the m-th sine coefficient of U_phi) makes a r h^(1 - 1/m) dominate the other terms for large R, a
contradiction.

Proof of Proposition 20 (outline). W1 = beta x + U1 is odd in x and W2 = beta y + U2 is odd in y, so smooth division
gives A, B0 with A - a, B0 - b = O(r^2) and DW = diag(a, b) + O(r^2). Near 0 the symmetric part of DW is bounded below
by (b - eps) I, so a small ball is backward invariant and the backward flow contracts exponentially together with all
its derivatives; every derivative of (A - a)(Phi_s X) decays like e^(2 (b - eps) s), so the integrals I_A, I_B converge in
every C^k norm on compact subsets of B (each compact subset enters the ball in a common backward time), with
I_A, I_B = O(r^2), W.grad I_A = A - a and W.grad I_B = B0 - b, which gives the conjugacy in (a). Injectivity: two points
with equal H values have equal H values after a common backward time inside the neighbourhood where H is injective.
Surjectivity: for Z in R^2, diag(e^(-a t), e^(-b t)) Z lies in the local image for large t, and its local preimage is
flowed forward (completeness). Differentiating the conjugacy and using det D Phi_t = e^(2 beta t) = e^((a + b) t) shows
det DH is constant along the flow, hence equal to det DH(0) = 1. Once H is constructed, the conjugacy and the local
inverse give the sharp backward estimate |Phi_(-t) X| <= C_K e^(-b t) on compact K. (b): eta solves the equation; a
second solution differs by D = o(|X|) with D(X) = e^(b t) D(Phi_(-t) X) -> 0. (c): Theta_x = x y R(X) with R smooth, the
integrand is O(|Phi_s X|^2) with all derivatives exponentially decaying, the shifted integral verifies the equation,
and a homogeneous difference bounded near 0 obeys D(X) = e^(-t) D(Phi_(-t) X) -> 0. (d): with Y = Phi_(-T) X one has
|Y| <= C_K e^(-b T), Theta(Y) - a0 Y_2 = O(|Y|^3), grad Theta(Y) - a0 e_y = O(|Y|^2), Omega(Y) = O(|Y|^2); the exact
gradient along the path solves the same equation q' = [b I - DW^T] q; near 0, b I - DW^T = diag(-4, 0) + O(r^2), whose
symmetric part is bounded above by C r^2 I, and the integral of r^2 along the near-origin part of the path is bounded
uniformly, so the gradient propagator is bounded uniformly in T; the initial errors O(e^(-2 b T)) therefore propagate
with bounded factors, and the vorticity error is -e^(-T) Omega(Y) + int_(-T)^0 e^s E_1(s) ds with E the gradient error.
For small T the bound follows by enlarging C_K.

Proof of Proposition 21 (outline). With t = log r and f = r^(-alpha) xi, the equation W.grad xi = a xi becomes
f_t + v f_phi = d_alpha f, v = U_phi/(beta r + U_r), d_alpha = (beta + 2)/(beta + U_r/r) - alpha, and similarly for
j = r^(-gamma) eta with d_gamma = (beta - 2)/(beta + U_r/r) - gamma; alpha and gamma are chosen so that d_alpha,
d_gamma -> 0, and the symbol bounds give v, d_alpha, d_gamma = O(e^(-delta t)) in every C^k(S^1) norm. For R large,
beta r + U_r >= beta r/2 on r >= R, and B = R^2 makes H smooth on the circle r = R. The angular characteristic map has
derivative exp(int v_phi), bounded above and away from 0, and converges with all derivatives, at rate e^(-delta t), to a
smooth circle diffeomorphism; the transport factors exp(int d) converge to positive limits at the same rate. Applied to
the data on r = R this gives the limits; the axes are invariant and each quadrant is preserved, which with the positive
factors gives the signs and the nonzero axis values, and parity comes from Proposition 20(a). The transport equations
give f_t, j_t = O(e^(-delta t)) in every C^k(S^1) norm. In polar coordinates det DH = 1 reads
(alpha f + f_t) j_phi - f_phi (gamma j + j_t) = 1 (using alpha + gamma = 2); its limit is the first identity, whose
values at the axes give alpha g(0) h'(0) = 1 and -gamma g'(pi/2) h(pi/2) = 1. On (0, pi/2) it is equivalent to
(g h^(-q))' = -(1/gamma) h^(-q-1); integrating from phi to pi/2 with g(pi/2) = 0 gives the formula for g. With
k = h/phi smooth, even and positive, and 2N < q < 2N + 2, subtracting the divergent primitives gives
g = (k^q/gamma) [sum_(j <= N) d_j phi^(2j)/(q - 2j) + C phi^q + O(phi^(2N + 2))], C the finite part; a nonzero C gives a
non-smooth term (a non-integer power, or |phi|^q with q odd, which is not C^q as an even function). When q = 2 l the term
d_l phi^(-1) produces -(d_l/gamma) h^q log phi unless d_l = 0, after which C h^q is smooth. For the explicit pair,
h' = cos(theta) theta', g' = -sin(theta) theta' with theta' = 1/(1 + 2 delta cos 2 theta) >= 1/(1 + 2 delta) > 0, and
alpha cos^2 theta + gamma sin^2 theta = 1 + 2 delta cos 2 theta; moreover h^(-q-1) = -gamma d/dphi [cos(theta)
sin(theta)^(-q)], so the integral equals gamma cos(theta) sin(theta)^(-q), which verifies the endpoint conditions directly.

Proof of Proposition 22 (outline). Along s -> Phi_s X the difference of the transport equations gives e' = b e - R_Theta;
differentiating W.grad e - b e = -R_Theta, the chain rule produces the term DW^T grad e, so
q' = (b I - DW^T) q - grad R_Theta; and z' = -z + q_1 - R_Omega. Variation of constants with the integrating factors
e^(-b s), P and e^s gives (a); P(t, s) = e^(b (t - s)) [D Phi_(t - s)]^(-T) because the inverse transposed flow derivative
solves v' = -DW^T v. (b) is the product rule, and under the stated parities each factor pair is odd in both variables.
(c): substitution gives R_Theta = a x y f'(k x) and W.grad Omega_k + Omega_k - partial_x Theta_k
= y [a zeta J' + (b + 1) J - f'](k x); differentiating t^(b + 1) f'(zeta t^a) in t and integrating over [0, 1] gives
a zeta J' + (b + 1) J = f', so R_Omega = 0. Since f >= 0 and a0 > 0, N_Theta >= |W2 Theta_y| + b |Theta| >= 2 b a0 |y|,
which gives the bound; J(3/2) > 0 because f' >= 0 on [0, 3/2] and f' > 0 on (1, 3/2); J is odd and vanishes on
[-1, 1], which gives the parity and the strip property. Uniqueness: a C^1 difference D of two temperatures with the
stated jet is o(|X|) at 0 and satisfies D(X) = e^(b T) D(e^(-a T) x, e^(-b T) y) -> 0; a difference of two vorticities
bounded near 0 satisfies D(X) = e^(-T) D(Phi_(-T) X) -> 0.

Proof of Proposition 23 (outline). (a): write xi~(x, eta) = xi(x, y(x, eta)). Then y_eta = 1/eta_y and
partial_x xi~ = xi_x - xi_y eta_x/eta_y = det DH/eta_y = 1/eta_y (Proposition 20(a): det DH = 1), so
d(y dx + xi~ d eta) = 0 and the form has a primitive G on the simply connected image, with A = y_eta. On a
reflection-invariant chart, eta even in x makes y(x, eta) even in x and xi~ odd in x, so G(x, eta) + G(-x, eta) has zero
gradient and vanishes at 0; the reflection in y is analogous; y = eta + O(3) gives the Taylor form. (b): mixed
differentiation gives Psi_eta = beta x A - M and partial_x Psi = -beta G_x + beta x B0 + b eta A at fixed eta, and the
chain rule turns these into -Psi_y = M/A - beta x and Psi_x = B0 M/A + b eta A - beta G_x in physical derivatives, which
are U1 and U2; div W = [partial_x M + partial_eta (b eta A)]/A = a + b; in the (x, eta) coordinates
W.grad = (M/A) partial_x + b eta partial_eta, which gives W.grad Theta = b Theta, Theta_x = a0 Dx eta = -a0 B0/A and the
scalar equation. (c): A > 0 and the limits make eta -> G_x(x, eta) an increasing bijection of R for each x, so the chart
is a global diffeomorphism; likewise x -> G_eta(x, eta) for each eta. Applying W.grad to G_eta gives
(M/A) A + b eta C = a G_eta, which with W.grad eta = b eta gives the conjugacy to a linear flow, complete with the whole
plane as backward basin. Odd G gives the parities, and Psi = (b - beta) x eta + O(4) = -2 x y + O(4). The last sentence
is the uniqueness statement of Section 2.3.

Proof of Proposition 24 (outline). Smoothness and uniform sublinearity give |W| <= C (1 + |X|), hence a complete
flow, and X.W >= beta |X|^2/2 for |X| >= R, so every backward half-orbit stays in the closed ball of radius
max(R, |X|); the order-y part of (P2) gives c = -2 and DW(0) = diag(beta + 2, b) as in Section 2.4. (a) "If":
V(x) = W1(x, 0) has V'(0) = beta + 2 > 0. At a first positive zero x* of V, W(x*, 0) = 0 by parity and
DW(x*, 0) = diag(lambda_u, lambda_v) with lambda_u = V'(x*) <= 0 and lambda_v = 2 beta - lambda_u > b. A contraction in
the space of paths on (-inf, 0] with the norm sup e^(-mu s) |z(s)|, b < mu < lambda_v, gives an orbit z(s) with
y(s) > 0 that tends to (x*, 0) as s -> -inf with |z(s) - (x*, 0)| <= C e^(mu s) (the case lambda_u = 0 included).
Since Theta is C^1 and vanishes on the axis, |Theta| <= C |y| near (x*, 0), and Theta(z(0)) = e^(-b s) Theta(z(s)) -> 0,
against the strict sign; so V has the sign of x. For any X the backward limit set is nonempty, compact and invariant,
and Theta vanishes on it because Theta(Phi_s X) = e^(b s) Theta(X); hence it lies on the x-axis, where every orbit
other than 0 is forward unbounded, so it is {0} and Phi_s X -> 0. "Only if": Theta(x, y) = y int_0^1 Theta_y(x, t y) dt
= y (a0 + o(1)) near 0; the x-axis is invariant, so a backward orbit from y > 0 stays in y > 0, eventually enters this
neighbourhood, and the transport identity carries the sign back to X. (b) Differentiating (P2) at a zero P of W gives
DW(P)^T grad Theta(P) = b grad Theta(P); with div W = 2 beta the eigenvalues of DW(P) are b and beta + 2, so every zero
is a hyperbolic source. For the reversed field the omega-limit set of any point is nonempty and compact; it is not a
periodic orbit (a periodic orbit bounds a disc on which the divergence -2 beta integrates to the zero outward flux),
so by the Poincare-Bendixson theorem it contains a zero, and the orbit then converges to that sink. The plane is the
disjoint union of the open basins of the zeros, and connectedness leaves only the origin (no finiteness assumption on
the zero set is needed). (c) is the contrapositive of (b), since grad Theta(0) = (0, a0) != 0; at such P,
b Theta(P) = W.grad Theta(P) = 0, (P1) gives Omega(P) = Theta_x(P) = 0, and curl U(P) = -Omega(P) = 0 makes DU(P),
hence DW(P), symmetric. (d) Differentiating W_k d_k Theta = b Theta twice at P, where W and grad Theta vanish, leaves
A^T H + H A = b H; differentiating (P1) once gives (A^T + I) v = H e_x. In an eigenbasis of the symmetric A the first
identity reads (l_i + l_j - b) H_ij = 0; for i != j the factor is 2 beta - b = beta + 2 > 0, and two nonzero diagonal
entries would force tr A = b < 2 beta. The degree-m part of (P2) at P is (A Z).grad p_m = b p_m, and (A Z).grad
multiplies z1^i z2^j by i l1 + j l2. (e) For 0 < mu < l_min, Z.W(P + Z) >= mu |Z|^2 on a small closed ball D about P,
so D is backward invariant and |Phi_(-t) X - P| <= e^(-mu t) |X - P|. If Theta is flat at P, then
|Theta(X)| = e^(bt) |Theta(Phi_(-t) X)| <= C_N |X - P|^N e^((b - N mu) t) on D, so Theta = 0 on D (take N mu > b);
then Theta_x = 0 there and Omega(X) = e^(-t) Omega(Phi_(-t) X) -> 0. B_P is the union over t >= 0 of the open sets
Phi_t(int D), hence open and flow invariant; every X in B_P has Phi_(-t) X in D for some t, so the same two transport
identities give Theta(X) = 0 and Omega(X) = 0; by continuity every derivative vanishes on the closure, which therefore
misses the origin, where grad Theta = (0, a0) != 0. Otherwise a mixed monomial of p_m would have
i l1 + j l2 >= l1 + l2 = 2 beta > b, so only a pure power z_k^m with m l_k = b occurs, and l_max >= beta > b/m forces
k = min.

Proof of Proposition 25 (outline). On the axis parity gives Theta = Theta_x = Theta_xx = W2 = d_y W1 = 0, and
div W = 2 beta gives d_y W2(x, 0) = 2 beta - V'(x); the y-derivative of (P2) at y = 0 is V tau' + (2 beta - V') tau =
b tau, i.e. V tau' = (V' - a) tau, and (tau/V)' = -(a/V)(tau/V) on J gives the formula; V'(0) = a is the centre strain
of Section 2.4 and V(x) = beta x + o(x) by sublinearity. Differentiating the axis equation n times at a zero x0 of V
at which the derivatives of tau of order below n vanish leaves ((n - 1) l + a) tau^(n)(x0) = 0 with l = V'(x0). If
l = 0 this gives tau^(n)(x0) = 0 for every n, the first sentence of (c). If l != 0, the formula of (a) gives
tau = K_(+-) |x - x0|^(1 - a/l) phi(x) on the two sides of x0 with phi smooth and positive, so a nonzero K_(+-) excludes
flatness; the first nonzero derivative then has order n with (n - 1) l = -a, so n = 0 and l = a, or n = k >= 2 and
l = -a/(k - 1); a nonzero Taylor coefficient makes tau nonzero on both sides; this is (b) (Theta_xy = tau' and
Theta_yy = 0 on the axis). On an outgoing side the backward orbit x(t) of a point x_S of that side tends to x0, and
d/dt log|V(x(t))| = V'(x(t)) -> 0 gives |V(x(t))| >= c e^(-eps|t|) for every eps > 0; if tau(x_S) != 0 the formula
gives |tau(x(t))| >= c' e^((a - eps)|t|) -> inf, against continuity at x0. (d): V > 0 on (0, x1) forces V'(x1) <= 0 and
sigma tau > 0 to the left of x1. (e): V < 0 on (x1, x2); the sign of the k-th Taylor coefficient of tau at x1 is
sigma (-1)^k and propagates to (x1, x2) by (a); V'(x2) = 0 is excluded because (x2 - e, x2) would be an outgoing side,
so (b) gives V'(x2) = a; a backward orbit has at most one limit, and the basin of a source with positive definite
linearization is the union of the forward images of a small backward invariant ball. (f): Taylor gives
|Theta(X)| = e^(bt) |Theta(Phi_(-t) X)| <= C' e^((b - 2 mu) t) -> 0. If l < 0, the local unstable manifold theorem and
the complete flow give the global unstable manifold, along which backward orbits approach P1 at every rate below
2 beta - l > b/2. If l = 0, the reversed field -W has eigenvalues 0 and -2 beta at P1, and the strong (pseudo-)stable
manifold theorem for a rate gap -2 beta < -mu < 0 gives a smooth local curve tangent to e_y consisting of the small
backward orbits that converge at rate at least mu; its forward images form the strong unstable curve. In both cases
the reflection R(x, y) = (x, -y) satisfies W(R X) = R W(X) and fixes P1, so it preserves the curve; the x-axis is
invariant, so each of the two branches stays in its half-plane.

Proof of Proposition 26 (outline). Proposition 23(b) applies to every polynomial truncation of G on a neighbourhood of 0 (there
A = G_(x eta) = 1 + O(2) > 0 and the chart y = G_x = eta + O(3) is locally invertible), and the formal fields are the
stable Taylor jets of these local fields. So the temperature equation holds
identically, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), div U = 0 and Psi = -2 x y + O(4); parity of G gives the A1 parities. If two
generating series agree below an even degree N and differ by H at degree N, then at fixed (x, y) the inverse chart
changes by -H_x + O(N + 1), so Theta changes by -a0 H_x + O(N + 1), and Psi changes by (L - 2 beta) H + O(N + 2) (the term
-2 x eta contributes 2 x H_x, the explicit degree N part contributes (beta x d_x + b y d_y - 2 beta) H). Writing delta for
these changes, apart from (L + 1) delta Omega - d_x delta Theta the terms of the change of the residual of (P1) have order at least N, so the degree
N - 2 change of the residual is T_N H. For H = x^i y^j (i, j odd, i + j = N) with M = a i + b j,
   T_N H = i (i - 1) [a0 - (M - 2 beta)(M - 2a + 1)] x^(i-2) y^j - j (j - 1) (M - 2 beta)(M - 2b + 1) x^i y^(j-2).
Order the columns i = 1, 3, ..., N - 3 (omitting i = N - 1) and the rows by the exponent of x of the output
(1, 3, ..., N - 3). The matrix is upper triangular with diagonal entries -j (j - 1)(M - 2 beta)(M - 2b + 1), where j >= 3,
M - 2 beta = a (i - 1) + b (j - 1) > 0 and M - 2b + 1 = a i + b (j - 2) + 1 > 0, so it is invertible for every a0. By
induction on N the residual of (P1) is removed degree by degree, H_N being unique once f_(N/2) is fixed. For a
truncation, A(0) = 1 gives A > 0 near 0, so the inverse function theorem gives smooth fields there; (P2) is exact and
the residual of (P1) vanishes through degree N - 2, hence (odd-odd parity) is O(|X|^N) for even N. The xy coefficient follows from the degree-4 computation. Full
proof: Appendix A.27.

Proof of Proposition 27 (outline). E, t, w and the patch factors are real analytic and even in x and in eta, so
G = x eta F with F even and F(0, 0) = h > 0; the implicit function theorem gives the analytic chart, and
Psi = -2h x eta + O(4) = -2xy + O(4), Theta = (a0/h) y + O(3). Suppose (P1) holds near 0 and put u = 1 + x^2. Expanding
in eta, G = eta g(x) + eta^3 k(x) + O(eta^5) with g = x u^(1/3) [p(t) + h_c(u)], k = x q(t)/s^2 + x u^(1/3) j_c(u),
where p = P(., 0), q = P_w(., 0), t = -log(1 - d u^(-1/6))/alpha, and h_c, j_c are finite sums of exponentials times
rational functions of u with poles only at u = 1 - R_l^2. Inverting y = G_x to third order gives Psi = yH + y^3 K3 +
O(y^5) and Omega = yv + O(y^3) with A = g', H = 3x - 5g/A, K3 = 5gk'/A^4 - 3k/A^3, v = -H'' - 6K3, and the coefficient
of y in (P1) is the identity (5g/A) v' + (4 + H') v + a0 A'/A^2 = 0 for real x near 0. Multiplied by A^6 it is
holomorphic in u on Im u > 0 (branches of u^(1/6), sqrt(u - 1) and of the logarithm fixed in A.28), so it holds there by
the identity theorem and extends to a short interval 0 < u < eps, where x -> i and t = log u/(6 alpha) + c(u^(1/6)) with
c holomorphic: at u = 0 the polynomial p(t) becomes a polynomial in log u, and h_c, j_c are meromorphic. With
f = p + h_c, ell = 1/3 + u f_u/f and N = u + 2(u - 1) ell one has A = u^(-2/3) f N and g/A = xu/N, and the operator
L_H[v] = (5g/A) v' + (4 + H') v satisfies L_H[v]/v -> 7 + 5(rho - 1)/ell0 for the factored terms v used below, for which
ell -> ell0 != 0, D_u ell -> 0 and D_u v/v -> rho (the derivative hypotheses are needed: an asymptotic form
v ~ C u^rho (log u)^m alone does not suffice). Three cases. (1) p nonconstant of degree n, h_c holomorphic at 0: -H'' ~ -90n x^3/(u (log u)^2) has
multiplier -23; the forcing a0 A'/A^2 = O(u^(-1/3) |log u|^(-n)) and the q part are smaller, and a pole u^mu of j_c
gives a term of power 7/3 + mu != -1 with multiplier 27 + 15 mu != 0. (2) p constant: f = u^nu F(u) with F(0) != 0; the
analytic part, the j_c part (powers in 1/3 + Z) and the forcing (powers in 2/3 + Z), together with a q term of power
2 - 3 nu times a power of log u and multiplier (22 - 24 nu)/(3 nu + 1) != 0, cannot cancel. (3) p nonconstant and h_c
with a pole of order kappa >= 1 at 0: L_H[-H''] is an analytic function plus C_* u^(kappa - 1) (log u)^n (1 + o(1)) with
C_* != 0, which an analytic function cannot cancel, and a j_c term has its power in 1/3 + Z. In each case one term of the continued identity dominates all
others and has a nonzero coefficient, a contradiction. Full proof: Appendix A.28.

Proof of Proposition 28 (outline). Say that f has mixed order q if |d_x^j d_eta^k f| <= C rho^(q - j - k/3) on R^2,
rho = E^(1/2). E^r has order 2r, T = E^(-1/6) and t = -log(1 - dT)/alpha have order -1/3, w and P(t, w) have order 0,
and every patch term G_l has every negative order (Gaussian decay; the rational patch variables have bounded
derivatives). So G, A and B0 = G_xx have orders 2, 2/3 and 0, and the Euler identity for D = 3x d_x + eta d_eta,
DE = 6(E - 1), gives Psi = x eta E^(1/3) [6(1 - 1/E) l P_t - 2P/E + 2w P_w/E] up to patch terms, with
l = -(e^(alpha t) - 1)/(6 alpha) of order -1/3, so Psi has order 5/3. By (H), 1/A has order -2/3 (induction on the
derivative order), so Dx = d_x - (B0/A) d_eta and Dy = (1/A) d_eta lower the order by 1. Integrating A in eta gives
c |eta| E^(1/3) <= |y| <= C |eta| E^(1/3); hence eta -> G_x is an increasing bijection for each x (global chart), rho is
comparable to <X>, and (c), (e) follow; parity of G gives the A1 parities. (P2) follows from W1 = (5G_eta -
eta G_(eta eta))/A, W2 = B0 W1 + eta A and grad_X eta = (-B0/A, 1/A). (b): in the mixed variables W = (M/A, eta),
M = 5G_eta - eta G_(eta eta); a zero has eta = 0 and G_eta(x, 0) = 0, and x -> G_eta(x, 0) is strictly increasing;
xi = G_eta satisfies xi' = A (M/A) + G_(eta eta) eta = 5 xi and d xi ^ d eta = A dx ^ d eta = dx ^ dy; A >= delta gives
G_eta(x, eta) >= delta x for x >= 0, so (x, eta) -> (G_eta, eta) is onto, and the explicit linear flow gives completeness,
the basin and the absence of periodic or bounded complete orbits. (d): Omega = O(<X>^(-1/3)) and
|K(X - Y) - K(-Y)| <= C_X |Y|^(-2) give absolute convergence; the integral V is smooth with div V = 0, curl V = -Omega,
V(0) = 0 and |V| <= C <X>^(2/3); U - V is harmonic of growth O(<X>^(2/3)), hence constant by the interior gradient
estimate, and zero at 0. (f) is a chain rule computation of (G_o)_(x eta) in the variables (t, w) and of (G_l)_(x eta)
in the variables (xi_l, zeta_l), z = x^2/E and v3 = (eta/s)^6/E. Full proof: Appendix A.29.

Proof of Proposition 29 (outline). With eta = lambda y, U_l = (U1, lambda^(-1) U2) and W_l = (W1, lambda^(-1) W2) at z, so
W_l.grad_X [f(x, lambda y)] = (W.grad f)(z) for every smooth f, and Omega_l = lambda H - lambda^(-1) J. Then
R_Omega = lambda (W.grad H + H - Theta_x) - lambda^(-1) (W.grad J + J) = -lambda^(-1) Q and R_Theta = lambda (W.grad Theta - (beta - 2) Theta) = 0
by (HS). Each term of N and of N2 is lambda times the corresponding entry of t - lambda^(-2) v or h - lambda^(-2) j, which gives
(c) with the reverse triangle inequality; parity and f = x eta int_0^1 int_0^1 f_(x eta)(s x, t eta) ds dt give the divided
forms. The linear part ((beta + 2) x, (beta - 2) eta) of W and J = 6 d1 x eta + O(|z|^4) give Q = 6 (2 beta + 1) d1 x eta + O(|z|^4).
(d): S_l is invertible; for fixed lambda the decay and sublinearity transfer to Omega_l and U_l, the canonical integral
converges for sigma > 0 and is o(|X|), and U_l minus it is harmonic and sublinear, hence zero. If Q vanished identically,
J would vanish (a nonzero extremum of the decaying J has grad J = 0, so Q = J != 0 there), so Psi = x A(eta) by oddness, and
sublinearity of U1 = -x A'(eta) forces A' = 0, contradicting Psi_(x eta)(0) = -2. Full proof: Appendix A.30.

Proof of Proposition 30 (outline). (a) Part (a) adapts the method of A.28 to a = beta + 2, p = 1/beta and m = beta/(beta - 2), with the exponents p, 3p - 1
and p/2 in place of 1/3, 0 and 1/6 and the corresponding residue-class computations in A.31 Steps 1 to 8. With u = 1 + x^2, G = eta g + eta^3 k + O(eta^5), g = x u^p f, f = P0(t) + h_c(u),
k = x s^(-2) u^(3p - 1) P1(t) + x u^p j_c(u), and the coefficient of y in (P1) is L_H[v] + a0 A'/A^2 = 0 with
L_H[v] = a (g/A) v' + (beta + 1 + H') v, H = beta x - a g/A, K3 = a g k'/A^4 + (beta - 6) k/A^3 and v = -H'' - 6 K3.
Multiplied by A^6 the identity is continued through Im u > 0 to a short interval 0 < u < eps, where, with z = u^(1/N)
(N = 5 at beta = 5/2, N = 16 at beta = 8/3), t is log u/(2 beta alpha) plus a function holomorphic in z, and
L_H[v]/v -> 2 beta + 1 + a (rho - 1)/ell0 for the factored terms used. (1) P0 nonconstant, h_c holomorphic at 0: -H''
has order u^(-1) (log u)^(-2) and multiplier 1 - 2 beta - 2 beta^2 != 0, and a pole u^mu of j_c gives a term of power
3 - 2p + mu != -1 with coefficient and multiplier proportional to beta a mu + 2 beta - 4 and 2 beta^2 + 4 beta - 3 +
beta a mu, both non-zero for integer mu. (2) P0 constant, f = u^nu F: the analytic part, the j_c part (powers in
1 - 2p + Z, that is 1/5 or 1/4 + Z) and the forcing (powers in 1 - p + Z, that is 3/5 or 5/8 + Z) cannot cancel, and a
P1 term of power 2 - 3 nu, whose coefficient and multiplier vanish only at the non-integers nu = (beta - 2)/(beta - 6)
and nu = (beta + 4 + p)/(beta + 5), either dominates (nu >= 2) or lies above the forcing (nu <= 1). (3) P0 nonconstant,
h_c with a pole of order k >= 1 at 0: L_H[-H''] is an analytic function plus C_* u^(k - 1) (log u)^(q0) (1 + o(1)) with
C_* != 0, and a j_c term has the non-integral power 3 - 2p + 3k + mu, a non-zero coefficient (by a congruence modulo 5
at beta = 5/2 and by parity at beta = 8/3) and, when it is the smaller power, a non-zero multiplier. In each case one
term of the continued identity dominates all others, a contradiction. (b) Under the chart bound, weighted bounds for the finite formulas and a cancellation in Psi give |U| <= C <X>^(1 - p),
polynomial bounds and every requirement of class A' except (P1). If (P1) held, Theorems 11(b) and 15(a) would make the
limit of |X|^(-1/m) Theta on rays a smooth function of the slope, which forces the limiting scaled chart
chi -> lim G_x(r, r^(1/m) chi)/r to be smooth near 0; its term P(0, 0) p (2p - 1) s^(-2m) chi |chi|^(2m), non-zero since
P(0, 0) >= kappa/(1 + 2p), then makes m = beta/(beta - 2) an integer, so m is 3, 4 or 5 and beta is 3, 8/3 or 5/2, and
h >= kappa > 0; Proposition 27 and (a) exclude these values. (c) The cases of (a) carry over to every integer m >= 2 other
than 3 with the general values of the constants (the Step 8 bracket times m(m - 1)/2 is congruent to -1 modulo m; at m = 2
the coefficient C1 of Case 2 vanishes only at nu = -1, where its non-vanishing is not needed, since the whole K3_1
contribution then has u-exponents at least 5, above the forcing exponent 3/4). For every beta > 2 the steps of (b) apply,
with the velocity exponent max(1 - p, 12p - 5) < 1 in place of 1 - p, and force m to be an integer, which the local
results exclude. (d) For every beta > 2 the three cases apply with the general
constants of (c), whose non-vanishing statements use only 0 < p < 1/2. In place of a common scale z = u^(1/N), finitely
many contributions are compared through their real exponents, with w = u^(p/2) and sigma = 1/log u as auxiliary
variables; for constant P1 the least exponents of three meromorphic contributions lie in the disjoint classes Z, Z - 2p
and Z - p; where C1 of Case 2 vanishes (beta = 6 + 4/(nu - 1)) the K3_1 term has the non-zero leading term
C1' u^(2 - 3 nu) (log u)^(q - 1); and the identity a (rho - (k - 1)) = B3 + 4(beta + 1) + (3 beta - 2) k shows that the
j_c bracket of Case 3 is non-zero wherever its non-vanishing is used. Full proof: Appendix A.31.

Proof of Proposition 31 (outline). The rescaled equations follow from U_r = -r psi_phi, U_phi = r (2 psi + eps psi_s),
beta r d_r = d_s on functions of (s, phi) and Delta(r^2 psi) = 4 psi + psi_phiphi + 4 eps psi_s + eps^2 psi_ss. (a) The
coefficients of eps^0 and eps^1 in (T), (V), (E) vanish. With p the sin 2phi coefficient of psi_0 and a' = -2 (1 + p) a,
a(s1) = a*, the deviation (theta_0 - a sin phi, omega_0) solves a linear transport system coupled through the elliptic
inverse of 4 + d_phi^2, which gains two angular derivatives; an H^1/L^2 energy estimate and zero data at s1 give the
leading harmonic branch. The order-1 equations without the sin phi projection of (T), in the unknowns p + 1, a - a*,
Q1 theta_1 and omega_1 (the fundamental temperature coefficient and the kernel coefficient of psi_1 being discarded),
form a closed system with the same structure, and the same estimate, applied in both directions of s, gives p == -1.
(b), (c) Dividing (V) by a0 gives the hydrostatic balance B eta_0 = 0, so eta_0 = alpha sin phi; the limit of (T) forces
psi_0 = p sin 2phi with alpha' = -2 (1 + p) alpha where alpha != 0, and the limit of (E) gives omega_0 = 0 there. In
(b), with L the left side of (V), L -> 0 in C^1 where omega_0 = 0, and the phi-derivative of (V) at phi = 0 is
L_phi(s, 0) = eps a0 eta_(s phi)(s, 0) exactly, because (B f)_phi = -sin phi (f + f_phiphi); as beta/a0 is bounded,
alpha' = eta_0,(s phi)(s, 0) = 0. In (c),
subtracting the limit equation from the exact (T) gives psi - psi_0 = O(eps) with two angular derivatives away from
the x-axis, hence omega = O(eps) there by (E); (V) tested against smooth functions supported there and divided by
a0 eps gives B eta_1 = -alpha' sin phi cos phi, whose solutions alpha' sin phi ln|sin phi| + C sin phi are not C^1 at
phi = 0 unless alpha' = 0. In both cases alpha is constant on each component of {alpha != 0}, which is therefore all
of R, and p == -1. In (d), if (d) failed for some Lambda, solutions with beta_n -> oo would satisfy (d1) to (d3); by
the Arzela-Ascoli theorem a subsequence of (eta, psi, omega) converges in C^2(Q), and the argument of (b) on the open
interval (-2, 2), with the lower bound (d3), gives p = -1 on (-2, 2), contrary to p(0) = -1/2. Full proof: Appendix
A.32.

Proof of Proposition 32 (outline). With f = sin phi F(z), g = sin 2phi G(z), h = sin 2phi H(z) and z = sin^2 phi, the
linearized angular equations become a linear system (*) for Y = (F', G, H', P) whose only singular points are the
regular singular points 0, 1 and oo. In the stated intervals of lam, the admissible solutions (strict integrability or
regularity inequalities on the Frobenius exponents) form a 3-dimensional space at z = 0 and a 2-dimensional space at
z = 1, which intersect in the 4-dimensional solution space. If P = 0, the admissible branch at z = 1 has -b, G and R
positive, a cooperative-system argument keeps G > 0 on (0, 1), and the integral identity
[D^(3/2) H']' = -(1/4) D^(1/2) (G + 4 lam P), D = z(1 - z), with vanishing end fluxes gives the integral of
D^(1/2) G = 0, a contradiction; so P != 0 and the dimension is 1. A C^oo solution is analytic at 0 and 1 (convergent
Taylor series by a majorant argument, and a Gronwall argument for the flat difference), hence entire and of polynomial
growth, hence a polynomial, and its top coefficients vanish. The lift uses a first integral of (*) and one constant.
Full proof: Appendix A.33.

Proof of Proposition 33 (outline). On y = 0 the parities give Theta = Theta_x = Omega = Omega_x = W2 = d_y W1 = 0, and
d_y W2(x, 0) = 2 beta - V' since div W = 2 beta. Proposition 25(a) gives V tau' = (V' - a) tau; with xi' = a xi/V this
is (tau xi/V)' = 0, so tau = a0 V/(a xi). Differentiating (P1) in y and putting y = 0 gives the first-order equation
(b) for w, with integrating factor E; E vanishes like x^((beta - 1)/a) at the origin, which removes the integration
constant. The bounds of Theorems 11(a) and 15(a) give V = beta x + O(x^(1 - delta)) and V' = beta + O(x^(-delta)),
hence power asymptotics for xi and E and absolute convergence of the integral; the C^1 convergence of Theorem 15(b)
identifies lim x^(1 + delta) w with A'(0). In (d) the weight is positive and V' - a is non-positive and not identically
zero, so the integral is negative; the sector follows from the uniform convergence of the angular derivative. Part (e)
follows from (d) applied with A = 0. Full proof: Appendix A.34.

Proof of Proposition 34 (outline). On x = 0 the parities give Theta_x = Theta_xxx = Omega = Omega_y = Omega_xx = 0,
W1 = W1_xx = 0 and W2_x = 0, and W1_x(0, y) = 2 beta - Y' since div U = 0. Restricting (P2), its second x-derivative
and the x-derivative of (P1) to the axis, and using the x-derivative of (P3) (Psi_xxx = -Omega_x - Psi_xyy), gives the
three equations of (a); with eta' = b eta/Y, (T/eta)' = 0 gives T = a0 eta. Matching finite Taylor coefficients gives
(b). In (c) the integrating factor E_v vanishes like y^((beta + 3)/b) at the origin, which removes the integration
constant; the bounds of Theorems 11(a) and 15(a) give power asymptotics and absolute convergence, and the C^1
convergence of Theorem 15(b) identifies lim y^(1 + delta) z with -A'(pi/2). Part (d) follows from the positive weight
and, as for Proposition 33, from the uniform convergence of the angular derivative. In (e), with d/dtau = Y d/dy:
under (H2) the equation for s is scalar with forcing T' q, q = -U2_xx(0, y) >= 0, and s is the forced integral from
tau = -inf; under (H1) the pair (s, z) solves a cooperative linear system with forcing (T' Y'', 0) >= 0, whose
propagator is entrywise nonnegative and, near tau = -inf, grows at most like exp(mu_+ (tau - sigma)), where
mu_+ < b exactly when a0 < D, so that (s, z) is again the forced integral from tau = -inf. Part (f) combines (d), (e),
Proposition 6 and Proposition 33(d). Full proof: Appendix A.35.

Proof of Proposition 35 (outline). In (a) the equations of Proposition 34(a) become (I_s s)' = -a0 b P C and
(E_v z)' = eta^(-h) I_s s with I_s = eta^((3 beta + 2)/b) Y^(-2); both integration constants at the origin vanish, and
exchanging the order of integration gives the positive kernel K_y; the second identity is the y-derivative of (P1) on
the horizontal axis, integrated over (0, inf). Under Omega <= 0 on Q1 the stream function is subharmonic on Q1 and
vanishes on its boundary, and a Phragmen-Lindelof comparison with r^k cos(k (phi - pi/4)), 2 - delta < k < 2, gives
Psi <= 0; the strong maximum principle and the Hopf lemma give (b). Part (c) follows from the uniform far-field
convergence, Theorem 12(ii) and the representation of Proposition 33(b), whose integrand is eventually negative; (d)
and (e) from (a), Omega_x(0, y) <= 0 and Proposition 34(d); (f) from the angular equation -H'' - d^2 H = A tested with
sin(d phi), Theorem 15(b) and Proposition 34(b), (e); (g) from the far behaviour of the two first-order equations of
(a) and Theorem 15(b); (h) from coefficient comparison in the Taylor jets at the origin. Full proof: Appendix A.36.

Proof of Proposition 36 (outline). Part (a) repeats Step 2 of A.36, which does not use the sign of a0, and adds the
signs of T from Proposition 34. In (b) the representation E w = I of Proposition 33(b) has, for a0 < 0, an eventually
positive integrand, so I <= 0 requires a region where U1_x(x, 0) > 2; the limit when A'(0) = 0 comes from the second
far-field term of Theorem 15(c), and the mean from the second identity of Proposition 35(a). In (c) the identity
E_v z = -a0 b J_y of Proposition 35(a) has the factor -a0 b > 0. Part (d) is coefficient comparison in the Taylor jets
at the origin, as in Step 7 of A.36 with the sign of a0 reversed. In (e) the sign of B gives F < 0 by integrating
(F/sin(phi)^gamma)', hence Theta < 0 outside a large disk; forward transport along orbits of W gives Theta <= 0 on the
upper half-plane, and a sublevel-set area argument with div W = 2 beta excludes zeros there. Part (f) integrates (P1)
multiplied by rho^(m - 1) over quarter disks. Full proof: Appendix A.37.

Proof of Proposition 37 (outline). Part (a) follows from the strict signs on both sides of the nodal graph, compared
on one vertical line near the axis (for z) and far out (for A, Theorem 11(b)). In (b) Taylor's formula in x with the
bound of Theorem 15(a) on Omega_xxx gives the estimate of the negative part of z, and the expansions of Theorem 16 on
the two axes give the first-nonzero-slope tests; the values of B' at the endpoints come from B of Theorem 15(c) and
the parities. Part (c) is coefficient comparison in the Taylor jets at the origin, with the relations of Step 7 of
A.36 that precede the use of a sign of Omega there. In (d) the first-order system S' = -a0 b P C, Z' = E_v s/Y of A.36
and Proposition 34(c), (d), none of which uses a sign of Omega, give the signs and the order of the first transitions,
and Steps 5 and 6 of A.36 give the tails. In (e) the identity of Proposition 35(a) gives the mean, and for a0 < 0 a
first positive zero of V would make the integrating-factor primitive of Proposition 33 diverge to -inf, against
w <= 0. Part (f) integrates (P1) multiplied by powers of the positive and negative parts of Omega over quarter disks.
In (g) a sign of Theta_x on the nodal graph makes one side of the graph forward invariant, which the backward limit at
the centre contradicts. Full proof: Appendix A.38.

Proof of Proposition 38 (outline). Two rays at a common large abscissa order the angular transitions of Theta_x, so
F/sin(phi)^gamma cannot dip below zero; a negative value of Theta would be carried by the flow to a far-field angle
where F would be negative. A first positive zero of the horizontal axis velocity would produce zeros of Theta, hence
zeros of Theta_x, accumulating on the axis, against the continuity of the nodal graph of Theta_x; Proposition 33 then
gives branch (i). Interior zeros of Theta are excluded by the area exponent 2 beta/b > 1 against the linear lower
bound on sublevel area furnished by the quadratic upper bound Theta(X) <= C|X - X0|^2 at an interior zero;
Proposition 24 then gives the complete backward basin. On the nodal graph of Theta_x, (P2) gives W2 Theta_y = b
Theta > 0. If Theta_xy > 0 everywhere on this graph, it is smooth. If also g < 0, the assumption U2_x >= 0 everywhere
on the graph would make the region below it forward invariant; the complete backward basin and Theta_x < 0 near the
origin would then force this region to be all of Q1, a contradiction. Parts (c) to (e) combine these facts with
Proposition 37, the weighted vertical system, the quartic centre block and the forward invariance of the region above
the vorticity nodal graph. Full proof: Appendix A.39.

Proof of Proposition 39 (outline). Along an outgoing trajectory X(t) whose angle tends to some theta in (0, L) with
A(theta) = 0, the leading vorticity term vanishes and e^t Omega(X(t)) -> 0, so (P1) can be integrated from infinity:
if Theta_x is eventually negative along it and e^t Theta_x(X(t)) is integrable, the vorticity is eventually positive
there, which class ST< forbids. If J_T(theta) < 0 this applies at once. If J_T(theta) = 0, the coefficient of
r^(-3 delta) in Theta_x(X(t)) is the leading coefficient M of U2_x times K_T = gamma F/sin(theta) > 0, by the first
temperature correction of Theorem 15(c) and a product-rule identity; at theta_A = sup {phi in (0, L) : A(phi) < 0} the
Green formula for H gives M(theta_A) < 0. Hence J_T(theta_A) > 0, and two rays slightly below theta_A separate the two
nodal graphs for all large x. Full proof: Appendix A.40.

Proof of Proposition 40 (outline). The argument of A.40 that gives M(theta_A) < 0 and J_T(theta_A) > 0 applies at every
angle of the interval [theta_A, theta_+] on which A vanishes. Rays at angles with A > 0, which exist arbitrarily close
above theta_+, eventually lie above the vorticity nodal graph. When theta_A < theta_+, each fixed ray with angle in
(theta_A, theta_+) eventually lies below it, because there the leading vorticity term vanishes and the next one, the
term -J_T r^(-2 delta) of Theorem 15(c), is negative; if the interval is a single point, rays with A < 0 just below
theta_A serve. Full proof: Appendix A.41.

## 5. Literature check
None of the theorems or computer-assisted proofs audited below (search as of 2026-10-20; the entry on arXiv:2603.26715
was added after a further search on 2026-10-22) decides existence or nonexistence in the class of Section 1; one
listed work (Ju, 2020) could not be checked at theorem level, so the statement is restricted to the audited works. The
closest works and their differences:
 - Chen and Hou, Stable nearly self-similar blowup of the 2D Boussinesq and 3D Euler equations with smooth data,
   I: Analysis (arXiv:2210.07191, version 4; Boussinesq results Theorems 1, 3, 4) and II: Rigorous Numerics
   (arXiv:2305.05660, version 3; Theorems 1, 3; Multiscale Model. Simul. 23 (2025)). Computer-assisted proof of
   blowup for Boussinesq in the half-plane y >= 0 with an impermeable wall (stream function zero on y = 0), from
   C^(k, alpha) data (k >= 5) close in a weighted energy to an approximate profile. Their symmetry class (Sym) has omega
   odd in x, theta even in x and theta(0, y) = 0, so theta_y vanishes at the blowup point, whereas the present class
   has a0 != 0; and the wall is a boundary, whereas the present problem is posed on the whole plane. The blowup is
   nearly self-similar: convergence to an exact profile is explicitly not proved, and no exact profile is constructed.
   In our convention the approximate profile has beta = -c_l/c_omega, about 2.92056 (their (2.6) and (2.14)).
   Verdict: disjoint (boundary problem; theta(0, y) = 0 against a0 != 0).
 - Chen and Hou, Finite time blowup of 2D Boussinesq and 3D Euler equations with C^(1, alpha) velocity and boundary
   (arXiv:1910.00173; Comm. Math. Phys. 383 (2021)). Theorem 1.1: in the upper half-plane, for small alpha > 0 and some
   data omega_0 in C_c^alpha, theta_0 in C_c^(1, alpha), the solution develops a focusing asymptotically self-similar
   singularity, and the limiting profile satisfies omega_inf, grad theta_inf in C^(alpha/40). This is an exact
   self-similar profile, of limited Holder regularity, for a boundary problem. Verdict: disjoint (half-plane with a wall;
   regularity far below C^infinity). Its exponent and full symmetry statement were not checked against the full text.
 - Elgindi and Pasqualotto, From instability to singularity formation in incompressible fluids (arXiv:2310.19780,
   version 1), with the companion Invertibility of a linearized Boussinesq flow: a symbolic approach (arXiv:2310.19781,
   version 2). Theorem 1.1 of the first: whole plane, no boundary, finite-energy data u_0, rho_0 in
   C^(1, alpha*) and C^infinity away from the origin, with vorticity and temperature gradient smooth in (r^alpha*, phi);
   Theorem 7.1 with Remark 7.3 constructs an exact self-similar profile in a weighted Sobolev space in these variables,
   with limited angular regularity at phi = pi/2, and Theorem 7.4 obtains the data by cutoff and perturbation. After a
   rotation of the axes and a change of sign of the temperature their parities agree with A1, but the profile is smooth
   only in (r^alpha, phi) and not C^infinity at the Cartesian origin. Their self-similar exponent translates to
   beta = lambda/alpha with lambda near 1 (their (19) and Remark 7.2), so beta is large when alpha is small. The
   companion paper proves operator statements (Theorem 1.1: a one-dimensional kernel and trivial intersection of kernel
   and range in a weighted space; Theorem 1.3: triviality of the kernel of a reduced operator), not statements about
   nonlinear profiles in the present class. Verdict: disjoint (Cartesian smoothness at the origin fails); this
   construction is the reason the fractional class is listed as not covered in Section 8.
 - Wang, Lai, Gomez-Serrano and Buckmaster, Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 244002 (2023) (arXiv:2201.06780, version 3):
   numerical (physics-informed neural network) self-similar profile for Boussinesq in the half-plane with a wall; no
   existence theorem. Their ansatz u = tau^lambda U(z / tau^(1 + lambda)), theta = tau^(lambda - 1) Theta gives
   beta = 1 + lambda, and lambda = 1.917 +- 0.002 gives beta about 2.917. Their symmetry has the vorticity odd in the
   first variable and the normalization Omega_(y1)(0, 0) = -1 at the wall. Verdict: disjoint (boundary problem; in
   the A1 class Omega is odd in y as well, so Omega_x(0, 0) = 0, and theta_y(0, 0) = a0 != 0 is not their setting).
 - Wang et al., Discovery of unstable singularities (arXiv:2509.14185, version 1, 2025): numerical stable and unstable
   self-similar profiles for Boussinesq with a boundary (and for IPM and the Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos model), with
   numerical stability calculations and no numbered existence theorem. Their table (Figure 2) lists lambda about
   1.92056, 1.39910, 1.25235, 1.18425 for the stable and first three unstable Boussinesq candidates, i.e. beta about
   2.92056, 2.39910, 2.25235, 2.18425; a fourth unstable candidate (lambda about 1.14488, beta about 2.14488) is
   labelled unvalidated by the authors. These decimals are numerical, not rigorous enclosures. Verdict: disjoint
   (boundary profiles; no whole-plane profile with the A1 parity and no existence proof).
 - Chae, Nonexistence of self-similar singularities for the 3D incompressible Euler equations (arXiv:math/0601060,
   version 2; Comm. Math. Phys. 273 (2007)). Theorem 2.4: for 2D Boussinesq there is no nontrivial self-similar
   solution with V in H^m(R^2), m > 2, and Theta in L^(p1) and L^(p2) for some 0 < p1 < p2 <= infinity (the proof
   first forces Theta = 0 by the transport argument). In the present class beta > 2, Theta is unbounded, and
   r^(-gamma) Theta tends to F, which is nonzero on an open set of directions around the y-axis (Corollary 4,
   Theorem 11(b)); hence Theta lies in no L^p (consistently with Proposition 5), U is unbounded, and both hypotheses
   fail. Verdict: disjoint.
 - Chae and Wolf (arXiv:1709.02030, version 3): blowup criteria for regular 2D Boussinesq solutions on [-1, 0) with
   v(-1), theta(-1) in W^(2, p)(R^2), p > 2; Theorem 1.2 excludes blowup at t = 0 if, for example,
   (i) limsup (-t) ||grad v(t)||_inf < 2, or (ii) the integral over [-1, 0] of (-t) ||grad theta(t)||_inf is finite.
   An exact self-similar solution in the present class fails the Sobolev hypothesis, and in any case it satisfies
   (-t) ||grad v(t)||_inf = ||grad U||_inf >= |partial_y U_2(0)| = 2 (the normalization c = -2 is forced by (P2) at
   the origin) and ||grad theta(t)||_inf >= |a0| (-t)^(-2), so neither (i) nor (ii) holds. Verdict: no conflict.
 - Abe, Ginsberg and Jeong, Stationary self-similar profiles for the two-dimensional inviscid Boussinesq equations
   (arXiv:2410.21765, version 1, 2024). They study stationary exactly (-alpha)-homogeneous solutions; in our
   convention beta = 1/(1 + alpha), so beta > 2 corresponds to -1 < alpha < -1/2. Half-plane solutions are identified
   with whole-plane ones by reflection in x2, and with their x1-symmetry (1.3) the combined parities are exactly
   those of A1 (their equation (1.1) has the force -rho e2, so their density rho corresponds to our theta, while their
   vorticity curl u is minus our omega). Theorem 1.2 excludes rotational homogeneous solutions that are C^1 or C^2
   away from the origin for 0 <= alpha <= 1 and -1/2 <= alpha < 0 (that is, beta in [1/2, 1] and (1, 2]). Theorem 1.3(i)
   constructs, for -1 < alpha < -1/2 (exactly the range beta > 2), continuous whole-plane weak solutions that are
   smooth off the coordinate axes, with the C^1 norm of u diverging on x1 = 0; Remark 1.4 states that existence of
   regular profiles in this range is open. Their profiles have the same homogeneity degrees as the far field of
   Theorem 11, but an exactly homogeneous Theta of degree 1 - 2/beta in (0, 1) cannot have finite nonzero
   Theta_y(0), and their profiles are not C^1. Verdict: disjoint (exact homogeneity, singular on the axes); neither
   theorem addresses smooth non-homogeneous profiles that share these far-field powers.
 - Chae and Shvydkoy (arXiv:1201.6009, version 2), Theorem 3.2, and Bronzi and Shvydkoy (arXiv:1310.8611, version 1),
   Theorem 1.1, exclude or constrain self-similar profiles of the Euler equations (without temperature) under the
   hypothesis v in L^p, 3 <= p <= infinity (the first), or for scalings corresponding to beta in (1/2, 1) and ambient
   H^s solutions (the second). The profiles of the present class have unbounded U and beta > 2, and the equations
   include buoyancy. Verdict: disjoint.
 - Luman Ju, On the profiles of locally self-similar solutions for the 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations, Journal of
   Mathematical Analysis and Applications (2020), DOI 10.1016/j.jmaa.2019.123671. The bibliographic record was
   confirmed, but the full text could not be retrieved (publisher access refused), so its theorem statements and
   hypotheses were not checked. Whether it decides or restricts the present class is an open literature gap of this
   report; nothing in this report uses it.
 - Chen (arXiv:2309.00150, 2023) and Chen, Huang and Li (arXiv:2604.01868, 2026) concern half-plane problems (smoothness
   away from the blowup point of the C^(1, alpha) singularity; numerical singular profiles), not the present class.
 - Shi, 2D inviscid Boussinesq equations and 3D axisymmetric Euler equations: (1) A unification (Em), (2) Finite-time
   blow-up of two unified (1+1)D systems rigorously derived from (Em) (arXiv:2603.26715, version 5, 2026).
   Time-dependent systems in polar variables obtained from the Boussinesq (m = 1) and axisymmetric Euler (m = 2)
   equations, their restrictions to the symmetry axes, and blowup of reduced (1+1)D systems; Theorem 2.11 states in
   its parts (A) to (D) that for every smooth solution with the stated evenness the restrictions to the two axes and
   to the apex close into equations without pressure terms (the strain equations of its (2.19) and (2.25), and at the
   apex its (2.21)), and Theorems 9.2 and 9.4 assume a background and estimates that are not constructed there. In the
   independent verification, an explicit smooth solution of the 2D Boussinesq equations with zero vorticity, velocity
   (x, -y) and temperature -y e^t (in our notation and coordinates) satisfies the full system of that work with that
   evenness, and the u equations of those closed systems, but not their strain equations, in particular not (2.21):
   the term omitted in (2.21) is proportional to the difference of the two diagonal second derivatives of the pressure
   at the apex (here that difference is e^t and the omitted term is e^t/2), and the parity does not force it to
   vanish. That solution is not stationary and its velocity is not o(|X|), so it is not in the present class and
   decides nothing about it. It refutes the restriction theorem as stated, which has no decay hypothesis; it does not
   refute the reduced ODE calculations or the other theorems of that work, and no realization for the axisymmetric
   Euler equations is checked. Verdict: disjoint (time-dependent reduced systems; no stationary profile of the present
   class).
The bibliographic details above were checked against the arXiv records. For the works of Chen and Hou, Elgindi and
Pasqualotto, Wang et al. (both), Chae, Chae and Wolf, Abe, Ginsberg and Jeong, Chae and Shvydkoy and Bronzi and
Shvydkoy, the theorem numbers, hypotheses and exponent translations were checked against the full texts of the
versions named (for arXiv:1910.00173 only the introduction, which contains Theorem 1.1; the supplementary information
of arXiv:2509.14185 was not available). For arXiv:2603.26715 the statements cited (Theorem 2.11 with its derivation,
and Theorems 9.2 and 9.4) were checked against the full text of version 5. For the remaining entries the distinctions
rest on the main results as stated in the arXiv records.

## 6. Numerical investigation
No numerical candidate has been accepted, and no numerical state is evidence of existence. All residual, inverse,
centre, far-field, stagnation and shape numbers given in 6.2 to 6.5 for the four least-squares states of the polar
representation were recomputed in the independent verification with code that does not use the solver's code; numbers
taken from solver logs are marked as such and were checked against the logs. Sections 6.6 to 6.9 state the source of
their numbers separately (the authors' computations, solver logs and stored records, or the independent verification);
a number there is an independent result only where it is attributed to the independent verification.

### 6.1 Representation and solver
Polar spectral representation on the quadrant with the A1 parity built in: Theta is expanded in the odd sine modes
sin((2n + 1) phi), n = 0, ..., NT - 1, and Omega and Psi in the even sine modes sin(2n phi), n = 1, ..., NO
("NT+NO angular modes" below); a compactified radial variable q = 1 - (1 + r^2/L^2)^(-1/(2 beta)) with Chebyshev
polynomials in q and the far-field exponents (Theta ~ r^(1 - 2/beta), Omega ~ r^(-1/beta)) built into the radial
factors; the canonical velocity from the modal Green formula (Gauss quadrature of the radial integrals, the part beyond the last radial node integrated from the basis's own continuation, so that the vorticity is not truncated); collocation of (P1)-(P2) up to q = q_max, i.e.
r_max = L ((1 - q_max)^(-2 beta) - 1)^(1/2) (q_max = 0.99 gives r_max = 1e6 L and q_max = 0.999 gives r_max = 1e9 L
at beta = 3; at fixed q_max the physical domain depends on beta); the centre strain condition c = -2 and the Taylor
identities as extra (soft) rows; Levenberg-Marquardt with column equilibration. L = 1 in all runs quoted.
Scale. The four least-squares states of 6.2 to 6.5 impose no gauge condition for the scaling symmetry of Section 2.4;
their scale is selected only implicitly by the basis and the least-squares weights, so they are compared only through
scale-invariant quantities (a0, c and the shape measures of 6.5). Under the scaling Theta -> l Theta(X/l),
Omega -> Omega(X/l) the residuals transform as R_Theta -> l R_Theta(X/l), R_Omega -> R_Omega(X/l), and the normalizers
in the same way, so the pointwise ratios |R|/N are invariant at corresponding points; the absolute residuals are
reported in each state's own scale, and the regions of 6.2, fixed in r, are not aligned between states of different
scale. The characteristic Newton-Krylov iterations of 6.8 impose one linear condition on their coefficient vector,
transverse to the scaling generator at the initial state.

### 6.2 Independent residuals of the four least-squares states

angular modes fitted to r <= 1e9 (q_max = 0.999, continued from the previous state with 100 further iterations);
32+32 angular modes fitted to r <= 1e6. Evaluation: seven-point Cartesian finite differences at three step sizes; an
independent physical-space full-plane inverse (Gaussian singularity splitting, no outer boundary); the prompt's
normalizers N_Omega = |W1 Omega_x| + |W2 Omega_y| + |Omega| + |Theta_x| and
N_Theta = |W1 Theta_x| + |W2 Theta_y| + |beta - 2| |Theta|, without floors or cutoffs; a ratio 0/0 (where parity makes
both vanish) is counted as zero, and no nonzero residual over a zero normalizer occurred. The points lie between the solver's collocation nodes, so the maxima are
sampled maxima, not continuum suprema. The sample sets differ between states (radii and numbers of points below), so
