## 8. Restrictions and limitations
 - Scope of the theorems. Each result holds under its stated hypotheses; the main admissible class is class A'
   (Section 2.3): Cartesian C^infinity profiles with the A1 parity, a0 != 0, the canonical sublinear velocity and
   polynomial bounds on Theta, Omega and their first derivatives. The exclusion of beta = 2 (Theorem 3, and hence
   Corollary 4 at beta = 2) is asserted only for C^infinity profiles (Theorem 3 uses flatness of every order; no C^k
   version is claimed); the results with weaker hypotheses (for example Theorems 1 and 2) keep their individually
   stated scopes. Not covered: profiles that are smooth only in a fractional radial variable such as r^alpha at the
   origin, velocities with added affine strain or other harmonic fields, a0 = 0 (degenerate leading temperature) and
   the other parity settings.
 - Neither existence nor nonexistence in the whole class A' is proved for beta > 2. Propositions 6, 7, 13, 18 and
   19 exclude restricted subclasses that contain values beta > 2. Theorems 11, 12, 15 and 16 and Propositions 13, 14 and 17
   to 21 are necessary conditions on a hypothetical profile (far-field structure, identities, Taylor jets, source
   coordinates; Proposition 20 reconstructs the fields on the backward basin of the origin, and its global application
   and Proposition 21 require that basin to be the whole plane, which by Proposition 24 is equivalent to the strict sign of the temperature and fails only if W has a zero P != 0 at which
   Theta, grad Theta and Omega vanish, a critical-temperature stagnation point; the local equations do not force
   DW(P) to be singular). Proposition 25 describes the possible zeros of W on the horizontal axis and the zero set
   of Theta they force; it does not decide whether such a zero exists. Proposition 26 shows that the Taylor coefficient
   identities at the centre are formally consistent for every beta > 2 and a0 != 0; it asserts no convergence and no
   realization by an actual solution.
   Propositions 27, 28 and 30 concern the logarithmic generating family of Section 6.9 and its free-exponent form only:
   no finite member with h > 0 solves (P1) near the centre at beta = 3 (Proposition 27) or, in the free-exponent form,
   at any beta > 2 (Proposition 30(a), (c), (d)); a member of the free-exponent form with a
   global chart bound A >= kappa E^p has every requirement of class A' except (P1) (A.31 Step 9) and does not solve (P1),
   for any beta > 2 (Proposition 30(c)); these arguments are for each fixed beta and give nothing uniform in beta; a
   member of the beta = 3 family of Proposition 27 with a global positive chart margin has the
   canonical velocity, the flow structure and the tail rates required by class A' (Proposition 28); none of them gives a residual floor or a
   statement about limits of members.
   Proposition 31 concerns hypothetical families indexed by beta -> oo with stated limits or expansions in the slow
   variable (ln r)/beta; at a finite beta it gives only (d), for beta above a non-explicit beta_0(Lambda) and under
   slow-variable bounds (d1) to (d3) that are not derived from (P); its hypotheses are not derived from (P) or from
   membership in class A'.
   Proposition 32 is a linear statement about separated modes of the closed order-1 system of Proposition 31 at the
   pure strain; it gives nothing non-linear, nothing at a finite beta and no statement about Setting A1 itself.
   Proposition 33 concerns profiles in class A' without positive stagnation points on the horizontal axis; it relates
   A'(0) to the axis velocity and gives a sufficient condition for branch (i) and a necessary condition for branch (ii)
   of Theorem 12, decides neither and excludes no beta.
   Proposition 34 concerns the vertical-axis traces of profiles in class A'; it expresses A'(pi/2) through
   Theta_xx(0, y) and gives sufficient conditions on these traces, not known to hold for a sought profile, for branch
   (i) of Theorem 12 and, when a0 > 0, for both signs of Omega on Q1; it decides neither and excludes no beta.
   Proposition 35 lists necessary conditions for Omega <= 0 on Q1 when a0 > 0 (a nonpositive stream function, signs on
   both axes and in the far field, a lower bound a0 >= 4 (beta + 2)(4 beta + 5) at a degenerate centre
   (Omega_xy(0, 0) = 0) with a nonzero quartic part of Omega); explicit angular data meet its angular sign conditions
   with negative two-term far-field vorticity on Q1 at large radii, without being matched to a centre or to a profile;
   it excludes neither this class nor any beta.
   Proposition 36 lists necessary conditions for Omega <= 0 on Q1 when a0 < 0 (a negative stream function,
   U1_x(x, 0) > 2 somewhere on the horizontal axis, the reversed sign of the vertical-axis kernel integral, vanishing
   quartic vorticity at a degenerate centre, negative temperature on the upper half-plane in branch (ii)); explicit
   centre data and explicit angular data meet some of these conditions without being matched to each other or to a
   profile; it excludes neither this class nor any beta.
   Proposition 37 lists necessary conditions for the class S of profiles whose vorticity changes sign once on every
   vertical line in Q1, negative below a graph y = G(x) and positive above it (orders of signs on the vertical axis
   and in the far field, centre and axis relations, U1_x(x, 0) > 2 somewhere when a0 < 0, branch (i) when a0 > 0 and
   the horizontal axis carries no positive stagnation point); a scalar model and explicit angular data meet some of
   these conditions without being matched to a centre or to a profile; it excludes neither this class nor any beta.
   Proposition 38 lists necessary conditions for the class T of profiles whose Theta_x changes sign once on every
   vertical line in Q1, negative below a graph y = G_T(x) and positive above it, and for its intersection ST with
   class S and the subclass ST< in which this graph lies below the nodal graph of Omega (in class T: a0 > 0, Theta > 0
   on the open upper half-plane, a complete backward basin, U1_x(x, 0) <= 2 on the horizontal axis and branch (i); in
   class ST: alpha < 0, or alpha, sigma and H'(L) all zero, A of both signs and, when g < 0, an order of the first
   transitions on the vertical axis); explicit angular data meet its angular restrictions without being matched to a
   centre or to a profile; it excludes from class ST< only the degenerate centres with a nonzero quartic block and
   a0 < D4, and it excludes neither these classes as a whole nor any beta.
   Proposition 39 shows that in class ST< the leading far-field coefficient J_T of Theta_x is nonnegative at every
   zero of A in (0, L) and positive at theta_A = sup {phi in (0, L) : A(phi) < 0}, and that the two nodal graphs
   satisfy G_T(x) < k1 x < k2 x < G(x) for all large x with constants 0 < k1 < k2; it excludes from class ST< only the
   profiles that violate one of these far-field conditions (for example those with liminf (G(x) - G_T(x))/x = 0), and
   explicit angular data with J_T(theta_A) = 0 that meet the angular restrictions of Proposition 38 are not the
   leading data of a profile in class ST<; it excludes neither the class as a whole nor any beta.
   Proposition 40 shows that in class ST< the vorticity nodal graph has the asymptotic slope tan(theta_+), with
   theta_+ = inf {phi in (0, L) : A(phi) > 0}, also when A vanishes on an interval, and that J_T > 0 on the whole
   interval [theta_A, theta_+]; it is a further necessary condition and excludes neither the class as a whole nor any
   beta.
   Proposition 22 concerns the transport problem with a prescribed velocity (it qualifies residual-based diagnostics)
   and Proposition 23 first gives local chart formulas (on sets where eta_y > 0 and the mixed coordinates are one to
   one), with additional hypotheses for its global conclusions; neither restricts beta. No
   contradiction among these formal conditions has been identified. The numerical states fail several of these
   necessary-condition tests (Section 6); compatibility within a controlled error budget has not been established.
 - Numerical restrictions. Section 6.9 searches only the positive-slope subclass (a0 > 0, Theta_y > 0) with a global
   mixed-coordinate chart, at beta = 3 except for the runs at other fixed exponents and with a free exponent; these
   properties are not proved for every class A' profile. The four polar least-squares states of 6.2 to 6.7 use a truncated
   compactified basis at fixed beta = 3 (6.1).
 - Physical meaning. A profile gives an exact self-similar solution with infinite kinetic energy and unbounded
   temperature at every t < T (Theorem 12, Corollary 4; reconstruction, limits and conservation laws in 2.5). No statement is made about localization to finite-energy
   data, stability of the profile, or asymptotically self-similar blowup.
 - Numerics. The numerical states are least-squares approximations, none is presented as a solution, and no quantity
   computed from them is used in any proof of existence or nonexistence; exact arithmetic certifies only the stated chart,
   centre-defect, amplitude and limiting-section properties of individual stored functions (6.9). For the four polar
   least-squares states (Sections 6.1 to 6.7),
   in the core r < 10 the largest sampled normalized residual of each state is 130 to 500 times the prompt's 1e-6
   target, the Taylor identity T2 fails in each state with relative defect 4.1e-3 to 2.1e-2 (Section 6.3), the
   next-order far-field coefficient equations fail in the three states where they were evaluated (Section 6.4), in the
   two 24+24 states, the only ones tested, the stored vorticity is not the one transported by the stored velocity near
   the vertical axis (Section 6.6), and these finite comparisons establish no convergence of a0 (Section 6.7).
   The states of the transport-exact representation (Section 6.9) satisfy the temperature equation and T1, T2
   identically; for the best of the states sampled independently at 10000 common points (degrees (96, 80), a0 held at
   600, beta = 3) the sampled maxima
   are 9.80e-7 (prompt ratio) and 7.83e-7 (grouped ratio) at 10000 points with r < 1e8 and 1.089e-6 and 8.65e-7 in
   directed zooms, up to 1.09 times the target; for the (80, 64) state it was refined from, the maximum of the grouped
   ratio at infinity lies in [1.54e-7, 2.91e-7], certified. These are sampled values except for the limit at infinity;
   there is no rigorous bound at finite radius, at an earlier setting the sampled maximum did not decrease with the
   angular degree beyond K = 64, along a resolution sequence of three fine members at the new setting (core degree 20
   throughout) the independent zoom maximum decreased by 17 percent and then 1.3 percent, raising the core degree to
   24, 28 and 32 at these degrees lowered the authors' largest sampled prompt ratios to 5.65e-7 at (96, 64) and 3.0e-7
   at (96, 80) (authors' samplings; independent checks at finite sets of points only, 6.9), and no domain sequence with the
   full row set at equal budgets was run, a0 is not determined and neither is beta (frozen-weight linearized widths
   0.007 to 0.08, at residual levels about 200 times the target), and no finite beta = 3 member of that family with
   h > 0 is an exact solution, nor any member of its free-exponent form with h > 0, at any beta > 2 (Section 6.9,
   Propositions 27 and 30).
   Rounding: certified bounds and enclosures are printed rounded outward; sampled values, including sampled maxima in
   tables, are printed at the stated number of digits, rounded to nearest or, in some places, upward, so a printed
   sampled value can differ from the stored value by up to one unit in the last printed digit.

## 9. Accompanying artifacts, software, compute and restart inputs
Scripts, coefficient files with their solver histories, check outputs and the selected code of the independent
verification are in the accompanying artifacts. Run logs are not published; the proofs are in Appendix A.
 - Appendix A (at the end of this report): complete proofs of all results of Section 3, in the order of Section 3 (A.1
   the canonical inverse and the centre strain formula of Section 2; A.2 to A.41 Theorem 1 to Proposition 40). Each
   section begins with a pointer to the statement in Section 3; scope notes in A.2, A.9 and A.21 record where the
   statement in Section 3 uses weaker hypotheses than the written proof and how the gap is closed. The proof outlines
   of Section 4 are summaries of these proofs.
 - Numerical states of Section 6 (coefficient files: angular and radial coefficients of Theta and Omega, beta, L,
   the basis sizes, the collocation grid and the solver history, from which a0 and all centre quantities are
   computed), each with its evaluation files and the commands that continue the least-squares search from a stored
   state and that evaluate a state. The four states are identified by the SHA-256 hashes of their coefficient files:

   | state | angular modes | radial functions K (Chebyshev degrees 0 to K - 1) | collocation points (radial x angular) | fitted domain | SHA-256 |

 - Independent verification code and reports: the Cartesian finite-difference residual evaluator (seven-point
   stencils at three step sizes, the prompt's normalizers without floors, desingularized axis residuals); the
   physical-space full-plane inverse with Gaussian singularity splitting and no outer boundary (for the states of 6.9, a
   parity-folded inverse in mixed coordinates with Duffy quadrature on the compactified quadrant); exact rational
   evaluation of the centre Taylor coefficients of stored states; a backward-characteristic checker (DOP853 integration
   with Cartesian finite differences) with a manufactured transport test; symbolic and exact-arithmetic checks of the
   proofs; for the states of 6.9 in addition raw high-precision differentiation at physical points, exact centre
   values, exact certificates of the global chart and of the limiting far section, and a separate implementation of
   the rescaled far evaluation; the proofs behind its interval and certificate scripts and summaries of its interval
   enclosure runs. The verifier's full reports, tables, sampled-point lists and audit inputs are not published; their
   conclusions are stated in this report, and the scripts that read those inputs cannot be rerun from the artifacts
   alone (the description in the artifacts names them).
Software. Python 3.9.25, NumPy 2.0.2, SciPy 1.13.1, SymPy 1.14.0, mpmath 1.3.0, PyTorch 2.8.0 (CUDA 12.8 build). The solvers
and the evaluators of the authors and of the second implementation use IEEE double precision (float64); the
finite-difference and core-field recurrences of the independent verification use extended precision (64-bit
mantissa), and its raw checks 85 to 130 decimal digits (mpmath); exact checks are in rational arithmetic (SymPy,
Python fractions). High-precision floating-point cross-checks are not certified bounds.
Hardware. Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL CPU (3.0 GHz); every CPU process single-threaded and below 16 GB of memory. One
NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU, shared between the authors' least-squares and slaved-transport solvers and their GPU
evaluators; the independent verification, the analytic work and the authors' exploratory computations used the CPU only.
Compute budget (the authors' approximate counts; final totals; according to the records of the numerical work, no
solver ran after 2026-10-22T00:56Z, which does not exclude an unrecorded process; jobs ran concurrently on the shared
GPU, and the hours below are job durations and estimates, not measured device occupancy). Polar least-squares
collocation solver about 20.6 hours and characteristic slaved-transport solver about 17.3 hours (wall-clock spans of
the runs); generating-function least-squares solver about 20.4 hours (the solver clock of the last saved record of
each distinct saved history; the sum over all saved files, about 25.1 hours, counts 38 duplicated histories twice; the
independent verification reproduced both sums from the stored records, which omit the work after the last accepted
update, Section 7); GPU evaluators about 9.5 hours (invocation counts times typical durations; about 1 hour of it for
diagnostics evaluated on request on 2026-10-22: a first attempt that failed after 2 min 42 s shortly before 02:37Z, a
run started at 02:37Z and stopped after 37 min, two runs of about 9 min each through 03:33Z, further evaluations, and
reproduction checks of the accompanying artifacts between 06:17Z and 06:32Z, about 5 min of GPU time); about 68 hours
of GPU jobs in all, a sum of run spans, stored solver clocks and estimates. The authors' checks of the numerical
states took about 6 single-core CPU hours (invocation counts times typical durations), and their analytic work and
other computations about 12 single-core CPU hours (an estimate from the run logs), of which about 9.5 for the
characteristic Newton-Krylov runs and under one for dynamic rescaling. The independent verification used no GPU and
only single-core CPU processes; process CPU time was recorded for only a subset of its computations (most of its logs
record wall-clock times, interrupted by pauses and restarts), so no total is stated for it. The external mathematical
reviews are not included.
Failures and stopped runs (recorded in the authors' run logs, which are not published). One characteristic
Newton-Krylov run (variant 1) stopped with an error when backward trajectories of a trial step did not reach the
centre within the integration limit; it was restarted from a refitted state. Dynamic-rescaling runs stopped on their
discrete blow-up criterion (from Gaussian data and with a0 < 0) after the centre strain changed sign. An earlier
version of the slaved-transport solver could reduce its objective by losing trajectories (failed points were given
weight zero); this was corrected by rejecting every trial step with a failed or nonfinite trajectory, and the results
quoted in Section 6 are from the corrected version.
Restart inputs. The SHA-256 digests listed above identify the reported states by their original coefficient files,
and every digest cited in this report has a coefficient file in the accompanying artifacts. In the published copies
of the generating-function states, one metadata field, which held the absolute path of the initial state on the
machine of the run, was shortened to a file name; every other stored array is unchanged. Those copies therefore have
other digests, and a table in the artifacts lists, for every coefficient file, the original digest cited here and the
digest of the published file. The artifacts also contain the solver scripts with documented invocations; run drivers
are not published. The documented invocations are script text, not a certificate of the historical executable; full
settings and the initialization must be read from the named script and the stored state, and a restart can reset the
gauge target and rebuild exponent-dependent points. The coefficient files store the discretization settings; the
residual passes of the verification are deterministic given the state file and the sampled-point list (the lists are
not published).

## 10. Outcome summary
Neither accepted endpoint has been reached. No numerical state of Section 6 meets the numerical requirements listed in
10.6, and no theorem excludes the whole admissible class (class A') for beta > 2. The outcome is UNRESOLVED. What was
established is summarized below.

### 10.1 Selected proved conclusions (complete statements and hypotheses in Section 3; complete proofs in Appendix A)
This subsection selects conclusions; the complete list of the numbered general results proved in this report, with
every lettered part and hypothesis, is the sequence of statements in Section 3: Theorems 1, 2, 3, 11, 12, 15 and 16,
Corollary 4 and Propositions 5 to 10, 13, 14 and 17 to 40 (auxiliary lemmas inside the proofs and the exact
certificates of Section 6 are not listed there).
 - Parameter-range exclusion: smooth A1 profiles with a0 != 0, sublinear velocity U = o(|X|) and
   0 < beta <= 2 do not exist (Theorems 1 to 3); every profile of
   class A' has beta > 2 and unbounded temperature, with Theta(0, y) strictly monotone (Corollary 4).
 - Subclass exclusions that contain values beta > 2: finite L^p temperature (Proposition 5), Omega >= 0 on the open
   first quadrant (Proposition 6), compactly supported vorticity (Proposition 7), Theta_x >= 0 on the open first
   quadrant (Proposition 13), exact finite angular spectra (Proposition 19), and exact membership in the finite
   compactified representation of Section 6 when 2 beta is not an integer (Proposition 18); and exact membership, for
   beta = 3, in the finite logarithmic generating family of Section 6.9 for members with h = G_(x eta)(0, 0) > 0
   (Proposition 27), and in its free-exponent form for members with h > 0 near the centre at every beta > 2, in
   particular under a global chart bound A >= kappa E^(1/beta), kappa > 0 (Proposition 30). Under that chart bound
   the fields of the family satisfy, for every beta > 2, every requirement of class A' except possibly (P1), with
   |U| <= C <X>^q, q = max(1 - 1/beta, 12/beta - 5) < 1 (Proposition 30, A.31 Step 9).
 - Necessary conditions on a profile with beta > 2: the far-field structure to leading, second and finite order
   (Theorems 11, 15, 16), the far-field dichotomy and infinite kinetic energy (Theorem 12), weighted integral identities
   (Proposition 14), the centre Taylor jets and the moment form of the strain condition (Proposition 17), the sign of
   the temperature on the backward basin of the origin (Proposition 8) and the equivalence of the full-basin property
   with the strict temperature sign (Proposition 24), the structure of possible stagnation points on the horizontal
   axis (Proposition 25), the characteristic formula for the vorticity (Proposition 9), the existence of the spatial
   gauge point (Proposition 10), and, under the full-basin assumption, the reconstruction of Theta and Omega from the
   velocity with angular compatibility conditions on the far-field temperature (Propositions 20, 21).
 - Consistency and reformulation results: the centre Taylor coefficient identities are formally consistent for every
   beta > 2 and a0 != 0, with one free coefficient at each even degree (Proposition 26); a reformulation as one scalar
   fourth-order equation for a generating function under a global chart assumption (Proposition 23); a transport
   error identity showing that, for a prescribed velocity, a small temperature residual does not control the
   reconstructed vorticity (Proposition 22); a description of the canonical velocity, flow and tail rates for members
   of the beta = 3 family of Proposition 27 with a global positive chart margin, which satisfy every requirement of class A' except (P1)
   (Proposition 28); and a conditional hydrostatic rescaling theorem (Proposition 29; a caution on the normalized
   residuals, not an existence or nonexistence result). It describes vertical compressions of a hypothetical
   profile satisfying (HS); they satisfy (P2) and (P3). Under the extra decay and sublinearity hypotheses of
   Proposition 29(d), they have the canonical inverse and no finite member satisfies (P1). On fixed compact rescaled
   sets with the stated positive leading normalizers, or their positive divided versions across the axes, both
   normalized vorticity residuals are bounded above by C/|a0_l| for sufficiently large lambda, with the threshold and
   constants depending on the base profile and set. The divided residual R_Omega/(x y) is independent of lambda at
   corresponding points. No hydrostatic base is constructed, and no nonexistence result for the full admissible
   class A' follows; membership in A' would also require polynomial tail control of Theta and the required derivatives.
   Conditional obstructions for large-beta asymptotic families (Proposition 31): for hypothetical families as

None of these excludes beta > 2 in class A', and none establishes existence.

### 10.2 The specific questions of the task statement
 - Exclusion of all A1 profiles by axis dynamics, the vorticity equation, global temperature transport, integral
   identities or far-field constraints: not achieved. Axis dynamics give beta > 2 and the monotone unbounded axis
   temperature (Theorem 1, Corollary 4) and restrict the stagnation points on the horizontal axis (Proposition 25);
   without positive stagnation points on that axis they express the far-field vorticity slope A'(0) as an integral of
   the axis velocity, with a sign criterion for the branches of Theorem 12 that leaves both open (Proposition 33). On
   the vertical axis the traces Theta_xx(0, y) and Omega_x(0, y) satisfy a linear system, A'(pi/2) is minus a
   positive-weight integral of Theta_xx(0, y), and sign conditions on these traces suffice for branch (i)
   (Proposition 34). The vorticity equation gives the characteristic formula (Proposition 9); Omega >= 0 and
   Theta_x >= 0 on the open first quadrant are excluded (Propositions 6, 13), while Omega <= 0 there (excluded for
   a0 > 0 only under sufficient conditions on vertical-axis traces that are not known for a sought profile,
   Proposition 34; necessary conditions for it in Proposition 35 for a0 > 0 and in Proposition 36 for a0 < 0) and
   sign-changing vorticity (necessary conditions for one sign change on every vertical line in Proposition 37, with
   one sign change of Theta_x on every vertical line in Proposition 38, and, in class ST<, a separation of the two
   nodal graphs by two rays of fixed positive slopes for all large x in Proposition 39 and an asymptotic slope of the
   vorticity nodal graph in Proposition 40) are not excluded in general. Global temperature transport gives the
   temperature sign on the backward basin and its characterization (Propositions 8, 24) and the L^p exclusion
   (Proposition 5). The integral identities (Proposition 14) contain profile-dependent integrals and fluxes and do not
   determine beta by themselves. In class A', the far-field recursions (Theorems 11, 12, 15 and 16, the last at the
   orders N < 4 beta - 1, below the first possible interior multipole) leave two leading angular functions
   undetermined at every proved order and produce no contradiction; the centre coefficient identities produce none at
   any finite order (Proposition 26). Whether the undetermined data can be realized by actual solutions is not proved
   at either end.
 - beta = 2: excluded in the smooth class (Theorem 3, a flatness argument at the neutral vertical eigenvalue). A
   bounded nonzero temperature forces beta = 2 (Theorem 1(c)); hence for beta > 2 every profile has a growing far field,
   Theta of order r^(1 - 2/beta) with a nonzero angular profile (Theorem 11), and arguments that use bounded temperature
   cannot apply. Such profiles have unbounded temperature (Corollary 4) and unbounded velocity with infinite kinetic
   energy (Theorem 12), so they do not themselves provide self-similar blow-up from bounded or finite-energy data.
 - Negative origin strain under the full-plane inverse: c = -2 is forced by the jet (Section 2.4), and under the
   canonical inverse it is the moment condition int_0^inf rho^(-1) Omega_2(rho) d rho = -4 (Proposition 17). For the
   four least-squares states of Section 6 the strain computed with the full-plane inverse deviates from -2 by 5.0e-8
   (16+16), 1.0e-8 and 8.7e-9 (the two 24+24 states) and 1.5e-8 (32+32); in each state between +0.017 and +0.020 of it
   comes from radii beyond 1e6 (Section 6.3). For the stored beta = 3 states of 6.9 with certified global chart bounds,
   Proposition 28 proves that the generated velocity is the canonical inverse of Omega and that c = -2, so for these
   stored functions the strain condition holds by proof and quadratures of it are finite consistency checks. The same
   holds, by A.31 Step 9, for the six stored states with beta != 3 of the free-exponent pairs of 6.9, whose global
   chart bounds were certified independently. No stored state meets the full acceptance package (Section 10.6).
 - Spatial scaling: it preserves beta, a0 and c (Section 2.4), so a0 is a genuine invariant of a profile and not a
   gauge; the gauge point Theta_y(x_h, 0) = a0/2 always exists (Proposition 10), so the gauge Theta_y(x*, 0) = a0/2
   at a prescribed x* excludes no profile. The four least-squares states of Section 6 impose no gauge condition and
   fix the scale only implicitly through the basis and the weights; they are compared through scale-invariant
   quantities, while their absolute residuals are reported in each state's own scale. The characteristic
   Newton-Krylov iterations impose one linear condition on their coefficients, transverse to the scaling generator at
   the initial state; whether it meets every scaling orbit was not established.

### 10.3 Best numerical states
See Section 6. The best of the states sampled independently at 10000 common physical points is a state of the
transport-exact representation of Section 6.9
(beta = 3, a generating function of the mixed variables, which satisfies the temperature equation and the Taylor
identities T1 and T2 identically); the four polar states below are earlier baselines with much larger residuals. This
state (coefficients 134d9098: degrees (96, 80) in the outer basis, a core patch of degree 20, a0 held at 600, beta = 3,
rows at infinity, in the intermediate far range and next to the axes, and a fourfold denser inner collocation; the
finest member of the resolution sequence of 6.9 from the state 62df5606) has sampled maxima 9.80e-7 (prompt ratio) and
7.83e-7 (grouped ratio) at 10000 independent points with r < 1e8, raised to 1.089e-6 and 8.65e-7 by directed zooms near
(x, y) = (0.0067, 0.051), next to the centre; and an exact centre prompt ratio of 1.29e-10. Its global chart was
certified independently, and its regional absolute residuals are tabulated in Section 6.9. It exceeds the target 1e-6 by
a factor of up to about 1.09 at the sampled points, its a0 was imposed and beta held rather than determined, and no
finite beta = 3 member of the family with h > 0 is exact. It does not meet the numerical-YES verification package (Section 10.6):
the finite cutoff and exponent studies of 6.9 establish neither full-plane domain convergence nor a refinement-stable
beta (the axis checks are finite, at 16 points per member). The state 62df5606 it was refined from has, in
addition, an exactly enclosed limit of the grouped ratio at infinity (maximum over directions between 1.54e-7 and
2.91e-7). The independently evaluated states of this representation with the full row set:

### 10.4 Most serious remaining obstacles
 (i) No stable value of the shape invariant a0 was obtained. The four least-squares states have a0 = 44.35, 52.35,
     52.83 and 59.10; their optimization histories are unequal, so the differences do not by themselves separate
     optimization from resolution (Section 6.7). The finite histories of the other methods include increases and decreases of a0:
     the characteristic Newton iterations with beta free reached a0 up to 229 (with beta between 2.47 and 3, and a
     decrease from 206.1 to 196.0 in one step); in dynamic rescaling the instantaneous a0 = 4 Theta_y(0)/c^2 grew to
     2.85e4 from Gaussian data while the centre strain c tended to zero, which by itself makes this diagnostic large,
     and decreased from about 6000 in the runs with amplified initial vorticity. These histories do not determine a
     limiting amplitude. In the transport-exact representation (Section 6.9) a0 is not determined either: reported
     free-amplitude endpoints include values near 404 and 600 and other values in the exponent studies, and none
     determines a profile amplitude; at (80, 40) and coarser resolutions fits at tested
     imposed values from 400 to 800 reach residuals of the same order, while with the full (80, 64) rows 450 and 800
     remained substantially worse than 600 after 100 iterations from a shape optimized at 600, excursions from
     62df5606 to 550, 650, 700 and 800 each ended above its own return to 600 in the objective (6.9; unconverged, the
     returns with twice the history), and the linearized a0 widths at (56, 30) are 6 to 120 percent of a0 depending on
     the definition. Whether a profile exists at some a0, whether
     the sequences approach a degenerate limit, or whether no profile exists was not decided.
 (ii) A defect that the prescribed normalized residual does not adequately constrain in these sampled states: near
     the y-axis an error in Theta_x enters the temperature residual only through W1 Theta_x, and the tested 24+24
     states, with normalized residuals near 1e-4, violate the transport consistency between velocity and vorticity by
     tens of percent there (Section 6.6). For prescribed velocities, Proposition 22 shows that the temperature residual
     alone does not control the reconstructed vorticity; no residual estimate for the coupled canonical problem has
     been excluded.
 (iii) The far field: the fixed-angle Fourier basis resolves the far-field angular layer near the x-axis poorly, the
     stored continuation beyond the fitted domain fails the far-field compatibility relations of the equations in
     each of the three states for which this was evaluated (Section 6.4), and the compactified radial basis cannot
     represent exact profiles when 2 beta is not an integer (Proposition 18).
 (iv) beta is not determined. The characteristic Newton
     iterations with beta free followed different beta paths. In the transport-exact representation at (56, 30) the
     linearized widths of beta are 0.007 to 0.08, at residual levels about 200 times the target, in a fixed-beta
     comparison there (not matched in cost) the terminal objectives at seven exponents are ordered 2.90, 2.80, 2.95,
     3.00, 3.05, 2.70, 2.50, free-exponent iterations from beta = 2.90, 3 and 3.05 drifted monotonically toward smaller
     beta (to 2.8920, 2.9925 and 3.0356) without stopping, and at (80, 64), from
     the state a7e057ae, beta moved by less than 1e-5 in 100 free-exponent iterations (after the first 60, with a0 held, the
     objective was below that of a 60-iteration control at beta = 3 by relative 3.5e-5; the further 40, with a0 also
     free, ended 1.4 percent below that control, which was not continued; finite trajectories, still moving; no stationarity established).
     These coarse runs do not identify an exponent; the reported widths describe frozen-weight linear models and
     establish neither nonlinear identifiability nor an optimum near 3. At (80, 64) from 62df5606 with a0 held at 600,
     runs at beta = 2.98 and 3.02, their returns to 3 and their continuations at their own exponents end at values that
     depend on continuation history or incomplete optimization, and from 62df5606 at equal history beta moved by less than
     1e-4 in 200 iterations with beta free and with beta and a0 free (Section 6.9); from the end states at 2.97 and
     3.03 at (80, 64), with a0 held, beta moved toward 3 in 200 iterations (by +1.2e-3 and -2.6e-3, every increment of
     one sign), with objectives 10.4 and 24.0 percent below those of fixed-exponent controls at equal history, finite
     trajectories that locate no minimum and do not separate the equations from the representation (Section 6.9); at
     (96, 64) the forward-versus-return contrast persists and neither return recovered its parent. Proposition 18
     gives an exact representation obstruction when 2 beta is not an integer, not a quantitative bias or a selection
     mechanism; Propositions 27 and 30 likewise exclude exact finite members of the generating family with h > 0 near
     the centre, at beta = 3 and in the free-exponent form at every beta > 2, and select no exponent.
 (v) No argument excludes the whole admissible class for beta > 2; Proposition 31(d) excludes only the families
     satisfying its uniform hypotheses. The centre is formally unobstructed (Proposition 26), the far field is
     consistent to every proved order (Theorem 16), and the identities contain unknown integrals. The realization of
     nontrivial formal centre jets and far-field data by actual solutions, estimates, higher-order far-field
     compatibility, the canonical moment constraints and the global matching between centre and far field all remain
     unresolved.
 (vi) The normalized vorticity residuals can conceal a persistent residual after division by x y. Conditional on a
     hydrostatic profile (equations (HS) of Proposition 29, which was not constructed), Proposition 29 gives vertical
     compressions that satisfy (P2) and (P3), keep the parities and Psi_xy(0) = -2, have centre slope lambda^2 a0 and,
     under the hypotheses of its part (d), the canonical velocity. On fixed compact sets of rescaled coordinates where
     the leading normalizers (or their divided versions across the axes) are bounded below, both normalized vorticity
     residuals are at most C/|a0_l| for sufficiently large lambda, with constants depending on the profile and the set, while R_Omega/(x y) is
     independent of lambda at corresponding points, and under the hypotheses of (d) no member satisfies (P1).
     Decreasing normalized residuals along a sequence whose centre slope varies therefore do not by themselves
     establish convergence; comparisons should also track the absolute residual after division by x y and account
     for amplitude and spatial scale (the genuine scaling preserves a0 and the normalized ratios but multiplies the
     divided residual by mu^(-2), so fixing a0 does not fix the spatial scale).
     The reported generating-family runs include imposed amplitudes and free-amplitude endpoints near 404 and near 600
     (the joint free run of 6.9 ends at stored amplitude about 600.0315), as well as other endpoints in the exponent
     studies (for example 746.07 at beta = 2.50 in 6.9); none determines a profile amplitude.
     When the centre coefficient G_xeta(0) is positive, the physical centre
     slope is a/G_xeta(0), as defined in Section 6.9; this formula is not a new numerical certification of those free-amplitude states.
     For the states 62df5606 and 134d9098 the divided residual is tabulated by region with

### 10.5 Strategies ruled out by proved results, and approaches that remained inconclusive
 - Arguments that require a bounded temperature or a finite L^p norm of the temperature, for beta > 2: every profile
   of class A' has unbounded temperature of order r^(1 - 2/beta) (Corollary 4, Theorem 11), so such arguments cannot
   reach the class. The other maximum-principle, integral-identity and far-field arguments that were tried have not
   produced a class-wide exclusion.
 - Local obstructions at the centre: the unrestricted formal centre identities are consistent for every beta > 2 and
   a0 != 0 (Proposition 26); this does not establish compatibility of prescribed jets, sign restrictions or canonical
   moments, or convergence of the formal series.
 - Far field: through the orders proved in Theorem 16 the recursions alone do not select beta; the two leading angular
   functions remain undetermined, and compatibility with the centre and with additional sign conditions remains open.
 - Exact finite angular representations, and the finite compactified radial basis when 2 beta is not an integer:
   no exact profile has this form (Propositions 18, 19). Exact finite members of the logarithmic generating family of
   Section 6.9: none with h > 0 satisfies (P1) near the centre, at beta = 3 or, in the free-exponent form, at any
   beta > 2, and in particular none with a global chart bound A >= kappa E^p is exact (Propositions 27, 30); these propositions make no assertion about approximation by members of the family, and no rate of approximation
   and no residual floor is known.
 - Sign arguments: they exclude only sign classes (Propositions 6, 13); Omega <= 0 on the first quadrant and
   sign-changing vorticity remain (Proposition 34 excludes Omega <= 0 for a0 > 0 only under sufficient conditions on
   the vertical-axis traces that are not known for a sought profile; Proposition 35 lists necessary conditions for
   this class, whose angular sign conditions explicit angular data, not matched to a centre or to a profile, satisfy;
   Proposition 36 gives the corresponding necessary conditions for a0 < 0, with explicit centre and angular data of
   the same limited kind; Proposition 37 gives necessary conditions for one sign change of the vorticity on every
   vertical line and Proposition 38 for one sign change of Theta_x on every vertical line, alone or together with it,
   the sign structure found on the sampled lines of the stored states of 6.9; Proposition 38 excludes only a
   degenerate-centre subclass of the sampled order, and Proposition 39 only the profiles of class ST< that violate one
   of its far-field conditions, such as those with liminf (G(x) - G_T(x))/x = 0 as x -> inf, and Proposition 40 those
   of class ST< whose vorticity nodal graph has no asymptotic slope or a slope other than the one fixed by the leading
   angular coefficient A).
 - Integral identities as a beta-selection mechanism: they hold for every exact profile and contain profile-dependent
   integrals (Proposition 14).
 - Large-beta limits in the slow variable s = (ln r)/beta (Proposition 31): the pure strain Theta = a0 y, Psi = -2xy
   solves the local equations for every beta, and on the leading harmonic branch the leading equations leave the
   strain coefficient p(s) free. The first-order data of (a), an exact identity on the x-axis in (b), or the next order
   in (c) (a non-constant leading amplitude alpha would force a first temperature correction alpha' sin phi
   ln|sin phi|, not C^1 at the x-axis) force p = -1, contrary to the normalized value p_beta(0) = -1/2. These are
   conditional nonexistence results for asymptotic families whose normalized fields satisfy the stated hypotheses:
   at a finite beta they give only (d), above a non-explicit beta_0 and under bounds not derived from (P); they give
   no unconditional nonexistence and select no beta. Open: bounded a0 when only
   the limits as s -> -oo are known (at the linear level, Proposition 32 shows that the energy argument of (a) cannot
   use such limits in place of the data at s1, in the energy class and in C^k for large a*), a0/beta -> 0 without an
   expansion, normalized temperatures tending to 0, and
   transitions through fast departures (for example the free centre coefficients of Proposition 26), angular layers or
   strong strain.
 - Accepting least-squares states on the prescribed normalized residuals alone: in the tested states these
   residuals did not detect transport inconsistencies of tens of percent (Section 6.6), and for prescribed velocities
   they do not control the reconstructed vorticity (Proposition 22), so additional checks (Taylor identities,
   transport reconstruction, far-field tests) are necessary.
 - Numerical approaches that have not produced a state meeting the verification package of 10.6 (finite computations;
   they do not rule out these methods in general): dynamic rescaling from Gaussian and
   least-squares data (no steady state was approached), characteristic Newton iterations (stalled with large
   closure defects and drifting beta and a0), and least squares in the transport-exact representation (sampled
   residual maxima near the target, down to 1.09e-6 in directed zooms at the finest of three resolutions, with a0
   imposed and beta held at 3, a0 undetermined, beta not determined, no sequence of fit domains).

## Appendix A. Complete proofs

### A.1 Canonical inverse

Report statement: see the canonical inverse and class A' in Section 2.3.

Proof.

Section A.1.1 proves existence, smoothness, parity and uniqueness of the canonical velocity in the decay class, uniqueness in the sublinear class, and the nondecaying example. Section A.1.2 derives the centre strain formula under power decay.

#### A.1.1 Canonical inverse and the scope of a decay subclass

##### Statement

Let Omega be smooth on R2, odd in each coordinate, tending uniformly to zero at infinity, and satisfying int_(|Y|>1) |Omega(Y)|/|Y|^2 dY < infinity. Put

    K(Z)=(Z2,-Z1)/(2 pi |Z|^2),
    U(X)=int [K(X-Y)-K(-Y)] Omega(Y) dY.

Then this absolutely convergent integral defines a smooth divergence-free U with curl U=-Omega, U=o(|X|), U(0)=0, and the A1 velocity parities. It is the unique smooth velocity with this curl, divergence, sublinear growth, and value zero at the origin. After fixing Psi(0)=0, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x) gives a streamfunction odd in each variable. The smooth parity quotient H=Psi/(xy) extends across the axes, tends uniformly to zero at infinity, and its rotational lift to R3 x R3 solves -Delta_6 H=G, where G=Omega/(xy) has its smooth extension. This decaying lifted solution is unique.

##### Convergence, regularity, and growth

For fixed X, K(X-Y)-K(-Y)=O_X(|Y|^-2) at infinity. Near Y=0 or Y=X the possible inverse-distance singularities are locally integrable. The tail hypothesis therefore proves absolute convergence. On a compact set of X, every positive derivative of the tail kernel has bound C_m |Y|^(-m-1), which is controlled by the weighted hypothesis. For the local part of the kernel, choose a compact smooth cutoff on Omega and transfer derivatives to this smooth compactly supported function in the convolution. This proves local smoothness to every order. Distributional differentiation gives divergence zero and curl -Omega; smoothness makes those identities classical. Direct substitution gives U(0)=0. Reflections of the integral give the stated parity because K(SZ)=-S K(Z) and Omega(SY)=-Omega(Y) for each coordinate reflection S.

To prove sublinearity, fix R, let eta_R=sup_(|Y|>R)|Omega(Y)|, and let A(s)=int_(|Y|>s)|Omega(Y)|/|Y|^2 dY. For r=|X|>2R split into |Y|<=R, R<|Y|<=2r, and |Y|>2r. Their contributions are bounded by C_R, C eta_R r, and C r A(2r). The middle estimate follows by integrating |X-Y|^-1+|Y|^-1 over |Y|<=2r. Therefore

    |U(X)|/r <= C_R/r + C eta_R + C A(2r).

First let r tend to infinity and then R tend to infinity. Both tail quantities vanish, proving uniform sublinearity.

##### Uniqueness and the six-dimensional representation

For two admissible velocities, their difference is divergence free and curl free, hence each component is harmonic. A harmonic scalar h=o(r) is constant: the harmonic interior gradient estimate on B_R(X0) gives |grad h(X0)| <= C R^-1 sup_B_R(X0) |h|, whose limit is zero. The origin value fixes the constant.

A smooth divergence-free field on the simply connected R^2 has a streamfunction. The velocity parity and Psi(0)=0 imply Psi=0 on both axes and oddness in both coordinates. Dividing a smooth odd function by its coordinate gives a smooth even function, as follows directly from f(x,y)/x=int_0^1 f_x(tx,y) dt. Apply this in each coordinate to extend H and G.

The identity

    -Delta_2(xy H)=-xy (H_xx+2H_x/x+H_yy+2H_y/y)

extends smoothly at the axes. The operator in parentheses is precisely Delta_6 on a function radial separately in two R3 variables. Smooth even profiles lift smoothly at the radial origins; this can be seen by Taylor expansion with a smooth remainder to arbitrary order.

For |x|>=|y| and large |x|, use Psi(x,y)=-int_0^y U1(x,s) ds. Sublinearity gives |H(x,y)|<=sqrt(2) epsilon once |x| is sufficiently large. For |y|>=|x| use Psi(x,y)=int_0^x U2(s,y) ds. The same bound holds. It extends to the axes by continuity. Thus H tends uniformly to zero in R6. The difference of two decaying lifted solutions is harmonic and vanishes by the maximum principle on expanding balls.

##### Why the hypotheses are a subclass

Set

    Psi(x,y)=sin(x)sin(y)/2,
    Omega(x,y)=sin(x)sin(y),
    U(x,y)=(-sin(x)cos(y), cos(x)sin(y))/2.

Direct differentiation gives all curl, divergence, parity, and origin gauge identities, with bounded U. Vorticity is bounded but does not decay, and the weighted absolute tail integral diverges. Its canonical Fourier inverse is defined mode by mode at the four nonzero frequencies; the same sublinear uniqueness principle fixes U. Thus decay of Omega and weighted absolute integrability are sufficient conditions, not necessary consequences of sublinear velocity. This example does not satisfy the center strain or stationary transport equations and is not an A1 profile. It refutes only an unjustified necessity claim about the inverse class.

##### Dependencies and scope

The only outside inputs are elementary harmonic interior estimates, the streamfunction construction on R^2, and the maximum principle. No exterior multipole, affine strain, wall image, or velocity gauge is appended.

#### A.1.2 The centre strain formula under power decay

Assume the smooth A1 equations on R^2

    W=beta X+U, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), Omega=-Delta Psi,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x, W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,

with beta>2, the specified fourfold parity, Theta_y(0)=a0!=0 and U=o(|X|). Impose the same additional hypotheses as Section A.12.2:

    |Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^(-alpha), alpha>0,
    |grad Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^m, m finite.                 (H)

Write Q={x>0,y>0}, k(X)=xy/|X|^4, and let Phi_t be the complete flow of W.

The far-field theorem of Section A.12.2 proves, under (H), with delta=1/beta,

    |Theta_x(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^(-2 delta),
    |Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^(-delta),
    |U(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^(1-delta).                          (5)

The center equation gives c=Psi_xy(0)=-2 and

    W1=x[beta+2+O(|X|^2)],
    W2=y[beta-2+O(|X|^2)], Theta_x=xy J(X),              (6)

where J is smooth locally.

For completeness the strain formula is obtained from the subtracted velocity, not from an unregularized log potential. Differentiate its first component at X=0. The derivative kernel is partial_x K1(-Y)=-xy/(pi |Y|^4). This is absolutely integrable against Omega: at infinity use power decay, and near zero use Omega=O(|Y|^2). To justify the difference quotient, remove |Y|<2|h| for a displacement h along x. This removed contribution after division by |h| is O(|h|^2), using the locally integrable inverse-distance kernels and Omega=O(|Y|^2). On the complement use the derivative bound C/|Y|^2 and dominated convergence. Hence c=-partial_x U1(0)=(1/pi) integral xy |Y|^-4 Omega. Sublinear uniqueness of the velocity, proved in Section A.1.1, removes any harmonic velocity remainder; an additive streamfunction constant has no derivative. The normalization and parity therefore give

    c=(1/pi) integral_R2 xy |X|^-4 Omega(X)dX
      =(4/pi) integral_Q k Omega=-2.

In the removed-disc argument the limiting derivative integral on |Y|<2|h| is also O(h^2): the integrand |xy| |Y|^-4 |Omega| is bounded by smooth odd-odd parity. Thus both the difference quotient and its proposed limit lose a vanishing contribution.

### A.2 Theorem 1 (axis exclusions)

Report statement: see Theorem 1 in Section 3.

Proof.

Theorem 1 is items 1 to 3 below together with their proofs. Item 5 and its proof give the finite L^p part of Proposition 5 (Section A.6).

Scope note. The proof below assumes C1 fields on R^2, U divergence free and uniformly sublinear, and DU(0)=diag(2,-2), which give V(y)/y -> lambda. These hypotheses hold in class A', so every use of Theorem 1 in the report is covered. Theorem 1 as stated in Section 3 assumes only that V is continuous and that U2(0,y)=o(y); for that version the step "V(y)/y -> lambda" is replaced by the mean value argument of the proof of Theorem 1 in Section 4 of the report: T has a point of (0,delta) where T' has the sign of a0, and there V = lambda T/T' has the sign of lambda.

#### Statement and notation

Let beta > 0. Let U and Theta be C1 on R2, with U divergence free, U=o(|X|) uniformly at infinity, and the A1 parities. Suppose

    W = beta X + U,       W.grad Theta = (beta-2) Theta,
    Theta_y(0)=a0 != 0,   DU(0)=diag(2,-2).

The last equality follows from the first-order temperature equation and the canonical A1 parity when the full profile assumptions hold. Set lambda=beta-2, T(y)=Theta(0,y), and V(y)=W2(0,y). Then:

1. If beta != 2, V has no positive zero. Its sign is the sign of lambda.
2. The range 0 < beta < 2 is impossible.
3. For beta > 2, T has the sign of a0 and |T| is strictly increasing on y>0. For every epsilon in (0,beta), there are positive c,C,R such that

       c y^(lambda/(beta+epsilon)) <= |T(y)| <= C y^(lambda/(beta-epsilon))   (y>=R).

   In particular log|T(y)|/log y -> lambda/beta, and the temperature is unbounded.
4. For beta=2, V vanishes near zero and Theta is bounded on R2. Analyticity of T alone, or of V alone, on the connected y-axis excludes this case. No analyticity is assumed in the main target.
5. No such nonzero Theta belongs to Lp(R2) for any finite p>0.
6. If beta>2, every continuous solution of this transport equation satisfies |Theta(X)| <= C_epsilon (1+|X|)^(lambda/(beta-epsilon)) for every epsilon in (0,beta). This conclusion requires no a priori polynomial tail bound.

#### Axis proof

Parity gives W1(0,y)=0, hence V T'=lambda T. The center limits are T(y)/y -> a0 and V(y)/y -> lambda. If lambda is nonzero, choose delta>0 on which both functions are nonzero. If V has a positive zero, its first positive zero y_* exists by continuity and this nonzero initial interval. On (0,y_*), V has the sign of lambda, and the regular linear ODE gives

    T(y)=T(y0) exp(int_[y0,y] lambda/V(s) ds).

The integrand is positive. Thus |T(y)|>=|T(y0)|>0 for y0<=y<y_*. Continuity makes T(y_*) nonzero, whereas the undivided equation at y_* gives 0=lambda T(y_*). This contradiction proves item 1. It needs no Lipschitz estimate at the zero beyond the displayed classical equation.

For beta<2, item 1 gives V<0 throughout the positive axis, contrary to V(y)=beta y+o(y)>0 at large y. For beta>2, item 1 gives V>0 throughout. At large y,

    (beta-epsilon)y <= V(y) <= (beta+epsilon)y.

Integrating the corresponding lower and upper bounds on (log|T|)'=lambda/V proves item 3. The logarithmic limit follows by sending epsilon down to zero. The argument does not prove convergence of T(y)/y^(lambda/beta); a slowly varying factor remains possible under sublinearity alone.

At beta=2 the equation becomes V T'=0. Since T'(0)=a0 and T' is continuous, T' is nonzero near zero, so V=0 there. At large positive y, V>0, so T is constant on a tail. If T is analytic, it is constant everywhere by analytic continuation, contradicting T'(0)!=0. If V is analytic, its initial interval of zeros makes V identically zero, contradicting sublinearity.

#### Complete flow and global bounds

Because U is continuous and sublinear, |W(X)| <= C(1+|X|). Local C1 regularity gives a unique local flow; this bound prevents escape to infinity in finite positive or negative time by Gronwall. Thus W has a complete C1 flow Phi_t, and

    Theta(Phi_t(X)) = exp(lambda t) Theta(X).

For each epsilon in (0,beta), choose R so large that |U(X)|<=epsilon|X| outside B_R. Along a trajectory outside the ball,

    beta-epsilon <= d(log|Phi_t(X)|)/dt <= beta+epsilon.

A backward trajectory from X outside B_R reaches the sphere in a finite time h with

    log(|X|/R)/(beta+epsilon) <= h <= log(|X|/R)/(beta-epsilon).

To justify finite hitting, if the backward trajectory stayed outside forever its radius would be at most |X| exp(-(beta-epsilon)s), which eventually falls below R. If Y is the first hit, Theta(X)=exp(lambda h)Theta(Y). For lambda=0 this is bounded by max_B_R |Theta|, proving the global assertion of item 4. For lambda>0, the upper hitting-time bound proves item 6. The ball itself is compact, so its values cause no problem.

#### Finite-Lp exclusion

The flow has Jacobian det D Phi_t=exp(2 beta t), since div W=2 beta. Change variables using the complete diffeomorphism Phi_t in the finite integral of |Theta|^p. The transport identity gives

    exp((p lambda+2 beta)t) int |Theta|^p = int |Theta|^p.

This calculation is valid for any p>0 and does not differentiate |Theta|^p at its zeros. If the integral is finite and nonzero, p(beta-2)+2 beta=0, hence beta=2p/(p+2)<2, already excluded by the axis argument. The integral cannot be zero because a0!=0. This proves item 5 without integration by parts or unstated boundary terms.

#### Dependencies and scope

Only elementary ODE existence, the Jacobian equation for a C1 flow, change of variables, and analytic continuation in the explicitly analytic subclasses are used. The vorticity transport equation and the inverse on R^2 are needed to construct U and to obtain the center strain, but are not used in these transport restrictions. Sublinearity only on the positive y-axis suffices for items 1 to 3; the global bounds and Lp result use sublinearity on R^2. No assertion of physical bounded-data blow-up follows from an unbounded profile.

### A.3 Theorem 2 (beta = 2 forces bounded temperature)

Report statement: see Theorem 2 in Section 3.

Proof.

Sublinearity makes W=2X+U globally of at most linear growth and smooth, so its flow exists for all finite positive and negative times. For a sufficiently large R, X.W>=|X|^2 on |X|>=R. Along the backward flow the radius decreases at least exponentially until entering the closed R ball, and this ball is backward invariant. Every point therefore reaches that ball in finite backward time. Temperature is constant along this flow, so

    |Theta(X)| <= max_{|Y|<=R}|Theta(Y)|.

Thus Theta is globally bounded, without assuming boundedness separately. In particular T(y)=Theta(0,y) is bounded and smooth.

For W in C^1 and continuous Theta the same bound is the case lambda=0 of the paragraph "Complete flow and global bounds" in Section A.2 (the global assertion of item 4 there).

### A.4 Theorem 3 (smooth beta = 2 is excluded)

Report statement: see Theorem 3 in Section 3.

Proof.

The exclusion is proved in Section A.4.1. It uses the nonlinear local flat-rigidity theorem of Section A.4.2, whose weight design comes from the linear results of Sections A.4.3 and A.4.4.

#### A.4.1 Exclusion of smooth beta = 2 profiles

##### Statement and dependencies

Suppose Psi and Theta are smooth on R2, Psi is odd in x and y, Theta is even in x and odd in y, and

    Omega=-Delta Psi, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), U(X)=o(|X|),
    (2X+U).grad Theta=0,
    (2X+U).grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
    Theta_y(0,0)=a0 != 0.

The conclusion is that no such fields exist. The canonical inverse is not an extra hypothesis for this restricted theorem: the actual smooth stream function and sublinearity suffice. All regularity here is C infinity. No analytic or vorticity integrability hypothesis is used.

The proof below uses the nonlinear local flat-rigidity theorem of Section A.4.2. Its hypothesis is flatness in x of phi=Psi+2xy along an open y interval. Its conclusion is phi=0 in a smaller relative one-sided neighborhood of each point of that interval. We restate and prove the additional continuation lemma needed here.

##### Part 1. Regular-interface continuation lemma

Let phi and Theta be smooth near a point p=(x0,y0) with x0>0, and put

    omega=-Delta phi, W=(4x-phi_y,phi_x).

Assume W.grad Theta=0 and W.grad omega+omega=Theta_x. Suppose that phi vanishes on the side x<g(y) of a smooth graph through p, where g(y0)=x0. Then phi vanishes in a neighborhood of p.

###### Part 1.1 Coordinates and an exact integral identity

Write r=x-g(y). All derivatives of phi vanish on r=0 because phi is smooth and zero on one side. The transverse velocity is

    V=W.grad r=4x-phi_y-g'(y)phi_x.

It is positive in a neighborhood of p, since V=4x0 at p. In coordinates (r,y), straighten W by solving

    partial_r Y(r,z)=phi_x(r+g(Y),Y)/V(r+g(Y),Y),
    Y(0,z)=z.

The integrand is smooth and flat in r on r=0. Hence Y-z and all mixed derivatives are flat in r, uniformly on a smaller compact interval; Y_z and 1/Y_z are bounded and positive. The physical coordinate map is

    X(r,z)=(r+g(Y(r,z)),Y(r,z)),  det D X=Y_z.

In these coordinates W=V partial_r. Thus Theta(X(r,z))=T(z), where T(z)=Theta(g(z),z). Put Phi=phi composed with X and omega_hat=omega composed with X. At fixed physical y, partial_x=partial_r at fixed y. The chain rule gives

    Theta_x=-T'Y_r/Y_z,
    phi_x=Phi_r-(Y_r/Y_z)Phi_z.

Consequently, with smooth bounded coefficients

    a=T'/(V^2 Y_z), d=a Y_r/Y_z,

we have

    omega_hat_r+omega_hat/V=-a Phi_r+d Phi_z.

Take I(r,z)=exp(integral_0^r dt/V(t,z)). It and its inverse are bounded on the small chart. Since Phi and omega_hat vanish to every order at r=0, integrating by parts gives the exact equation

    (Delta phi)(X(r,z))=a Phi(r,z)
       -I(r,z)^(-1) integral_0^r I(t,z)
            [(a_r+a/V)Phi(t,z)+d Phi_z(t,z)] dt.             (1)

In particular this equation has no second derivative in its integral. Although its coefficients depend on the given solution, they are fixed smooth bounded coefficients for the following estimates. The integral curves from 0 to r all stay in one chart after that chart is shrunk.

###### Part 1.2 Carleman estimate for a curved interface

Translate y and, if necessary, change the common length unit so a compact z interval is [-1,1]. A common scaling of both physical coordinates preserves the form of the equations after scaling phi by length squared and Theta by length; horizontal translation is not used. Set

    b(z)=1-z^2,
    D={|z(x,y)|<1, 0<r(x,y)<delta b(z(x,y))},
    f=log b(z(x,y))-log r(x,y).

All differential operators and norms below are in the physical Euclidean coordinates. The functions r and z are smooth on a slightly larger closed chart; |grad r|>=1, and the derivatives of r through order four are bounded. Flatness of z-y in r lets us choose, after shrinking the chart,

    |D^j(z-y)| <= epsilon r^4, 1<=j<=4.

This means derivatives in physical coordinates; the assertion follows by the chain rule from flatness in (r,y). Constants below may depend on this fixed chart and on g, but not on the Carleman parameter sigma.

We first establish bounds for the weight. Write n=grad r, q=(log b)'=-2z/b, and k=-(log b)''=2(1+z^2)/b^2. Then

    Hess f=r^(-2)n tensor n-r^(-1)Hess r
                     -k grad z tensor grad z+q Hess z.

For constants M,C fixed by the chart, the nonnegative function

    K=M/r+C/b(z)^2+4 epsilon/r^2

bounds the absolute sizes of the last three quadratic forms. One may require the following estimates, with an arbitrarily small eta>0 and fixed positive constants c0,Cg,C4:

    Hess f >= r^(-2)n tensor n-K Id,
    K <= eta/r^2,  |Delta K| <= eta/r^4,
    |grad f|^2 <= Cg/r^2,
    Hess f(grad f,grad f) >= c0/r^4,
    |Delta^2 f| <= C4/r^4.                                (2)

Here are the choices and order estimates. First bound n and derivatives of r on an initial chart, and take M at least the operator norm bound on Hess r. Bound |grad z| by 2, so C/b^2 bounds k|grad z|^2. The remaining term |q Hess z| is bounded by 4 epsilon/r^2 on a sufficiently small chart with r<=1 and delta<=1/4. Since r/b<=delta,

    r^2 K <= M delta+C delta^2+4 epsilon,
    r^4 |Delta K| <= C'(delta+delta^4+epsilon).

For the second inequality use Delta(r^-1)=2|n|^2/r^3-Delta r/r^2, the chain rule for b(z)^-2, and Delta(r^-2)=6|n|^2/r^4-2 Delta r/r^3. Derivatives of z of order at least two are flat; their contribution is bounded by a constant times epsilon. Constants depend on the initial chart, not on its subsequent small width.

Also grad f=-n/r+q grad z. The second term has norm at most 4 delta/r. Thus Cg can be fixed using the bound on n. Moreover

    |n.grad f| >= (|n|^2-4 delta|n|)/r.

As |n|>=1, first choose delta small enough that the last numerator is at least 1/2. By the first two lines of (2),

    Hess f(grad f,grad f) >= (1/4-eta Cg)/r^4.

Choose eta small enough that c0=1/8 is valid, and also eta<c0/(4 Cg). The fourth derivatives of -log r have leading term of order r^-4 and lower terms involving bounded derivatives of r, while the fourth derivatives of log b(z) are bounded by C/b^4 plus flat lower terms. This proves the last bound in (2) with a finite C4 after decreasing delta. These choices are consistent: fix the initial chart and derivative bounds, including M, C=16 and Cg; choose eta with eta Cg<1/8 and eta<c0/(4 Cg); choose epsilon sufficiently small; shrink the chart to obtain the stated flatness bounds; choose delta below its width and below all the displayed smallness conditions; and only then choose sigma0.

For a smooth u flat at r=0, supported where r/(delta b)<=3/4, put

    v=e^(sigma f)u, A=Delta+sigma^2|grad f|^2,
    B=-2 sigma grad f.grad-sigma Delta f,
    P=||e^(sigma f)Delta u||_2, Z=||r^-2 v||_2.

A is symmetric, B is skew symmetric. The exact conjugation and commutator identity give

    P^2=||Av||^2+||Bv||^2
        +4 sigma integral Hess f(grad v,grad v)
        +4 sigma^3 integral Hess f(grad f,grad f)v^2
        -sigma integral Delta^2 f v^2.

Bound the possibly negative gradient contribution by the identity

    integral K|grad v|^2=-<Kv,Av>
       +sigma^2 integral K|grad f|^2v^2+(1/2)integral Delta K v^2,

and 4 sigma|<Kv,Av>| <= (1/2)||Av||^2+8 sigma^2||Kv||^2. This yields

    P^2 >= (1/2)||Av||^2
       +[4c0 sigma^3-4 Cg eta sigma^3-8 eta^2 sigma^2
                                      -(C4+2 eta)sigma] Z^2.

Our choice of eta makes the cubic coefficient positive. For sigma>=sigma0, with sigma0 fixed by the chart,

    P^2 >= (1/2)||Av||^2+c0 sigma^3 Z^2.                  (3)

There is also the gradient estimate

    G:=||r^-1 e^(sigma f)grad u|| <= C sigma^-1/2 P.       (4)

Indeed integration by parts with r^-2 gives

    integral r^-2|grad v|^2 <= Z||Av||+(Cg sigma^2+C)Z^2,

because |Delta(r^-2)|<=C/r^4. Apply (3), and then use e^(sigma f)grad u=grad v-sigma grad f v. This proves (4).

To justify the computations, first use cutoffs away from r=0 and the two tips b=0. For each fixed sigma, flatness bounds every differentiated integrand by arbitrarily high powers of r. On the support under consideration b>=r/delta; therefore the weight and every derivative of the cutoffs or weight cost only finite powers of r^-1. The cutoff errors tend to zero, establishing (3)-(4) for the stated u. All integrations use dx dy=Y_z dr dz with bounded density; the commutator itself was computed in the Euclidean coordinates, so no variable elliptic principal part has been omitted.

###### Part 1.3 Absorbing the integral and localizing the conclusion

At fixed z the weight is b(z)^sigma r^-sigma. Boundedness of I, I^-1 and Y_z reduces the estimates to elementary dilation inequalities. For delta<=1, Minkowski's inequality gives

    ||e^(sigma f) integral_0^r |Phi_u(t,z)|dt||
          <= C delta^3/(sigma+5/2) Z,
    ||e^(sigma f) integral_0^r |partial_z Phi_u(t,z)|dt||
          <= C delta^2/(sigma+3/2) G,                    (5)

where Phi_u=u composed with X. To check the exponents, substitute t=sr. Relative to Z the first integrand is r^3 s^(sigma+2) Z(sr,z), and L2 dilation contributes s^-1/2. Relative to G the second is r^2 s^(sigma+1)G(sr,z). The factor |partial_z X| is bounded, since it is Y_z times (g'(Y),1). Multiplication by bounded coefficients changes only C.

Choose a smooth chi equal to one on [0,1/2] and zero on [3/4,infinity), and set u=chi(r/(delta b(z)))phi. Commuting this cutoff in (1) gives the same operator applied to u and an error F. Every local error, the integral commutator chi(r,z)-chi(t,z), and the term containing partial_z chi(t,z) is zero for r/(delta b)<1/2. Flatness makes ||F||_2 finite, independent of sigma. Hence

    ||e^(sigma f)F|| <= (2/delta)^sigma ||F||.

Equations (1), (3)-(5) imply, with constants independent of sigma,

    P <= C[1+1/(sigma+5/2)]Z+C/(sigma+3/2)G
                                          +(2/delta)^sigma||F||.

The first two terms are absorbed for large sigma. On r<(delta/4)b the cutoff is one and the weight is at least (4/delta)^sigma. Equation (3) now bounds the unweighted L2 norm of phi there by C delta^2 sigma^-3/2 2^-sigma ||F||. Letting sigma tend to infinity proves phi=0 in that smaller wedge. Together with the already zero side r<=0, this is a neighborhood of p. This proves the regular-interface lemma.

##### Part 2. A pure-strain patch cannot end at finite horizontal distance

Assume the equations of the lemma hold globally for x>0. Suppose phi=0 in a neighborhood of [0,epsilon] times [y0-Y,y0+Y], with epsilon,Y>0. We show phi(X,y0)=0 for every X>0.

If not, take X with phi(X,y0)!=0; increase X if needed so X>epsilon. In the compact rectangle

    R=[0,X+1] times [y0-Y,y0+Y],

Use parity to extend the initial zero patch across x=0, and let S be the intersection of R with the closed support of phi in R^2. It is nonempty and compact. Choose K>0 with K Y^2>X+1 and minimize F(x,y)=x+K(y-y0)^2 on S. Its minimum m is at most X. A minimizer p lies at x>=epsilon>0, away from y=y0+-Y because F>=K Y^2 there, and away from x=X+1 because F>=X+1 there. It is thus interior to the rectangle and has x>0.

Near p, the side F<m is disjoint from the support, hence phi=0 there. The level surface F=m is the smooth graph

    x=g(y)=m-K(y-y0)^2.

At p, all jets of phi vanish from the zero side, so W.grad(x-g(y))=4x>0. The lemma applies and makes phi zero in a whole neighborhood of p, contradicting p in the support. Thus phi(X,y0)=0 for all X. Repeating the argument for every center in a smaller initial y interval gives an open horizontal strip of zeros. On that strip phi_y=0 and therefore U1=2x, contradicting U=o(|X|) along a fixed horizontal line. Any such pure-strain patch is consequently impossible in a sublinear global profile.

##### Part 3. Every proposed beta=2 profile supplies a forbidden patch

###### Part 3.1 Boundedness from the complete backward flow

Sublinearity makes W=2X+U globally of at most linear growth and smooth, so its flow exists for all finite positive and negative times. For a sufficiently large R, X.W>=|X|^2 on |X|>=R. Along the backward flow the radius decreases at least exponentially until entering the closed R ball, and this ball is backward invariant. Every point therefore reaches that ball in finite backward time. Temperature is constant along this flow, so

    |Theta(X)| <= max_{|Y|<=R}|Theta(Y)|.

Thus Theta is globally bounded, without assuming boundedness separately. In particular T(y)=Theta(0,y) is bounded and smooth.

###### Part 3.2 A nonresonant stagnation interval exists

On the y-axis, parity gives W1=0 and the temperature equation reads

    V(y)T'(y)=0,  V(y)=2y+Psi_x(0,y).

Let

    Lambda={4(m-1)(4m-7): m=3,5,7,...}={40,208,504,...}.

If T'(y) took values only in {0} union Lambda, continuity on the connected real line would make T' constant, since that set is discrete. Its value at zero is a0!=0. A nonzero constant would make T unbounded. Hence there is a point where T' lies outside this set. On a small open interval I around that point, T' is nonzero and avoids all of Lambda. There V=0, so phi=Psi+2xy satisfies phi_x(0,y)=0 on I; parity also gives phi(0,y)=0 and all its even transverse jets vanish.

###### Part 3.3 Finite Taylor induction gives flatness

Write Theta=T(y)+eta. On I the exact equations are

    (4x-phi_y)eta_x+phi_x(T'+eta_y)=0,
    (4x-phi_y)omega_x+phi_x omega_y+omega=eta_x,
    omega=-Delta phi.

The function phi is odd in x, eta is even in x, eta(0,y)=0, and the linear coefficient of phi is zero. Suppose inductively that the odd coefficients of phi below an odd m>=3 vanish identically on I. The lower even coefficients of eta also vanish: compare successively the corresponding orders in the first displayed equation, whose leading operator on eta is 4x partial_x. Finite Taylor's theorem, with smooth coefficient functions, then permits writing at the first still unknown orders

    phi=phi_m(y)x^m+O(x^(m+2)),
    eta=eta_(m-1)(y)x^(m-1)+O(x^(m+1)),
    omega=-m(m-1)phi_m(y)x^(m-2)+O(x^m).

All statements about lower coefficients hold identically on I and can be differentiated in y. Comparing order x^(m-1) in temperature and x^(m-2) in vorticity gives

    4(m-1)eta_(m-1)+mT'phi_m=0,
    -m(m-1)(4m-7)phi_m=(m-1)eta_(m-1).

The products involving phi_y or phi_x times a perturbation derivative are of strictly higher order, including m=3. Eliminating eta_(m-1) gives

    [T'-4(m-1)(4m-7)]phi_m=0.

Our interval avoids every resonance, so phi_m and then eta_(m-1) vanish. This proves the induction at all finite orders. Thus phi and eta, and consequently omega, are flat in x on the entire interval I, uniformly on its compact subintervals. Taylor series convergence has not been assumed.

Apply the nonlinear local flat-rigidity theorem of Section A.4.2 at an interior point of I. It gives a relatively open one-sided patch of phi=0. A smaller patch contains [0,epsilon] times a closed y interval, with a relative neighborhood in x>=0. This is sufficient for part 2, because its support minimizer has x>0. If a full neighborhood at x=0 is desired, parity supplies the zero patch on x<0. Part 2 now contradicts sublinearity. This proves the beta=2 exclusion.

##### Scope

This argument concerns smooth exact profiles on R^2 at beta=2. It does not exclude beta>2 and does not concern finite-regularity profiles.

#### A.4.2 Local rigidity of a flat nonlinear beta = 2 perturbation

##### Statement

Let phi and Theta be smooth on a neighborhood of {0} times an open y interval I. Set omega=-Delta phi and suppose, for x>0 near this interval,

    W=(4x-phi_y,phi_x),
    W.grad Theta=0,
    W.grad omega+omega=Theta_x.                              (1)

Suppose phi is flat in x on {0} times I: every transverse derivative vanishes there. Then for every y0 in I there is a relative one-sided neighborhood of (0,y0) on which

    phi=0, omega=0, Theta(x,y)=Theta(0,y).

The statement is local. Global propagation is not asserted. In the A1 beta=2 application, phi=Psi+2xy and flatness follows on any stagnation interval where T'=Theta_y(0,y) avoids the transverse resonance set. The resonance derivation and all global questions are separate.

##### Part 1. Smooth straightening of the transverse flow

Work on a slightly larger compact interval around y0 so that flatness and all its differentiated forms are uniform. Put V=4x-phi_y. Then V=x alpha with alpha=4 plus a smooth flat function. On a sufficiently small neighborhood, alpha>2. The quotient

    h0(x,y)=phi_x/V

extends smoothly and flatly across x=0. Solve the ordinary differential equation

    Y_x(x,z)=h0(x,Y(x,z)),    Y(0,z)=z.                       (2)

Smooth dependence of ordinary differential equations, or differentiation of their integral form, shows that Y-z is smooth and flat in x, including all mixed derivatives. In particular 1/2<Y_z<2 after shrinking the neighborhood. Its inverse z=z(x,y) satisfies z-y flat in x as well.

In (x,z) coordinates, W is V(x,Y) partial_x. Write T(z)=Theta(0,z). The first transport equation therefore gives exactly

    Theta(x,Y(x,z))=T(z).                                  (3)

We use hats only where necessary: Phi(x,z)=phi(x,Y(x,z)), and omega_hat(x,z)=omega(x,Y(x,z)). Let alpha=V(x,Y)/x, and define

    a=T'(z)/(alpha^2 Y_z),     d=a Y_x/Y_z.

All these coefficients are bounded locally; t a_t is bounded. The second equation in (1) becomes

    omega_hat_x + omega_hat/(x alpha)
         = -a Phi_x/x^2 + d Phi_z/x^2.                     (4)

For verification, Theta_x in physical coordinates equals -T'Y_x/Y_z, and phi_x=Phi_x-(Y_x/Y_z)Phi_z. Substitution into (1) gives (4).

##### Part 2. Exact Volterra form

Define

    I0(x,z)=x^(1/4) m(x,z),
    m=exp( integral_0^x [1/alpha(t,z)-1/4] dt/t ).

The integral is smooth and flat, so m and 1/m are bounded. I0_x/I0=1/(x alpha). Flatness kills every endpoint term below. Multiplying (4) by I0, integrating from zero, and integrating the Phi_x term by parts gives

    (Delta phi)(x,Y)=a Phi/x^2
       -I0(x,z)^(-1) integral_0^x I0(t,z)
          { [a_t/t^2+a(1/alpha-2)/t^3] Phi(t,z)
                     +d Phi_z(t,z)/t^2 } dt.              (5)

This is an exact identity for the given nonlinear solution. Its coefficients are now fixed smooth functions when estimating that solution. It contains no second derivative inside the Volterra integral.

##### Part 3. A Carleman estimate in physical coordinates

Translate y and rescale both coordinate lengths so that the chosen compact z interval is [-1,1]. The displayed local equations have the same form after rescaling phi by length squared, Theta by length, and omega without amplitude change. Let

    b(z)=1-z^2,   D={ |z(x,y)|<1, 0<x<delta b(z(x,y)) },
    f(x,y)=log b(z(x,y))-log x.

For sufficiently small delta, every smooth u flat at x=0 and supported in x/(delta b)<=3/4 obeys, for sigma>=2,

    P^2 := ||e^(sigma f) Delta u||_2^2
        >= (1/2)||A0 v||_2^2+2 sigma^3||x^(-2)v||_2^2,
    v=e^(sigma f)u,   A0=Delta+sigma^2|grad f|^2.          (6)

All norms and derivatives in this part use physical dx dy, so the Laplacian remains Euclidean. Also

    ||x^(-1)e^(sigma f) grad u||_2 <= C sigma^(-1/2) P.    (7)

Here C is independent of sigma.

We give the details establishing stability of the weight under the flat coordinate change; no second derivative perturbation is discarded. By shrinking the neighborhood, for 1<=j<=4 one may require

    |D^j(z-y)| <= epsilon1 x^4,  |grad z|<=2.

This follows from uniform smooth flatness. Put q=(log b)'=-2z/b and k=-(log b)''=2(1+z^2)/b^2. Then

    Hess f=x^(-2)e_x tensor e_x-k grad z tensor grad z+q Hess z.

For a nonnegative function K=16/b^2+4 epsilon1/x^2, and after taking delta and epsilon1 sufficiently small, the following bounds hold with eta=1/1000:

    Hess f >= x^(-2)e_x tensor e_x-K Id,
    0<=K<=eta x^(-2),   |Delta K|<=eta x^(-4),
    |grad f|^2<=4x^(-2),
    Hess f(grad f,grad f)>=(1-eta)x^(-4),
    |Delta^2 f|<=(6+eta)x^(-4).                           (8)

Here is a direct check of the orders needed in these choices. In D, 1/b<=delta/x. The j-th derivative of log b is bounded by C_j/b^j for j<=4. Thus K x^2<=16 delta^2+4 epsilon1, and x^4|Delta K|<=C delta^4+C epsilon1, by the chain rule and the displayed bounds on z. Also grad f=-e_x/x+q grad z, so its norm is at most (1+4 delta)/x. Its x component is -1/x+q z_x. The error in its squared x component, after multiplication by x^2, is O(delta epsilon1). The remaining terms in Hess f(grad f,grad f), multiplied by x^4, are O(delta^4+delta epsilon1). Finally Delta^2 f=6/x^4+Delta^2(log b(z)), and the chain rule bounds the second term multiplied by x^4 by C(delta^4+delta epsilon1). The constants are independent of small delta and epsilon1. Fix eta first, then choose epsilon1 small enough to control the terms C epsilon1 (including 24 epsilon1 in Delta K). Next shrink the straightened chart to obtain the stated flat derivative bounds, and finally choose delta below the chart width and small enough to control C delta^2 and C delta^4. This proves all of (8). All of D and the complete fixed-z integration segments lie in this one chart, with |z|<=1 and x<delta. The inequality for Hess f uses k|grad z|^2<=16/b^2 and |q Hess z|<=4 epsilon1/x^2 when x<=1 and delta<=1/4.

For completeness, conjugation yields A0+B0, where B0=-2 sigma grad f.grad-sigma Delta f is skew symmetric. The exact commutator identity gives

    P^2=||A0v||^2+||B0v||^2
        +4 sigma int Hess f(grad v,grad v)
        +4 sigma^3 int Hess f(grad f,grad f)v^2
        -sigma int Delta^2 f v^2.

Bound its negative gradient contribution using

    int K|grad v|^2=-<Kv,A0v>+sigma^2 int K|grad f|^2v^2
                         +(1/2)int Delta K v^2,
