    4 sigma |<Kv,A0v>| <= (1/2)||A0v||^2+8 sigma^2||Kv||^2.

The coefficient of ||x^(-2)v||^2 left after these estimates is at least

    4 sigma^3(1-5 eta)-(6+3 eta)sigma-8 eta^2 sigma^2.

For eta=1/1000 and sigma>=2 this is larger than 2 sigma^3, proving (6). To prove (7), integration by parts gives

    int x^(-2)|grad v|^2
       =-<x^(-2)v,A0v>+sigma^2 int x^(-2)|grad f|^2v^2
                              +3 int x^(-4)v^2
       <= ||x^(-2)v|| ||A0v||+(4 sigma^2+3)||x^(-2)v||^2.

Equation (6) bounds this by C P^2/sigma. Now e^(sigma f)grad u=grad v-sigma grad f v, so (7) follows. Flatness removes the boundaries at x=0 and the two corners, just as in the linear tapered-domain estimate of Section A.4.4. All weights and cutoff derivatives cost only finite powers of x^(-1) for each fixed sigma.

##### Part 4. Volterra bounds and cutoff

For the two kernel types appearing in (5), the ratio I0(t,z)/I0(x,z) is bounded by C(t/x)^(1/4). The physical measure is Y_z dx dz, with Y_z and its reciprocal bounded. Under t=sx this changes the fixed-z L2 dilation bound only by a constant. Minkowski therefore gives

    || e^(sigma f) x^(-1/4) integral_0^x t^(-11/4)|u(t,Y(t,z))| dt ||
         <= C/(sigma-1/4) ||x^(-2)e^(sigma f)u||,

and

    || e^(sigma f) x^(-1/4) integral_0^x t^(-7/4)|partial_z u(t,Y(t,z))| dt ||
         <= C/(sigma-1/4) ||x^(-1)e^(sigma f)grad u||.          (9)

In the second line partial_z is taken after composition with Y. The bound |partial_z u|<=2|grad u| follows from Y_z<=2. Coefficient multipliers in (5) are bounded independently of sigma, including t a_t.

Take chi equal to one on [0,1/2] and zero on [3/4,infinity), and put

    u=chi(x/(delta b(z(x,y)))) phi.

Applying (5) to phi and commuting this cutoff produces the same linear Volterra operator applied to u, plus F0. Its local terms come from Delta(chi phi), its integral terms from chi(x,z)-chi(t,z), and from partial_z chi(t,z) in the derivative kernel. Every term of F0 vanishes where x/(delta b)<1/2, since the entire preceding integration segment then has chi=1 and its derivatives zero. F0 has finite unweighted L2 norm by uniform flatness, and is independent of sigma. Consequently

    ||e^(sigma f)F0|| <= (2/delta)^sigma ||F0||.

Equations (5) and (9) yield

    P <= C0[1+1/(sigma-1/4)] Z + C1/(sigma-1/4) G
                       +(2/delta)^sigma||F0||,
    Z=||x^(-2)e^(sigma f)u||, G=||x^(-1)e^(sigma f)grad u||.

By (6)-(7), Z<=C sigma^(-3/2)P and G<=C sigma^(-1/2)P. For large sigma the first two terms can be absorbed, giving P<=2(2/delta)^sigma||F0||. On x<(delta/4)b, the weight is at least (4/delta)^sigma and chi=1. Equation (6) then forces

    ||phi||_{L2(x<(delta/4)b)} <= C delta^2 sigma^(-3/2) 2^(-sigma)||F0||.

Let sigma tend to infinity. Thus phi=0 on that smaller domain. Equation (3) and Y_x=0 there give Theta=T(y), and omega=-Delta phi=0. Smoothness includes the axis. This proves the proposed local statement.

##### Dependencies

The proof uses the exact local equations, elementary smooth ODE dependence, integration by parts, the explicit tapered logarithmic weight, and weighted Volterra estimates. The earlier linear interval theorem (Section A.4.4) supplied the weight design but is not invoked as a black box. The local conclusion alone is not a beta=2 nonexistence theorem. The regular-interface continuation and global beta=2 exclusion are in Section A.4.1.

#### A.4.3 Flat transverse perturbations of the beta = 2 source line

##### Part 1. Exact nonlinear equations near the segment

Assume beta = 2 and that an open interval of the y-axis consists of stagnation points with T(y) = Theta(0,y). Write

    Psi = -2xy + phi, Theta = T(y) + eta, omega = -Delta phi.

Then W = (4x-phi_y, phi_x), and the exact equations are

    (4x-phi_y) eta_x + phi_x (T'(y)+eta_y) = 0,
    (4x-phi_y) omega_x + phi_x omega_y + omega = eta_x,
    omega = -Delta phi.

Parity makes phi odd in x and eta even in x. At each first nonzero odd transverse order m >= 3, comparison gives

    [T'(y) - 4(m-1)(4m-7)] phi_m(y) = 0.

For m = 2k+3 the coefficient is 8(k+1)(8k+5). By induction on finite Taylor orders, if T' avoids this discrete set on an open interval, phi, eta and omega are flat in x there. Flat means that every transverse derivative vanishes at x = 0; it does not by itself mean the function vanishes nearby.

##### Part 2. Linearization and a Volterra identity

Linearize the equations at phi = eta = omega = 0, keeping a(y) = T'(y) fixed. They become

    4x eta_x + a(y) phi_x = 0,
    4x omega_x + omega = eta_x,
    omega = -Delta phi.

Elimination gives

    16x^2 phi_xxx + 4x phi_xx - a(y) phi_x
       + 16x^2 phi_xyy + 4x phi_yy = 0.

With z = log x this reads

    16 phi_zzz - 44 phi_zz + (28-a) phi_z
       + exp(2z) (16 phi_zyy + 4 phi_yy) = 0.

There is a more useful integral form when phi is smooth and flat at x = 0. From the first two equations,

    (x^(1/4) omega)_x = -(a/16) x^(-7/4) phi_x.

Integrating from zero and integrating by parts is legitimate because flatness kills every endpoint term. Therefore

    Delta phi = (a/16) [ x^(-2) phi + (7/4) J phi ],
    J phi(x,y) = x^(-1/4) integral_0^x t^(-11/4) phi(t,y) dt.             (V)

This identity is exact for flat solutions of the linearized equations. It is not the nonlinear equation.

##### Part 3. A weighted estimate

Let x range over (0,delta) and let y be periodic with any fixed period. For a smooth function u compactly supported away from x = delta and flat at x = 0, all norms below use dx dy. For sigma > 1/4,

    || x^(-sigma) J u ||_2
       <= [1/(sigma-1/4)] || x^(-sigma-2) u ||_2.                      (H)

Indeed, with f = x^(-sigma-2) u the left-hand expression inside the norm is

    integral_0^1 s^(sigma-3/4) f(sx,y) ds.

Minkowski and ||f(sx,y)||_{0<x<delta} <= s^(-1/2)||f|| give (H). The integral of s^(sigma-5/4) is 1/(sigma-1/4).

A direct Carleman estimate for the Laplacian is

    || x^(-sigma) Delta u ||_2^2
       >= (4 sigma^3-6 sigma) || x^(-sigma-2) u ||_2^2,                (C)

provided 4 sigma^3-6 sigma is positive. To prove it put v = x^(-sigma)u and decompose the conjugated operator as A+B, where

    A = Delta + sigma^2/x^2,
    B = (2 sigma/x) partial_x - sigma/x^2.

A is symmetric and B is skew symmetric. The commutator is

    [A,B] = -4 sigma x^(-2) partial_xx + 8 sigma x^(-3) partial_x
                + (4 sigma^3-6 sigma) x^(-4).

After integration by parts, its quadratic form is

    4 sigma integral x^(-2) |v_x|^2
       + (4 sigma^3-6 sigma) integral x^(-4) |v|^2.

The identity ||(A+B)v||^2 = ||Av||^2 + ||Bv||^2 + <v,[A,B]v> proves (C). First prove the calculation for support away from zero. Flatness then permits removal of a cutoff near zero for each fixed sigma, with all error terms tending to zero. Periodicity removes the tangential boundary terms.

##### Part 4. Linear flat uniqueness on a periodic strip

Statement. Let a(y) be bounded and periodic. Suppose phi is smooth on [0,delta) times the y-circle, flat at x=0 uniformly in y, and satisfies (V). Then phi vanishes on a smaller strip 0 <= x < delta0. Thus every smooth, uniformly flat solution of the linearized system on this periodic strip is locally zero in its streamfunction perturbation.

Proof. Choose a smooth cutoff chi(x) equal to one for x <= delta/2 and zero for x >= 3 delta/4, and set u = chi phi. Multiplying (V) by chi gives

    Delta u = (a/16)[x^(-2)u + (7/4)Ju] + f,

where

    f = 2 chi' phi_x + chi'' phi + (7a/64)(chi Jphi - J(chi phi)).

The function f vanishes for x < delta/2 and has a finite unweighted L2 norm on (0,delta) times the circle. The Volterra commutator need not vanish beyond the support of chi, but this causes no difficulty: it is still supported in x >= delta/2, away from the singular boundary.

By (H), the norm of the first right-hand term is at most

    C_sigma ||x^(-sigma-2)u||_2,
    C_sigma = ||a||_infinity/16 [1 + 7/(4(sigma-1/4))].

By (C), for sufficiently large sigma,

    [sqrt(4 sigma^3-6 sigma)-C_sigma] ||x^(-sigma-2)u||_2
       <= (delta/2)^(-sigma) ||f||_2.

On x < delta/4, chi = 1. Bounding the left weight below by (delta/4)^(-sigma-2) shows that ||phi|| on this smaller strip is at most a constant times 2^(-sigma) divided by a quantity growing like sigma^(3/2). Letting sigma tend to infinity gives phi = 0 there. Smoothness converts the L2 conclusion into pointwise equality. This proves the statement. For a flat solution of the whole linearized system, eta_x then vanishes and eta(0,y)=0 gives eta=0 on this smaller strip; omega=-Delta phi vanishes there as well.

#### A.4.4 Local interval uniqueness for a flat linear perturbation

##### Statement and notation

Let I be an open interval and epsilon>0. Let A(y) be a bounded function on compact subintervals of I. Suppose phi is smooth on [0,epsilon) times I, with every transverse derivative zero on x=0, and satisfies

    Delta phi = (A(y)/16) [x^(-2) phi + (7/4) J phi],
    J phi(x,y) = x^(-1/4) integral_0^x t^(-11/4) phi(t,y) dt.       (1)

Then phi vanishes in a relative one-sided neighborhood of every point (0,y0), y0 in I. Consequently every smooth flat solution of the linearized beta=2 system

    4x eta_x + A phi_x = 0,
    4x omega_x + omega = eta_x,
    omega = -Delta phi

vanishes locally in all three unknowns. Flatness of eta is part of this last conclusion's hypothesis.

All assertions are local. They do not concern the nonlinear equations or propagation to infinity.

##### Part 1. Reduction and tapered domain

Fix y0 and choose a closed interval centered at y0 contained in I. Translate y and rescale both spatial coordinates by its half-length so that this interval is [-1,1]. Both the Laplacian and the right side of (1) scale by the inverse square of this length, so (1) keeps its form. Shrink epsilon if needed. Smooth flatness is uniform on this compact interval.

Put b(y)=1-y^2 and choose 0<delta<=min(1/10,epsilon/2). Define

    D = { -1<y<1, 0<x<delta b(y) },
    f(x,y)=log b(y)-log x,
    q(y)=f_y=-2y/b,
    k(y)=-f_yy=2(1+y^2)/b^2.

The explicit bounds are

    0<k<=4/b^2, q^2<=4/b^2,
    k''=(12+72y^2+12y^4)/b^4, 0<k''<=96/b^4.            (2)

In D, x/b<delta. The domain tapers to zero width at the endpoints. This geometry will place all cutoff errors on a set where b/x is bounded.

##### Part 2. Carleman estimate

For u smooth and flat at x=0, supported away from the upper boundary x=delta b(y), and zero outside the tapered domain, all norms below use dx dy on D. For sigma>=2,

    || exp(sigma f) Delta u ||_2^2
         >= 2 sigma^3 || x^(-2) exp(sigma f) u ||_2^2.            (3)

Proof. Put v=exp(sigma f)u. The conjugated Laplacian is A0+B0 with

    A0=Delta+sigma^2 |grad f|^2,
    B0=-2 sigma grad f.grad-sigma Delta f.

A0 is symmetric and B0 is skew symmetric. Thus

    ||(A0+B0)v||^2 = ||A0v||^2+||B0v||^2+<v,[A0,B0]v>.

The commutator quadratic form, obtained by two integrations by parts, is

    4 sigma int Hess(f)(grad v,grad v)
    + 4 sigma^3 int Hess(f)(grad f,grad f) v^2
    - sigma int Delta^2(f) v^2.

Since Hess(f)=diag(x^(-2),-k), this equals

    4 sigma int x^(-2) v_x^2 - 4 sigma int k v_y^2
    + (4 sigma^3-6 sigma) int x^(-4)v^2
    - 4 sigma^3 int k q^2 v^2 + sigma int k''v^2.                 (4)

The sole negative gradient term can be controlled without assuming a bound for second derivatives. Indeed

    int k |grad v|^2
       = -<kv,A0v> + sigma^2 int k(x^(-2)+q^2)v^2
           + (1/2) int k''v^2.

Use v_y^2<=|grad v|^2, drop the positive x-gradient term, and apply

    4 sigma |<kv,A0v>| <= (1/2)||A0v||^2+8 sigma^2||kv||^2.

Writing J0=int x^(-4)v^2, the result is

    ||(A0+B0)v||^2 >= (1/2)||A0v||^2+||B0v||^2
      + [4 sigma^3-6 sigma-16 sigma^3 delta^2-128 sigma^3 delta^4
          -128 sigma^2 delta^4-96 sigma delta^4] J0.             (5)

For example, int k x^(-2)v^2<=4 delta^2 J0 and int kq^2v^2<=16 delta^4 J0 follow directly from (2). For delta<=1/10 and sigma>=2, the bracket divided by sigma^3 is at least

    4-.16-.0128-.0064-1.5024 = 2.3184 > 2.

This proves (3). Initially use support away from x=0 and the two corners. For each fixed sigma, smooth flatness and b>=x/delta ensure that every derivative of v decays faster than any prescribed power of x at the remaining boundary. All cutoff-removal errors therefore tend to zero. This justifies the integrations by parts and gives (3) for the stated u. For complex functions apply the same argument to real and imaginary parts.

##### Part 3. Weighted Volterra bound

For the same domain and sigma>1/4,

    || exp(sigma f) Ju ||_2
       <= [1/(sigma-1/4)] || x^(-2) exp(sigma f) u ||_2.        (6)

Let F=x^(-sigma-2)b^sigma u. Changing variables t=sx gives the integrand on the left as

    integral_0^1 s^(sigma-3/4) F(sx,y) ds.

For each fixed y the x interval is (0,delta b(y)), so dilation in x has L2 norm at most s^(-1/2). Minkowski gives (6). No y derivative enters this step.

##### Part 4. Cutoff and uniqueness

Choose chi in C-infinity([0,infinity)), equal to one on [0,1/2] and zero on [3/4,infinity), and set

    u=chi(x/(delta b(y))) phi.

Extend u by zero outside D. Uniform flatness and the inequality b>=x/delta on its support imply that this extension is smooth at the corners. Derivatives of the cutoff cost only finite powers of x^(-1), which flatness absorbs. Equation (1) gives

    Delta u=(A/16)[x^(-2)u+(7/4)Ju]+F0,

where

    F0=2 grad chi.grad phi+(Delta chi)phi
           +(7A/64)[chi Jphi-J(chi phi)].

Here chi denotes the displayed composite cutoff. F0 is in L2(D) and vanishes wherever x/(delta b)<1/2. The Volterra commutator can persist beyond the support of chi, but remains in that same outer portion of D. Consequently

    ||exp(sigma f)F0|| <= (2/delta)^sigma ||F0||.

Combining (3) and (6), for sufficiently large sigma,

    [sqrt(2)sigma^(3/2)-C_sigma] ||x^(-2)exp(sigma f)u||
         <= (2/delta)^sigma ||F0||,
    C_sigma=||A||_infinity/16 [1+7/(4(sigma-1/4))].

On the smaller domain D0={0<x<(delta/4)b(y), |y|<1}, u=phi and exp(sigma f)>=(4/delta)^sigma. Also x^(-2)>=delta^(-2). Hence

    ||phi||_{L2(D0)} <= delta^2 2^(-sigma)||F0|| /
        [sqrt(2)sigma^(3/2)-C_sigma].

Let sigma tend to infinity. Then phi=0 on D0, first in L2 and then pointwise. Since b(y0)>0 in these coordinates, D0 contains a one-sided neighborhood of (0,y0). Smoothness includes x=0. In the linearized system, eta_x=0 there and eta(0,y)=0, so eta=0; omega=-Delta phi=0. This proves the statement.

##### Dependencies and limits

The Volterra identity is derived in Section A.4.3. The present proof replaces its periodic tangential hypothesis by a tapered local domain. It uses only explicit integration by parts and inequalities. No claim about the nonlinear beta=2 system is made: straightening its flat tangential drift changes the elliptic operator and requires a further estimate with variable coefficients. Even nonlinear local rigidity would not by itself provide global exclusion.

### A.5 Corollary 4

Report statement: see Corollary 4 in Section 3.

Proof.

The axis theorem (Theorem 1, Section A.2) and the smooth beta=2 theorem (Theorem 3, Section A.4) exclude beta<=2. For beta>2, the axis theorem gives |Theta(0,y)| increasing without bound as y tends to infinity. The sign of Theta(0,y), its strict monotonicity on y>0 and the lower bound c y^(lambda/(beta+epsilon)) are item 3 of Section A.2; the hypotheses used there hold in class A' by the center identity DU(0)=diag(2,-2) stated in Section A.2.

### A.6 Proposition 5 (finite L^p norms)

Report statement: see Proposition 5 in Section 3.

Proof.

The finite L^p part of Proposition 5 is item 5 of Section A.2 and its proof; the Jacobian computation there is valid for every p > 0. The part for beta = 2 and Theta -> 0 at infinity is part 1 below.

#### Hypotheses and notation

Unless stated otherwise, let a smooth Setting A1 profile on R^2 satisfy

    W = beta X + U, div U = 0, U = o(|X|),
    W dot grad Theta = (beta-2) Theta,
    W dot grad Omega + Omega = Theta_x,
    -Delta Psi = Omega, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x),
    Theta_y(0) = a0 != 0.

Use Phi_t for the complete flow of W. Sublinear U makes W at most linear in size, so smoothness gives global existence for positive and negative finite times. The Jacobian determinant is exp(2 beta t). Section A.2 supplies the beta < 2 exclusion and the finite-Lp exclusion; its flow argument applies for every finite p > 0.

#### Part 1. Invariant level bands at beta = 2

Statement. If beta = 2, every nonempty open set of the form

    A = {X : t1 < Theta(X) < t2},  t1 < t2,

has infinite area. For each value v in the range of Theta there is a sequence |X_n| -> infinity with Theta(X_n) -> v. If Theta tends to zero at infinity, or belongs to some Lp with finite p > 0, there is no nontrivial profile.

Proof. Transport gives Theta(Phi_t X) = Theta(X), hence Phi_t A = A for every real t. By the change-of-variables formula, |A| = exp(4t)|A|. If A is nonempty, it is open and has positive area. The identity rules out finite positive area, proving |A| = infinity. For any v in the range and each integer n, the band |Theta-v| < 1/n is nonempty and therefore unbounded; choose X_n there with |X_n| > n.

If Theta tends to zero and has a nonzero value v, a sufficiently narrow band around v is bounded, contradicting its infinite area. If Theta is in Lp, choose a nonempty band with |Theta| >= epsilon > 0. Infinite area contradicts finite integral of |Theta|^p. Thus Theta must vanish in either case, contradicting a0 != 0. No integration by parts or boundary flux assumption is used.

### A.7 Proposition 6 (sign of the vorticity)

Report statement: see Proposition 6 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and hypotheses

Let a smooth Setting A1 profile satisfy the equations on R^2 with beta > 0, nonzero a0 = Theta_y(0), and the canonical sublinear velocity U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x). Thus Theta is even in x and odd in y, Psi and Omega are odd in both coordinates, -Delta Psi = Omega, and U(X) = o(|X|). Then Omega cannot be nonnegative throughout Q = {x > 0, y > 0}.

No decay or absolute integrability of Omega is assumed beyond existence of this smooth sublinear velocity. More generally, if a smooth odd-odd Psi has sublinear rotated gradient and -Delta Psi is nonnegative in Q, then Psi/(xy) is nonnegative everywhere. It is strictly positive everywhere if Omega is not identically zero.

#### Notation and dependencies

Write Psi(x,y) = xy H(x,y) and Omega(x,y) = xy G(x,y), with H and G extended smoothly and evenly across both axes. Lift these functions to R^6 = R^3 times R^3 by h(p,q) = H(|p|,|q|), g(p,q) = G(|p|,|q|). Smooth even radial functions have smooth lifts. Section A.1.1 establishes h -> 0 uniformly at infinity under U = o(|X|), and the exact identity -Delta_6 h = g. The only additional dependency is the strong minimum principle for C^2 superharmonic functions on Euclidean balls.

#### Proof

The sign of Omega in Q implies G >= 0 on Q. Even reflection and continuity imply G >= 0 everywhere, hence g >= 0 on R^6. Therefore Delta_6 h <= 0.

If h(z0) < 0 at some point, uniform decay h -> 0 implies that the global minimum of h is achieved in a finite ball and is negative. The strong minimum principle forces h to be constant on R^6. Its limit at infinity then makes that constant zero, a contradiction. Thus h >= 0. If h vanished anywhere, the same strong minimum principle would make it identically zero; its equation would give g = 0 and Omega = 0. Consequently h > 0 for nonzero Omega.

For a profile, expansion of W dot grad Theta = (beta-2) Theta at the origin gives a0(Psi_xy(0)+2) = 0. Since a0 != 0, h(0) = H(0,0) = Psi_xy(0) = -2. This contradicts h >= 0 and completes the proof.

#### Scope

The result excludes only Omega >= 0 in Q. It permits negative or sign-changing quadrant vorticity. In particular it does not constrain the sign of a0 by itself. It strengthens the strain-integral argument because it requires neither a convergent first-quadrant strain integral nor cancellation estimates at infinity.

### A.8 Proposition 7 (compactly supported vorticity)

Report statement: see Proposition 7 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Compactly supported Omega is impossible, for every beta > 0

Statement. A smooth Setting A1 profile with canonical sublinear velocity cannot have compactly supported vorticity.

Proof. Suppose supp Omega lies in {|X| <= R}. The ordinary Biot-Savart integral converges. Odd-odd parity makes its subtracted constant zero, and this velocity tends to zero as |X| -> infinity, since for |X| > 2R the kernel is O(1/|X|). Uniqueness in the sublinear parity class identifies it with U.

On {|X| > R}, Omega and its derivatives vanish. The vorticity equation gives Theta_x = 0 there. Set F(y) = Theta(R+1,y); on the right exterior horizontal ray Theta = F(y), and evenness in x gives the same value on the left ray. When |y| > R the whole horizontal line is exterior, so again Theta = F(y). Therefore Theta(X) = F(y) throughout the exterior of the ball, and F is smooth and odd.

For fixed y, let x -> positive infinity in the exterior temperature equation. Since U2(x,y) -> 0, it gives

    beta y F'(y) = (beta-2) F(y).

On y > 0 this has F(y) = C y^gamma, gamma = 1-2/beta < 1. Smoothness and oddness give F(0) = 0 and F(y) = O(y) near zero. These force C = 0: for gamma < 0 continuity already fails if C != 0; for gamma = 0 it contradicts F(0) = 0; and for 0 < gamma < 1 differentiability fails. Oddness gives F = 0 on the negative axis as well.

Thus Theta has compact support and belongs to every finite Lp. The finite-Lp exclusion (Proposition 5, Section A.6) rules out the profile. Alternatively, combine beta < 2 exclusion with the level-band result of Section A.6 for beta = 2 and unbounded axis temperature for beta > 2. This completes the proof.

### A.9 Proposition 8 (sign of the temperature, beta > 2)

Report statement: see Proposition 8 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Hypotheses and notation

Let beta>2, lambda=beta-2 and alpha=beta+2. Let W=beta X+U be a C1 vector field on R2, with div U=0, U=o(|X|), and the A1 velocity parities. Assume DW(0)=diag(alpha,lambda). (This follows from the hypotheses of Proposition 8 in Section 3: the parities give W1(0,y)=0 and W2(x,0)=0, so DW(0) is diagonal; dividing (P2) on the y-axis, W2(0,y) Theta_y(0,y)=lambda Theta(0,y), by y and letting y -> 0 gives a0 (dW2/dy)(0)=lambda a0; and div W=2 beta gives (dW1/dx)(0)=alpha.) Let Theta be a C1 solution of W.grad Theta=lambda Theta, even in x and odd in y, with Theta_y(0)=a0!=0. When used, Omega is a C1 solution of W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x. Write Phi_t for the complete flow of W and B for the set of points whose backward trajectory tends to 0. The completeness proof is in Section A.2. Higher smoothness is stated where it is needed.

#### Area expansion and the global basin

The flow Jacobian is exp(2 beta t). Consequently a bounded invariant region of positive area is impossible: invariance and change of variables would give |D|=exp(2 beta t)|D|. In particular there is no periodic orbit, since its Jordan interior is invariant, and no finite separatrix cycle forming the boundary of such a region. This is also the Bendixson divergence argument. A sink or center is excluded: the trace at an equilibrium is 2 beta>0, so a sink cannot have the required stable linear spectrum, and a center would give periodic orbits. Here 'sink' means a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium, not a saddle with a lower-dimensional stable set.

Suppose 0 is the only equilibrium. For sufficiently large R, W points strictly outwards on and outside the circle of radius R. Every backward trajectory enters the closed ball and remains there. Its backward limit set is nonempty and compact. If this limit set avoids 0, the two-dimensional Poincare-Bendixson theorem gives a periodic orbit, a contradiction. If it contains 0, the trajectory enters a small attracting neighborhood for the reversed flow, since -DW(0) has strictly negative eigenvalues. It then converges to 0. Thus B=R2.

Under the same hypothesis, every nonzero forward trajectory tends to infinity. A trajectory which leaves a sufficiently large circle cannot return and its radius grows at least exponentially. A bounded forward trajectory would have a compact limit set. It cannot accumulate at 0, because W points strictly outwards on a sufficiently small circle around this source. A limit set with no equilibrium would again contain a periodic orbit. This proves the assertion.

#### Uniqueness and the sign of the temperature on B

Suppose Theta_1 and Theta_2 have the same W and a0. Their difference D has zero value and derivative at 0, so D=o(|X|). Near 0, Theta_1(x,y)=y(a0+o(1)), uniformly, by the fundamental theorem of calculus in y. Thus |y|<=C|Theta_1(x,y)| there. Parity also gives W1=x A(x,y), with A continuous and A(0)=alpha.

Fix X in B and take t negative enough that its entire earlier trajectory stays in this neighborhood. Along that trajectory, Theta_1(Phi_t X)=exp(lambda t)Theta_1(X). For any epsilon in (0,alpha-lambda), the x equation gives |x(Phi_t X)|<=C_X exp((alpha-epsilon)t). Combining these two estimates gives |Phi_t X|<=C_X exp(lambda t), including points on the x-axis. Hence

    D(X)=exp(-lambda t)D(Phi_t X) -> 0  as t -> -infinity.

Therefore Theta_1=Theta_2 on B. The use of an existing nondegenerate temperature to control the slow coordinate avoids an unjustified exact exponential rate from C1 linearization alone.

For X in B with y>0, parity and uniqueness of the flow keep its backward trajectory in y>0. Eventually Theta(Phi_t X)/y(Phi_t X) has the sign of a0. The positive factor exp(-lambda t) preserves this sign. Thus Theta has the sign of a0 on B intersected with {y>0}. No assertion about Theta_x follows from this sign result.

### A.10 Proposition 9 (characteristic formula)

Report statement: see Proposition 9 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and hypotheses

Let beta>0 and let smooth A1 fields solve

    W=beta X+U, div U=0, U=o(|X|),
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
    W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,
    U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), Omega=-Delta Psi,
    Theta=a0 y+O(|X|^3), a0!=0.

The usual parity holds, so both axes and the open quadrants are invariant. Then the reconstruction formula below holds everywhere, not merely in the backward basin of the origin. The sign conclusions use the already proved fact that Omega>=0 on Q1 contradicts the A1 strain c=-2 (Proposition 6, Section A.7), in smooth sublinear class A' without extra integrability. The reconstruction and one-sign arguments require no behavior of derivatives at infinity.

#### Reconstruction without a basin assumption

The vector field W has at most linear growth, so its smooth flow Phi_t exists for all finite positive and negative times. Outside a fixed ball, X.W>=beta|X|^2/2. The backward vector field therefore points strictly inward there. Every backward trajectory stays in a compact ball depending on its starting point. In particular Omega and Theta_x are bounded along that trajectory.

Integrate d[e^t Omega(Phi_t X)]/dt=e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) from -T to zero. Since the bounded endpoint is multiplied by e^-T, it tends to zero. Thus

    Omega(X)=integral_-infinity^0 e^t Theta_x(Phi_t X) dt.       (1)

The integral is absolutely convergent for each X. No claim about a common integrable bound over all X or about Fubini with the strain kernel is needed. The formula in fact holds for every beta>0 in this sublinear setting. For beta=2 it also shows Omega=0 on the critical set of Theta, since that set is invariant by the invertible gradient-transport equation. The same conclusion holds for all beta: grad Theta evolves by (beta-2)Id-DW^T, so a zero gradient stays zero in both time directions.

### A.11 Proposition 10 (spatial gauge)

Report statement: see Proposition 10 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and assumptions

A1 means Theta is even in x and odd in y; U1 is odd in x and even in y; U2 is even in x and odd in y.

Let beta>0 and let smooth fields satisfy the temperature equation of (P), the A1 parities, div U=0, U=o(|X|), and Theta_y(0,0)=a0!=0. The origin temperature equation forces U1_x(0,0)=2. Define

    w(x)=beta x+U1(x,0),   tau(x)=Theta_y(x,0),   x>=0.

Then tau attains a0/2 at some positive finite x before the first positive zero of w, if such a zero exists. In particular the spatial normalization Theta_y(1,0)=a0/2 is available for every smooth profile in the target class, including a profile with Theta_xxy(0)=0. It does not set a0.

If w has no positive zero then tau has the sign of a0 for every x>0 and

    lim_{x->infinity} log |tau(x)| / log x = -2/beta.

This is a logarithmic decay exponent, not an asymptotic power with a proved amplitude.

#### Proof

Differentiate W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta with respect to y and restrict to y=0. Parity gives Theta(x,0)=Theta_x(x,0)=W2(x,0)=W1_y(x,0)=0. The divergence identity gives W2_y(x,0)=2 beta-w'(x). Therefore

    w tau'=(w'-beta-2)tau.                              (1)

Near zero w=(beta+2)x+O(x^3) and tau=a0+O(x^2). Let x* be the first positive zero of w if one exists, otherwise infinity. Then w>0 on (0,x*). At any fixed x0 in that interval, (1) has the exact solution

    tau(x)=tau(x0) [w(x)/w(x0)]
        exp( -(beta+2) integral_{x0}^x ds/w(s) ).        (2)

Choose x0 sufficiently small that tau(x0) has the sign of a0. Formula (2), applied on every compact subinterval, preserves that sign throughout (0,x*).

If x*<infinity, then w(x)->0 as x increases to x*. For x>=x0 the exponential in (2) is at most one, since beta+2>0 and w>0. It follows that tau(x)->0. No assumption on the order of the zero or on a finite integral is needed.

If x*=infinity, sublinearity gives w(x)/x->beta. Hence log w(x)/log x->1 and

    (1/log x) integral_{x0}^x ds/w(s) -> 1/beta.

The latter limit follows directly by comparison with 1/((beta+-epsilon)s), outside a sufficiently large fixed interval, and then epsilon->0. Taking logarithms in (2) proves the displayed exponent -2/beta<0, and therefore tau(x)->0.

In either case tau starts at a0 and tends to zero at the end of the interval. The intermediate value theorem gives tau(xh)=a0/2 for a finite xh in (0,x*). The first such xh is well-defined: the level set is closed in (0,x*), nonempty, and separated from zero by continuity and a0!=0.

The full profile system is W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x, W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta, -Delta Psi=Omega and U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x). Under the spatial change below, also set Omega_l(X)=Omega(X/l) and Psi_l(X)=l^2 Psi(X/l). Then W_l=lW(X/l), derivatives of Omega_l bring a factor 1/l, derivatives of Theta_l bring no factor, and -Delta Psi_l=Omega_l. Thus every displayed equation and the canonical sublinear inverse are preserved.

Under this exact spatial symmetry

    Theta_l(X)=l Theta(X/l), U_l(X)=l U(X/l),

one has tau_l(x)=tau(x/l) and a0_l=a0. Taking l=1/xh puts the first half-height at x=1. A tangential crossing could make this gauge poorly conditioned for the numerical states, but does not prevent its existence. No monotonicity of tau is assumed.

#### Dependencies and scope

Only the temperature equation, smooth parity, divergence, sublinearity and the nondegenerate center jet are used. The vorticity equation and any integral inverse formula are not needed. The local center identity and spatial symmetry are proved in Sections A.2 and A.1. This argument strengthens the justification of the normalization Theta_y(1,0)=a0/2; it does not decide existence or fix the exponent beta.

### A.12 Theorem 11 (far field for beta > 2)

Report statement: see Theorem 11 in Section 3.

Proof.

Theorem 11 is assembled from four parts. Section A.12.1 proves that the polynomial bounds imply the power decay hypothesis (H). Section A.12.2 proves, under (H), the rates in (a), the limits F, A, V in (b) and the annular bound (d) (take p=1 in (7) there). Section A.12.3 proves the Holder continuity of A, the description of V through H, the sign of F(pi/2) and (c). Section A.12.4 proves the gradient limit in (b).

#### A.12.1 Polynomial tails bootstrap to power decay

##### Exact statement

Let beta>2. Let U,Theta,Omega be smooth on R2, with

    div U=0, curl U=-Omega, U=o(|X|),
    W=beta X+U, W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x.                         (P)

Sublinearity is uniform: sup_{|X|>=R}|U(X)|/|X| tends to zero as R tends to infinity. Assume only the polynomial bounds

    |Omega(X)|+|grad Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^m,

for some finite m, increased to be nonnegative. No bound on higher derivatives is used. Then for some a>0,

    |Omega(X)|<=C_a(1+|X|)^(-a).                        (1)

The A1 parity and nonzero temperature jet are not needed for this preliminary decay conclusion. For an A1 profile they are retained when invoking the far-field theorem of Section A.12.2: (1), the polynomial gradient bound, and that theorem give delta=1/beta and

    |Theta|=O(r^(1-2 delta)), |grad Theta|=O(r^-2 delta),
    |Omega|=O(r^-delta), |U|=O(r^(1-delta)),
    |DU|=O(r^-delta log r),

as well as its C1 nonzero temperature angular limit, continuous vorticity angular limit and annular Lp obstruction. Thus those conclusions hold in the full smooth class A' with polynomial tails specified in Section 2.3. No profile is constructed or excluded for beta>2 by this bootstrap.

##### Part 1. A local elliptic estimate without prior vorticity decay

For any fixed N>0 and r=|X| sufficiently large,

    |DU(X)| <= C_N [r^-1 sup_{B(X,r/2)}|U|
                 +(1+log r) sup_{B(X,r/2)}|Omega|
                 +r^-N].                              (2)

Here all constants may depend on the polynomial gradient bound and N.

Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on B(X,r/4), supported in B(X,r/2), with first derivative bounded by C/r. Let v be its compact-vorticity Biot-Savart velocity with the same minus-curl convention. The locally integrable kernel has size C/|Z|, so

    sup_{B(X,r/3)}|v| <= C r sup_{B(X,r/2)}|Omega|.

Both div(U-v) and curl(U-v) vanish on B(X,r/4). Its components are harmonic there. The interior harmonic gradient estimate bounds its derivative at X by
C r^-1 sup_{B(X,r/4)}|U-v|, hence by the first term of (2) plus C sup|Omega|.

For Dv(X), the distributional derivative kernel is a principal-value kernel of order |Z|^-2, plus a fixed local multiple of Omega(X). It has angular cancellation. On |Z|<r/4 subtract Omega(X). Split at epsilon=r^(-m-N), taking r large enough that epsilon<r/4. The innermost integral is bounded by

    C sup_{B(X,r/4)}|grad Omega| integral_0^epsilon ds
       <= C r^m epsilon=C r^-N.

On epsilon<|Z|<r/4 the bound is
C sup|Omega| log(r/epsilon)<=C_N sup|Omega|(1+log r). The cutoff annulus r/4<|Z|<r/2 and the local distributional multiple cost C sup|Omega|. This proves (2). This argument uses only a local compact-vorticity inverse; it does not presume convergence of a global inverse before (1) is known.

In particular if Omega=O(r^p), with any real p, sublinearity and (2) imply

    |DU|+|U|/r <= C (1+r^q)(1+log r), q=max(p,0).        (3)

The annular comparison |Y| comparable to r on B(X,r/2) justifies using r^p uniformly there.

##### Part 2. Exact gradient transport with a controlled source

Use J(v1,v2)=(-v2,v1), h=J grad Theta, and M=DW. Differentiating the temperature equation and using trace M=2 beta gives

    W.grad h=M h-(beta+2)h,                             (4)

since JM^T=(trace M)J-MJ. Write polar components W_r,W_phi. On an exterior region where W_r>0 define

    f=-Theta_phi/(r W_r),
    h=f W+a e_phi, a=(beta-2)Theta/W_r.                 (5)

Indeed the radial component is h_r=-Theta_phi/r=f W_r, and
 det(W,h)=W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta=a W_r. Thus both components agree.

Taking the radial component of (4), after differentiating (5), yields

    W.grad f+(beta+2)f
       = (beta-2)Theta [partial_phi W_r]/(r W_r^2).      (6)

For explicit verification, (M e_phi).e_r=(partial_phi W_r-W_phi)/r and
((W.grad)e_phi).e_r=-W_phi/r. The two W_phi terms cancel. The derivative of the scalar a contributes only in the e_phi direction. Also

    |partial_phi W_r|/r <= |DU|+|U|/r.                  (7)

The dilation field beta X has zero angular derivative of its radial component, so no derivative estimate on the full W is hidden in (7).

##### Part 3. A gain in the polynomial vorticity exponent

We prove the following implication for every p in R and every eta>0:

    Omega=O(r^p)
      implies grad Theta=O(r^(max(p,0)-2/beta+eta)),
      and Omega=O(r^(max(-1/beta,max(p,0)-2/beta)+eta)).  (8)

Fix a small epsilon>0, to be chosen after p and eta. By uniform sublinearity, outside a sufficiently large circle Sigma,

    (beta-epsilon)r<=W_r<=(beta+epsilon)r.

Every exterior point is Phi_t Z for a unique Z on Sigma and t>=0. The flow is complete by the global linear growth bound. Its radius satisfies uniformly over Sigma

    c e^((beta-epsilon)t)<=r(t)<=C e^((beta+epsilon)t).   (9)

Exact temperature transport gives Theta(Phi_t Z)=e^((beta-2)t)Theta(Z), with uniformly bounded Theta(Z). Integrating (6) and using (7) and W_r comparable to r gives

    |f(Phi_t Z)| <= C e^(-(beta+2)t)
        [1+integral_0^t e^(2 beta s) r(s)^-2
                         (|DU|+|U|/r)(Phi_s Z) ds].     (10)

The initial f is bounded on the fixed circle. This estimate remains valid at zeros of Theta or of its derivatives; no division by Theta has occurred.

Let q=max(p,0). From (3) and (9), the integrand in (10) is bounded by
C(1+s) exp([q beta+(q+2)epsilon]s). Since q>=0 and epsilon>0, integration and absorption of the polynomial factor give

    integral_0^t (...) ds <= C_epsilon
                    exp([q beta+(q+3)epsilon]t).

Equation (5), |W|<=Cr, and |a|<=C e^((beta-2)t)/r now give

    |grad Theta(Phi_t Z)|
       <=C_epsilon exp([q beta-2+(q+4)epsilon]t).        (11)

For a real exponent b, conversion of exp(bt) using (9) gives a power r^(b/(beta-epsilon)) if b>=0 and r^(b/(beta+epsilon)) if b<0. As epsilon tends to zero, the exponent in (11) therefore tends to q-2/beta. This proves the first statement of (8), with any prescribed positive loss eta.

For the vorticity equation use the exact forward formula

    Omega(Phi_t Z)=e^-t Omega(Z)
             +integral_0^t e^(-(t-s))Theta_x(Phi_s Z)ds.

With b=q beta-2+(q+4)epsilon, the right side is bounded by

    C(1+t)exp(max(-1,b)t).

For any epsilon>0, the factor 1+t is at most C_epsilon e^(epsilon t). Converting to a radial power as above, its exponent tends, as epsilon tends to zero, to max(-1/beta,q-2/beta). Choosing epsilon sufficiently small proves the second statement in (8). The choice may depend on p and eta; only finitely many applications are needed below. All constants are uniform in direction.

##### Part 4. Finite iteration to actual decay

Set delta=1/beta and eta=delta/4. Start with p0=m>=0 from the assumed polynomial vorticity bound, and apply (8) successively with

    p_{j+1}=max(-delta,max(p_j,0)-2 delta)+delta/4.

While p_j>=delta this gives p_{j+1}=p_j-7 delta/4. If 0<=p_j<delta, it gives p_{j+1}=-3 delta/4. Thus after finitely many steps p_j<0. This is precisely (1), with a=-p_j>0. If an earlier step already gives a negative p_j, stop immediately. No limit of constants over infinitely many iterations is taken.

For an A1 profile, positive power decay together with the original polynomial grad Omega bound supplies exactly hypothesis (H) of Section A.12.2. That proof gives all the sharp rates and limits listed after (1). Its use of the canonical subtracted inverse is now justified by actual positive power decay; sublinear harmonic uniqueness and parity identify it with the prescribed U. This removes the formerly additional power-decay hypothesis for solutions of the full coupled class A'.

##### Dependencies and scope

Standard inputs are local harmonic gradient estimates, the two-dimensional div-curl identity, and complete-flow calculus; all applications and boundary assumptions are specified above. Sharp rates use the conditional far theorem of Section A.12.2 only after (1) is established. There is no claim that sublinearity alone forces vorticity decay: the coupled transport equations and polynomial gradient bound are essential to this argument. No conclusion of existence or nonexistence for the remaining range beta>2 follows.

#### A.12.2 Far-field limits and vorticity integrability

##### Exact hypotheses and conclusions

Let beta>2 and lambda=beta-2. Suppose smooth fields on R^2 satisfy

    W=beta X+U, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), Omega=-Delta Psi,
    W.grad Theta=lambda Theta, W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x.

Theta is even in x and odd in y; Psi and Omega are odd in both variables. Suppose Theta_y(0)=a0!=0 and U=o(|X|). In addition assume, for some alpha>0 and finite m,C,

    |Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^(-alpha),
    |grad Omega(X)|<=C(1+|X|)^m.                          (H)

Both additional conditions are retained explicitly. Write delta=1/beta and gamma=1-2/beta. There are F in C1 of the angular circle and A continuous on that circle such that, uniformly in angle,

    r^(-gamma)Theta(r,.) -> F in C1,
    r^delta Omega(r,.) -> A in C0,
    r^(-(1-delta))U(r,.) -> V in C0.                     (1)

F is nonzero and has the inherited even-x, odd-y parity. In particular,

    |grad Theta|=O(r^(-2/beta)),
    |Omega|=O(r^(-1/beta)), |U|=O(r^(1-1/beta)).          (2)

There is a constant c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large R,

    integral_{R<|X|<2R} Omega^2 >= c R^(2-4/beta).        (3)

More generally Omega cannot belong to Lp(R2) for any 0<p<=beta, and uniform Omega=o(r^(-2/beta)) is impossible. No sign condition on Theta_x or Omega is imposed. The limit A is allowed to vanish; its C1 regularity is not claimed from (H).

##### Part 1. Canonical inverse and derivative bounds

Replace alpha by a smaller number in (0,1) if necessary. The subtracted inverse

    U_0(X)=integral [K(X-Y)-K(-Y)]Omega(Y)dY,
    K(Z)=(Z2,-Z1)/(2 pi |Z|^2)

converges absolutely and obeys |U_0(X)|<=C(1+r)^(1-alpha). The proof is the three-region estimate: for |Y|>2r the kernel difference is O(r/|Y|^2); the two locally integrable singularities in |Y|<=2r contribute O(r^(1-alpha)) after rescaling. Smoothness near finite points follows from the local elliptic equation. U-U_0 is a smooth divergence-free and curl-free sublinear field, so each component is harmonic and sublinear and hence constant. The A1 parity and U(0)=U_0(0)=0 eliminate that constant.

The polynomial gradient bound in (H) gives

    |DU(X)|<=C r^(-alpha) log(2+r), r>=2.                 (4)

Here is the local principal-value estimate. Near X subtract Omega(X) in the homogeneous derivative kernel, split at epsilon=r^(-m-2) after increasing m to be nonnegative, and then at r/2. The inner contribution is O(r^m epsilon)=O(r^-2). The intermediate contribution is O(r^-alpha log(r/epsilon)). The far region is O(r^-alpha), by splitting near the origin and beyond 2r. The local distributional multiple of Omega is O(r^-alpha). Because alpha<1, the first term is bounded by the stated right side. Thus all constants are uniform in direction.

##### Part 2. Outgoing flow coordinates and a differentiable angular limit

Take a large circle Sigma on which W has strictly positive radial component and outside which

    (beta-epsilon)r <= d r/dt <= (beta+epsilon)r

for some fixed epsilon<beta/2. Every point outside Sigma is represented uniquely as Phi_t Z, with Z in Sigma and t>=0. Backward crossing follows from the positive lower radial bound. The complete finite-time flow exists because W has at most linear growth.

Using |U|=O(r^(1-alpha)),

    d(log r)/dt=beta+O(r^-alpha).

The error is integrable by the initial exponential lower bound on r(t). Hence r(t) is uniformly comparable to e^(beta t). Equation (4) is integrable in t along all these trajectories, uniformly over Sigma.

Put M_t(Z)=e^(-beta t)D Phi_t(Z). Then

    d M_t/dt=DU(Phi_t Z) M_t, det M_t=1.

The integrable coefficient bounds M_t and its inverse and makes them converge uniformly to M_infinity, with determinant one. Also

    a(Z)=lim_{t->infinity}e^(-beta t)Phi_t Z

exists in C1 on Sigma. The derivative is M_infinity restricted to the tangent. To see existence, integrate e^(-beta t)U(Phi_t Z)=O(e^(-alpha beta t)); the derivative convergence follows from the already proved convergence of M_t. The norm rho=|a| is bounded above and below by positive constants.

Parametrize Sigma counterclockwise by sigma. The flow identity D Phi_t W(Z)=W(Phi_t Z) yields

    beta a=M_infinity W(Z),
    det(beta a,a')=det(W(Z),Z')>0.

Thus sigma -> arg a is a local C1 diffeomorphism. It has degree one, since the nonzero curves e^(-beta t)Phi_t(Sigma) are homotopic to Sigma and converge uniformly without touching zero. It is therefore a global C1 diffeomorphism of circles.

##### Part 3. Transport limits and improved rates

Exact differentiation of Theta(Phi_t Z)=e^(lambda t)Theta(Z) gives

    grad Theta(Phi_t Z)
       =e^(lambda t)D Phi_t(Z)^(-T)grad Theta(Z)
       =e^(-2t)M_t(Z)^(-T)grad Theta(Z).                  (5)

This proves the gradient bound in (2), and also uniform convergence of e^(2t)grad Theta(Phi_t Z). The forward vorticity identity gives

    e^t Omega(Phi_t Z)=Omega(Z)+integral_0^t e^s Theta_x(Phi_s Z)ds.

The integrand is O(e^-s), uniformly. Hence the right side converges uniformly to a continuous b(Z). It follows that Omega=O(r^-delta), and the canonical inverse estimate improves to U=O(r^(1-delta)). Repeating the derivative estimate if desired gives DU=O(r^-delta log r).

Define

    F(arg a(Z))=rho(Z)^(-gamma)Theta(Z),
    A(arg a(Z))=rho(Z)^delta b(Z).

These have the asserted C1 and C0 regularities. To justify the limits at fixed radius, let t=t(R,sigma) be the unique crossing time of the radius-R circle. Differentiating r(t,sigma)=R gives

    t_sigma=-r_sigma/r_t.

Since D Phi_t=O(e^(beta t)) and r_t is comparable to r, this is uniformly bounded. Moreover e^(-beta t)Phi_t, its sigma derivative at fixed t, and its time derivative converge uniformly; the time derivative tends to zero. Thus the fixed-radius limiting-angle maps converge in C1 to arg a and their inverses converge in C1. The identities

    R^(-gamma)Theta(Phi_t Z)
       =(e^(-beta t)r(t,Z))^(-gamma)Theta(Z),
    R^delta Omega(Phi_t Z)
       =(e^(-beta t)r(t,Z))^delta e^t Omega(Phi_t Z)

then prove the first two limits in (1), including the first angular derivative for Theta. No derivative of b is used or assumed.

F cannot vanish identically. If Theta were zero on Sigma, it would be zero at every exterior point. A nonzero point exists by a0!=0. Its forward trajectory cannot remain in the closed Sigma disk, because |Theta(Phi_t X)|=e^(lambda t)|Theta(X)| would become unbounded on that compact disk. It must cross Sigma, where the temperature would be nonzero, a contradiction.

Finally scale the absolutely convergent subtracted inverse. The improved bound |Omega(X)|<=C(1+r)^(-delta) and the continuous angular limit A provide an integrable dominator for the scaled kernel at zero, infinity and the target. Uniformity follows by first removing uniformly small neighborhoods of these regions and then using uniform convergence on the remaining compact set. This proves the third limit in (1). If psi is the unique periodic solution of

    -(psi''+(2-delta)^2 psi)=A,

then V_r=-psi' and V_phi=(2-delta)psi. Invertibility holds because 2-delta lies strictly between 3/2 and 2, so it is not an integer Fourier frequency. This leading inverse formula does not assert a next-order expansion.

##### Part 4. A finite-annulus argument excluding integrable vorticity

On D={1<|X|<2}, set

    T_R(X)=R^(-gamma)Theta(RX),
    Z_R(X)=R^(2 delta)Omega(RX),
    W_R(X)=beta X+U(RX)/R.

The exact scaled vorticity equation is W_R.grad Z_R+Z_R=partial_x T_R, since 1-gamma=2 delta. Also div W_R=2 beta. For every smooth eta compactly supported in D, integration by parts on this fixed bounded set gives

    integral_D T_R eta_x
       =integral_D Z_R[W_R.grad eta+(2 beta-1)eta].         (6)

There is no integration by parts at physical infinity. The left side tends to integral_D T_infinity eta_x, where

    T_infinity(X)=|X|^gamma F(arg X).

For some eta this limit is nonzero. Otherwise partial_x T_infinity=0 distributionally, hence classically since T_infinity is C1 on D. Its angular equation is

    gamma cos(phi)F(phi)-sin(phi)F'(phi)=0.

On the upper semicircle its solutions are F(phi)=C_+ sin(phi)^gamma; on the lower semicircle they are C_- |sin(phi)|^gamma. Since 0<gamma<1, C1 regularity at the x-axis forces both constants to vanish. This contradicts F!=0. Thus fix eta with nonzero limit in (6).

W_R converges uniformly to beta X, so the coefficient on the right side of (6) is bounded in every finite Lq(D), including q=infinity. For each p>=1, Holder's inequality yields ||Z_R||_Lp(D)>=c_p>0, with c_p depending on the fixed test function and p, for all sufficiently large R. Consequently

    integral_{R<|X|<2R}|Omega|^p >= c_p R^(2-2p/beta).    (7)

For p=2 this is (3). For 1<=p<beta the bound grows with R, and for p=beta it stays bounded below on every disjoint dyadic annulus. Either case excludes a finite global Lp integral. Smoothness and the decay bound make Omega globally bounded. For 0<p<1, this boundedness and the inequality |Omega|<=||Omega||_infinity^(1-p)|Omega|^p show that a finite Lp integral would imply a finite L1 integral, already excluded.

Uniform Omega=o(r^(-2/beta)) would make Z_R tend uniformly to zero on D and contradict (6). This proves all the stated conclusions.

##### Dependencies, limitations and next coefficients

The proof uses only the stated smooth equations, parity, nondegenerate jet, sublinearity and additional hypotheses (H), plus the displayed kernel estimate and standard complete-flow calculus. In particular it does not use the origin being the only equilibrium, a global origin basin, or any sign of vorticity.

The power bound (H) does not follow merely from smooth sublinear velocity and a convergent strain tail. The general class of sublinear velocities in Section 2.3 is broader. We do not claim Omega is C1 in limiting angle from the assumptions above. The present proof establishes only the leading limits and integrability obstruction.

#### A.12.3 Regularity of the limits and the first temperature correction

##### Statement and hypotheses

Assume a smooth A1 profile on R^2 with beta>2, W=beta X+U, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x)=o(r) uniformly, Omega=-Delta Psi, Theta even in x and odd in y, Omega and Psi odd in both variables, Theta_y(0)=a0!=0, and the exact coupled equations (P). Assume polynomial Omega and grad Omega bounds, as in class A'. The power-decay bootstrap (Section A.12.1) and far theorem (Section A.12.2) then apply. Set

    delta=1/beta, gamma=1-2 delta, 0<delta<1/2.

Their limits are F in C1(S1), A in C0(S1), and V in C1(S1), with

    r^-gamma Theta -> F,
    r^(2 delta)grad Theta -> G=gamma F e_r+F' e_phi,
    r^delta Omega -> A,
    r^(-(1-delta))U -> V,                               (1)

uniformly in angle. F is nonzero. The scalar velocity potential H is the unique periodic solution of

    -(H''+(2-delta)^2 H)=A,
    V_r=-H', V_phi=(2-delta)H.

The C1 regularity of V here follows directly from this scalar ODE with continuous A; it is regularity of the limit, not convergence of DU.

The following conclusions hold.

1. If |grad Omega|<=C(1+r)^m with m>=0, then A belongs to C^(0,eta) for eta=1/[beta(m+1)+2]. Higher angular smoothness is not asserted.

2. The first temperature correction is rigorous in C0(angle):

    r^-gamma Theta=F+r^-delta F1+o(r^-delta),
    F1=gamma V_r F+V_phi F'.                            (2)

No angular differentiation of this remainder is claimed. In branch (ii), V=0 and F1=0, so this assertion gives only an o(r^-delta) remainder; it does not supply the next nonzero temperature coefficient there.

##### Part 1. Regularity and the nonzero vertical-axis limit

For a large outgoing circle Sigma, the far theorem provides uniform relations

    r(Phi_t Z) comparable to e^(beta t),
    e^(-beta t)D Phi_t(Z) -> M_infinity(Z),
    e^(-beta t)Phi_t Z -> a(Z), rho=|a|>0,

where the derivative convergence is uniform on Sigma. Thus a and rho are C1, and Z -> arg a(Z) is a C1 diffeomorphism. The coefficient identity is A(arg a(Z))=rho(Z)^delta b(Z). The theorem also proves

    e^t Omega(Phi_t Z) -> b(Z),
    sup_Z |e^t Omega(Phi_t Z)-b(Z)| <= C e^-t.           (4)

The final error bound follows from the exact forward integral and
|Theta_x(Phi_s Z)|<=Ce^-2s.

Parametrize Sigma smoothly. Differentiating the finite-time expression on the left of (4), the polynomial gradient bound and D Phi_t=O(e^(beta t)) give a Lipschitz constant at most

    C exp([1+beta(m+1)]t).

For two labels at distance d<=1, compare both limiting values to the finite-time expression, obtaining

    |b(Z)-b(Z')| <= C[e^-t+d exp([1+beta(m+1)]t)].

Choose t=log(1/d)/[2+beta(m+1)]. Both terms are bounded by C d^eta. Smoothness on the compact circle covers d>=1. Multiplication by rho^delta and composition with the C1 angular diffeomorphism preserve this exponent, so A is Holder as stated.

The positive y-axis is invariant, and its rescaled vertical speed is strictly positive for every y>0 by the axis theorem (Theorem 1(b), Section A.2). Starting from a small positive y, the trajectory reaches Sigma in finite time; otherwise its radius would remain bounded and temperature, which grows as e^((beta-2)t), would be unbounded on a compact set. Temperature on this trajectory has the sign of a0 and is nonzero. Its limiting direction is the positive y-axis and rho>0. Thus

    F(pi/2) has the sign of a0 and is nonzero.           (5)

This also proves F!=0 without assuming a global origin basin.

The full gradient convergence in (1) follows from angular C1 convergence together with the exact radial temperature equation, as proved in Section A.12.4. In particular no derivative of A is used.

##### Part 2. Integration of the radial temperature equation

Let f(r,phi)=r^-gamma Theta(r,phi). The exact equation is

    beta r f_r=-r^-gamma U.grad Theta.

By (1), the right side is -r^-delta[Q(phi)+o(1)] uniformly, where Q=gamma V_r F+V_phi F'. Since f tends uniformly to F, integrate from r to infinity:

    f(r,phi)-F(phi)
       =(1/beta) integral_r^infinity s^(-delta-1)
                                         [Q(phi)+o(1)]ds.

The uniform error is bounded in absolute value by
sup_{s>=r,phi}|o(1)| times r^-delta/(beta delta), which is o(r^-delta). Since beta delta=1, (2) follows. No prescribed convergence rate beyond the uniform limit is needed.

#### A.12.4 Convergence of the temperature gradient

The far theorem of Section A.12.2 under its hypothesis (H), which holds by Section A.12.1, gives, uniformly in angle as R tends to infinity,

    R^-gamma Theta(R,phi)->F(phi) in C1(phi),
    R^delta Omega(R,phi)->A(phi),
    R^(-(1-delta))U(R,phi)->V(phi).

For the temperature gradient, angular differentiation already gives
R^(-gamma)Theta_phi -> F'. The radial part follows from the exact transport equation:

    beta R Theta_R=(beta-2)Theta-U.grad Theta.

The bounds U=O(R^(1-delta)), grad Theta=O(R^-2 delta) imply
R^-gamma U.grad Theta=O(R^-delta), since gamma=1-2 delta. Therefore

    R^(1-gamma)Theta_R -> gamma F.

Together the radial and angular limits give
R^(1-gamma)grad Theta -> gamma F e_r+F' e_phi.

### A.13 Proposition 13 (one-signed horizontal temperature derivative)

Report statement: see Proposition 13 in Section 3.

Proof.

The hypotheses and the reconstruction formula (1) are those of Section A.10.

#### Signs and finite Lp vorticity

If Theta_x>=0 on Q1, (1) implies Omega>=0 there. The R6 sign theorem (Proposition 6, Section A.7) excludes this. Thus Theta_x cannot be everywhere nonnegative on Q1.

Suppose instead Theta_x<=0, and put f=-Omega>=0, h=-Theta_x>=0. The equation along the forward flow gives

    f(Phi_t X)=e^-t f(X)+integral_0^t e^(s-t)h(Phi_s X)ds
             >=e^-t f(X), t>=0.                           (2)

The quadrant is invariant under the complete flow and its Jacobian is e^(2 beta t). If 0<M=integral_Q1 f^p<infinity, then

    M=e^(2 beta t)integral_Q1 f(Phi_t X)^p dX
      >=e^((2 beta-p)t)M.

For 0<p<2 beta this is impossible. At p=2 beta, equality of the finite integrals forces equality in (2) for almost every X, because raising nonnegative numbers to the positive power p is strictly increasing. If h were positive at any point, continuity and short-time flow dependence would make its integral in (2) strictly positive on a nonempty open set, contradicting that equality. Hence h=0 and (1) gives f=0. Parity then gives Omega=0 on all of R^2. Both components of U are harmonic and sublinear, hence constant by the harmonic Liouville theorem; parity makes the constant zero, contradicting c=-2. The case M=0 is excluded in the same way. Therefore one-signed Theta_x is incompatible with Omega in Lp(Q1) for any 0<p<=2 beta. No integration by parts at infinity or differentiation of f^p is used.

### A.14 Theorem 12 (far-field dichotomy; velocity growth)

Report statement: see Theorem 12 in Section 3.

Proof.

The hypotheses, the notation and equations (1), (2), (4) and (5) are those of Section A.12.3, which also contains parts 1 and 2 of the argument. Items 3 and 4 of the statement there are as follows. The kinetic energy statement uses the physical reconstruction of Section A.14.2.

#### A.14.1 Far-field dichotomy and velocity growth

3. Exactly one of the following alternatives occurs.

    (i) A is nonzero; V is nonzero and
        U=r^(1-delta)[V+o(1)].

    (ii) A is identically zero; putting
        B=-(gamma cos(phi)F-sin(phi)F'),
        B is continuous, nonzero, and
        Omega=r^(-2 delta)[B+o(1)],
        U=r^(1-2 delta)[V2+o(1)],                         (3)

    uniformly in angle. Here V2 is nonzero and comes from
        -(H2''+(2-2 delta)^2 H2)=B,
        V2_r=-H2', V2_phi=(2-2 delta)H2.

Thus the velocity is necessarily unbounded and has infinite kinetic energy in either branch. More precisely, for h=1-delta in (i) or h=1-2 delta in (ii), and every 0<p<infinity,

    integral_{R<|X|<2R}|U|^p >= c_p R^(2+hp)

for all large R. In particular U belongs to no finite global Lp space, and the exact physical reconstruction has infinite kinetic energy at every t<T.

4. In branch (ii), Theta_x takes both signs on the open first quadrant. If a0>0, Omega also takes both signs there. The proof uses the global characteristic identity and, for the first assertion, the one-sign Lp obstruction of Proposition 13 (Section A.13).

##### Part 3. The branch with vanishing leading vorticity

Suppose A=0, equivalently b=0 on Sigma. The exact forward vorticity integral now gives an integral from the observation time to infinity:

    Omega(Phi_t Z)=-e^-t integral_t^infinity
                                      e^s Theta_x(Phi_s Z)ds. (6)

This follows by subtracting the finite-time integral from its limit b=0. The integral is absolutely convergent because Theta_x=O(e^-2s) there. Thus (6) does not estimate or discard U.grad Omega, and it uses no bound on derivatives of Omega beyond those already used for the far theorem.

By the full gradient limit and r(Phi_s Z)e^-beta s -> rho(Z),

    e^(2s)Theta_x(Phi_s Z)
       -> C(Z)=rho(Z)^(-2 delta) G_x(arg a(Z))

uniformly on Sigma. If e(s,Z) denotes the uniform o(1) error, then

    integral_t^infinity e^s Theta_x(Phi_s Z)ds
       =e^-t[C(Z)+epsilon(t,Z)],
    |epsilon(t,Z)|<=sup_{s>=t,Z}|e(s,Z)| ->0.

Multiplying (6) by e^(2t) proves uniform convergence to -C(Z). Outgoing trajectories from Sigma cover the far exterior, and their flight times tend uniformly to infinity as radius tends to infinity. Their angular maps and inverses converge uniformly; multiplying by r^(2 delta)e^-2t ->rho^(2 delta) cancels the rho factor. This gives exactly

    r^(2 delta)Omega(r,phi)->-G_x(phi)=B(phi).

There is no need for a quantitative rate in the gradient limit: the exponential integration kernel gives the displayed uniform remainder directly.

B cannot vanish identically. If it did, the C1 homogeneous function r^gamma F would have zero x derivative. Equivalently on the upper semicircle,

    F'=gamma cot(phi)F,

so F=C_+ sin(phi)^gamma. On the lower semicircle F=C_-|sin(phi)|^gamma. Since 0<gamma<1, C1 regularity at the x-axis forces C_+=C_-=0. This contradicts (5).

##### Part 4. The inverse limit and lower bounds on velocity

We spell out the inverse argument for either exponent a=delta in branch (i) or a=2 delta in branch (ii). In each case 0<a<1, Omega=O((1+r)^-a), and r^a Omega tends uniformly to a continuous angular coefficient C_a. For branch (i) C_a=A!=0; for branch (ii) C_a=B!=0. Positive power decay makes the subtracted inverse absolutely convergent:

    U(X)=integral [K(X-Y)-K(-Y)]Omega(Y)dY,
    K(Z)=(Z2,-Z1)/(2 pi|Z|^2).

The difference from the prescribed sublinear velocity is harmonic and constant, and parity fixes that constant to zero. Rescaling Y=RZ gives

    R^(-(1-a))U(RX)
       =integral [K(X-Z)-K(-Z)] R^a Omega(RZ)dZ.         (7)

The bound |R^a Omega(RZ)|<=C|Z|^-a holds for all Z!=0 and R>=1. For X on a fixed compact annulus, the kernel difference times this bound is integrable at Z=0 since a<1, at Z=X since K is locally integrable, and at infinity since the kernel difference is O(|Z|^-2) and a>0. Remove small disks around both singularities and a large exterior region; their integrals are uniformly small in X. On the remaining compact set, the vorticity convergence is uniform. This proves uniform convergence in (7).

The limiting velocity is the homogeneous inverse of r^-a C_a. Let d=2-a in (1,2). The unique periodic solution of

    -(H_a''+d^2 H_a)=C_a

exists because d is not an integer frequency. It is C2 when C_a is continuous, and inherits odd-odd parity. Its rotated gradient is the homogeneous vector

    r^(1-a)[-H_a' e_r+d H_a e_phi].

This is the same limit as (7). Both fields have zero divergence and curl -r^-a C_a in distributions on all of R^2. For the explicit homogeneous field this holds across the origin because the boundary term on a circle of radius epsilon is O(epsilon^(2-a)), tending to zero. For the integral it follows by the fundamental-solution identity, local integrability and the subtracted kernel. Their difference is therefore an entire distributionally harmonic vector field, hence smooth. It is homogeneous of degree 1-a in (0,1), whereas a nonzero smooth homogeneous function at the origin can only have a nonnegative integer degree. Thus the difference vanishes. If the angular vector were zero, its phi component d H_a would force H_a=0 and hence C_a=0. Therefore V and V2 are nonzero in their respective branches.

Continuity gives an angular interval E of positive length on which the corresponding limiting vector has norm at least 2c>0. Uniform convergence implies |U(r,phi)|>=c r^h for every phi in E and all r>=R0, with h=1-a>0. Integrating on R<r<2R proves the announced lower bound for every p>0, and also unboundedness. Physical scaling multiplies the positive infinite energy integral by the finite positive factor tau^(4 beta-2); the energy remains infinite for every t<T.

##### Part 5. Sign consequences in branch (ii)

The decay Omega=O(r^-2 delta) makes Omega belong to Lp(R2) for every p>beta. The global characteristic formula applies: parity makes Q invariant, at most linear growth gives complete flow, and every backward orbit stays in a compact ball; hence its exponentially weighted vorticity endpoint vanishes. The sign-class theorem of Section A.13 (Proposition 13) assumes exactly Theta_x<=0 on Q and the present smooth A1 equations with sublinear velocity. Its proof uses the nonnegative forward Duhamel formula and Jacobian e^(2 beta t), covering all 0<p<=2 beta, including the equality endpoint. Suppose Theta_x>=0 on Q. Its global characteristic formula gives Omega>=0 there, contrary to the established strain/sign obstruction c=-2 (Proposition 6). Suppose instead Theta_x<=0 on Q. Then Omega<=0 by the same characteristic formula, and the sign-class theorem of Section A.13 requires Omega to lie outside Lp(Q) for every p<=2 beta. Choose beta<p<=2 beta to contradict the decay integrability. Hence Theta_x has both signs. All sign assertions mean actual strict signs somewhere, since the fields are continuous and neither one-sign alternative is possible.

For a0>0, (5) gives F(pi/2)>0. On 0<phi<pi/2,

    B=sin(phi)^(gamma+1) d/dphi [F(phi)/sin(phi)^gamma].

Since F is C1 and F(0)=0, F(phi)/sin(phi)^gamma tends to zero as phi tends to zero. Its value at pi/2 is positive. The mean value theorem therefore makes its derivative positive somewhere in the open quadrant, so B>0 there. Uniform asymptotics make Omega>0 at sufficiently distant points of that angle. On the other hand the absolutely convergent strain identity (Section A.1.2)

    -2=(4/pi)integral_Q xy|X|^-4 Omega(X)dX

forces Omega<0 somewhere on Q. Thus Omega changes sign. No corresponding two-sign conclusion for Omega when a0<0 is asserted.

##### Dependencies and limits of this result

The outgoing maps and leading limits are from Section A.12.2; their hypotheses follow for A-prime from Section A.12.1. The global sign-class Lp obstruction is proved in Section A.13, and the strain formula in Section A.1.2. The radial gradient argument is also written in Section A.12.4. Equations (2), (3), their uniform remainders, the inverse lower bound and sign argument are fully proved here.

The dichotomy does not prove A!=0 and does not construct the A=0 branch. The general next vorticity coefficient involving A' remains unproved under these minimal hypotheses, since C1 regularity of A has not been established. Formal logarithmic and multipole expansions are separate questions. Infinite energy excludes a finite-energy subclass, not the broad class of sublinear velocities of Section 2.3.

#### A.14.2 Physical reconstruction

Equation labels (P) and (1) in this subsection are local to it.

Let beta>0 and let C-infinity fields Theta,Psi on R2 satisfy the exact A1 parity (Theta even in x and odd in y, Psi odd in both x and y), Theta_y(0)=a0!=0, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x)=o(|X|), Omega=-Delta Psi, and

    W=beta X+U,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
    W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta.                          (P)

The canonical inverse fixes the sublinear velocity and its parity. For every T and t<T put tau=T-t and X=z/tau^beta. Then

    omega(t,z)=tau^-1 Omega(X),
    theta(t,z)=tau^(beta-2) Theta(X),
    u(t,z)=tau^(beta-1) U(X),
    psi(t,z)=tau^(2 beta-1) Psi(X).                       (1)

These fields are a classical solution on R^2 of the original vorticity-temperature system, with complete physical flow on every compact time interval contained in (-infinity,T).

For any scalar f(t,z)=tau^a F(z/tau^beta), the chain rule, using d tau/dt=-1, gives

    partial_t f=tau^(a-1)[-a F+beta X.grad F],
    grad_z f=tau^(a-beta)grad F.

Applying this with a=-1 and a=beta-2 gives respectively

    omega_t+u.grad omega-theta_z1
       =tau^-2[W.grad Omega+Omega-Theta_x]=0,
    theta_t+u.grad theta
       =tau^(beta-3)[W.grad Theta-(beta-2)Theta]=0.

Moreover -Delta_z psi=tau^-1 Omega=omega and
(-psi_z2,psi_z1)=tau^(beta-1)U=u. Thus (1) solves exactly the required signs and domain.

Sublinear U has a global linear bound |U(X)|<=C(1+|X|). For t in any compact interval below T, the powers of tau are bounded above and below by finite positive constants, so |u(t,z)|<=C_I(1+|z|), uniformly in t. The smooth nonautonomous vector field has unique local trajectories. The linear growth bound and Gronwall prevent a trajectory escaping to infinity during a finite interval; the flow is therefore complete on every such interval. Smoothness gives the usual flow differentiation locally, and div u=0 gives physical Jacobian one. No uniform bound on all spatial derivatives is required for this completeness claim.

### A.15 Proposition 14 (weighted integral identities)

Report statement: see Proposition 14 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement, notation and hypotheses

Let beta>2 and let a smooth A1 profile on R^2 solve

    W=beta X+U, div U=0, U=o(r),
    W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
    U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x), -Delta Psi=Omega,

with Theta even in x and odd in y, Psi and Omega odd in both variables, and nonzero a0=Theta_y(0). In particular Theta(0)=0 and U(0)=0; smoothness then gives Theta=O(r), U=O(r) locally. Assume polynomial bounds on Omega and grad Omega, as in A-prime. Put delta=1/beta and gamma=1-2 delta. The full-class bootstrap and far theorem (Sections A.12.1 and A.12.2) give, uniformly in angle,

    Theta=r^gamma(F+o(1)), grad Theta=O(r^-2 delta),
    Omega=r^-delta(A+o(1)), U=O(r^(1-delta)),

where F is C1 and nonzero and A is continuous. No derivative of A is needed. Define

    k_star=2+2 gamma=4-4/beta,
    I_k=integral_R2 Theta^2 r^-k dX,
    J_k=integral_R2 Theta^2 (U.X) r^(-k-2) dX.

Then:

1. For k_star<k<4, both integrals are absolutely convergent and

    [beta(4-k)-4] I_k=k J_k.                          (1)

   In particular J_k<0: a0!=0 implies I_k>0, k>k_star implies beta(4-k)-4<0, and k>0.

2. At the lower endpoint k=k_star, J_k remains absolutely convergent, whereas I_k diverges. The exact surviving flux is

    beta integral_0^(2 pi) F(phi)^2 dphi=-k_star J_k_star. (2)

3. For every m>2 beta, the following integrals are absolutely convergent and satisfy

    (1-2 beta/m) integral_R2 |Omega|^m dX
      =integral_R2 Theta_x Omega |Omega|^(m-2) dX.     (3)

4. For m=2 beta the source integral remains absolutely convergent, and

    integral_R2 Theta_x Omega |Omega|^(2 beta-2) dX
      =(1/2) integral_0^(2 pi) |A(phi)|^(2 beta) dphi.   (4)

   This identity requires no finite integral of |Omega|^(2 beta). If A=0, its right side is zero. The dichotomy theorem (Theorem 12, Section A.14) then gives faster vorticity decay, but is not needed to prove (4).

#### Part 1. Weighted temperature divergence and integrability

For r>0 the smooth equations give the exact identity

    div(Theta^2 W r^-k)
      =[beta(4-k)-4] Theta^2 r^-k
         -k Theta^2 (U.X) r^(-k-2).                  (5)

Indeed div W=2 beta and 2 Theta W.grad Theta=2(beta-2)Theta^2. Differentiating r^-k gives -k r^(-k-2)X, whose beta X term is -k beta r^-k.

Near the origin, Theta=O(r), U=O(r), W=O(r). The absolute radial integrands for I_k and J_k are therefore O(r^(3-k)), and the flux on a circle of radius epsilon is O(epsilon^(4-k)). Thus both local integrals converge and that flux vanishes whenever k<4.

At infinity the I_k radial integrand is O(r^(2 gamma+1-k)); this is integrable if k>k_star. The J_k radial integrand is O(r^(2 gamma+1-delta-k)), which is integrable whenever k>k_star-delta, including k=k_star. The outer flux is

    integral_0^(2 pi) Theta(R,phi)^2
                        [beta R+U_r(R,phi)] R^(1-k) dphi.

For k>k_star it is O(R^(k_star-k)) and vanishes. Integrating (5) on epsilon<r<R and taking both limits proves (1).

At k=k_star the coefficient of I_k in (5) is identically zero, so no divergent integral is formed. Uniform far convergence and U_r/R->0 make the outer flux tend to beta integral F^2. The inner flux still vanishes and J_k is absolutely integrable. This proves (2). Finally F!=0, so for sufficiently large R the angular integral of Theta(R,phi)^2 is at least c R^(2 gamma), and the radial integral for I_k_star is bounded below by c integral dR/R. Hence I_k_star actually diverges.

#### Part 2. Vorticity moments, including the critical exponent

For m>=2 beta>4, the function |Omega|^m is continuously differentiable even at Omega=0, and

    div(W |Omega|^m/m)+(1-2 beta/m)|Omega|^m
       =Theta_x Omega |Omega|^(m-2).                 (6)

This uses only the first derivative chain rule. At infinity the absolute radial integrand of |Omega|^m is O(r^(1-m delta)), so it is integrable for m>2 beta. The absolute source integrand is O(r^(1-(m+1)delta)), so it is integrable already for m>2 beta-1, in particular throughout the claimed range. Smoothness handles finite radii.

The boundary term obtained by integrating (6) over B_R is

    (1/m) integral_0^(2 pi) [beta R+U_r(R,phi)]
                                      |Omega(R,phi)|^m R dphi.

For m>2 beta this is O(R^(2-m delta)) and tends to zero, proving (3).

For m=2 beta the volume coefficient in (6) vanishes exactly, and uniform vorticity convergence gives the flux limit

    (beta/m) integral |A|^m=(1/2) integral |A|^(2 beta).

The source integral converges absolutely, as already shown. This proves (4) without treating zero times an infinite volume integral as a number.

#### Dependencies and scope

The full-class tail bounds follow from Sections A.12.1 and A.12.2. All integration-by-parts limits used here are explicitly estimated above. Angular integrals are over the full circle. No positivity of Omega or Theta_x, finite temperature norm, finite energy, origin-basin assumption or angular derivative of A is used. These identities constrain exact profiles; they are not by themselves contradictions or an exponent-selection theorem.

### A.16 Theorem 15 (smooth far field and second-order terms)

Report statement: see Theorem 15 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement, hypotheses and notation

Assume a smooth exact A1 profile in the coupled class A-prime with beta>2: the parity and nonzero a0 of Section 2.2, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x)=o(r) uniformly, Omega=-Delta Psi, polynomial bounds on Omega and grad Omega, and the full stationary equations. Put delta=1/beta in (0,1/2), gamma=1-2 delta, d=2-delta. Previous complete proofs give

    |Omega|<=C(1+r)^(-delta), |grad Theta|<=C(1+r)^(-2 delta),
    |U|<=Cr(1+r)^(-delta), |Theta|<=Cr(1+r)^(-2 delta),
    |DU|<=C(1+r)^(-delta) log(2+r).

The bounds for U and Theta near zero use smoothness and parity: U(0)=0 and Theta(0)=0. Oddness of Omega in both variables gives grad Omega(0)=0, also used below. They also give uniform angular limits F,A,V of r^-gamma Theta, r^delta Omega, r^(-1+delta)U. Here F is initially C1, A Holder, and V the canonical homogeneous inverse of A. These hypotheses are consequences of Sections A.12 and A.14.

Then F,A,V are C-infinity in angle. For every integer k>=0,

    |D^k Omega(X)|<=C_k r^(-delta-k),
    |D^k Theta(X)|<=C_k r^(gamma-k),
    |D^k U(X)|<=C_k r^(1-delta-k)                     (1)

for r>=1. The angular and annular rescaled limits hold in every finite Ck norm.

Moreover the first two vorticity and velocity terms satisfy, in every finite angular Ck norm,

    Omega = r^-delta A + r^(-2 delta) B + o(r^(-2 delta)),
    U = r^(1-delta) V + r^(1-2 delta) V2 + o(r^(1-2 delta)),  (2)

where

    B = -delta V_r A + V_phi A' - gamma cos(phi)F + sin(phi)F',
    V2=-H2' e_r+(2-2 delta)H2 e_phi,
    -H2''-(2-2 delta)^2 H2=B.

The first temperature correction also holds in every finite angular Ck norm:

    Theta=r^gamma[F+r^-delta F1+o(r^-delta)],
    F1=gamma V_r F+V_phi F'.                          (3)

All remainders here are uniform in angle. No higher complete expansion, absence of logarithms, or smoothness in time through T is asserted.

#### Part 1. Uniform physical bounds and the inverse away from the singular point

Translate T to zero if desired, and put tau=T-t>0. Use the exact physical fields

    omega=tau^-1 Omega(z/tau^beta),
    theta=tau^(beta-2)Theta(z/tau^beta),
    u=tau^(beta-1)U(z/tau^beta), q=grad_z theta.

They solve

    D_t omega=q_1, D_t q=-(Du)^T q, div u=0,
    D_t=partial_t+u.grad, curl u=-omega.              (4)

For 0<tau<=1 and all z!=0, the profile bounds imply

    |u(t,z)|<=C |z|^(1-delta),
    |theta(t,z)|<=C |z|^gamma,
    |omega(t,z)|<=C |z|^-delta,
    |q(t,z)|<=C |z|^(-2 delta).                       (5)

For |z|>=tau^beta these are the far bounds. For |z|<=tau^beta, smoothness gives |u|<=C tau^-1 |z|, |theta|<=C tau^-2 |z|, |omega|<=C tau^-1 and |q|<=C tau^-2. The inequalities |z|^delta<=tau and |z|^(2 delta)<=tau^2 imply (5) also there. On each fixed compact annulus K, the derivative bound gives

    ||Du(t)||_(Linf(K))<=C_K(1+|log tau|).             (6)

This bound is integrable in time up to T. The physical velocity is the same canonical subtracted inverse of omega, by its homogeneity and parity.

We will use the following local elliptic fact. Let B be a fixed ball whose closure avoids zero and let chi0 be smooth, compactly supported away from zero, and identically one on a neighborhood of B. On B,

    Du = T(chi0 omega)+h,                             (7)

where T is the fixed matrix of order-zero Calderon-Zygmund operators for the divergence/curl system on R^2, including its possible local multiplication terms. Every spatial derivative of h is uniformly bounded for t<T close to T. Indeed h is the integral of derivatives of the Biot-Savart kernel against (1-chi0)omega. The target is separated from that support locally. Near the origin, |omega|<=Cr^-delta is integrable against the smooth target kernel since delta<2. At infinity, the kernel for D^m Du is O(r^(-2-m)), and integral_1^infinity r^(-2-m-delta)r dr is finite. No high derivative of distant omega is used. For the velocity itself the canonical subtraction makes the tail O(r^-2)omega; its origin subtraction is O(r^-1)omega, integrable since delta<1.

#### Part 2. A weighted local elliptic estimate

For 1<p<infinity, a smooth compactly supported multiplier phi, and f supported in a fixed compact set, an order-zero operator T as in (7) satisfies

    ||[phi,T]partial_j f||_Lp<=C_(phi,p)||f||_Lp.     (8)

The constants are uniform when finitely many derivatives of phi are uniformly bounded and the supports stay in fixed compact sets. Here [phi,T]g=phi Tg-T(phi g).

For completeness, write its principal-value kernel as (phi(x)-phi(y))K(x-y), with K smooth off zero, homogeneous of degree -2 and of zero circular mean. Integration by parts once in y moves partial_j off f. Terms with a derivative on phi give T((partial_j phi)f), bounded on Lp. For the derivative of K, split |x-y|<1 and its complement. In the first region expand

    phi(x)-phi(x-h)=grad phi(x).h+O(|h|^2).

The remainder times D K is O(|h|^-1), hence an integrable kernel, with bounds for its transpose as well. The principal kernels h_l partial_j K(h), of degree -2, have zero circular mean: integrate partial_j(h_l K) on an annulus; the outer and inner fluxes agree by homogeneity, and the remaining delta_(jl)K term has zero mean. They are therefore classical smooth Calderon-Zygmund kernels and bounded on Lp. Integration across a small deleted disk can also give a bounded multiplication term proportional to grad phi(x)f(x); this is included in (8). On bounded x and |h|>=1 all terms are integrable. Outside a fixed large ball, phi(x)=0 and integration by parts leaves kernels O(|x|^-2) times f and bounded derivatives of phi; these are in Lp for p>1 and bounded by ||f||_Lp on its fixed support. Local multiplication parts of T commute with phi. This proves (8), using only the usual Lp theorem for smooth mean-zero homogeneous singular integral kernels.

Apply (8) with f a derivative of order m-1 of chi0 omega, and use (7). If phi is supported where chi0=1, then for each integer m>=1,

    ||phi D^m Du||_Lp
       <=C ||phi D^m omega||_Lp
          +C ||omega||_(W^(m-1,p)(supp chi0))+C.       (9)

Here and below sums over all derivatives of the indicated order are understood. The first term follows from T(phi D^m(chi0 omega)); the commutator follows from (8). Derivatives of chi0 are supported away from phi and involve only lower derivatives in the commutator norm. The last constant is the distant term in (7). This estimate localizes the highest vorticity derivative without assuming any high derivative bound outside the larger compact set.

#### Part 3. Local derivative induction without nested top-order losses

We prove, simultaneously for every finite p>2, every integer m>=0, and every compact K away from zero,
