    sup_(t0<=t<T) (||omega(t)||_(W^(m,p)(K))
                       +||q(t)||_(W^(m,p)(K)))<infinity,  (10)

for some t0<T; earlier compact time intervals are already smooth. The case m=0 is (5).

For the induction step fix a ball B_R(z0) whose closure avoids zero, and suppose (10) for order m-1 on a slightly larger compact set and for every finite exponent. Take chi0 equal to one on B_R and supported in that larger set. Let M be a uniform bound for |u| on B_R, and choose t0 sufficiently close to T that M(T-t0)<R/8. Let chi be a smooth nonincreasing function equal to one on (-infinity,1/4] and zero on [1/2,infinity), and put

    phi(t,z)=chi((|z-z0|+M(t-t0))/R).

This is smooth: chi is constant near z0 throughout the chosen time interval. It is supported in B_(R/2), equals one on B_(R/8), has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order, and

    D_t phi<=0,                                    (11)

since the argument has material derivative (M+u.grad|z-z0|)/R>=0. Thus cutoff flux is favorable.

Differentiate (4) m times, then take the weighted Lp energy with weight phi^p. By incompressibility and (11), the differentiated transport produces no positive cutoff contribution. For each component this is justified first for the integral of phi^p |f|^p, using a smooth approximation at f=0, and then by a limit. Passing from this pth-power energy to its norm uses division by p times the (p-1)st norm power where positive, or an epsilon regularization followed by a limit where zero. The resulting norm inequality is understood in its integral form. The terms with exactly one derivative on u are bounded by C||Du||_Linf(B_R) times the weighted top-order norm. In the omega equation the differentiated source is D^m q_1. In the q equation the other highest-order term is (D^m Du)^T q; by (5) and (9), its weighted Lp norm is bounded by

    C||phi D^m omega||_Lp+C.

Every remaining product involves only derivatives of omega and q of order at most m-1. More explicitly, in the transport commutator, terms with j>=2 derivatives on u have derivatives D^j u and D^(m-j+1)omega or D^(m-j+1)q; j<=m, so the elliptic derivative count for u is at most m-1 on omega. In D^m((Du)^Tq), the mixed terms have D^j Du and D^(m-j)q with 1<=j<=m-1, also within the preceding induction order. Each factor is uniformly bounded in L^(2p) on the larger compact set by the induction hypothesis and the local elliptic estimate without weights. Holder's inequality bounds their product in Lp uniformly. This use of all finite p at the preceding order avoids an unproved L-infinity estimate for its top derivative. At m=1 these mixed products do not occur.

Let E_m,p be the sum of the weighted Lp norms of D^m omega and D^m q. The preceding estimates give

    d E_m,p/dt <=C(1+||Du||_Linf(B_R))(1+E_m,p).       (12)

The constants may depend on previously bounded lower derivatives but not on t near T. The right-hand coefficient is integrable by (6), and E_m,p(t0) is finite by smoothness at a time before T. Gronwall proves (10) on B_(R/8). Covering any target compact set by finitely many such smaller balls and choosing the latest of their finitely many initial times t0 proves the induction. The larger compact sets only enter lower-order estimates, so there is no unresolved nested estimate at the same derivative order.

Local elliptic estimates from (7), the uniform bound for u, and q=grad theta now give uniform W^(m,p) bounds for u and theta as well, for all finite m,p. Sobolev embedding yields uniform spatial Ck bounds of every finite order on compact annuli.

#### Part 4. Terminal smoothness and symbol bounds

The far-field theorem of Section A.12 gives uniform limits on every physical annulus:

    omega(t,z)->omega0(z)=r^-delta A(phi),
    theta(t,z)->theta0(z)=r^gamma F(phi),
    u(t,z)->u0(z)=r^(1-delta)V(phi).                  (13)

Uniform spatial bounds of every higher order upgrade these convergences to Ck on each smaller compact set, for every finite k. One justification is compact embedding on nested compact sets followed by uniqueness of the known uniform limit; every subsequence has the same Ck limit. Therefore these terminal fields are C-infinity away from zero, and F,A,V are smooth angular functions.

Fix a unit physical annulus and set tau=r^-delta, so tau^beta=r^-1. The identities for kth physical derivatives read

    D^k omega(t,z)=tau^(-1-beta k)(D^k Omega)(rz),
    D^k theta(t,z)=tau^(beta-2-beta k)(D^k Theta)(rz),
    D^k u(t,z)=tau^(beta-1-beta k)(D^k U)(rz).

Their uniform local bounds prove (1), and their Ck limits prove the corresponding smooth annular rescaled convergence. No time differentiability through the singular point is used.

#### Part 5. First time derivative and the next far coefficients

By (4) and the Ck convergence in (13), on every compact annulus,

    partial_t omega -> -u0.grad omega0+partial_x theta0,
    partial_t theta -> -u0.grad theta0

in every finite spatial Ck norm. Integrate from t=T-tau to T. The resulting one-sided first-order expansion gives

    omega(t,z)=omega0(z)+tau[u0.grad omega0-partial_x theta0]+o(tau),
    theta(t,z)=theta0(z)+tau[u0.grad theta0]+o(tau),     (14)

in every such norm. Direct polar differentiation shows

    u0.grad omega0-partial_x theta0=r^(-2 delta)B(phi),
    u0.grad theta0=r^(gamma-delta)F1(phi),

with the coefficients stated above. Substituting r_profile=tau^-beta at unit physical radius gives the vorticity part of (2) and (3).

For the velocity coefficient, one must also control the nonlocal origin and tail before interchanging this first time difference with the inverse. Equation (1) at k=1 and smoothness at the profile origin give globally, for z!=0,

    |grad omega(t,z)|<=C |z|^(-1-delta).

Inside |z|<=tau^beta, odd-odd parity gives |grad Omega(X)|<=C|X|, so tau^(-1-beta)|grad Omega(z/tau^beta)|<=C tau^(-1-2 beta)|z|<=C|z|^(-1-delta). Outside, (1) applies. Equations (4) and (5) therefore yield

    |partial_t omega(t,z)|<=C |z|^(-2 delta),
    |(omega(t,z)-omega0(z))/tau|<=C |z|^(-2 delta).     (15)

The latter follows by integrating the first bound to T using (13). The first difference converges to r^(-2 delta)B by (14). In the canonical inverse

    K(z)=(z2,-z1)/(2 pi |z|^2),
    u(X)=integral [K(X-Y)-K(-Y)]omega(Y)dY,

the majorant in (15) is integrable near Y=0 against the subtracted kernel because 2 delta<1, near Y=X because K is locally integrable and the majorant is bounded there, and at infinity because the kernel difference is O(|Y|^-2) and 2 delta>0. Dominated convergence thus gives

    (u(t,z)-u0(z))/tau -> inverse[r^(-2 delta)B](z).

Uniform convergence on compact annuli follows by uniformly controlling a small disk about each target and then using the continuous kernel on its complement. For derivatives, split with a cutoff equal to one near the target compact set. The local vorticity differences converge in every Ck norm by (14); the local singular-integral map gives convergence in arbitrarily high finite W^(k,p) norms, and Sobolev embedding gives convergence of velocity derivatives there. No boundedness of an order-zero singular integral on Ck alone is asserted. The distant differentiated kernels have the same integrable majorant from (15). Thus the velocity limit holds in every finite Ck norm locally. The inverse is homogeneous by scaling the subtracted integral. The stated field V2 has the same divergence and curl distributionally on all of R^2: boundary terms at a small circle vanish since 2 delta<1. Their difference is an entire harmonic vector field of noninteger homogeneous degree 1-2 delta, and hence vanishes. The angular equation has a unique periodic solution because 2-2 delta lies strictly between 1 and 2 and is not an integer. This proves the rest of (2).

#### Dependencies and limitations

The only standard functional-analytic ingredients are Lp boundedness of smooth mean-zero homogeneous Calderon-Zygmund kernels for 1<p<infinity, Holder's inequality, Sobolev embedding on nested bounded sets, and Gronwall. The localized commutator estimate is proved above, and every distant inverse term is bounded using only the explicit pointwise majorants (5) and (15). The prior full A-prime decay bootstrap and canonical inverse are essential dependencies. No global finite-energy or bounded-temperature assumption is made. No statement about higher time derivatives, a full asymptotic series, or an actual solution beyond T follows from this proof.

### A.17 Theorem 16 (finite far expansion)

Report statement: see Theorem 16 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement

Assume the same full smooth coupled A-prime hypotheses as in Theorem 15 (Section A.16). Put delta=1/beta in (0,1/2), gamma=1-2 delta. Let N be any nonnegative integer with

    N < 4 beta - 1.                                  (1)

Then there are smooth angular functions A_j,F_j,V_j such that, in every finite angular Ck norm,

    Omega(r,phi)=r^-delta sum_(j=0)^(N+1) r^(-j delta) A_j(phi)
                      +o(r^(-(N+2)delta)),
    Theta(r,phi)=r^gamma sum_(j=0)^(N+1) r^(-j delta) F_j(phi)
                      +o(r^(gamma-(N+1)delta)),
    U(r,phi)=r^(1-delta) sum_(j=0)^N r^(-j delta) V_j(phi)
                      +o(r^(1-(N+1)delta)).          (2)

The leading functions are the previously proved A,F,V. For 0<=j<=N, put a_j=(j+1)delta, d_j=2-a_j. On the odd-odd angular parity class,

    -H_j''-d_j^2 H_j=A_j,
    V_(j,r)=-H_j', V_(j,phi)=d_j H_j.                (3)

This equation is uniquely invertible because 0<a_j<4, hence |d_j|<2, while the odd-odd stream modes are sin(2n phi), n>=1. Even when d_j=0 or +/-1 there is no kernel in this parity class.

For 0<=j<=N the coefficients obey

    (j+1)A_(j+1)
      =sum_(k+l=j)[-a_l V_(k,r) A_l+V_(k,phi)A_l']
                  -(gamma-j delta) cos(phi)F_j+sin(phi)F_j',

    (j+1)F_(j+1)
      =sum_(k+l=j)[(gamma-l delta)V_(k,r)F_l+V_(k,phi)F_l']. (4)

The inverse (3) is not asserted for A_(N+1) when (N+2)delta>=4. At beta=3 one may take N=10, proving pure-power expansions through j=10 for velocity and through j=11 for vorticity and temperature. This does not exclude a logarithmic or independent interior-moment contribution beginning at j=11 for velocity and j=12 for the transported fields. No complete expansion beyond (1) is claimed.

#### Part 1. The quadrant-folded kernel and its larger origin range

For Y=(y1,y2) in the open first quadrant Q, write Y_epsilon=(epsilon1 y1,epsilon2 y2), and set

    K(Z)=(Z2,-Z1)/(2 pi |Z|^2),
    K_Q(X,Y)=sum_(epsilon1,epsilon2=+/-1)
                            epsilon1 epsilon2 K(X-Y_epsilon).

If f is odd in both Cartesian coordinates, define

    B_Q f(X)=integral_Q K_Q(X,Y) f(Y)dY, X!=0.         (5)

For smooth decaying f in the original class this equals the canonical subtracted Biot-Savart inverse. Indeed the quadrant sum of epsilon1 epsilon2 K(-Y_epsilon) vanishes identically, component by component, so the canonical subtraction drops out after folding. This exact cancellation also permits additional singular behavior at the origin for other functions f in (5).

Suppose

    |f(Y)|<=C|Y|^-a, 0<a<4.                          (6)

For fixed X!=0, (5) is absolutely convergent as a folded integral. For |Y|<|X|/2, its constant and linear Taylor terms in Y cancel, leaving

    |D_X^k K_Q(X,Y)|<=C_k |Y|^2 |X|^(-3-k).

Thus the origin integral is bounded by a constant times integral_0^1 r^(3-a)dr. For |Y|>2|X|, K_Q(0,Y)=0 and the mean value theorem gives |K_Q(X,Y)|<=C|X||Y|^-2. The tail is bounded by integral_1^infinity r^(-1-a)dr. Near a target or its reflections, each individual velocity kernel is locally integrable and the bound on f is uniform. Rescaling Y=|X|Z proves

    |B_Q f(X)|<=C_a C |X|^(1-a).                     (7)

The constants in these estimates are uniform for X on the unit circle, including its axes. The possible target singularities are bounded separately by translated integrals of |Z|^-1 over fixed disks.

If, in addition, f is smooth away from zero and |D^k f(Y)|<=C_k |Y|^(-a-k) for every finite k, then

    |D^k B_Q f(X)|<=C'_k |X|^(1-a-k).                (8)

To prove this, rescale X to a fixed unit annulus, split the source with a cutoff equal to one on a larger target annulus, and use the usual local elliptic Lp estimates for the smooth source there. The remainder uses the differentiated folded kernel near zero, still O(|Y|^2), and its differentiated kernel at infinity, at least O(|Y|^-2). Derivatives on the local source are bounded uniformly on the rescaled annulus. Sobolev embedding supplies (8). Thus no derivative estimate is obtained by taking the absolute value of a nonintegrable target derivative kernel.

The same estimates prove local smooth convergence B_Q f_n -> B_Q f when f_n -> f in C-infinity on compact subsets away from zero, all f_n obey the same majorant (6), and their local derivatives converge. For the values use dominated convergence with small neighborhoods of targets controlled uniformly; for derivatives use the preceding local elliptic split and the integrable distant differentiated kernels.

The inverse in (5) is divergence-free off zero and has zero flux through each circle centered at zero. For the flux, first interchange the circle integral with the FOLDED integral (5). The folded origin/tail bounds justify this Fubini step; the logarithmic singularity from integrating a target kernel along the circle is integrable in the source variable. Only after this interchange, at each fixed Y, split the folded kernel into its four summands. Every individual Biot-Savart kernel then has zero radial flux through the circle, so the resulting flux is zero. Splitting before Fubini would not be justified for a>=2 and is not used. This excludes a possible radial source field proportional to X/|X|^2 in the homogeneous degree -1 case. Such a field would otherwise share the component parity and would not be excluded by divergence-free behavior only off zero.

#### Part 2. The homogeneous inverse for 0<a<4

If f=r^-a A(phi) has odd-odd parity, (5) is homogeneous of degree 1-a by changing variables. Its angular velocity components V_r,V_phi satisfy, off zero,

    (2-a)V_r+V_phi'=0,
    (2-a)V_phi-V_r'=-A.                              (9)

The inherited velocity parity makes V_r even under both angular reflections and V_phi odd under both. If d=2-a!=0, set H=V_phi/d. Equations (9) give V_r=-H' and -H''-d^2H=A, with H odd-odd. If d=0, the first equation makes V_phi constant; its odd reflection parity makes it zero. The second gives V_r'=A. The zero radial flux proved above makes V_r have mean zero. It is then the negative derivative of a unique odd-odd periodic H, which solves -H''=A. In either case H has only sin(2n phi) modes, and 4n^2-d^2>0 because |d|<2. This proves (3) including the potentially delicate a=2 case.

No locally integrable distributional vorticity at the origin is assumed when a>=2. The folded integral, local equations away from zero, parity and zero flux are the exact definitions and hypotheses used here. This is not the addition of a free harmonic field.

#### Part 3. Uniform physical derivative bounds and time differentiation

Let omega,theta,u be the exact physical fields with tau=T-t, and let q=grad theta. The scaling convention is

    omega(t,z)=tau^-1 Omega(z/tau^beta),
    theta(t,z)=tau^(beta-2) Theta(z/tau^beta),
    u(t,z)=tau^(beta-1) U(z/tau^beta).

At every finite time, omega is odd in both coordinates, theta is even in x and odd in y, and u has the component parity stated in Section 2.2. All time derivatives retain those parities. Their local terminal limits and the coefficients below therefore have the same parities. The spatial theorem gives for every k>=0 and all z!=0, uniformly for 0<tau<=1,

    |D^k omega|<=C_k r^(-delta-k),
    |D^k theta|<=C_k r^(gamma-k),
    |D^k u|<=C_k r^(1-delta-k).                       (10)

For r>=tau^beta this is its symbol estimate after scaling. For r<=tau^beta, smooth bounded derivatives of the profiles give (10) whenever the displayed exponent is negative. The only positive-exponent cases, k=0 for theta and u, follow from theta(t,0)=u(t,0)=0 and their local linear bounds. All constants are independent of tau.

Write f^[n]=partial_t^n f. We claim that whenever (n+1)delta<4,

    |D^k omega^[n]|<=C_(n,k) r^(-(n+1)delta-k),
    |D^k theta^[n]|<=C_(n,k) r^(gamma-n delta-k),
    |D^k u^[n]|<=C_(n,k) r^(1-(n+1)delta-k),
    u^[n]=B_Q(omega^[n]).                            (11)

All these estimates hold globally off zero, uniformly in tau, for every finite k. The case n=0 is (10) and canonical inversion.

Assume (11) through n. From the physical equations,

    omega^[n+1]=-sum_(j=0)^n binom(n,j)
                         u^[j].grad omega^[n-j]+partial_x theta^[n],
    theta^[n+1]=-sum_(j=0)^n binom(n,j)
                         u^[j].grad theta^[n-j].     (12)

Leibniz's rule at every spatial order and (11) bound the right sides by

    |D^k omega^[n+1]|<=C r^(-(n+2)delta-k),
    |D^k theta^[n+1]|<=C r^(gamma-(n+1)delta-k).

For example each velocity-vorticity product has exponent
1-(j+1)delta-1-(n-j+1)delta=-(n+2)delta; the differentiated temperature term has the same exponent. If (n+2)delta<4, the folded inverse (5)-(8) applies to omega^[n+1]. Differentiation under its folded integral is justified by the uniform majorant at both endpoints, first on compact time intervals and then uniformly up to T. It gives u^[n+1]=B_Q omega^[n+1] and the remaining bounds in (11). The velocity gauge is fixed by the original parity and the exact folded formula at every finite time. This proves the induction up to n=N. Formula (12) additionally bounds omega^[N+1] and theta^[N+1], even if their vorticity exponent has reached or crossed 4; we do not invert that extra derivative.

#### Part 4. One-sided terminal limits and finite Taylor series

At n=0, the spatial theorem already proves C-infinity local terminal limits of omega,theta,u away from zero. Suppose these limits have been established through n. Formula (12) then gives C-infinity local limits of omega^[n+1] and theta^[n+1] by products of lower time derivatives and their spatial derivatives. If n+1<=N, (11) supplies the uniform origin/tail majorant with exponent (n+2)delta<4. The convergence statement following (8) therefore gives the C-infinity local limit of u^[n+1]. This induction proves local one-sided C^N regularity in time for u, and C^(N+1) for omega and theta, all with values in every finite local spatial Ck space away from zero.

Taylor's theorem from the left, equivalently repeated integration of these continuous one-sided derivatives, gives

    omega(T-tau,z)=sum_(j=0)^(N+1) tau^j O_j(z)+o(tau^(N+1)),
    theta(T-tau,z)=sum_(j=0)^(N+1) tau^j T_j(z)+o(tau^(N+1)),
    u(T-tau,z)=sum_(j=0)^N tau^j U_j(z)+o(tau^N),      (13)

locally in every finite spatial Ck norm, where each coefficient is (-1)^j/j! times its terminal time derivative. The recursions from (12), or direct comparison of powers of tau in the equations, give

    (j+1)O_(j+1)=sum_(k+l=j) U_k.grad O_l-partial_x T_j,
    (j+1)T_(j+1)=sum_(k+l=j) U_k.grad T_l.             (14)

Here U_j=B_Q O_j for j<=N. Induction in (14), starting from the known homogeneous leading fields and using the homogeneous inverse in part 2, proves

    O_j=r^(-(j+1)delta) A_j(phi),
    T_j=r^(gamma-j delta) F_j(phi),
    U_j=r^(1-(j+1)delta) V_j(phi).

Polar differentiation of (14) is exactly (4). Substituting unit physical radius and tau=r_profile^-delta into (13) proves (2) with its Ck angular remainders.

#### Part 5. Threshold and scope

The first possible failure of absolute origin convergence in the folded inverse occurs at a=4, when its leading quadratic kernel term is integrated against r^-4. This is the same threshold d=2-a=-2 where the sin(2 phi) homogeneous Poisson inverse can resonate. A nonzero coefficient in that mode may require a logarithmic particular solution. A global interior contribution to the stream multipole r^-2 gives a physical velocity term of order tau^(4 beta-1). Neither the coefficient nor its nonvanishing is determined by the present theorem. A vanishing resonant projection could remove a logarithm; it cannot be assumed either way.

The recurrence contains no automatic exponent-selection equation before that threshold: F0 and A0 remain unknown smooth angular data subject to the full interior equations. The theorem proves an actual finite asymptotic expansion, not merely formal matching, but does not prove a full polyhomogeneous series, analyticity, a continuation through the physical singularity, or any profile's existence.

#### Dependencies

The spatial estimates and terminal limits are proved in Section A.16. Canonical inversion on R^2 and parity are defined in Section A.1. The larger origin range (0<a<4), its zero-flux clause and the finite time-derivative induction are proved here. Standard local singular-integral Lp estimates and Sobolev embedding are used only after localization to a compact annulus.

### A.18 Proposition 17 (centre jets)

Report statement: see Proposition 17 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and scope

Let beta>2. On a neighborhood of the origin consider smooth real functions Theta,Omega,Psi satisfying

    W=beta(x,y)+(-Psi_y,Psi_x),
    W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,  -Delta Psi=Omega.

Require Theta even in x and odd in y, and Omega,Psi odd in both variables, with Theta_y(0)=a0!=0 and Psi_xy(0)=-2. Write its Taylor coefficients without factorials as

    Theta = sum a_ij x^(2i) y^(2j+1),
    Psi   = sum h_ij x^(2i+1) y^(2j+1),
    Omega = sum g_ij x^(2i+1) y^(2j+1).

Here each equality means a finite Taylor expansion with its smooth remainder. Thus a_00=a0 and h_00=-2. Let C_(2n+2) be the coefficient of r^(2n+2) sin((2n+2)phi) in the homogeneous degree 2n+2 Taylor part of Psi.

For each n>=1, the equations determining the new blocks h_ij,a_ij with i+j=n, and g_ij with i+j=n-1, reduce to n adjacent linear relations among the n+1 new h-coefficients, followed by the one prescribed harmonic coefficient C_(2n+2). All other terms depend only on lower blocks. The adjacent relations never require division by zero for beta>2.

If

    a0 < 2(beta+2)(2 beta+1),                                      (1)

this square system is invertible at every order n. Consequently beta,a0 and the harmonic coefficients C_4,C_6,... and h_00=-2 uniquely determine all Taylor jets of a smooth local solution. Through block n the determined degrees are 2n+1 for Theta, 2n+2 for Psi and 2n for Omega, with the other parity coefficients zero. This is uniqueness of the formal jets, not uniqueness of a smooth solution from its jets and not an analyticity theorem.

For a solution on R^2 in the broad coupled class A-prime, the power-decay theorem of Section A.12.1 justifies

    C_m = (1/(2m)) int_0^infinity rho^(1-m) Omega_m(rho) d rho,
    Omega_m(r) = (1/pi) int_0^(2 pi) Omega(r,phi) sin(m phi) dphi,   (2)

for even m>=4. These are canonical inverse moments, not freely appended harmonic fields.

Without (1), a finite-order scalar coefficient described below may vanish. This does not itself rule out a profile; compatibility of the prescribed moment and lower jets must then be checked. At n=1 the exceptional amplitude is

    a0 = 4(beta+2)(2 beta+1).                                    (3)

At this amplitude one must have C_4=0. If C_4=0 the block-1 equations leave h_10 undetermined. This is a formal freedom at that finite order; its extension to higher compatible jets or smooth local solutions is not established. A global solution must still satisfy the global equations. No claims about all higher exceptional values are made.

#### Dependencies

Only the stationary equations, A1 parity, ordinary finite Taylor calculus and the modal Green formula on R^2 are used for the recurrence. Equation (2) additionally uses Section A.12.1 and the inverse uniqueness in Section A.1.

#### Derivation of every block equation

Put lambda_x=beta+2 and lambda_y=beta-2. Since h_00=-2, the linear part of W is (lambda_x x,lambda_y y). Poisson inversion at each coefficient gives

    g_ij = -(2i+3)(2i+2) h_(i+1,j)
           -(2j+3)(2j+2) h_(i,j+1).                           (4)

The temperature coefficient at x^(2i)y^(2j+1), for i+j=n>=1, is

    L_ij a_ij + (2i+1)a0 h_ij + P_ij = 0,
    L_ij = 2i lambda_x + 2j lambda_y,                         (5)

where the explicit lower-block expression is

    P_ij = sum {[-2u(2q+1)+(2p+1)(2v+1)] h_pq a_uv:
                 p+u=i, q+v=j, 1<=p+q<=n-1}.               (6)

The degree-1 temperature coefficient is a0(c+2), already zero because c=-2; since a0!=0 this row forces c=-2, so the strain condition is not a freely chosen gauge. It does not fix a0. The first nonzero-parity vorticity coefficient has degree 2 and belongs to block n=1. An empty sum is zero. Formula (6) follows directly from U1=-Psi_y and U2=Psi_x. The term with p+q=n has u=v=0, which gives the displayed a0 term; the p=q=0 term belongs to the linear part of W. Since beta>2, L_ij>0 for n>=1.

For the vorticity coefficient at x^(2i+1)y^(2j+1), put i+j=n-1. Its equation is

    M_ij g_ij - 2(i+1)a_(i+1,j) + Q_ij = 0,
    M_ij = (2i+1)lambda_x+(2j+1)lambda_y+1,                  (7)

where

    Q_ij = sum {[-(2q+1)(2u+1)+(2p+1)(2v+1)] h_pq g_uv:
                 p+u=i, q+v=j, p+q>=1}.                    (8)

Every h in (8) has construction block at most n-1. Every g has index sum u+v at most n-2, hence construction block at most n-1, since g_uv is determined in block u+v+1. Thus it is already known when constructing block n. Moreover M_ij>0.

Substitute (4) and (5) into (7). Define A_i=(2i+3)(2i+2) and B_j=(2j+3)(2j+2). The resulting adjacent relation is

    h_(i,j+1)
      = -(A_i/B_j)[1-a0/(L_(i+1,j) M_ij)] h_(i+1,j)
        + [Q_ij+2(i+1)P_(i+1,j)/L_(i+1,j)]/(M_ij B_j).      (9)

All divisions are by strictly positive quantities. Starting with h_(n,0), apply (9) for i=n-1,n-2,...,0 and j=n-1-i. This determines every other h in block n as an affine function of h_(n,0). Then (5) fixes the a-block and (4) fixes the g-block.

#### The harmonic coefficient and the sufficient invertibility bound

The highest angular sine coefficient of x^(2i+1)y^(2j+1), i+j=n, restricted to r=1 is 2^(-2n-1)(-1)^j. To see the sign and constant, use cos(phi)=(e^(i phi)+e^(-i phi))/2 and sin(phi)=(e^(i phi)-e^(-i phi))/(2i). The coefficient of e^((2n+2)i phi) is -i(-1)^j 2^(-2n-2); multiplying by 2i gives the sine coefficient. Therefore

    C_(2n+2) = 2^(-2n-1) sum_(j=0)^n (-1)^j h_(n-j,j).    (10)

For i+j=n-1,

    L_(i+1,j) = 2n(beta-2)+8i+8,
    M_ij      = 2n(beta-2)+8i+5.                            (11)

The product in (11) increases with i and with n, since beta>2. Its minimum over all n>=1 and admissible i is

    [2(beta-2)+8][2(beta-2)+5]
      = 2(beta+2)(2 beta+1).                                (12)

Under (1), each bracket 1-a0/(L M) in (9) is strictly positive. The homogeneous response to increasing h_(n,0) by one consequently has entries (-1)^j k_j, where k_0=1 and every k_j>0. Its contribution to (10) is 2^(-2n-1)sum k_j>0. Hence the final scalar equation fixing C_(2n+2) has a nonzero coefficient. This proves the claimed block invertibility and its iteration over n.

For larger a0 the same recurrence still gives an explicitly computable polynomial in a0 multiplying h_(n,0). Its degree is at most n. It may or may not vanish; the proof does not replace this test by a general claim of invertibility. For block n alone the same sign proof works under a0<[2n(beta-2)+8][2n(beta-2)+5]. At beta=3 these sufficient bounds are 70, 108, 154 for n=1,2,3. They are not a table of actual exceptional amplitudes.

#### First block and exceptional amplitude

At n=1 all lower sums vanish. Let D=2(beta+2)(2 beta+1). Equations (9),(10) become

    h_01=-(1-a0/D)h_10,
    C_4=(h_10-h_01)/8=(2-a0/D)h_10/8.                     (13)

The scalar coefficient vanishes exactly at a0=2D, giving (3). In that case C_4=0 is necessary. Conversely with C_4=0, any h_10 and h_01=h_10 solve this block, with the a- and g-coefficients then determined by (4),(5). This is only finite-jet compatibility.

For beta=3 the sufficient all-order bound is a0<70, while the first-block exceptional amplitude is 140. These two numbers express different statements; neither is an admissible normalization of a0.

#### Canonical moment formula

The canonical inverse of Section A.1 excludes homogeneous additions and has Psi_m=o(r^m) at infinity for every even m>=2. For a fixed such mode, its Green formula on R^2 is

    Psi_m(r)=(1/(2m))[
        r^(-m) int_0^r rho^(m+1)Omega_m(rho)d rho
        + r^m int_r^infinity rho^(1-m)Omega_m(rho)d rho].        (14)

Smoothness and parity imply Omega_m(r)=O(r^m) as r decreases to zero, for each fixed m, because lower-degree Taylor polynomials have no angular harmonic m. The first term in (14) is therefore O(r^(m+2)); removing the interval (0,r) from the second integral also changes Psi_m by O(r^(m+2)). At infinity Omega=O(r^(-1/beta)), so the integral in (2) converges for m>=2. Its coefficient is thus precisely the homogeneous r^m sine coefficient of Psi. This proves (2), including its normalization. At m=2 the center condition gives C_2=c/2=-1, an additional compatibility condition on the global vorticity.

### A.19 Proposition 18 (representation obstruction of the compactified basis)

Report statement: see Proposition 18 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Exact statement

Consider a smooth A1 solution on R^2 with beta>2, a0=Theta_y(0)!=0, the sign conventions of Section 2.1

    W=beta X+(-Psi_y,Psi_x),  -Delta Psi=Omega,
    W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,  W.grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,

canonical velocity U=o(r) uniformly, and polynomial bounds on Omega and grad Omega. These are exactly the hypotheses used in Theorem 15 (Section A.16), in addition to the displayed equations, A1 parity and nonzero a0. Polynomial bounds for Theta and its gradient follow from the preceding coupled results. Put delta=1/beta, gamma=1-2 delta, p=2 beta and n=ceil(p). Assume p is not an integer.

For a fixed positive odd angular mode m write

    Theta_m(r)=(1/pi) integral_0^(2 pi) Theta(r,phi)sin(m phi)dphi.

Suppose its nonzero leading coefficient F_m=lim r^(-gamma)Theta_m(r) is nonzero. This mode cannot have a representation

    Theta_m(r)=rho(r)^m E(r)^(gamma/2) P_m(1-2E(r)^(-delta/2)),
    E(r)=1+(r/L)^2, rho(r)=(r/L)/sqrt(E(r)), L>0,           (1)

in which P_m is C^n from the left at its endpoint 1. In particular no exact A-prime profile at non-half-integer beta can lie in the finite Chebyshev temperature representation used for the numerical states. The statement concerns any finite polynomial degree, including coefficients unrelated to the numerical states. At half-integer beta this particular obstruction vanishes; existence does not follow.

Every actual profile has a nonzero smooth leading angular temperature F, by the cited far-field theorem. Hence at least one positive odd mode has F_m!=0. It suffices to apply the statement to that mode; no finite angular truncation assumption is needed if (1) is asserted mode by mode.

#### Dependencies

The nonzero smooth far limit is proved in Sections A.12.2, A.12.1 and A.16. The stronger necessary fact used here is proved in Section A.17: theta(T-tau,z)=tau^(beta-2)Theta(z/tau^beta) extends one-sided C^(N+1) in tau, locally in every spatial Ck away from z=0, for each integer N<4 beta-1. Choose N=n-1. Since n<2 beta+1<4 beta, that hypothesis holds. Consequently its angular coefficient on the unit physical circle is C^n at tau=0. Only that already proved finite regularity fact is needed below.

#### Proof by the physical-time expansion

At physical radius 1, substitute r=tau^(-beta) into (1) and multiply by tau^(beta-2). Exact cancellation of the pure powers gives

    theta_m(tau)=L^(-gamma)(1+L^2 tau^p)^alpha
        P_m(1-2L^delta tau(1+L^2 tau^p)^(-delta/2)),
    alpha=(gamma-m)/2.                                    (2)

As tau decreases to 0, the argument of P_m differs from 1-2L^delta tau by O(tau^(p+1)). Since P_m is C^n and hence locally Lipschitz, this changes its value by O(tau^(p+1)). Moreover

    (1+L^2 tau^p)^alpha=1+alpha L^2 tau^p+O(tau^(2p)),
    P_m(1-2L^delta tau)=P_m(1)+O(tau).

Since p>4 and p<n<p+1, both p+1 and 2p exceed n. Therefore

    theta_m(tau)=L^(-gamma)P_m(1-2L^delta tau)
        +alpha L^(2-gamma)P_m(1)tau^p+o(tau^n).            (3)

The first term has a degree-n Taylor polynomial with o(tau^n) remainder. The left side also has such a Taylor polynomial by the dependency above. Subtract them. A nonzero multiple of tau^p, with n-1<p<n, cannot equal an integer-power polynomial of degree n plus o(tau^n): successively divide by the smallest integer power, then by tau^p. Thus the coefficient in (3) must vanish.

But 0<gamma<1 and m is a positive odd integer, so alpha!=0. The limit in (1) is F_m=L^(-gamma)P_m(1), nonzero by hypothesis. This is a contradiction and proves the theorem.

#### The endpoint term a true profile requires

The same fact can be read directly in the compact coordinate z=E^(-delta/2), which tends to 0 at infinity. Then

    rho=sqrt(1-z^p), r=L z^(-beta)sqrt(1-z^p).

Use the finite far expansion through integer index n, available by the same dependency:

    Theta_m(r)=r^gamma sum_(j=0)^n F_(m,j)r^(-j delta)
                        +o(r^(gamma-n delta)).

Dividing by rho^m E^(gamma/2) gives

    P_m(1-2z)=sum_(j=0)^n B_j z^j
         +(m-gamma)B_0 z^p/2+o(z^n),
    B_j=L^(gamma-j delta)F_(m,j).                          (4)

Indeed each term has the exact extra factor (1-z^p)^((gamma-m-j delta)/2). Its first correction is order p+j; only j=0 contributes before order n. Formula (4) exhibits a nonzero fractional endpoint term when B_0!=0. The lack of C^n regularity is a property of this compactified representation, not a lack of smoothness of the physical profile at finite radius.

#### Independent residual argument for two finite polynomial coefficient fields

This additional statement does not use the physical-time regularity theorem. Suppose both Theta and Omega are finite angular sums of the compactified basis, with a common L and beta>2, finite polynomials P_m for positive odd temperature modes and Q_m for positive even vorticity modes:

    Theta_m=rho^m E^(gamma/2) P_m(1-2E^(-delta/2)),
    Omega_m=rho^m E^(-delta/2) Q_m(1-2E^(-delta/2)).

Let U be the canonical modal Green inverse on R^2, and assume 2 beta is noninteger. The inverse identification is proved in Section A.1: regularity at zero excludes r^(-m), and U=o(r) excludes every added r^m harmonic mode for the even m>=2. With the sign convention -Delta Psi=Omega of Section 2.1 the radial Green formula is positive:

    Psi_m(r)=[r^(-m) integral_0^r s^(m+1)Omega_m(s)ds
              +r^m integral_r^infinity s^(1-m)Omega_m(s)ds]/(2m).
 Let F(phi)=lim r^(-gamma)Theta be nonzero. Then the actual temperature residual has a finite expansion

    r^(-gamma) R_Theta(r,phi)
        =sum_(1<=k<2 beta) B_k(phi)r^(-k delta)
          +C(phi)r^(-2)+o(r^(-2)),
    C(phi)=beta L^2 sum_(m odd) (m-gamma)F_m sin(m phi).   (5)

Here each B_k is some smooth angular trigonometric polynomial, and the sum is over integer k only. The function C is nonzero by orthogonality and 0<gamma<1. Thus R_Theta cannot vanish identically. Equation (5) excludes exact solutions in this finite representation without assuming any local jet, the vorticity transport equation, or the general profile asymptotic theorem.

To prove this, expand each finite polynomial in z=E^(-delta/2). At infinity an individual temperature monomial z^j gives a constant multiple of

    r^(gamma-j delta)(1+L^2/r^2)^((gamma-m-j delta)/2).

Consequently all temperature exponents relative to gamma are j delta+2l with nonnegative integers j,l. At relative exponent 2 the only term is j=0,l=1, because 2 beta is noninteger. Its angular coefficient is

    S(phi)=(L^2/2) sum_m (gamma-m)F_m sin(m phi).

The linear operator beta r d_r-(beta-2) multiplies that term by -2 beta, giving C=-2 beta S in (5). Its other terms with relative exponent<2 are exactly integer multiples k delta.

Similarly a vorticity monomial gives powers r^(-a), with a=(j+1)delta+2l. The Green formula on R^2 for each even mode m sends a tail power with a<2 into the power r^(1-a) in velocity. Its denominator m^2-(2-a)^2 is nonzero. All homogeneous interior-moment velocity terms have powers r^(-m-1), corresponding to a=m+2>=4. To justify the truncated expansion, subtract the finitely many vorticity tail powers with a<2, using a smooth radial cutoff away from zero. The remaining tail begins at a strictly larger exponent a_next>2; one can bound it by r^(-a_star) for some 2<a_star<min(a_next,4). The elementary two modal Green integrals then give a remainder O(r^(1-a_star)), plus O(r^(-m-1)), uniformly in the finitely many angles and after the needed derivatives. No velocity term with a=2 occurs because 2 beta is noninteger.

It follows that a nonlinear product U.grad Theta with relative exponent at most 2 can only have the form

    (j+1)delta+k delta=(j+k+1)delta,

since any geometric correction already adds 2 and is followed by a strictly positive velocity exponent. Neither an interior multipole nor a remainder can contribute at relative exponent 2. No integer j+k+1 equals 2 beta. This proves (5), including its little-o remainder, and shows that its nonzero fractional term cannot be canceled by the lower integer-power terms if the residual were zero.

The surviving term in (5) decays like r^(-2) relative to the leading temperature. Its nonvanishing is not a lower bound of fixed size on the residual on a chosen box or at a chosen resolution.

#### Removing the nonzero leading-limit condition for finite polynomials

In the direct finite-polynomial statement with noninteger 2 beta, every nonzero Theta is excluded. Nonzero a0 implies Theta is nonzero for A1, without invoking an asymptotic theorem. If F=0 but Theta is nonzero, let j0>=1 be the smallest z-power with a nonzero angular coefficient T0. The finite representation gives, with differentiated remainder,

    Theta=r^(gamma-j0 delta)(T0(phi)+O(r^(-delta))),
    grad Theta=O(r^(gamma-j0 delta-1)).

The finite-basis vorticity has Omega=O(r^(-delta)), so its canonical inverse has U=O(r^(1-delta)). Therefore the temperature residual's leading term is

    R_Theta=-j0 r^(gamma-j0 delta)T0(phi)
                          +O(r^(gamma-(j0+1)delta)),

which is nonzero. This simple leading-order obstruction works at every beta>2 when F=0. When F!=0 and 2 beta is noninteger, equation (5) gives the obstruction. Thus the direct finite-basis result needs no local jet or general exact-profile far-field theorem. It still excludes only this finite representation.

### A.20 Proposition 19 (finite angular spectra are excluded)

Report statement: see Proposition 19 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and hypotheses

Consider a smooth A1 profile on R^2 solving

    (beta X+U).grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x,
    (beta X+U).grad Theta=(beta-2)Theta,
    -Delta Psi=Omega, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x),

with beta>2, Theta_y(0)=a0!=0, the stated fourfold parity, canonical U=o(r) uniformly, and polynomial bounds on Omega and grad Omega. Suppose both Omega and Theta have finite angular Fourier spectra. Then no such profile exists.

Put delta=1/beta and gamma=1-2 delta. The already proved broad A-prime far-field results give

    |Theta|<=C r^gamma,
    |D^j Psi|<=C_j r^(2-delta-j),
    |D^j Omega|<=C_j r^(-delta-j), r>=1, j>=0.

For Psi itself integrate its gradient along an axis-compatible path; its odd-odd normalization eliminates a constant. Radial modal derivatives inherit these bounds. Only these bounds, not a full time expansion, are used below. Dependencies: Sections A.12.1 and A.16. The canonical inverse acts mode by mode; smoothness at zero and sublinearity exclude its homogeneous additions, as proved in Section A.1.

The first-order temperature equation and a0!=0 force Psi_xy(0)=-2. If Omega is identically zero, canonical uniqueness gives U=0 and hence Psi_xy(0)=0, a contradiction. Thus Omega is nonzero. Parity excludes cosine modes and leaves precisely the sine modes described next.

Write m>=2 for the largest nonzero even angular mode of Omega and hence Psi, and n>=1 for the largest nonzero odd mode of Theta. Equality of the highest Psi and Omega modes follows because any extra homogeneous stream mode is excluded by regularity at zero and sublinearity, using Section A.1. Their radial coefficients are

    Psi_m=p(r), Omega_m=g(r), Theta_n=t(r),
    g=-p''-p'/r+m^2 p/r^2.                               (1)

They are smooth on r>0. At the origin p=O(r^m). Neither p nor t is identically zero.

#### Exact highest-mode equations

For a single stream mode p sin(m phi), the polar velocity is

    U_r=-(m/r)p cos(m phi), U_phi=p' sin(m phi).

Consequently the coefficient of sin((m+n)phi) in U.grad Theta is

    [-m p t'+n p't]/(2r).

No lower modes can reach m+n, so the temperature equation forces

    m p t'=n p't.                                       (2)

The highest possible vorticity advection mode is 2m; its coefficient is

    m(p'g-pg')/(2r).

The coefficient of sin((n+1)phi) in Theta_x is

    (t'-n t/r)/2.                                       (3)

If n+1>2m, equation (3) must vanish, hence t=C r^n. The bound t=O(r^gamma), with gamma<1<=n, forces t=0, a contradiction. Thus n+1<=2m.

If n+1<2m, the highest vorticity equation gives p'g-pg'=0. On a nonzero component of p, g=k p for a constant k. This relation extends globally by linear ODE uniqueness: at a finite endpoint the Cauchy pair p,p' cannot both vanish, and a simple zero allows g/p to extend with the same constant, using smoothness of g and g'. Therefore p solves the fixed radial Helmholtz equation globally. The lemma below excludes it.

Only the critical case n=2m-1 remains. Then

    m(p'g-pg')=r t'-n t.                                (4)

#### A radial Helmholtz lemma

A smooth regular m-th mode p with g=k p, equation (1), and all symbol bounds above must vanish. For k=0, regularity gives p=C r^m, excluded by sublinearity. For k!=0, repeated use of the radial Laplacian and the all-order symbol bounds gives p and p' faster than every negative power at infinity. If k<0, multiplication of the radial equation by rp and integration yields

    integral_0^R [r(p')^2+m^2 p^2/r-k r p^2]dr=R p(R)p'(R).

The right side tends to zero, and the integrand is nonnegative. Thus p=0. If k>0, set v=sqrt(r)p. It solves

    v''+[k-(m^2-1/4)/r^2]v=0.

For large R the coefficient Q(r) lies between k/2 and 2k. The energy E=(v')^2+Qv^2 obeys E'=Q'v^2 and |E'|<=C r^-3 E. If E(R)>0, integrating the logarithmic inequality gives a strictly positive lower bound for E at infinity. The rapid decay of v,v' gives E->0, a contradiction. Thus E(R)=0 and ODE uniqueness gives p=0.

#### Critical highest-mode reduction on a nonzero component

Let I be a connected interval where p!=0, put h=|p|>0 and epsilon=sign(p), and b=n/m=2-1/m. Equation (2) gives

    t=C h^b                                                (5)

with a constant C on I. If C=0, equation (4) gives g=k p. At any finite endpoint, regular linear ODE uniqueness makes the zero of p simple. Smooth t and b in (1,2) then force C=0 on the adjacent nonzero interval too: a nonzero multiple of |r-r0|^b cannot be C2. Smooth g/p fixes the same k. Propagating this argument, including the impossibility of a finite accumulation of simple zeros of a nontrivial fixed linear ODE, gives a global Helmholtz solution, already excluded. Propagation holds down to every positive radius by ordinary linear ODE uniqueness. Smoothness of the original mode at zero supplies p=O(r^m), so the boundary term r p p' vanishes there; no uniqueness assertion for singular initial data at r=0 is needed.

Assume C!=0 and define a=C n/m. Since p'g-pg'=-p^2(g/p)', substituting (5) into (4) gives

    (g/p)'=a (r h^(-1/m))'.

Thus a second constant k exists and

    g=k p+a r epsilon h^(1-1/m),
    h''+h'/r-m^2 h/r^2+k h+a r h^(1-1/m)=0.              (6)

This calculation fixes the signs; t=C|p|^b is permitted for either sign of p.

#### Endpoints of a component, and propagation of the constants

First, a finite positive endpoint r0 of I cannot be a flat zero of p. The following finite-interval interpolation inequality follows from Taylor's formula at finitely many points, optimizing the step, with a fallback step equal to the interval length:

    ||f^(j)||_infinity <= C_lj [M^(1-j/l) H^(j/l)+M/L^j],
    M=||f||_infinity, H=||f^(l)||_infinity, 0<j<l.        (7)

Here is a proof of (7), including the endpoint issue. At any point choose the direction having at least L/2 of the interval available. Evaluate Taylor's formula of order l-1 at l fixed, distinct multiples of a step h0 in that direction, all within the interval. Inverting the fixed Vandermonde matrix bounds the j-th derivative by C(M/h0^j+H h0^(l-j)). Choose h0 a fixed fraction of min(L,(M/H)^(1/l)). If the L restriction is active, H L^l<=C M and the second term is absorbed into C M/L^j. This gives (7). The H=0 case follows by the same finite polynomial argument. On a half-line all l points can be chosen forward at any scale, so there is no M/L^j term. If H=0 and M is finite there, the polynomial is constant.

The interval has length L; the bound includes its endpoints using these one-sided points. Apply (7) to h=epsilon p on the one-sided interval of length L next to r0, with l=2m and j=1,2. Flatness implies M and H are smaller than every power of L. At a point where h attains its maximum M, equation (6), after division by M^(1-1/m), gives

    |a| inf_(one-sided interval) r <= C [H^(1/m)
       +M^(1/(2m))H^(1/(2m))+M^(1/m)(1+L^-2)],          (8)

where 1/r, k and m are bounded constants near r0. The right side tends to zero, while the left tends to |a|r0>0. This is impossible.

Hence any finite positive endpoint is a nonflat zero. Let its order be l. Smoothness of t=C|p|^b from the I side first implies lb is an integer, so m divides l, since gcd(m,2m-1)=1. In (6), the nonzero leading term h'' has order l-2, and the nonlinear term has order l(1-1/m); all other terms have higher order. Equality forces l=2m. Since 2m is even, p has the same sign and is nonzero on both sides of r0. The smooth leading coefficients of p and t force the same C, hence a, on the adjacent component. More precisely h=(r-r0)^(2m)A(r), A smooth and positive. Then h^(1-1/m)=(r-r0)^(2m-2)A(r)^(1-1/m) is smooth. The smooth quotient

    [g-a r epsilon h^(1-1/m)]/p

has its left value k and extends across r0 by Taylor divisibility. Its right constant is therefore the same k.

The constants propagate through every isolated zero. The maximal propagated interval cannot have a finite boundary where p is nonzero or has an isolated zero: smoothness and the preceding extension continue it. They cannot stop at a finite accumulation of zeros: that point is flat by smoothness, and (7)-(8) apply on the propagated side, which now satisfies (6) across its zeros, with h=epsilon p>=0. They cannot stop at an open zero interval for the same reason. For the argument below only rightward propagation is needed: C,a,k and the sign epsilon extend over (r_I,infinity), for any chosen r_I inside the starting component, with only isolated zeros of order 2m. Equations (5)-(6) hold on that interval. We make no assertion about accumulation at the singular endpoint r=0. At an isolated zero the leading positive h'' coefficient in (6) also forces a<0; this extra fact is not needed.

#### Exclusion at infinity

The temperature bound and (5) give

    h(r)<=C r^nu, nu=m gamma/(2m-1)<1.

Equation (6) in the form g=epsilon[kh+a r h^(1-1/m)] then implies, for all sufficiently large r where h>0,

    |g| >= (|a|/2) r h^(1-1/m),

because |k|h/[r h^(1-1/m)]=|k|h^(1/m)/r tends to zero. Since |g|<=C r^-delta,

    h(r)<=C r^(-(1+delta)/(1-1/m)).                      (9)

Thus h tends to zero. Let M_R=sup_(r>=R) h(r), and H_R=sup_(r>=R)|h^(2m)(r)|. The symbol bounds give H_R<=C R^(2-delta-2m), which tends to zero. The half-line version of (7), with no interval-length term, gives

    ||h''||_(R,infinity)<=C M_R^(1-1/m) H_R^(1/m),
    ||h'||_(R,infinity)<=C M_R^(1-1/(2m)) H_R^(1/(2m)).

It follows either by one-sided optimized finite differences or by applying (7) on intervals of arbitrarily large length. If M_R>0, its maximum is attained because h->0. Evaluate (6) there and divide by M_R^(1-1/m):

    |a| R <= C H_R^(1/m)
        +(C/R) M_R^(1/(2m)) H_R^(1/(2m))
        +(m^2/R^2+|k|)M_R^(1/m).                        (10)

The right side tends to zero, whereas the left diverges. Hence M_R=0 for large R. This contradicts the component propagation just proved, or gives a finite flat endpoint already excluded. Therefore the critical case is impossible, completing the proof.

#### Scope

The conclusion concerns exactly finite angular spectra, not fast angular decay and not a finite truncation of an infinite-spectrum profile. It gives no numerical lower bound and no exclusion of the full A1 class. Every use of all-order symbol bounds depends on the smooth-angular result (Section A.16).

The proof only uses finitely many of the already established symbol bounds once m is fixed, including radial derivatives through order 2m and enough derivatives for the Helmholtz step. We retain Theorem 15 (Section A.16) as the source: the polynomial-to-power bootstrap of Section A.12.1 alone did not establish these higher derivative bounds.

### A.21 Proposition 20 (source coordinates; reconstruction of Theta and Omega from the velocity)

Report statement: see Proposition 20 in Section 3.

Proof.

Item (a) of Proposition 20 is formula (4) below together with (1) and the diffeomorphism and area statements; items (b), (c) and (d) are (2), (3) and (6)-(7) with their proofs. The consequence for class A' profiles is the third sentence of the final paragraph, combined with the identity DU(0)=diag(2,-2) stated in Section A.2 and the uniqueness of the canonical inverse in Section A.1.1.

#### Statement

Let beta>2 and let U be a smooth divergence-free vector field on R2 with the A1 velocity parity, U=o(r) uniformly, and DU(0)=diag(2,-2). Put a=beta+2, b=beta-2 and W=beta X+U. Both axes are invariant. The flow Phi_t is complete because W has at most linear growth. Let B be the open basin of the origin under the backward flow. It contains a neighborhood of zero.

There is a smooth, parity-preserving, area-preserving diffeomorphism H=(xi,eta) from B onto R2, tangent to the identity at zero, such that

    H(Phi_t X)=(exp(a t) xi(X), exp(b t) eta(X)).          (1)

For every a0 the unique C1 function on B with the A1 temperature parity, origin jet a0 y+o(r), and W.grad Theta=b Theta is

    Theta[U,a0]=a0 eta.                                  (2)

It is smooth. Among vorticities bounded near zero, the unique solution on B of W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x is

    Omega[U,a0](X)=integral_(-infinity)^0 exp(s)
                  Theta_x(Phi_s X) ds.                  (3)

It too is smooth and odd in each coordinate. Equation (3) does not assert that its canonical inverse equals the prescribed U. That equality is the remaining nonlinear coupled equation. No claim is made about extending (2)-(3) across the boundary of B, or about decay and inverse admissibility of the constructed source.

#### Smooth local coordinates

Write W=(x A(x,y),y B0(x,y)), where the smoothly divided functions A and B0 are even in both coordinates, A(0)=a and B0(0)=b. Smooth division follows by the integral form of Taylor's formula, including the axes. Thus A-a and B0-b are O(r^2), with gradients O(r).

For X in the backward basin define

    I_A(X)=integral_(-infinity)^0 [A(Phi_s X)-a] ds,
    I_B(X)=integral_(-infinity)^0 [B0(Phi_s X)-b] ds,
    xi=x exp(-I_A), eta=y exp(-I_B).                      (4)

The backward flow contracts in a sufficiently small ball. For any fixed epsilon in (0,b), the symmetric part of DW is bounded below by (b-epsilon)Id there. The radial scalar product has the same lower bound. Consequently, writing t=-s>=0,

    |Phi_-t X|<=C exp(-(b-epsilon)t),
    |D^k Phi_-t X|<=C_k exp(-(b-epsilon)t), k>=1,          (5)

locally uniformly in that ball. The first derivative bound follows from the variational equation. For higher derivatives, the equation for D^k Phi has the same stable homogeneous matrix and a sum of products containing at least two lower flow derivatives. Induction and variation of constants give (5). All spatial derivatives of W are bounded on the ball.

Every derivative of (A-a) composed with Phi_-t decays like exp(-2(b-epsilon)t). For derivative order zero use A-a=O(r^2); for the chain-rule term with one differentiated A use D A=O(r) and (5); terms with two or more factors of flow derivatives also have this decay. The same argument applies to B0-b. Thus the integrals in (4) converge in every local Ck norm. They define smooth functions with I_A,I_B=O(r^2). Shifting the integration interval verifies W.grad I_A=A-a and W.grad I_B=B0-b. Equations (1) follow. H(X)=X+O(r^3), so H is a local diffeomorphism at zero.

Every compact subset of the basin enters the contracting ball in a common finite backward time. Transporting (4) over the remaining finite interval proves smoothness throughout the basin. The parity of the flow and of A,B0 makes xi odd in x and even in y, and eta even in x and odd in y. Their signs equal those of x,y.

#### Global diffeomorphism on the basin and preservation of area

The basin is invariant under every finite flow time. If H(X)=H(Y), take a common large backward time so Phi_-t X and Phi_-t Y lie in the neighborhood where H is injective. Equation (1) gives equal H values there, hence equal backward points and X=Y.

For any Z in R2, diag(exp(-a t),exp(-b t))Z lies in the local image of H for large t. Take its preimage X0 near zero and put X=Phi_t X0. Completeness gives this point, which still belongs to the backward basin. Equation (1) gives H(X)=Z. Hence H is onto R2.

Differentiating (1), using div W=a+b=2 beta and the exact flow Jacobian, gives

    det DH(Phi_t X)=det DH(X).

This formula does not presume invertibility: take determinants of the differentiated identity and divide only by the nonzero flow Jacobian. On letting t tend to minus infinity, continuity and DH(0)=Id give det DH(X)=1 everywhere in the basin. Thus H is a smooth area-preserving diffeomorphism.

#### Transported temperature and vorticity

Equation (2) follows directly from W.grad eta=b eta. Conversely, let another C1 temperature have the same first-order jet and transport equation. Its difference D from a0 eta is o(r) at zero. Equation (4) implies the exact component asymptotics

    x(Phi_-t X)=exp(-a t)[xi(X)+o(1)],
    y(Phi_-t X)=exp(-b t)[eta(X)+o(1)],

and in particular |Phi_-t X|<=C_X exp(-b t). Therefore

    D(X)=exp(b t)D(Phi_-t X)->0.

This proves uniqueness without assuming analyticity or a sign for a0.

The integrand in (3) converges in every Ck norm on compact subsets of the basin. Indeed Theta_x=O(xy)=O(r^2), D Theta_x=O(r), and the chain-rule argument used after (5) applies, with the additional integrable factor exp(s). Differentiating its shifted integral proves W.grad Omega+Omega=Theta_x. For any other solution bounded near zero, the homogeneous difference obeys D(X)=exp(-t)D(Phi_-t X), which tends to zero. Smoothness and parity follow from the integral. Near zero, Omega=O(xy).

#### Finite-time diagnostic and its error

Fix a compact subset K of the basin. For T>0 let Y=Phi_-T X and define

    Theta_T(X)=a0 exp(b T)Y_y.

On the exact path Phi_s X, -T<=s<=0, solve forward

    q'=[b Id-DW(Phi_s X)^T]q, q(-T)=a0 e_y,
    w'=q_x-w, w(-T)=0.                                  (6)

Then, uniformly for X in K,

    |Theta_T-Theta|+|q(0)-grad Theta|+|w(0)-Omega|
         <= C_K exp(-2b T)                               (7)

for large T, say T >= T_0. This is an exact truncation estimate. For 0 < T <= T_0 the left side of (7) is bounded on the compact set K by continuity of the flow and of the solutions of the ordinary differential equations, so after enlarging C_K the bound (7) holds for all T > 0, as stated in Proposition 20(d).

To prove it, the local parity jet gives Theta-a0 y=O(|y|r^2), grad Theta-a0 e_y=O(r^2), Omega=O(r^2). Formula (4) gives |Y|<=C_K exp(-b T), and |Y_y|<=C_K exp(-b T), proving the temperature estimate. The exact gradient along the path obeys (6), but with initial value grad Theta(Y). Near zero,

    b Id-DW^T=diag(-4,0)+O(r^2).

Its symmetric part has upper bound C r^2 Id. The integral of r^2 over the long near-origin portion of the path is bounded, uniformly in T and X in K; the rest of the path has uniformly bounded duration and coefficients. Thus the gradient propagator from any intermediate time to zero is uniformly bounded, giving the gradient error O(|Y|^2). The same estimate holds at intermediate times. The scalar w equation multiplies the missing origin value Omega(Y) by exp(-T) and integrates the gradient error against exp(s). Both are bounded by C_K exp(-2b T). This proves (7).

#### Dependencies and scope

Only standard finite-dimensional ODE existence, variation of constants, the chain rule, determinant differentiation and elementary smooth division are used. The proof does not invoke an exact coupled profile or the far-field theorems. For a genuine profile on a region of its origin basin, (2)-(3) necessarily reproduce its fields. A global fixed-point formulation requires separately proving that the basin is all of R^2 and that the constructed Omega has an admissible canonical inverse.

### A.22 Proposition 21 (angular limits of the source coordinates)

Report statement: see Proposition 21 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and hypotheses

Let beta>2, delta=1/beta, alpha=1+2 delta and gamma=1-2 delta. Let U be smooth, divergence free, with A1 parity, DU(0)=diag(2,-2), and suppose that for every k>=0

    |D^k U(X)| <= C_k r^(1-delta-k), r>=1.

Assume every backward trajectory of W=beta X+U tends to zero. Let (xi,eta) be the canonical source coordinates constructed in Section A.21, tangent to the identity at zero. They have determinant one and satisfy W.grad xi=(beta+2)xi and W.grad eta=(beta-2)eta.

There are smooth angular functions g,h with, in every angular Ck norm,

    xi=r^alpha(g(phi)+O(r^-delta)),
    eta=r^gamma(h(phi)+O(r^-delta)).                    (1)

The same O(r^-delta) bound holds for one logarithmic radial derivative of the rescaled functions. On 0<phi<pi/2, g,h>0; g(0)>0, h(pi/2)>0; h is odd about zero and even about pi/2, while g is even about zero and odd about pi/2. They satisfy

    alpha g h' - gamma g' h = 1.                       (2)

In particular, alpha g(0)h'(0)=1 and -gamma g'(pi/2)h(pi/2)=1. For a genuine coupled profile, equation (2) of Section A.21 gives Theta=a0 eta everywhere under the full-basin assumption. Taking its leading limit gives F=a0 h.

Put q=alpha/gamma>1. Then in the first quadrant

    g(phi)=(1/gamma) h(phi)^q
             integral_phi^(pi/2) h(s)^(-q-1) ds.       (3)

There is a necessary endpoint condition. Write the even Taylor expansion

    (h(phi)/phi)^(-q-1)=sum_(j>=0) d_j phi^(2j),

where any use of this series means a finite Taylor expansion with its remainder. If q is not an even integer, the finite part

    lim_(eps->0+) [ integral_eps^(pi/2) h(s)^(-q-1) ds
       - sum_(2j<q) d_j eps^(2j-q)/(q-2j) ]             (4)

is zero. If q=2 ell is an even positive integer, the necessary condition is d_ell=0. These are necessary conditions only. They do not select beta: a smooth positive pair satisfying all conditions exists for every beta>2, as constructed below.

#### Smooth limits

Set t=log r. For sufficiently large r, W_r=beta r+U_r>=beta r/2. Dividing the equation for xi by W_r/r and putting f=r^-alpha xi gives

    f_t+v(t,phi)f_phi=d_alpha(t,phi)f,
    v=U_phi/(beta r+U_r),
    d_alpha=(beta+2)/(beta+U_r/r)-alpha.

All angular derivatives of v and d_alpha are O(exp(-delta t)). The same equation holds for j=r^-gamma eta with d_gamma=(beta-2)/(beta+U_r/r)-gamma. The symbol assumptions imply these statements by the chain rule, including one or more radial derivatives when needed.

On the circle r=R the two coordinate functions are smooth. The angular characteristic equation phi'=v has a limiting smooth circle diffeomorphism as t tends to infinity. Indeed its first derivative solves the scalar variational equation and stays bounded above and below because integral ||v_phi|| is finite. Each higher derivative solves a linear equation whose inhomogeneous terms contain derivatives of v and previously bounded flow derivatives; induction gives bounded derivatives, and their tails are O(exp(-delta t)). The inverse maps have the same properties. The multiplicative factors exp(integral d_alpha), exp(integral d_gamma) likewise converge in every Ck norm with this rate. This proves (1). The transport equations give f_t,j_t=O(exp(-delta t)) in every Ck norm.

Parity is inherited from xi,eta. The angular diffeomorphisms fix both axes and preserve the intervening quadrant. The source-coordinate formulas xi=x exp(-I_A) and eta=y exp(-I_B) show their precise signs and zero sets, and also their A1 parities. Positivity in the open quadrant and the nonzero values on the appropriate axes follow from these formulas at r=R and from their positive finite multiplicative factors.

The determinant identity in polar coordinates is

    1=(alpha f+f_t)j_phi-f_phi(gamma j+j_t),

since alpha+gamma=2. Taking the smooth limit proves (2) and its axis identities.

#### The endpoint condition

Equation (2) gives

    (g h^-q)'=-(1/gamma) h^-q-1.

At pi/2, g=0 and h>0, proving (3). At zero, h'(0)>0 by (2). Thus h(phi)/phi extends to a positive smooth even function near zero and the displayed finite Taylor expansions are legitimate.

If q is not an even integer, subtract from the integral all divergent power primitives corresponding to 2j<q. The remaining integrand is locally integrable, so the limit in (4) exists. Integrating a Taylor expansion to arbitrarily high finite order shows that (3) is a smooth even power expansion plus (C/gamma)h(phi)^q, with a remainder of arbitrarily high prescribed order; C is (4). If q is noninteger, a nonzero C produces a noninteger power at zero, incompatible with smooth g. If q is an odd integer, even parity would extend its leading phi^q term as |phi|^q, which is not C^q. Hence C=0 in both cases.

If q=2 ell, the term d_ell phi^-1 in the integrand produces -d_ell log phi in the integral. After multiplication by h^q it produces a nonzero multiple of phi^(2 ell) log phi unless d_ell=0. No other term can cancel that logarithm. Smoothness requires d_ell=0. The finite constant multiplying h^q is now compatible with even smoothness, so no zero finite-part assertion is made in this case.

#### Explicit angular pairs for every beta

Let theta be the unique smooth angle defined by

    phi=theta+delta sin(2 theta),
    g(phi)=cos theta, h(phi)=sin theta.                (5)

The derivative dphi/dtheta=1+2 delta cos(2 theta) is at least 1-2 delta=gamma>0, so this defines a smooth orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism with the required parity. Direct differentiation gives

    alpha g h'-gamma g'h
      =(alpha cos^2(theta)+gamma sin^2(theta))
         /(1+2 delta cos(2 theta))=1.

The endpoint conditions already proved therefore hold for these functions for every beta>2. There is no inference that they solve the coupled vorticity or inverse equations.

More concretely, the map of the punctured R^2

    (r,phi) -> (r^alpha cos theta, r^gamma sin theta)

has determinant one and is a global smooth diffeomorphism of R^2 minus the origin. Given a nonzero target (z1,z2), its radius is the unique positive solution of z1^2 r^(-2 alpha)+z2^2 r^(-2 gamma)=1. The left side decreases strictly from infinity to zero. Then cos theta=z1 r^-alpha and sin theta=z2 r^-gamma determine theta, and (5) gives phi. Smoothness of the inverse follows from the nonzero radial derivative. This map is not asserted smooth at the origin and is not a coupled profile. It explicitly refutes exponent selection from (2) or its endpoint condition alone.

#### Scope and dependencies

The full-basin assumption remains unproved for the sought A1 profiles. The symbol bounds follow for a coupled admissible profile from Theorem 15(a) (Section A.16), but the proof here also applies to prescribed velocities satisfying them. The argument uses only the source-coordinate theorem of Section A.21, elementary ODE estimates, finite Taylor expansions and the inverse function theorem. No complete angular profile, error floor for the numerical states, or existence or nonexistence result for the full A1 problem follows.

### A.23 Proposition 22 (transport errors; the temperature residual does not control the reconstruction)

Report statement: see Proposition 22 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and hypotheses

Let beta>2, b=beta-2, and let U be a prescribed smooth velocity. Put W=beta X+U and DW_ij=partial_j W_i. Assume the flow line Phi_s X exists on -T<=s<=0. On a flow tube containing it, let smooth fields Theta, Omega have residuals

    RT = W.grad Theta-b Theta,
    RO = W.grad Omega+Omega-Theta_x,

and let smooth Theta^, Omega^ on the same tube solve W.grad Theta^=b Theta^ and W.grad Omega^+Omega^=Theta^_x. Write e=Theta^-Theta, q=grad e, z=Omega^-Omega, and let q_1 be the first component of the vector q (not a derivative).

#### The error identities

Subtracting the two temperature equations gives W.grad e-b e=-RT. Differentiation gives

    grad(W.grad e)=DW^T grad e+(W.grad) grad e,

so

    (W.grad) q=(b I-DW^T) q-grad RT.

Subtracting the vorticity equations gives W.grad z+z=q_1-RO. Along s->Phi_s X these are linear inhomogeneous ordinary differential equations:

    e'=b e-RT,   q'=(b I-DW^T)q-grad RT,   z'=-z+q_1-RO.

Let P(t,s) solve partial_t P(t,s)=(b I-DW(Phi_t X)^T)P(t,s), P(s,s)=I. The matrix [D Phi_(t-s)(Phi_s X)]^(-T) solves v'=-DW^T v with the value I at t=s, so P(t,s)=exp(b(t-s))[D Phi_(t-s)(Phi_s X)]^(-T). Multiplying the first equation by exp(-bs), variation of constants for the second, and multiplying the third by exp(s), then integrating over [-T,0], gives

    e(X)=exp(bT)e(Phi_-T X)-int_-T^0 exp(-bs)RT(Phi_s X) ds,
    q(X)=P(0,-T)q(Phi_-T X)-int_-T^0 P(0,s)grad RT(Phi_s X) ds,
    z(X)=exp(-T)z(Phi_-T X)+int_-T^0 exp(s)[q_1-RO](Phi_s X) ds.

These are finite-time identities. A boundary term may be discarded only on the basis of separate estimates; under the hypotheses of Proposition 20 the origin jet and the quantitative estimate of Proposition 20(d) (Section A.21) justify the infinite-time limits.

#### The differentiated residual

Direct differentiation gives

    partial_x RT = W1 Theta_xx+W2 Theta_xy+(partial_x W1)Theta_x+(partial_x W2)Theta_y-b Theta_x.

Assume W1 odd in x and even in y, W2 even in x and odd in y, and Theta even in x and odd in y. Substitution shows that every summand is odd in x and odd in y. If f is smooth and odd in x, then f(x,y)/x extends smoothly as int_0^1 f_x(tx,y)dt; applying this in both variables, each summand has a smooth quotient by xy, and the sum of the absolute values of the five summands divided by |xy| extends continuously. Where xy is nonzero, the ratio of partial_x RT to this sum equals the ratio of their quotients. The quotient of the divided residual by the divided normalizer need not extend continuously where the divided normalizer vanishes; the conventions 0/0=0 and nonzero/0=infinity are reported separately. A common parity factor cancels in such a ratio and does not by itself make a relative residual small. The parity of Theta alone does not give these conclusions.

#### A transport-only counterexample

Fix a0>0, a=beta+2, b=beta-2 and U=(2x,-2y), so W=(a x,b y). This velocity is divergence free and smooth, but it is not sublinear.

Uniqueness of the reconstructed fields. Phi_-T(x,y)=(exp(-aT)x,exp(-bT)y), and since a>b>0, |Phi_-T X|<=exp(-bT)|X|. A C1 solution Theta^ on the plane with Theta^(0)=0 and grad Theta^(0)=(0,a0) obeys

    Theta^(X)=exp(bT)Theta^(Phi_-T X)=exp(bT)[a0 exp(-bT) y+o(|Phi_-T X|)] -> a0 y.

Its x derivative is zero, so a vorticity bounded near the origin obeys Omega^(X)=exp(-T)Omega^(Phi_-T X)->0. Hence Theta^=a0 y and Omega^=0.

The family. Take the smooth, nonnegative, even function

    f(s)=exp(-1/[(s^2-1)(4-s^2)])  if 1<|s|<2,   f(s)=0 otherwise.

For 1<s<3/2 the polynomial D(s)=(s^2-1)(4-s^2) has D'(s)=2s(5-2s^2)>0, so f'(s)=f(s)D'(s)/D(s)^2>0; also f'=0 on [0,1]. For integers k>=1 put

    Theta_k=a0 y+k^-1 y f(kx),   J(zeta)=int_0^1 t^b f'(zeta t^a) dt,   Omega_k=y J(kx).

The integral defining J converges with all derivatives because b>0 and f has bounded derivatives. J is odd (f' is odd) and vanishes on [-1,1]. Hence Theta_k is even in x and odd in y, Omega_k is odd in both variables, and Theta_k=a0 y, Omega_k=0 on the strip |x|<1/k; there the fields agree with Theta^ and Omega^ to every order.

Residuals. Direct differentiation gives

    RT_k=a x y f'(kx)=(a/k) y (kx) f'(kx).

Since zeta f'(zeta) is bounded, RT_k->0 uniformly on bounded sets. With the term-sum normalizer

    NT_k=|a x partial_x Theta_k|+|b y partial_y Theta_k|+|b Theta_k|

and partial_y Theta_k=a0+k^-1 f(kx)>=a0, the last two terms give NT_k>=2 b a0 |y|. Consequently

    |RT_k|/NT_k <= a sup|zeta f'(zeta)|/(2 b a0 k)

for y nonzero, and 0/0=0 on y=0; the bound is uniform on the plane. Since d/dt[t^(b+1) f'(zeta t^a)]=(b+1)t^b f'(zeta t^a)+a zeta t^(a+b) f''(zeta t^a) and the lower boundary term vanishes,

    a zeta J'(zeta)+(b+1)J(zeta)=f'(zeta).

Therefore W.grad Omega_k+Omega_k=y[a zeta J'+(b+1)J](kx)=y f'(kx)=partial_x Theta_k, and RO_k=0 exactly.

Lower bound. The integrand of J(3/2) is positive when 1<(3/2)t^a<3/2 and zero for smaller t, so J(3/2)>0. At X_k=(3/(2k),1), in a fixed bounded rectangle, Omega_k(X_k)=J(3/2) for every k, while the reconstructed vorticity is zero. The derivative partial_x RT_k=a y[f'(kx)+kx f''(kx)] is not small, in agreement with the error identities.

#### Scope and dependencies

The identities and the counterexample use only elementary flow theory and differentiation; no whole-plane inverse is used. The velocity of the counterexample is affine, is not the canonical sublinear velocity of its vorticity, and the fields are not Boussinesq profiles; no estimate for the coupled problem in other norms is excluded. A differentiated residual is an additional necessary-condition diagnostic and does not replace any acceptance requirement.

### A.24 Proposition 23 (a generating function for the source coordinates)

Report statement: see Proposition 23 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Statement and notation

Let beta>2, a=beta+2, b=beta-2. Let U be a smooth divergence-free velocity with the A1 parity, U=o(r) uniformly and DU(0)=diag(2,-2). On the backward basin B of the origin let (xi,eta) be the area-preserving source coordinates of Proposition 20(a) (Section A.21): W.grad xi=a xi, W.grad eta=b eta, (xi,eta)=(x,y)+O(r^3), det D(xi,eta)=1, xi odd in x and even in y, eta even in x and odd in y.

#### Existence of the generating function

On a simply connected open set V of B where eta_y>0 and (x,y)->(x,eta) is one-to-one, write y=y(x,eta). Implicit differentiation at fixed eta gives y_x=-eta_x/eta_y and y_eta=1/eta_y. Area preservation gives

    partial_x[xi(x,y(x,eta))] = xi_x+xi_y y_x = (xi_x eta_y-xi_y eta_x)/eta_y = 1/eta_y = y_eta.

Thus the one-form y dx+xi d eta is closed on the simply connected image of V and equals dG for a smooth G, with G_x=y, G_eta=xi and A=G_(x eta)=y_eta=1/eta_y(x,G_x(x,eta))>0.

Parity. Let V be a connected neighbourhood of 0 invariant under (x,y)->(-x,y) and (x,y)->(x,-y). Since eta is even in x, y(x,eta) is even in x; since xi is odd in x, xi(x,y(x,eta)) is odd in x. Hence G(x,eta)+G(-x,eta) has zero gradient and equals 2G(0,0)=0 after normalization. Since eta is odd in y and xi even in y, y(x,eta) is odd in eta and xi(x,y(x,eta)) is even in eta, so G(x,eta)+G(x,-eta)=0 likewise. The parity of xi is essential: at beta=4 (a=3b), xi+kappa eta^3 also satisfies W.grad(xi+kappa eta^3)=a(xi+kappa eta^3), is area preserving with eta and equals x+O(r^3), but it is even in x in its correction and adds kappa eta^4/4 to G, which no additive constant makes odd. The coordinate change is tangent to the identity, so y=eta+O(r^3) and xi=x+O(r^3), and integration gives G=x eta+O(r^4); odd-odd parity excludes cubic terms.

Global chart. If B=R^2, eta_y>0 everywhere and eta(x,y)->+-inf as y->+-inf for each x, then y->eta(x,y) is an increasing bijection of R for each x, and the inverse function theorem makes (x,y)->(x,eta) a global diffeomorphism.

#### The converse formulas

Let G be smooth on an open set of the (x,eta) plane with A=G_(x eta)>0, and put B0=G_xx, C=G_(eta eta), M=a G_eta-b eta C, with (x,y)=(x,G_x) one-to-one. For a function f(x,eta), the physical derivatives are

    Dx f=f_x-(B0/A)f_eta,   Dy f=f_eta/A,

since y_x=B0 and y_eta=A at fixed eta and x respectively. Dx^2 and Dy^2 are compositions of these operators.

The field W. If W is to satisfy W.grad xi=a xi and W.grad eta=b eta with xi=G_eta, then along the flow eta'=b eta and A x'+C eta'=a G_eta, so x'=M/A, and y'=(d/dt)G_x=B0 x'+A eta'=B0 M/A+b eta A. Define W1=M/A, W2=B0 M/A+b eta A and U=W-beta(x,G_x). In the (x,eta) coordinates the physical derivative along W is W.grad f=(M/A)f_x+b eta f_eta.

The stream function. With Psi=beta x G_x+b eta G_eta-2 beta G, mixed differentiation gives

    Psi_eta = beta x A+b G_eta+b eta C-2 beta G_eta = beta x A-M,
    Psi_x = beta G_x+beta x B0+b eta A-2 beta G_x = -beta G_x+beta x B0+b eta A.

Consequently

    -Dy Psi = M/A-beta x = W1-beta x = U1,
    Dx Psi = -beta G_x+beta x B0+b eta A-(B0/A)(beta x A-M) = -beta G_x+b eta A+B0 M/A = W2-beta G_x = U2.

Hence U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x) and div U=0.

Divergence check. The physical area element is A dx d eta, so

    div W = [partial_x M+partial_eta(b eta A)]/A = [a A-b eta A_eta+b A+b eta A_eta]/A = a+b = 2 beta,

using partial_x M=a G_(eta x)-b eta C_x=a A-b eta A_eta.

Temperature and vorticity. With Theta=a0 eta, W.grad Theta=b eta partial_eta(a0 eta)=b Theta exactly, and Theta_x=Dx(a0 eta)=-a0 B0/A. With Omega=-(Dx^2+Dy^2)Psi, the remaining equation (P1) reads

    [(M/A)partial_x+b eta partial_eta]Omega+Omega = -a0 B0/A.

Psi uses first derivatives of G, U derivatives up to order two, Omega up to order three, and the equation up to order four (differentiating the coefficient B0/A uses third derivatives of G, applied to functions that use at most second derivatives at that stage).

#### The global converse

Let G be smooth on R^2 with A>0 everywhere, odd in x and in eta, G=x eta+O((|x|+|eta|)^4), G_x->+-inf as eta->+-inf for each x, and a0 != 0. For each x, eta->G_x(x,eta) is increasing (its derivative is A>0) with limits +-inf, hence a bijection of R; the inverse function theorem makes (x,eta)->(x,G_x) a global diffeomorphism. Since G is odd in each variable, G_x is even in x and odd in eta, so the inverse eta(x,y) is even in x and odd in y; then Psi is odd in each variable, Theta=a0 eta is even in x and odd in y, and U, Omega have the A1 parities. From G=x eta+O(4), y=eta+O(3), and Psi=(beta+b-2beta)x eta+O(4)=-2xy+O(r^4), so Psi_xy(0)=-2 and Theta=a0 y+O(r^3).

If moreover G_eta->+-inf as x->+-inf for each eta, then x->G_eta(x,eta) is increasing (derivative A) with these limits, and (x,eta)->(G_eta,eta) is a global diffeomorphism; composed with the physical chart it gives a diffeomorphism H of the physical plane onto R^2. Applying W.grad to G_eta gives (M/A)A+b eta C=a G_eta, so H conjugates the flow of W to (xi,eta)->(exp(at)xi,exp(bt)eta). This linear flow is complete and every backward orbit tends to 0, so the flow of W is complete and its backward basin of 0 is the whole plane.

Canonical velocity. If U=o(r) uniformly, any divergence-free field with curl -Omega, sublinear growth and the A1 parity differs from U by a field whose components are harmonic and sublinear, hence constant by Liouville, and the constant is 0 by parity. So U is the canonical velocity in the sense of Section 2.3; convergence of the subtracted kernel integral is a separate matter (it holds, for example, under the sufficient condition of Section 2.3). If also Theta, Omega and their first derivatives are polynomially bounded, the fields form a class A' profile whenever the scalar equation holds.

Dilation. For l>0, G_l(x,eta)=l^2 G(x/l,eta/l) corresponds to Theta_l(X)=l Theta(X/l), U_l(X)=l U(X/l), Omega_l(X)=Omega(X/l), and preserves beta, a0 and the equation.

#### Remark: a smooth search family at beta = 3 (not part of Proposition 23)

At beta=3 put E=1+x^2+eta^6, f(E)=sum_(j=0)^K c_j E^((2-j)/6) with sum c_j=1, p=f'(1), d=p(a0-70)/14 and

    G = x eta [f(E)+d eta^2/E].

Every member is smooth and odd in each variable, and G=x eta+p x^3 eta+d x eta^3+O(r^6). The inverse map gives eta=y-3p x^2 y-d y^3+O(r^5), and in the notation of Section 2.4 the formulas above give d1=10p, d2=2d, b1=-3a0 p, b2=-a0 d, g=-60p-12d; the relations (T1), (T2) hold identically and (T3), 7g=2b1, is equivalent to (a0-70)p=14d, which the choice of d enforces. If c0>0 and A>0 everywhere, the two onto conditions hold (at fixed x, y grows like c0 eta^3; at fixed eta, xi grows like c0 sign(x)|x|^(5/3)), r is comparable to R=E^(1/2) at infinity, and differentiation of the finite powers gives D^k U=O(r^(2/3-k)), D^k Omega=O(r^(-1/3-k)), D^k Theta=O(r^(1/3-k)); in particular U is uniformly sublinear and Omega=O(r^(-1/3)) makes the subtracted kernel integral absolutely convergent. For the subfamily with c1=c3=...=0 and c2=1-c0>=0 one has A>=c0/3+c2-3|d| everywhere; for example c0=1/100, c2=99/100, a0=52 gives p=1/300, d=-3/700 and A>0.98. These are manufactured fields satisfying (P2), the Poisson relation and the low-order centre relations; they are not solutions of the scalar equation, and no member is claimed to be one.

#### Scope and dependencies

The formulas are exact calculus on the stated chart and use only Proposition 20(a) (Section A.21) and the uniqueness statement of Section 2.3 (Section A.1). They do not show that an arbitrary A1 profile has eta_y>0 or a global mixed chart, do not give a solution of the scalar equation, and do not select beta.

### A.25 Proposition 24 (backward basin, temperature sign and stagnation points)

Report statement: see Proposition 24 in Section 3.

Proof.

#### Standing facts

Let beta>2, a=beta+2, b=beta-2. W=beta X+U is smooth with div W=2beta (div U=0), W1 odd in x and even in y, W2 even in x and odd in y. Write Psi=cxy+O(r^4), so U=(-cx,cy)+O(r^3). With Theta=a0 y+o(r), the coefficient of y in W.grad Theta=b Theta is (beta+c)a0=(beta-2)a0, so c=-2 and DW(0)=diag(a,b) (the off-diagonal entries vanish by parity). Since U is smooth and U=o(r) uniformly, |W(X)|<=C(1+|X|), so solutions of X'=W(X) exist for all finite positive and negative times; and there is R>0 with X.W(X)>=beta|X|^2/2 for |X|>=R, so d|Phi_s X|^2/ds=2X.W>=beta|Phi_s X|^2 whenever |Phi_s X|>=R; hence |Phi_s X| decreases as s decreases outside B_R, the closed ball B_R is backward invariant and the backward half-orbit of X stays in the closed ball of radius max(R,|X|). Along any orbit, Theta(Phi_s X)=exp(bs)Theta(X).

#### A local orbit lemma, including a zero eigenvalue

Suppose a smooth field near (0,0), in coordinates z=(u,v), has the form

    u'=lambda_u u+f(u,v),  v'=lambda_v v+g(u,v),  lambda_u<=0,  lambda_v>b>0,
    f(0)=g(0)=0,  Df(0)=Dg(0)=0,  g(u,0)=0.

Then there is an orbit z(s), -infinity<s<=0, with v(s)>0 for all s, z(s)->0 as s->-infinity and |z(s)|<=C exp(mu s) for some mu>b.

Choose mu with b<mu<lambda_v.
