Multiply f, g by a smooth cutoff equal to 1 on a small ball and 0 outside the ball of twice the radius; since f, g=O(|z|^2) and Df, Dg=O(|z|), the global Lipschitz constant L of the cut-off functions (max norm) can be made as small as desired by shrinking the ball, and the cutoff preserves g(u,0)=0. On the Banach space of continuous paths on (-infinity,0] with norm ||z||_mu=sup_(s<=0) exp(-mu s)max(|u(s)|,|v(s)|) define, for epsilon>0,

    Tu(s)=int_(-infinity)^s exp(lambda_u(s-t)) f(z(t)) dt,
    Tv(s)=epsilon exp(lambda_v s)-int_s^0 exp(lambda_v(s-t)) g(z(t)) dt.

Integrating exp(lambda_u(s-t))exp(mu t) over t<s and exp(lambda_v(s-t))exp(mu t) over s<t<0 shows that the Lipschitz constants of the two integral maps are at most L/(mu-lambda_u) and L/(lambda_v-mu); both denominators are positive also when lambda_u=0. For L small the map is a contraction, and its fixed point has norm at most 2 epsilon; for epsilon small the whole path lies in the ball where the cutoff equals 1, and differentiating the absolutely convergent integrals shows that it solves the original system, with v(0)=epsilon. The bound |z(s)|<=2 sqrt(2) epsilon exp(mu s) gives z(s)->0 as s->-infinity. Since {v=0} is invariant and the field is locally Lipschitz, the orbit cannot reach v=0 at a finite s, so v(s)>0 for all s<=0.

#### (a), "if"

Assume a0>0 (otherwise replace Theta by -Theta, which leaves the transport equation unchanged) and Theta(x,y)>0 for y>0, Theta(x,y)<0 for y<0. Put V(x)=W1(x,0); V is odd and V'(0)=a>0, so V>0 just to the right of 0. Suppose V has a positive zero and let x* be the smallest one (the zero set is closed and bounded away from 0). Then V'(x*)<=0. At p=(x*,0), W(p)=0 (W2 vanishes on the x-axis by parity), and DW(p) is diagonal because W1 is even in y and W2(x,0)=0 for all x:

    DW(p)=diag(lambda_u,lambda_v),  lambda_u=V'(x*)<=0,  lambda_v=2beta-lambda_u>=2beta>b.

In the coordinates u=x-x*, v=y the remainders satisfy the hypotheses of the lemma, including g(u,0)=0. The lemma gives an orbit z(s) with y(s)>0 that tends to p as s->-infinity with |z(s)-p|<=C exp(mu s), mu>b. As Theta is C^1 and vanishes on the x-axis, |Theta(x,y)|<=M|y| near p, so

    |Theta(z(0))|=exp(-bs)|Theta(z(s))|<=MC exp((mu-b)s)->0  (s->-infinity),

hence Theta(z(0))=0 with y(z(0))>0, a contradiction. So V>0 on (0,infinity) and, by oddness, V<0 on (-infinity,0).

Let X be arbitrary and let L_X be its backward limit set (limits of Phi_(s_n)X with s_n->-infinity). By the boundedness of backward half-orbits, L_X is nonempty and compact, and it is invariant under the full flow by continuity of Phi_t. Since Theta(Phi_s X)=exp(bs)Theta(X)->0, Theta=0 on L_X, so L_X lies in {y=0} by the strict signs. A point (x,0) with x>0 cannot lie in a compact invariant set: its forward x-coordinate increases strictly (x'=V(x)>0), and a bounded increasing trajectory would converge to some ell>0 with V(ell)=0, impossible; x<0 is symmetric. Hence L_X={0}, and since the half-orbit is bounded, Phi_s X->0 (otherwise a subsequence outside a fixed neighbourhood of 0 would produce a second limit point). So B=R^2.

#### (a), "only if"

Let B=R^2 and y>0. Near 0, Theta(x,y)=y int_0^1 Theta_y(x,ty) dt=y(a0+o(1)), so there is a neighbourhood N of 0 in which a0 Theta>0 at every point with y>0. The x-axis is invariant (W2(x,0)=0), so by uniqueness the backward orbit of X stays in {y>0}; it converges to 0 and therefore enters N, and Theta(Phi_s X)=exp(bs)Theta(X) shows that a0 Theta(X)>0. The case y<0 is the same by oddness.

#### (b)

At a zero P of W, (P2) gives b Theta(P)=W(P).grad Theta(P)=0, and differentiating (P2) at P gives DW(P)^T grad Theta(P)=b grad Theta(P). Under the hypothesis of (b), b is an eigenvalue of DW(P), and since tr DW(P)=div W=2beta the other eigenvalue is beta+2. Both are positive and distinct, so P is a hyperbolic source of W, that is, a hyperbolic sink of -W; in particular the zeros of W are isolated.

For the reversed field -W every forward orbit stays in a compact disc (standing facts), so its omega-limit set is nonempty and compact. We use the Poincare-Bendixson theorem in the form: a nonempty compact omega-limit set of a C^1 planar field that contains no equilibrium is a periodic orbit. A periodic orbit of -W is a simple closed curve; the outward flux of -W through it is 0, while by the divergence theorem it equals -2beta times the enclosed area, and the area is positive, so the flux is negative, a contradiction. Hence the omega-limit set contains a zero P of W. P is a hyperbolic sink of -W, so it has a positively invariant neighbourhood in which all orbits converge to P; the orbit enters it and converges to P.

So the plane is the union of the basins (for -W) of the zeros of W. These basins are pairwise disjoint and open (each contains a positively invariant attracting neighbourhood, and every point of a basin enters that neighbourhood in finite time, so by continuous dependence an open set around it does too). If there were two or more zeros, one basin and the union of all the others would disconnect the plane; no finiteness of the zero set is needed. The origin is a zero, so it is the only one and B=R^2.

#### (c)

The origin satisfies the hypothesis of (b) because grad Theta(0)=(0,a0)!=0. If B!=R^2, (b) fails, so there is a zero P of W with grad Theta(P)=0, and P!=0. At P, b Theta(P)=0 with b!=0, and (P1) gives Omega(P)=Theta_x(P)=0. Since curl U=-Omega, the off-diagonal entries of DU(P), hence of DW(P)=beta I+DU(P), are equal, and tr DW(P)=2beta. This proves (c); it gives at least one such point and does not describe every additional zero of W.

#### (d)

Let P be as in (c), A=DW(P) (so A_kj=d_j W_k(P), symmetric with trace 2beta), H=D^2 Theta(P), v=grad Omega(P), e_x=(1,0). Differentiating W_k d_k Theta=b Theta (summation over k) with respect to x_i and x_j gives

    (d_ij W_k) d_k Theta+(d_i W_k) d_jk Theta+(d_j W_k) d_ik Theta+W_k d_ijk Theta=b d_ij Theta.

At P the first and last terms vanish because grad Theta(P)=0 and W(P)=0, leaving sum_k A_ki H_kj+sum_k H_ik A_kj=b H_ij, that is A^T H+HA=bH. Differentiating W_k d_k Omega+Omega=d_x Theta with respect to x_j gives at P sum_k A_kj v_k+v_j=H_jx, that is (A^T+I)v=He_x. Under an orthogonal change of coordinates Z=Qz the objects become Q^TAQ, Q^THQ, Q^Tv and Q^Te_x, so both identities hold in an orthonormal eigenbasis of A with e_x expressed in that basis. There the first identity reads (l_i+l_j-b)H_ij=0. For i!=j the factor is l1+l2-b=2beta-b=beta+2>0, so H_12=0, and the diagonal equations are (2 l_i-b)H_ii=0. Both diagonal entries cannot be nonzero, since then l1=l2=b/2 and tr A=b<2beta. Hence H=0 unless an eigenvalue equals b/2; if H!=0, H has rank one and the eigenvalues are b/2 and 2beta-b/2, both positive, so A is positive definite, A+I is invertible and v=(A+I)^(-1)He_x (which may vanish). By contraposition, if A is not positive definite then H=0. If H=0, then (A+I)v=0, so v=0 when -1 is not an eigenvalue of A.

If Theta has a first nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial p_m at P, then m>=2 because Theta(P)=0 and grad Theta(P)=0. With Z=X-P, Taylor's theorem gives W(P+Z)=AZ+O(|Z|^2), Theta(P+Z)=p_m(Z)+O(|Z|^(m+1)) and grad Theta(P+Z)=grad p_m(Z)+O(|Z|^m), so the degree-m part of W.grad Theta=b Theta is (AZ).grad p_m=b p_m. In eigen-coordinates (l1 z1 d_z1+l2 z2 d_z2)(z1^i z2^j)=(i l1+j l2)z1^i z2^j, so every monomial with a nonzero coefficient in p_m satisfies i+j=m and i l1+j l2=b.

#### (e)

Let A be positive definite with smaller eigenvalue l_min, and fix 0<mu<l_min. By Taylor expansion of W there is a small closed ball D about P with Z.W(P+Z)>=mu|Z|^2 for P+Z in D. Along the backward flow, d/dt |Phi_(-t)X-P|^2=-2(Phi_(-t)X-P).W(Phi_(-t)X)<=-2mu|Phi_(-t)X-P|^2 while Phi_(-t)X is in D; so D is backward invariant and |Phi_(-t)X-P|<=e^(-mu t)|X-P| for X in D and t>=0.

Flat case. Suppose all Taylor coefficients of Theta at P vanish. Then for every N there is C_N with |Theta(P+Z)|<=C_N|Z|^N on D. Since Theta(Phi_s X)=e^(bs)Theta(X), for X in D and t>=0,

    |Theta(X)|=e^(bt)|Theta(Phi_(-t)X)|<=C_N|X-P|^N e^((b-N mu)t).

Choosing N with N mu>b and letting t->infinity gives Theta=0 on D. On the interior of D, Theta_x=0, so (P1) reads W.grad Omega+Omega=0 there and d/ds Omega(Phi_s X)=-Omega(Phi_s X) as long as the orbit stays in D; for X in int D and t>=0 this gives Omega(X)=e^(-t)Omega(Phi_(-t)X), and boundedness of Omega on D gives Omega(X)=0.

Extension to the basin. Let B_P be the set of X with Phi_(-t)X -> P as t -> infinity. Every point of B_P enters int D after a finite backward time, and every point whose backward orbit enters int D tends to P by the contraction estimate; hence B_P is the union over t>=0 of the open sets Phi_t(int D), so B_P is open, contains a neighbourhood of P and satisfies Phi_s(B_P)=B_P for every real s. For X in B_P choose t with Phi_(-t)X in int D. Then Theta(X)=e^(bt)Theta(Phi_(-t)X)=0, so Theta and Theta_x vanish on the open set B_P; the orbit segment from Phi_(-t)X to X lies in B_P, where (P1) is homogeneous, so Omega(X)=e^(-t)Omega(Phi_(-t)X)=0. Thus U is curl-free (curl U=-Omega) and divergence-free on B_P. By continuity Theta, Omega and all their derivatives vanish on the closure of B_P; since grad Theta(0)=(0,a0)!=0, the origin is not in that closure. Distinct sources have disjoint basins, since a backward orbit has at most one limit. Nothing is asserted outside the closure of B_P, and the argument does not exclude such a basin. This is alternative (e1).

Non-flat case. Then Theta is not identically zero on any neighbourhood of P and its first nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial p_m exists, with m>=2 by (d). Since both eigenvalues are positive, a monomial with i,j>=1 has i l1+j l2>=l1+l2=2beta>b, contradicting the resonance condition of (d); so only pure powers z_k^m occur, and a nonzero coefficient of z_k^m requires l_k=b/m. The larger eigenvalue satisfies l_max>=beta>b/2>=b/m, so k is the index of the smaller eigenvalue: l_min=b/m, l_max=2beta-b/m and p_m=C z_min^m with C!=0. This is alternative (e2). If l_min>b/2, no integer m>=2 satisfies m l_min=b, so Theta is flat and (e1) holds. The alternatives are exhaustive by the flat/non-flat dichotomy and exclusive because (e1) gives vanishing on a neighbourhood of P while (e2) has a nonzero Taylor coefficient. Analyticity is not used; the conclusion concerns the leading Taylor term and does not assert that Theta equals that monomial near P.

#### Remark (the local equations do not force DW(P) to be singular)

Let k=beta-b/2=(beta+2)/2 and put Psi=-kxy, U=(-Psi_y,Psi_x)=(kx,-ky), W=beta X+U=((2beta-b/2)x,(b/2)y), Omega=0, Theta=y^2. Then -Lap Psi=0=Omega, (P1) holds since Omega=0 and Theta_x=0, and W.grad(y^2)=(b/2)y(2y)=by^2, so (P2) holds. At the equilibrium 0, Theta, grad Theta and Omega vanish and DW(0)=diag(2beta-b/2,b/2) is positive definite, with det DW(0)>0; this is an instance of (e2) with m=2. The example violates the oddness of Theta in y, the condition a0!=0 and the sublinearity of U, so it is not a class A' profile and makes no existence claim; it shows only that the local equations and the vanishing conditions at P are compatible with a nonsingular linearization.

#### Scope and dependencies

Only elementary ODE existence and uniqueness, the contraction mapping principle, the divergence theorem and the planar Poincare-Bendixson theorem (no-equilibrium form) are used; no Poisson inverse, polynomial tail bound or vorticity sign enters (a) and (b). The strict temperature sign in (a) is indispensable to the argument: a zero curve of Theta in the upper half-plane would invalidate both the horizontal-axis contradiction and the localization of the backward limit set. Numerical sign checks at sample points do not verify either hypothesis. Parts (d) and (e) use only Taylor's theorem at P, symmetric-matrix diagonalization and the local backward contraction estimate near a positive definite source, together with the complete flow and (P1), (P2) on B_P for the extension of (e1) to the basin; the parity, normalization, canonical-velocity condition and polynomial bounds enter only through the existence of P in (c).

### A.26 Proposition 25 (stagnation points on the horizontal axis)

Report statement: see Proposition 25 in Section 3.

Proof. Throughout, beta > 2, a = beta + 2, b = beta - 2, sigma = sign(a0), V(x) = W1(x, 0), tau(x) = Theta_y(x, 0).
The flow Phi_s of W exists for all real s (Appendix A.25, standing facts), and Theta(Phi_s X) = e^(b s) Theta(X).

(a) By the parities, W1 is odd in x and even in y, W2 is even in x and odd in y, and Theta is even in x and odd in y.
So V is odd, tau is even, and on the axis Theta(x, 0) = 0, Theta_x(x, 0) = 0, Theta_xx(x, 0) = 0, W2(x, 0) = 0 and
d_y W1(x, 0) = 0. Differentiating (P2), W1 Theta_x + W2 Theta_y = b Theta, in y and putting y = 0 gives
V tau' + d_y W2(x, 0) tau = b tau. Since div W = 2 beta and d_x W1(x, 0) = V'(x), d_y W2(x, 0) = 2 beta - V'(x), so
V tau' = (V' - (2 beta - b)) tau = (V' - a) tau. DW(0) = diag(a, b) (Section 2.4) gives V'(0) = a, and tau(0) = a0.
U = o(|X|) gives V(x) = beta x + o(x), so V(x) > 0 for all large x. On an interval J without zeros of V,
(tau/V)' = tau'/V - tau V'/V^2 = -a tau/V^2 = -(a/V)(tau/V), which integrates to
tau(x) = tau(x_J) (V(x)/V(x_J)) exp(-a int_{x_J}^x du/V(u)); this includes the zero solution and does not divide by
tau. As J is connected, V(x)/V(x_J) > 0, so a solution that is not identically zero on J has constant sign there.
Since V'(0) = a > 0 and the zero set of V is closed, V > 0 on (0, x1); tau(0) = a0, continuity gives sigma tau > 0 just
to the right of 0, and the formula gives sigma tau > 0 on [0, x1) (tau is even, so also on (-x1, 0]).

(b) Write h = x - x0 and V = h v1 with v1 smooth, v1(x0) = l != 0. Then 1/V = 1/(l h) + g with g smooth near x0. Fix a
primitive G of g on a neighbourhood of x0 and put phi = |v1| e^(-a G), smooth and positive. On each side of x0 the
formula of (a) gives tau = K_(+-) |h|^p phi with p = 1 - a/l and side constants K_(+-) (the signs of h and v1 are
absorbed into the constants). If one of K_(+-) is nonzero, tau is not flat at x0: for an integer N > p the expression
is not O(|h|^N) on that side. So tau(x0 + h) = c_n h^n + O(|h|^(n+1)) with c_n != 0 for some n >= 0, and comparison
with K |h|^p phi forces p = n, K_+ phi(x0) = c_n and K_- phi(x0) = (-1)^n c_n; in particular tau is nonzero on both
sides for small h != 0, so the hypothesis "tau does not vanish identically on any neighbourhood of x0" is exactly the
condition that one, hence both, constants are nonzero. Now p = n reads (n - 1) l = -a. The case n = 1 is impossible
(a != 0). If n = 0 then l = a and tau(x0) != 0: this is (b1), and DW(x0, 0) = diag(V'(x0), 2 beta - V'(x0)) =
diag(a, b) (diagonal by the parities), grad Theta(x0, 0) = (0, tau(x0)). If n = k >= 2 then l = -a/(k - 1) < 0 and tau
vanishes to order exactly k: this is (b2). On the axis grad Theta = (0, tau) and the Hessian of Theta has entries
Theta_xx = 0, Theta_xy = tau', Theta_yy = 0 (Theta_yy is odd in y), so Theta, grad Theta and D^2 Theta vanish at
(x0, 0) when k >= 2. The two cases are exclusive (l > 0 in (b1), l < 0 in (b2)).

(c) Flatness at every degenerate zero. Differentiating V tau' = (V' - a) tau n times gives
   sum_(i=0)^n C(n, i) V^(i) tau^(n+1-i) = sum_(i=0)^n C(n, i) V^(i+1) tau^(n-i) - a tau^(n).
Let x0 be a zero of V with V'(x0) = l and suppose tau^(j)(x0) = 0 for all j < n. At x0 the left side reduces to the
term i = 1, n l tau^(n)(x0) (the term i = 0 contains V(x0) = 0, the terms i >= 2 contain tau^(j)(x0) with j < n), and
the right side reduces to l tau^(n)(x0) - a tau^(n)(x0). Hence ((n - 1) l + a) tau^(n)(x0) = 0. If l = 0 this says
tau^(n)(x0) = 0, and induction on n (starting at n = 0) shows that tau is flat at x0.
Outgoing side. Let S be (x0, x0 + e) with V > 0 on S, or (x0 - e, x0) with V < 0 on S, and x_S in S. The backward
orbit x(t), t <= 0, of the axis flow x' = V(x) through x_S stays in S and tends to x0 as t -> -infinity. Along it
d/dt log|V(x(t))| = V'(x(t)), and |V'(x(t))| <= eps for t <= -T_eps since V'(x0) = 0; integrating backward from -T_eps,
|V(x(t))| >= c_eps e^(-eps |t|) for t <= -T_eps. The formula of (a) along the orbit reads
tau(x(t)) = tau(x_S) (V(x(t))/V(x_S)) e^(-a t). If tau(x_S) != 0, then |tau(x(t))| >= c'_eps e^((a - eps)|t|), which
tends to infinity for 0 < eps < a, against continuity of tau at x0. So tau = 0 on S.
(On an incoming side the forward orbit stays in the side and the analogous estimate |tau| <= C_eps |x - x0|^(a/eps)
gives flatness again; this is contained in the first part.)

(d) If V has a positive zero, x1 > 0 exists (V'(0) = a > 0 excludes zeros near 0 and the zero set is closed), V > 0
on (0, x1) and V'(x1) <= 0. By (a), sigma tau > 0 on [0, x1), so tau does not vanish identically near x1. If
V'(x1) != 0, then V'(x1) < 0, case (b1) is excluded and (b2) holds. If V'(x1) = 0, tau is flat at x1 by (c). In
both cases W(x1, 0) = (V(x1), 0) = 0 and Theta = Theta_x = 0, Theta_y = tau(x1) = 0 at (x1, 0).

(e) In the first case of (d), V'(x1) = l < 0, so V < 0 on (x1, x1 + e) for some e > 0; V > 0 for large x, so V has
zeros in (x1, infinity), and since x1 is isolated and the zero set is closed there is a smallest one, x2, with V < 0
on (x1, x2) and V'(x2) >= 0. Write tau(x1 + h) = c_k h^k + O(|h|^(k+1)), c_k != 0. Since sigma tau > 0 for small h < 0,
sign(c_k) = sigma (-1)^k, so sigma (-1)^k tau > 0 for small h > 0, and by (a) on all of (x1, x2). If V'(x2) = 0, the
interval (x2 - e', x2) carries V < 0 and is an outgoing side (motion under x' = V is to the left, away from x2), so
tau = 0 there by (c), a contradiction. So V'(x2) > 0 and (b) gives (b1): V'(x2) = a and tau(x2) != 0; by continuity
sigma (-1)^k tau(x2) > 0. At P2 = (x2, 0), DW(P2) = diag(a, b) with a, b > 0. For the reversed field near P2,
d/dt |Z|^2 = 2 Z . (-W(P2 + Z)) <= -b |Z|^2 on a small ball, so that ball lies in the backward basin of P2, and the basin
is the union of its forward images under Phi_t, hence open. The same holds at the origin. A backward orbit has at most
one limit, so the two basins are disjoint.

(f) Since Theta(P) = 0 and grad Theta(P) = 0, Taylor's theorem gives |Theta(P + Z)| <= M |Z|^2 for |Z| small. For t
large, |Theta(X)| = e^(b t) |Theta(Phi_(-t) X)| <= M C^2 e^((b - 2 mu) t), which tends to 0 when mu > b/2; so
Theta(X) = 0. (At mu = b/2 the argument gives only a bound.) In the first case of (d), DW(P1) is diagonal by the
parities with entries V'(x1) = l < 0 and lambda_u = 2 beta - l > 0 (div W = 2 beta), so P1 is a hyperbolic saddle
with unstable direction e_y. The local unstable manifold theorem gives a locally embedded C^1 curve through P1 tangent
to e_y; near P1 write it as (x1 + h(y), y), h(0) = h'(0) = 0, so that W2 = lambda_u y + o(|y|) along it. Its images
under the complete flow form the global unstable manifold W^u(P1) = {X : Phi_(-t) X -> P1 as t -> infinity}, an
injectively immersed C^1 one-dimensional manifold (no global embeddedness or graph property is claimed). Every X in
W^u(P1) lies on the local curve after a finite backward time, and integrating the scalar equation for y gives, for
every 0 < eps < lambda_u, |Phi_(-t) X - P1| <= C_(X,eps) e^(-(lambda_u - eps) t) for all t >= 0 (the constant
absorbs the initial finite time interval). Choose 0 < eps < lambda_u - b/2 (possible since lambda_u > 2 beta > b/2);
the first statement gives Theta = 0 on W^u(P1). The reflection R(x, y) = (x, -y) satisfies W(R X) = R W(X) (W1 even
in y, W2 odd in y), so R Phi_s = Phi_s R, and R fixes P1; hence R preserves W^u(P1). W^u(P1) minus P1 consists of two
orbits, tangent at P1 to +e_y and -e_y. The horizontal axis is invariant under the flow, and by uniqueness an orbit
starting off the axis never meets it in finite time; so one orbit stays in y > 0 and the other in y < 0, and R
exchanges them. The orbit in y > 0 is a nonempty subset of the zero set of Theta in the open upper half-plane, with
P1 in its closure.
In the second case of (d), V(x1) = V'(x1) = 0, so DW(P1) = diag(0, 2 beta) by the parities and div W = 2 beta, and
Theta(P1) = 0, grad Theta(P1) = 0 by (d). The reversed field -W has eigenvalues 0 (eigenvector e_x) and -2 beta
(eigenvector e_y) at P1. Fix mu with b/2 < mu < 2 beta. The strong stable manifold theorem for an equilibrium with the
spectral gap -2 beta < -mu < 0 (which allows the zero eigenvalue in the complementary direction; for example Dutilleul,
arXiv:1804.06126, Theorem 1.1, with gamma = -mu) gives a C^1 local curve through P1, tangent to e_y, consisting of the
points whose orbits under -W stay in a small neighbourhood of P1 and converge to P1 at the rate e^(-mu t); by this
characterization and W(R X) = R W(X) it is invariant under R. Every point X of the curve satisfies
|Phi_(-t) X - P1| <= C_X e^(-mu t), so Theta(X) = 0 by the first statement; transport carries the vanishing to the
forward images Phi_t of the curve, and their union is the strong unstable curve of (f). Its two branches are single
orbits, tangent at P1 to +e_y and -e_y, and stay in the open half-planes by invariance of the axis, as before. This
curve need not contain every point whose backward orbit converges to P1 (slower convergence along the zero eigenvalue
is not excluded).

Hypotheses used: smoothness, the A1 parities, (P2), div W = 2 beta, U = o(|X|), DW(0) = diag(a, b) and the complete
flow. (P1), (P3), the canonical-velocity condition beyond these consequences and the polynomial bounds are not used.

### A.27 Proposition 26 (formal centre jets exist for every beta > 2 and a0 != 0)

Report statement: see Proposition 26 in Section 3.

Proof. Throughout, beta > 2, a = beta + 2 > 0, b = beta - 2 > 0, a0 != 0 and L = a x d_x + b y d_y. For a polynomial
(or smooth) function F we write F = O_k if F(X) = O(|X|^k) near 0; for smooth F this is equivalent to the vanishing of
the Taylor polynomial of F of degree k - 1, and then every derivative of order l is O_(k-l) and x F_x, y F_y are O_k.
"Odd-odd" means odd in x and odd in the second variable.

Step 1 (polynomial generating functions). Let G be a polynomial in (x, eta), odd-odd, with G = x eta + O_4. Then
A = G_(x eta) = 1 + O_2, so A > 0 on a disc around 0, and the map (x, eta) -> (x, G_x(x, eta)) has Jacobian determinant A;
by the inverse function theorem it is a diffeomorphism of a smaller disc D_G onto a neighbourhood N_G of 0, with smooth
inverse (x, y) -> (x, eta(x, y)), eta = y + O_3 (since G_x = eta + O_3). On D_G the hypotheses of Proposition 23(b)
hold (A > 0, the coordinates are one-to-one), so the fields Theta = a0 eta, Psi = S(x, eta) with
S = beta x G_x + b eta G_eta - 2 beta G, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), Omega = -Lap Psi and W = beta X + U are smooth on N_G and
satisfy W.grad Theta = b Theta identically (Proposition 23(b) defines W by explicit formulas and proves
U = W - beta X = (-Psi_y, Psi_x); so the W of Proposition 23(b) is the W used here). Parity: G_x is even in x and odd in
eta, so eta(x, y) is even in x and odd in y; hence Theta is even in x and odd in y, and S(x, eta(x, y)) is odd-odd, so
Psi and Omega are odd-odd, W1 is odd in x and even in y, W2 is even in x and odd in y: the A1 parities. Since
S = (beta + b - 2 beta) x eta + O_4 = -2 x eta + O_4 and eta = y + O_3, Psi = -2 x y + O_4, so Psi_xy(0) = -2,
U = (2x, -2y) + O_3, W = (a x, b y) + O_3, Omega = O_2; and Theta = a0 y + O_3, so Theta_y(0) = a0. Put
R_G = W.grad Omega + Omega - Theta_x, the residual of (P1) on N_G. R_G is odd-odd (each term is), so its Taylor
polynomial contains only odd-odd monomials, all of even total degree. For G = x eta the fields are Theta = a0 y,
Psi = -2xy, Omega = 0, W = (a x, b y), and R_G = 0.

Step 2 (effect of one homogeneous term). Let G be as in Step 1 and H a homogeneous odd-odd polynomial of degree N >= 4,
G' = G + H, and compare the fields at the same point (x, y) of N_G intersected with N_G'. Let eta, eta' be the two
inverse charts. From G_x(x, eta') + H_x(x, eta') = y = G_x(x, eta) and the mean value theorem,
A(x, eta*)(eta' - eta) = -H_x(x, eta'), with eta* between eta and eta'. So eta' - eta = O_(N-1); then
H_x(x, eta') = H_x(x, y) + O_(N+1) (H_x is homogeneous of degree N - 1 and eta' - y = O_3) and A(x, eta*) = 1 + O_2,
hence eta' - eta = -H_x(x, y) + O_(N+1). Therefore
   Theta' - Theta = -a0 H_x + O_(N+1).
For the stream function, Psi' - Psi = [S(x, eta') - S(x, eta)] + [beta x H_x + b eta H_eta - 2 beta H](x, eta'). By
Taylor's formula in the second variable, S(x, eta') - S(x, eta) = S_eta(x, eta)(eta' - eta) + O(|S_(eta eta)| |eta' - eta|^2)
= (-2x + O_3)(-H_x + O_(N+1)) + O_(2N) = 2 x H_x + O_(N+2), and the second bracket equals
beta x H_x + b y H_y - 2 beta H evaluated at (x, y), up to O_(N+2). Hence
   Psi' - Psi = (L - 2 beta) H + O_(N+2),
since 2 x H_x + beta x H_x = a x H_x. Both differences are smooth, so by the remark at the start
Omega' - Omega = -Lap (L - 2 beta) H + O_N, W' - W = (-d_y, d_x)(L - 2 beta) H + O_(N+1) = O_(N-1) and
(Theta' - Theta)_x = -a0 H_xx + O_N. Now
   R_G' - R_G = (W' - W).grad Omega' + W.grad(Omega' - Omega) + (Omega' - Omega) - (Theta' - Theta)_x.
The first term is O_(N-1) O_1 = O_N (Omega' = O_2). In the second, W = (a x, b y) + O_3 and Omega' - Omega = O_(N-2), so
W.grad(Omega' - Omega) = L(Omega' - Omega) + O_N = -L Lap (L - 2 beta) H + O_N. Altogether
   R_G' - R_G = T_N H + O_N,  T_N H := -(L + 1) Lap (L - 2 beta) H + a0 H_xx,
where T_N H is homogeneous of degree N - 2. Consequently the Taylor parts of R of degree < N - 2 are unchanged, and the
degree N - 2 part changes by T_N H. Applied with H of degree N >= k + 3, this also shows that the Taylor parts of degree
<= k of R, Theta, Psi, Omega and W depend only on the homogeneous parts of G of degree <= k + 2 (for Theta, Psi, W even
less).

Step 3 (the matrix of T_N). For H = x^i y^j with i, j odd, i + j = N, put M = a i + b j. Since L x^k y^l =
(a k + b l) x^k y^l,
   T_N x^i y^j = i(i - 1)[a0 - (M - 2 beta)(M - 2a + 1)] x^(i-2) y^j - j(j - 1)(M - 2 beta)(M - 2b + 1) x^i y^(j-2):
indeed (L - 2 beta) multiplies by M - 2 beta, Lap gives i(i - 1) x^(i-2) y^j + j(j - 1) x^i y^(j-2), on which L + 1
acts by M - 2a + 1 and M - 2b + 1 respectively, and a0 H_xx = a0 i(i - 1) x^(i-2) y^j. Let P_N be the span of the
odd-odd monomials of degree N other than x^(N-1) y, i.e. x^i y^(N-i) with i = 1, 3, ..., N - 3 (dimension (N - 2)/2), and
Q_(N-2) the span of the odd-odd monomials of degree N - 2, x^k y^(N-2-k) with k = 1, 3, ..., N - 3 (also dimension
(N - 2)/2). T_N maps P_N into Q_(N-2) (both outputs are odd-odd of degree N - 2; for i = 1 the first term vanishes). In
the bases ordered by the exponent of x, column i has the entry -j(j - 1)(M - 2 beta)(M - 2b + 1) in row i and (for
i >= 3) an entry in row i - 2, so the matrix is upper triangular. For i <= N - 3 we have j = N - i >= 3, so j(j - 1) > 0,
M - 2 beta = a(i - 1) + b(j - 1) >= 2b > 0 (using 2 beta = a + b) and M - 2b + 1 = a i + b(j - 2) + 1 > 0. All diagonal
entries are negative, so T_N : P_N -> Q_(N-2) is a bijection, for every a0. (For N = 4 the single entry is
-6(2b)(a + b + 1) = -12 b (2 beta + 1).)

Step 4 (induction). Fix f_2, f_3, .... Let G_2 = x eta. Suppose G_(N-2) = x eta + H_4 + ... + H_(N-2) (N >= 4 even)
has been constructed, odd-odd, with R_(G_(N-2)) = O_(N-2), i.e. its Taylor parts of degree <= N - 4 vanish (for N = 4
this is vacuous). Let r be the degree N - 2 Taylor part of R_(G_(N-2)), an element of Q_(N-2) by Step 1. By Step 2, for
H = f_(N/2) x^(N-1) y + H~ with H~ in P_N, the degree N - 2 part of R_(G_(N-2) + H) is r + f_(N/2) T_N(x^(N-1) y) + T_N H~,
and its lower parts vanish. By Step 3 there is exactly one H~ in P_N making this zero. Put H_N = f_(N/2) x^(N-1) y + H~
and G_N = G_(N-2) + H_N; then R_(G_N) = O_N. This defines the series G = x eta + sum H_(2n), with the prescribed
coefficients f_n. By the last sentence of Step 2, for each k the degree <= k Taylor parts of Theta, Psi, Omega, W and
R computed from G_N do not depend on N once N >= k + 2; these stable jets define the formal fields of the statement,
which therefore satisfy (P2) exactly at every degree (Step 1) and (P1) at every degree (R_(G_N) = O_N for all N), and
have the A1 parities, Theta_y(0) = a0 and Psi_xy(0) = -2 (Step 1). For even N the truncation G_N defines smooth fields on N_(G_N)
with (P2) exact and R = O_N, which is the statement about truncations. For odd N the truncation through degree N equals
G_(N-1) and in general R is not O_N: at beta = 3, a0 = 70, f_2 = 1 (so d = 0 and G_4 = x eta + x^3 eta) the exact fields
are Theta = 70y/(1 + 3x^2), Psi = (-2x + 4x^3) y/(1 + 3x^2) and R = 720 x^3 y (16x^4 + 19x^2 + 9)/(1 + 3x^2)^5
= 6480 x^3 y + O_6.
Uniqueness: let G and G' be two such series with the same f_n, and suppose they first differ at degree N, with
H = H'_N - H_N. Let G_N and G'_N = G_N + H be their truncations at degree N. By Step 2 the degree N - 2 Taylor parts of
R computed from G_N and from G agree (the later terms have degree >= N + 2), so they vanish, and likewise for G'_N.
Hence T_N H = 0 by Step 2. H has no x^(N-1) y term (equal f_(N/2)), so H is in P_N and H = 0 by Step 3, a contradiction.

Step 5 (the vorticity coefficient). Let H_4 = p x^3 eta + d x eta^3. By Step 2 applied to G = x eta and H = H_4,
Theta = a0 y - a0(3p x^2 y + d y^3) + O_5, so the x^2 y coefficient of Theta is b1 = -3 a0 p. Write Omega = g x y + O_4.
The degree 2 part of (P1) with W = (a x, b y) + O_3 reads (a + b + 1) g x y = 2 b1 x y, so g = 2 b1/(2 beta + 1)
= -6 a0 p/(2 beta + 1), which is nonzero when p = f_2 != 0. (For general beta, Psi = -2xy + 2a p x^3 y + 2b d x y^3 + O_6,
the degree 2 residual is [6(a0 - D) p - 12 b (2 beta + 1) d] x y with D = 2(beta + 2)(2 beta + 1), so
d = (a0 - D) p/(2b(2 beta + 1)) and h_10 = 2a p, h_01 = 2b d = -(1 - a0/D) h_10, the relation of Proposition 17; at
beta = 3, d = p(a0 - 70)/14.)

Step 6 (consequence and comparison). Since the construction works for every beta > 2 and a0 != 0, with an arbitrary
sequence f_n, the Taylor coefficient identities at the centre are formally consistent for every (beta, a0); any argument
excluding some (beta, a0) must use more than coefficientwise compatibility, for example convergence or estimates,
realization by actual solutions, the canonical inverse and its moment conditions, or the global and far-field structure.
Put F(x) = G_eta(x, 0) = x + sum f_n x^(2n-1). Since eta(x, 0) = 0, eta_y(x, 0) = 1/A(x, 0) = 1/F'(x) and
S_eta(x, 0) = beta x F' + (b - 2 beta) F = beta x F' - a F, so Psi_y(x, 0) = beta x - a F(x)/F'(x). Hence the coefficient
h_(n-1,0) of x^(2n-1) y in Psi equals 2a(n - 1) f_n + C_n with C_n a polynomial in f_2, ..., f_(n-1) (h_10 = 2a f_2,
h_20 = 4a f_3 - 6a f_2^2): with the lower coefficients fixed, f_n and h_(n-1,0) determine each other by an affine bijection.
The formal existence also follows from the coefficient equations behind Proposition 17, run forwards: with
t_ij the coefficient of x^(2i) y^(2j+1) in Theta and h_ij that of x^(2i+1) y^(2j+1) in Psi, the equations are
L_ij t_ij + a0(2i + 1) h_ij + P_ij = 0 (i + j >= 1) and M_ij(-A_i h_(i+1,j) - B_j h_(i,j+1)) + Q_ij = 2(i + 1) t_(i+1,j),
with P_ij, Q_ij depending only on earlier blocks; prescribing h_(n,0), one computes h_(n-1,1), ..., h_(0,n) by the recursion
displayed there and then the t_ij of the block. Its divisors L_(i+1,j) >= 2a, M_ij >= 2 beta + 1 and B_j >= 6 do not
involve a0, and the base block (L_00 = 0) is never divided by. The present proof adds that the truncations give exact
solutions of (P2). Exact symbolic
computations (degrees N = 4 and 6, rational beta and a0) confirm that the linear part of the degree N - 2 residual in
H_N equals T_N H and that the restricted matrix is upper triangular with the stated diagonal.
Not proved: convergence of the series, realization of a prescribed formal jet by an actual local or global solution,
compatibility with the canonical global inverse or its moment constraints, or any global statement. QED

### A.28 Proposition 27 (no finite member of the logarithmic generating family solves (P1) near the centre)

Report statement: see Proposition 27 in Section 3.

Proof. Throughout, beta = 3, a = 5, b = 1, d = 1 - e^(-alpha) in (0, 1), and the notation of the statement is used.
Primes denote derivatives in x. Orders of meromorphic functions such as h_c, j_c below always refer to the finite sums,
not to single patches; cancellations between patches are allowed.

#### Step 1 (local chart and centre)
E >= 1, 1 - d E^(-1/6) >= 1 - d = e^(-alpha) > 0 and R_l^2 + x^2, R_l^2 + eta^2 > 0, so E^(1/3), t, w, xi_l, zeta_l and
the Gaussian factors are real analytic on R^2 and even in x and in eta. Hence G = x eta F(x, eta) with F real analytic
and even in each variable. At the origin E = 1, t = -log(e^(-alpha))/alpha = 1, w = xi_l = zeta_l = 0 and the Gaussians
equal 1, so F(0, 0) = P(1, 0) + sum_l Q_l(0, 0) = h and
   G = h x eta + O((|x| + |eta|)^4),   G_x = h eta + O((|x| + |eta|)^3),   G_(x eta)(0, 0) = h > 0.
The analytic implicit function theorem gives a unique real analytic eta(x, y) near 0 with G_x(x, eta(x, y)) = y. Since
G_x is even in x and odd in eta, uniqueness gives eta even in x and odd in y, and eta = y/h + O(|X|^3). Proposition 23(b)
applies on this neighbourhood: (P2), (P3) and U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x) hold identically. In the mixed variables Psi is odd in
x and in eta, so Psi(X) is odd in x and in y, Theta is even in x and odd in y, Omega is odd-odd, and U has the A1 parity.
Finally Psi = (3h + h - 6h) x eta + O(4) = -2h x eta + O(4) = -2xy + O(|X|^4) and Theta = (a0/h) y + O(|X|^3). (These
centre facts are also in the source derivation of the centre expansion; the rest of the proof uses only the local
inverse and A(0) = h > 0.)

#### Step 2 (expansion in eta on the horizontal axis)
Fix real x near 0 and put u = 1 + x^2. Since E = u + (eta/s)^6, E depends on eta only from order six, so
E^(1/3) = u^(1/3) + O(eta^6), t = t(u) + O(eta^6) with t(u) = -log(1 - d u^(-1/6))/alpha, and
w = (eta/s)^2 u^(-1/3) + O(eta^8). Put p(t) = P(t, 0) and q(t) = P_w(t, 0). For a patch, exp(-(x^2 + eta^2)/L^2) =
exp(-(u - 1)/L^2)(1 - eta^2/L^2 + O(eta^4)), zeta = eta^2/R^2 + O(eta^4) and xi = (u - 1)/(R^2 + u - 1). Hence
   G = eta g(x) + eta^3 k(x) + O(eta^5),
   g = x u^(1/3) [p(t) + h_c(u)],   k = x q(t)/s^2 + x u^(1/3) j_c(u),                                       (28.1)
   h_c(u) = sum_l exp(-(u - 1)/L_l^2) Q_l((u - 1)/(R_l^2 + u - 1), 0),
   j_c(u) = sum_l exp(-(u - 1)/L_l^2) [ R_l^(-2) (d_2 Q_l)((u - 1)/(R_l^2 + u - 1), 0)
                                        - L_l^(-2) Q_l((u - 1)/(R_l^2 + u - 1), 0) ],
with t = t(u), d_2 the derivative in the second variable, and an analytic remainder. The functions h_c, j_c are finite
sums of entire functions times polynomials in (u - 1)/(R_l^2 + u - 1); they are meromorphic on C with poles only at the
real points u = 1 - R_l^2. A pole at u = 0 is possible exactly when some R_l = 1.

#### Step 3 (the coefficient of y in (P1))
Let A = g'. Then A(0) = G_(x eta)(0, 0) = h > 0, so A > 0 for real x near 0, and G_x = eta A + eta^3 k' + O(eta^5).
Inversion gives eta = y/A - k' y^3/A^4 + O(y^5). The mixed stream function is
   Psi = 3x G_x + eta G_eta - 6G = eta (3xA - 5g) + eta^3 (3xk' - 3k) + O(eta^5),
and substitution of the inverse gives, since -(3xA - 5g) k'/A^4 + (3xk' - 3k)/A^3 = 5gk'/A^4 - 3k/A^3,
   Psi = y H + y^3 K3 + O(y^5),   H = 3x - 5g/A,   K3 = 5gk'/A^4 - 3k/A^3.                                   (28.2)
All remainders are analytic, so they may be differentiated. Hence U1 = -Psi_y = -H + O(y^2), U2 = Psi_x = yH' + O(y^3),
Omega = y v + O(y^3) with v = -H'' - 6K3, Theta = a0 y/A + O(y^3), Theta_x = -a0 y A'/A^2 + O(y^3),
W1 = 3x - H + O(y^2) = 5g/A + O(y^2) and W2 = y (3 + H') + O(y^3). The coefficient of y in
W1 Omega_x + W2 Omega_y + Omega - Theta_x is therefore
   (5g/A) v' + (4 + H') v + a0 A'/A^2 = 0,                                                                  (28.3)
which holds for real x in an interval (0, x0) if (P1) holds on a neighbourhood of 0. The highest power of 1/A in (28.3)
is the sixth (from (5g/A) times the derivative of 5gk'/A^4), so A^6 (28.3) has no denominator A.

#### Step 4 (continuation to the point x = i)
Let S = {u : Im u > 0}. On S take u^(1/6) = exp((log u)/6) with arg u in (0, pi), so arg u^(1/6) is in (0, pi/6);
x = sqrt(u - 1) with arg(u - 1) in (0, pi), which tends to the positive root for real u > 1 and to i as u -> 0; and,
since arg u^(-1/6) is in (-pi/6, 0), 1 - d u^(-1/6) has positive imaginary part on S, and its logarithm is taken with
argument in (0, pi). With these branches t(u), x, u^(1/3), p(t), q(t), h_c, j_c are holomorphic on S, x-derivatives
are computed as d_x = 2x d_u, and derivatives of t only add denominators 1 - d u^(-1/6), which do not vanish on S. Thus
I(u) := A^6 times the left side of (28.3) is holomorphic on S. All ingredients extend holomorphically across the real
interval 1 < u < 1 + x0^2, where they coincide with the real functions of Steps 2 and 3; I vanishes on that interval,
hence on a complex neighbourhood of it (identity theorem), hence on the connected set S. Now choose eps > 0 with
eps < d^6 and eps below every positive pole 1 - R_l^2. For 0 < u < eps the boundary values are u^(1/6) > 0,
x = i sqrt(1 - u), and 1 - d u^(-1/6) < 0 is approached from positive imaginary part, so the logarithm extends
holomorphically across each such point with argument near pi; h_c and j_c are analytic there. So I extends
holomorphically across (0, eps) and vanishes there. In each case below A != 0 on a shorter interval (0, eps'), so (28.3)
itself holds there for the continued ingredients. From now on all limits are u -> 0+ along this boundary interval, not
the physical origin u = 1. Write Lu = log u (real, negative), z = u^(1/6), sigma = 1/Lu and Du = u d/du. Since
1 - d/z = -(d/z)(1 - z/d),
   t = Lu/(6 alpha) - (log d)/alpha - i pi/alpha - log(1 - z/d)/alpha = 1/(6 alpha sigma) + c(z),              (28.4)
with c holomorphic near z = 0.

#### Step 5 (factored forms and the transport multiplier)
Functions of (z, sigma) holomorphic near (0, 0) are evaluated on the curve (z, sigma) = (u^(1/6), 1/log u). On such
compositions, since u dz/du = z/6 and u d sigma/du = -sigma^2,
   Du = (z/6) d_z - sigma^2 d_sigma,   d_x = 2x d_u = (2x/u) Du,
   d_x^2 = 2 d_u + 4x^2 d_u^2 = (4x^2/u^2)(Du^2 - Du) + (2/u) Du.                                          (28.5)
If p has degree n >= 1 and leading coefficient p_n, then by (28.4)
   p(t) = Lu^n b_p(z, sigma),   b_p holomorphic near (0, 0),   b_p(z, 0) = c_p := p_n/(6 alpha)^n != 0,        (28.6)
since t^j = sigma^(-j) (1/(6 alpha) + sigma c(z))^j. If q != 0 has degree m, likewise q(t) = Lu^m b_q(z, sigma) with
b_q(z, 0) = c_q := q_m/(6 alpha)^m != 0. An analytic function of u near 0 is an analytic function of z (of z^6), and a
meromorphic one is an integer power of u times an analytic unit. Every derivative below is computed from such explicit
factorizations by (28.5); no derivative bound is obtained by differentiating an unspecified O-term.
Put f = p(t) + h_c(u), so g = x u^(1/3) f, ell = Du log(u^(1/3) f) = 1/3 + Du f/f and N = u + 2(u - 1) ell. Wherever
f != 0 and N != 0,
   A = u^(-2/3) f N,   g/A = xu/N,   H = 3x - 5xu/N,                                                       (28.7)
because A = u^(1/3) f + (2x^2/u) Du(u^(1/3) f) = u^(1/3) f (1 + 2(u - 1) ell/u). Put
   L_H[v] = (5g/A) v' + (4 + H') v,
so that, with k = k_q + k_j, k_q = x q(t)/s^2, k_j = x u^(1/3) j_c and K3 = K3_q + K3_j accordingly (K3 is linear in k),
(28.3) reads L_H[-H''] + L_H[-6 K3_q] + L_H[-6 K3_j] + a0 A'/A^2 = 0. The operator is linear in v; its coefficients
depend on g only. Suppose that ell -> ell0 != 0 and Du ell -> 0 as u -> 0+ (both hold in each case below, from the
factored forms). Then N -> -2 ell0, Du N -> 0, and
   H' = 3 - 5 [u/N + 2x^2 (1/N - Du N/N^2)] -> 3 - 5/ell0,   (5g/A)(2x/u) = 10x^2/N -> 5/ell0.               (28.8)
Hence, for v = C u^rho Lu^m (1 + o(1)) with C != 0 and Du v/v -> rho (both established from a factored form),
   L_H[v]/v = (10x^2/N)(Du v/v) + 4 + H' -> Lambda(ell0, rho) := 7 + 5(rho - 1)/ell0.                         (28.9)
The cases below are exhaustive: p nonconstant with h_c holomorphic at 0; p constant; p nonconstant with h_c having a pole
at 0.

#### Step 6 (Case 1: p nonconstant, h_c holomorphic at u = 0)
Let n = deg p >= 1. Then f = Lu^n b~(z, sigma) with b~ = b_p + sigma^n h_c(z^6) holomorphic and b~(z, 0) = c_p. Hence
ell = 1/3 + n sigma + Du b~/b~, and since b~(z, 0) is constant, d_z b~ is divisible by sigma, so
   ell = 1/3 + n sigma + z sigma ell_1(z, sigma) + sigma^2 ell_2(z, sigma),   ell_1, ell_2 holomorphic.
So ell0 = 1/3, Du ell -> 0, N(0, 0) = -2/3 and 1/N is holomorphic near (0, 0); at sigma = 0 it equals 3/(5u - 2), and
its coefficient of sigma at z = 0 is 9n/2. Taylor expansion gives the exact representation
   H = 3x + (15/2) xu - (45/2) n xu sigma + R1 + R2 + R3,
   R1 = xu sigma^2 r1(z, sigma),   R2 = xu z sigma r2(z, sigma),   R3 = xu^2 r3(z, sigma),
with r1, r2, r3 holomorphic and bounded with all fixed-order derivatives on a small polydisc (x = i sqrt(1 - u) is
analytic near u = 0). Using (28.5) and the cancellation (Du^2 - Du)(u Q) = u (Du^2 Q + Du Q),
   R1'' = O(u^(-1) |sigma|^3) + O(u^(-5/6) |sigma|^2) + O(|sigma|^2),
   R1''' = O(u^(-2) |sigma|^3) + O(u^(-11/6) |sigma|^2) + O(u^(-1) |sigma|^2),
   R2'' = O(u^(-5/6) |sigma|),   R2''' = O(u^(-11/6) |sigma|),   R3'' = O(1),   R3''' = O(u^(-1));
derivatives falling on x add only terms within these bounds. Every second-derivative remainder is o(u^(-1) sigma^2) and
every third-derivative remainder is o(u^(-2) sigma^2), since u^e |log u|^r -> 0 for e > 0. Direct differentiation gives
   d_x^2 (xu/Lu) = 6x (1/Lu - 1/Lu^2) + (4x^3/u)(-1/Lu^2 + 2/Lu^3),
and 3x + (15/2) xu has bounded derivatives. Therefore
   H'' = 90 n x^3/(u Lu^2) (1 + o(1)),   H''' = -180 n x^4/(u^2 Lu^2) (1 + o(1)),
   H' -> -12,   5g/A = -(15/2) xu (1 + o(1)).                                                             (28.10)
So v_H := -H'' has v_H'/v_H = -(2x/u)(1 + o(1)), and, as x^2 -> -1,
   L_H[v_H]/v_H -> (-(15/2) xu)(-2x/u) + 4 - 12 -> -15 - 8 = -23 = Lambda(1/3, -1).
q part: if q != 0 let m = deg q, otherwise m = 0 and the coefficients below vanish. q(t) = sigma^(-m) c0(z, sigma), and
   g = u^(1/3) sigma^(-n) c1,   A = u^(-2/3) sigma^(-n) c2,   k_q = sigma^(-m) c3,   k_q' = u^(-1) sigma^(-m) c4,
with c_i holomorphic near (0, 0) (the factor x = i sqrt(1 - u) and the constant s included); by (28.7) c2 = b~ N, so
c2(0, 0) = -2 c_p/3 != 0. Substitution gives K3_q = u^2 sigma^(3n - m) c5 = u^2 sigma^(-M1) c6, M1 = max(m - 3n, 0), so
K3_q = O(u^2 |Lu|^M1) and K3_q' = O(u |Lu|^M1), and L_H[-6 K3_q] = O(u^2 |Lu|^M1). Forcing: 1/A = u^(2/3) sigma^n/c2,
so a0 A'/A^2 = -a0 d_x(1/A) = O(u^(-1/3) |Lu|^(-n)). Both are o(u^(-1) Lu^(-2)).
j part. If j_c = 0, dividing (28.3) by v_H gives -23 = 0 in the limit, a contradiction. Otherwise j_c = u^mu J(u) with
mu in Z, J analytic, J(0) != 0. In K3_j = A^(-3) [5 (g/A) k_j' - 3 k_j] one has 5(g/A) k_j' = (10x^2/N) Du k_j and
Du k_j/k_j -> 1/3 + mu, 10x^2/N -> 15, so the bracket is (15 mu + 2)(1 + o(1)) k_j, with 15 mu + 2 != 0. With
A^(-3) = u^2 sigma^(3n)/c2^3,
   K3_j = C u^(7/3 + mu) Lu^(-3n) (1 + o(1)),   C = (15 mu + 2) i J(0)/c2(0, 0)^3 != 0,   Du K3_j/K3_j -> 7/3 + mu,
both from the factored form u^(7/3 + mu) sigma^(3n) times a holomorphic unit in (z, sigma). By (28.9) the multiplier is
Lambda(1/3, 7/3 + mu) = 27 + 15 mu != 0. If mu <= -4, then 7/3 + mu < -1 and L_H[-6 K3_j] dominates L_H[v_H], the q
term and the forcing; if mu >= -3, then 7/3 + mu > -1 and L_H[v_H] dominates all other terms. Equality is impossible
since mu is an integer. Both alternatives contradict (28.3).

#### Step 7 (Case 2: p constant)
Let p = p0 (p0 = 0 allowed). Then f = p0 + h_c is meromorphic at 0 and not identically zero: otherwise f = 0 on C minus
the poles, so g = 0 for real x near 0, against A(0) = h > 0. Write f = u^nu F(u), nu in Z, F analytic, F(0) != 0. Then
ell = nu + 1/3 + Du F/F is analytic with ell0 = nu + 1/3 != 0 and Du ell -> 0, N is analytic with N(0) = -2 ell0 != 0,
and
   A = u^(nu - 2/3) a1(u),   a1 = F N analytic,   a1(0) = -2 ell0 F(0) != 0,
so A != 0 on a short interval. By (28.7), g/A = xu/N and H are analytic at 0 (as functions of u, with x = i sqrt(1 - u)),
g/A is divisible by u, and d_x = 2x d_u preserves analyticity. The forcing is
   a0 A'/A^2 = -2 a0 x d_u (u^(2/3 - nu)/a1) = u^(-nu - 1/3) c(u),   c(0) = -2 i a0 (2/3 - nu)/a1(0) != 0,     (28.11)
using a0 != 0 and nu in Z. F0 := L_H[-H''] is analytic at 0. Since k_j = x u^(1/3) j_c, A^(-3) = u^(2 - 3nu) a1^(-3) and
(5g/A) d_x = (10x^2/N) Du, K3_j is u^(7/3 - 3nu) times a meromorphic function, and
   L_H[-6 K3_j] = u^(7/3 - 3nu) F1(u),   F1 meromorphic at 0, possibly identically zero.                       (28.12)
If F1 != 0, the first nonzero power in (28.12) lies in 1/3 + Z; the powers of (28.11) lie in 2/3 + Z; those of F0 are
nonnegative integers.
q = 0. Then (28.3) is F0 + u^(7/3 - 3nu) F1 + u^(-nu - 1/3) c = 0 on (0, eps'). Put v0 = u^(1/3) and multiply by a large
integer power of v0: the three terms become convergent power series in v0 with exponents in the three distinct residue
classes 0, 1, 2 modulo 3 (before the common shift). By uniqueness of convergent power series all coefficients vanish,
in particular c(0) = 0, a contradiction.
q != 0 of degree m. Then k_q = x Lu^m b_q/s^2 and Du k_q/k_q -> 0, so the bracket of K3_q is -3 k_q (1 + o(1)) (the term
5(g/A) k_q' = (10x^2/N) Du k_q is of lower order), and
   K3_q = C_q u^(2 - 3nu) Lu^m (1 + o(1)),   C_q = -3 i c_q/(s^2 a1(0)^3) != 0,   Du K3_q/K3_q -> 2 - 3nu,     (28.13)
from the factored form u^(2 - 3nu) sigma^(-m) times a holomorphic unit. (The value of C_q is a direct evaluation; the
source derivation states only C_q != 0.) The multiplier is
   Lambda(nu + 1/3, 2 - 3nu) = (22 - 24 nu)/(3 nu + 1) != 0   for nu in Z.                                       (28.14)
If nu >= 2: the q term has the negative integer leading power 2 - 3nu; it dominates the bounded F0 and the forcing,
whose ratio to it is O(u^(2nu - 7/3) |Lu|^(-m)) -> 0. If F1 != 0, its first power (in 1/3 + Z) differs from the integer
2 - 3nu; whichever is smaller has a nonzero coefficient and dominates all other terms. This contradicts (28.3).
If nu <= 1: the q contribution is o(u^(-nu - 1/3)), since the power difference is 7/3 - 2nu > 0. The first nonzero
powers of F0, of (28.12) (if F1 != 0) and of (28.11) have three distinct fractional parts; the smallest occurs once and
has a nonzero coefficient, and the q contribution lies above the forcing power, hence above this smallest power. No
cancellation in (28.3) is possible. This settles Case 2 for every nu in Z.

#### Step 8 (Case 3: p nonconstant, h_c with a pole at u = 0)
Let n = deg p >= 1, h_c = u^(-kappa) phi(u) with kappa >= 1 an integer, phi analytic, phi(0) = phi0 != 0, c_p as in
(28.6), and ell0 = 1/3 - kappa < 0. Then
   f = u^(-kappa) phi(u) (1 + eps(u)),   eps = u^kappa Lu^n b_p(z, sigma)/phi(u),
and for every fixed integer r >= 0, by the product rule and (28.5),
   Du^r eps = kappa^r (c_p/phi0) u^kappa Lu^n (1 + o(1)):                                                      (28.15)
terms in which Du falls on b_p/phi are smaller because its Du derivatives tend to 0, and Du lowers the degree of Lu^n.
So eps and its fixed-order Du derivatives tend to 0 and 1 + eps is a unit on the interval. Let g_b = x u^(1/3) h_c and
let N_b, H_b and S_b = 5 g_b/g_b' be the expressions (28.7) for g_b alone; they are analytic at 0 and N_b(0) = -2 ell0.
From (28.7), since ell - ell_b = Du eps/(1 + eps),
   N - N_b = 2x^2 Du eps/(1 + eps),   H - H_b = 5xu (N - N_b)/(N_b N),
and (28.15) gives, with C_H = -5 i kappa c_p/(2 ell0^2 phi0) != 0,
   H - H_b = C_H u^(kappa + 1) Lu^n (1 + o(1)),
   v_H - (-H_b'') = 4 C_H kappa (kappa + 1) u^(kappa - 1) Lu^n (1 + o(1)),                                    (28.16)
using d_x = 2x d_u, d_x^2 = 2 d_u + 4x^2 d_u^2 and x^2 -> -1; the fixed-order differentiated remainders follow from
(28.15) and the unit denominators. In particular Du of the second expression divided by itself tends to kappa - 1 (to 0
if kappa = 1, where the factor Lu^n still diverges since n >= 1). The coefficient differences of L_H and L_Hb are
S - S_b = -(H - H_b) = O(u^(kappa + 1) |Lu|^n) and H' - H_b' = O(u^kappa |Lu|^n). Since v_b = -H_b'' and its derivative are
bounded, their products with these differences are o(u^(kappa - 1) Lu^n); products of the differences with the
perturbation in (28.16) are smaller still, by a factor of order u^kappa |Lu|^n. By (28.9) with ell0 = 1/3 - kappa,
   L_H[-H''] = F0(u) + C_* u^(kappa - 1) Lu^n (1 + o(1)),                                                      (28.17)
   F0 = L_Hb[-H_b''] analytic at 0,   C_* = 4 C_H kappa (kappa + 1) Lambda(1/3 - kappa, kappa - 1),
   Lambda(1/3 - kappa, kappa - 1) = (6 kappa + 23)/(3 kappa - 1) > 0,   so C_* != 0.
The forcing is O(u^(kappa - 1/3)) (1/A = O(u^(2/3 + kappa)) from the factored form) and the q contribution is
O(u^(2 + 3 kappa) |Lu|^M) for a finite M (A^(-3) = O(u^(2 + 3 kappa))); both are negligible against the logarithmic term
of (28.17).
j_c = 0. If F0 has first power below kappa - 1, that analytic term dominates; otherwise the logarithmic term dominates at
the power kappa - 1 (|Lu|^n -> inf). Either way (28.3) fails.
j_c = u^mu J(u) != 0. The bracket of K3_j now has the leading factor 5(mu + 1/3)/ell0 - 3 = (5 mu + 2/3 + 3 kappa)/ell0,
which does not vanish for integers mu, kappa. Hence
   K3_j = C_j u^rho (1 + o(1)),   C_j != 0,   rho = 7/3 + 3 kappa + mu,   Du K3_j/K3_j -> rho.                     (28.18)
rho lies in 1/3 + Z, so rho != kappa - 1. If rho > kappa - 1, L_H[-6 K3_j] = O(u^rho) is negligible against (28.17),
whether or not its multiplier vanishes, and the argument for j_c = 0 applies. If rho < kappa - 1, the multiplier
Lambda(ell0, rho) is nonzero, because its only zero is rho_* = 1 - 7 ell0/5 = 8/15 + 7 kappa/5 > kappa - 1; so
L_H[-6 K3_j] has the nonzero leading power u^rho. The first power of F0 is an integer and differs from rho; if it is
smaller, F0 dominates, otherwise the j term dominates, and all other terms are of higher order than rho. Either
alternative contradicts (28.3). This finishes Case 3.

In all cases the continued identity (28.3) fails, so (P1) cannot hold on any neighbourhood of 0. QED

#### Checks
The independent verification checked the three forms of the result separately. Polynomial form (no patches, P(1,0) > 0):
ten exact symbolic identities and 24 high-precision rows at u = 1e-60, 1e-180, 1e-540, 1e-1620 for three example
polynomials (working precision 3 |log10 u| + 100 and + 150 digits); two earlier attempts with insufficient precision
failed and are retained as failures. Patch form with R_l != 1: eleven exact symbolic checks (direct differentiation of
a raw patch, the chart centre and the axis expansion). Meromorphic form (the statement above): twenty exact symbolic
identities (among them the chart inversion, the coefficient of y, the transport multipliers and the pole perturbation
coefficients) and 24 high-precision rows for four manufactured axis cases at u = 1e-20, 1e-60, 1e-180 at
6 |log10 u| + 100 and + 140 digits (agreement gate 1e-40 between the two precisions), with targets such as -33 (Case 1
with mu = -4) and -26/7 (Case 2 with nu = 2). These rows show precision stability
only; convergence in log u is slow (some normalized pole terms still have imaginary part about 0.09 at u = 1e-180), and
they are not part of the proof. External review: three case reviews and a follow-up that rederived K3 and the axis
identity (28.3).

#### Scope and dependencies
Uses: the analytic implicit function theorem, finite Taylor expansion in eta, the one-variable identity theorem and
explicit asymptotics on one boundary branch; Proposition 23(b) for the local identities. The centre hypothesis h > 0 is
used only for the local inverse and to exclude g = 0; no global positivity is used. The polynomial degrees and the
number of patches are finite and alpha > 0; both are essential (alpha = 0 changes the map t). Not covered: limits of
increasing degree, other beta, other maps or exponents, different radii in the two patch variables, general analytic
or smooth G, residual lower bounds, and Setting A1 in general.



### A.29 Proposition 28 (canonical velocity and flow for members with a global positive chart)

Report statement: see Proposition 28 in Section 3.

Proof. Throughout, beta = 3, a = 5, b = 1, rho = E^(1/2), B0 = G_xx, C = G_(eta eta), M = 5 G_eta - eta C, and
Dx = d_x - (B0/A) d_eta, Dy = (1/A) d_eta are the physical derivatives of Proposition 23(b). Constants depend on alpha, s,
delta and the member.

#### Step 1 (mixed orders)
A function f on R^2 has mixed order q if |d_x^j d_eta^k f| <= C_(j,k) rho^(q - j - k/3) on R^2 for all j, k >= 0.
Products add orders (Leibniz rule), and order q implies order q' for q <= q' since rho >= 1. x and eta have orders 1
and 1/3 (|eta| <= s rho^(1/3)). E has order 2 by direct polynomial differentiation, and by the chain rule d^j d^k E^r is
a sum of terms C E^(r - l) prod_(i <= l) d^(j_i) d^(k_i) E with sum j_i = j, sum k_i = k, so E^r has order 2r for every
real r. So T = E^(-1/6) has order -1/3 and w has order 0, with 0 <= T, w <= 1. Let F(T) = -log(1 - dT)/alpha; F and its
derivatives are bounded on [0, 1] and F(0) = 0, so F(T) = T H1(T) with H1(T) = int_0^1 F'(rT) dr smooth. For a smooth
H on [0, 1], a term of d^j d^k H(T) with l derivatives of H has the factor rho^(-l/3 - j - k/3), so H(T) has order 0;
hence t = T H1(T) has order -1/3, and P(t, w) and all its t, w derivatives have order 0. No infinite series is used.

#### Step 2 (patches)
For every j, k and every M > 0, |d_x^j d_eta^k G_l| <= C_(j,k,M) rho^(-M - j - k/3) on R^2: since E >= 1,
R_l^2 + x^2 >= R_l^2 and R_l^2 + eta^2 >= R_l^2, differentiating the finite expression of G_l gives a finite sum of
products of rational and fractional-power factors bounded by a polynomial in |x| + |eta|, times exp(-(x^2 + eta^2)/L_l^2);
since rho <= C (1 + |x| + |eta|^3), the Gaussian absorbs every power of rho. Finite sums preserve this. (As in the source
derivation, this extension lemma is proved there for the patches present in a particular application; the argument uses
only the displayed facts and applies to any finite set of patches.)

#### Step 3 (orders of G, A, B0 and Psi)
By Steps 1 and 2, G has order 2, A order 2/3 and B0 order 0. For the stream function let D = 3x d_x + eta d_eta and
l = E d_E t (at fixed eta) = -(e^(alpha t) - 1)/(6 alpha); l = T H2(T) with H2 smooth (t = 0 at T = 0), so l has order
-1/3. Direct differentiation gives DE = 6(E - 1), Dt = 6(1 - 1/E) l, Dw = 2w/E and D(x eta E^(1/3)) =
(6 - 2/E) x eta E^(1/3). Since Psi = 3x G_x + eta G_eta - 6G = DG - 6G, the outer part of Psi is
   Psi_o = x eta E^(1/3) [6(1 - 1/E) l P_t - 2P/E + 2w P_w/E].                                               (29.1)
The prefactor has order 2 and the bracket order -1/3 (the last two terms have order -2), so Psi_o has order 5/3; the
patch part of Psi has every negative order. Hence Psi has order 5/3. By (H), 1/A <= delta^(-1) rho^(-2/3);
differentiating A (1/A) = 1 and inducting on the derivative order, every derivative of 1/A is a finite sum of products of
derivatives of A divided by powers of A, so 1/A has order -2/3 and B0/A has order -2/3. If f has order q, then Dx f and
Dy f have order q - 1 (d_x lowers the order by 1, the coefficient of d_eta has order -2/3 and d_eta lowers it by 1/3),
including all their mixed derivatives; by induction every composition of n physical derivatives lowers the order by n.

#### Step 4 (global chart and radius)
By Step 3, A <= C rho^(2/3), and by (H) A >= delta E^(1/3). Since y(x, 0) = G_x(x, 0) = 0 and y is odd in eta,
   c |eta| E^(1/3) <= |y(x, eta)| <= C |eta| E^(1/3).                                                       (29.2)
For the lower bound integrate A over [|eta|/2, |eta|], where E(x, r) >= E(x, eta)/64, which gives at least
delta |eta| E^(1/3)/8; the upper bound uses monotonicity of E in |eta|. Already A >= delta makes eta -> y strictly
increasing and onto R for each x; the implicit function theorem and uniqueness give a global smooth inverse eta(x, y),
so (x, eta) -> (x, G_x) is a diffeomorphism of R^2. Since |eta| <= s rho^(1/3), (29.2) gives |y| <= C rho, so
<X> <= C rho. Conversely, if rho >= 2 then x^2 >= 3 rho^2/8 or (eta/s)^6 >= 3 rho^2/8; in the first case |x| >= c rho, in
the second |eta| >= c s rho^(1/3) and (29.2) gives |y| >= c' rho; for rho <= 2 both quantities lie in [1, C]. So rho and
<X> are comparable on R^2, and the mixed orders of Step 3 for Psi (order 5/3), U = (-Dy Psi, Dx Psi) (order 2/3),
Omega = -(Dx^2 + Dy^2) Psi (order -1/3) and Theta = a0 eta (order 1/3) give (c).

#### Step 5 (parities, centre, transport)
E, t, w and the patch factors are even in x and in eta and G is odd in each, so y = G_x is even in x and odd in eta,
uniqueness of the inverse makes eta(x, y) even in x and odd in y, and Psi, Theta, Omega, U have the A1 parities (on the
axes by smoothness). At the origin A = h, so h >= delta > 0, and G = h x eta + O((|x| + |eta|)^4), y = h eta + O(3),
Psi = -2h x eta + O(4) = -2xy + O(|X|^4) and Theta = (a0/h) y + O(|X|^3); h = 1 is not assumed. Direct differentiation
gives Psi_eta = 3xA - 5G_eta + eta C, so W1 = 3x - Psi_eta/A = M/A, W2 = 3y + Dx Psi = B0 W1 + eta A and
grad_X eta = (-B0/A, 1/A); hence W.grad_X eta = eta, i.e. (P2) for Theta = a0 eta. div U = 0 and (P3) hold by the
definitions of U and Omega. This proves (a).

#### Step 6 (the flow)
This step uses only that G is smooth, odd in x and in eta, with A > 0, and the onto conditions; it is written for
beta = 3 (for general beta > 2 the same computation with the fields of Proposition 23(b) gives M = a G_eta - b eta C,
W = (M/A, b eta) in mixed variables, xi' = a xi and eta' = b eta, a = beta + 2, b = beta - 2, and every step below
goes through with 5, 1 replaced by a, b). In the mixed variables W is the field x' = M/A, eta' = eta: indeed
y' = B0 x' + A eta' = B0 M/A + eta A = W2. If W vanishes then eta = 0 (b > 0), and then W1 = 5 G_eta(x, 0)/A(x, 0); the
function x -> G_eta(x, 0) vanishes at 0 and has derivative A(x, 0) > 0, so x = 0. Thus 0 is the only zero. At the
centre M = 5h x + O(3) and A = h + O(2), so W = (5x, y) + O(|X|^3), DW(0) = diag(5, 1) and DU(0) = DW(0) - 3I =
diag(2, -2). A >= delta and oddness give G_x(x, eta) >= delta eta for eta >= 0 (<= for eta <= 0) and
G_eta(x, eta) >= delta x for x >= 0 (<= for x <= 0), so both onto conditions hold, and (x, eta) -> (xi, eta) = (G_eta, eta)
is a global smooth bijection with smooth inverse (x -> G_eta is strictly increasing). Composed with the chart it is a
diffeomorphism of R^2; since d xi = A dx + C d eta and dy = B0 dx + A d eta, d xi ^ d eta = A dx ^ d eta = dx ^ dy, so
it preserves area. Along W, xi' = A x' + C eta' = M + eta C = 5 G_eta = 5 xi, and eta' = eta. So the flow from X0 is the
inverse diffeomorphism applied to (e^(5 sigma) xi0, e^sigma eta0), defined for all real sigma; as sigma -> -inf the
coordinates tend to 0 and so does the orbit. For X0 != 0 one coordinate grows exponentially forward; a bounded complete
orbit would have bounded image under the continuous map X -> (xi, eta), and a periodic orbit would have periodic
coordinates; both are impossible. Reflection symmetry of W gives the invariance of the axes. This proves (b).

#### Step 7 (the subtracted integral)
Let V(X) = int [K(X - Y) - K(-Y)] Omega(Y) dY, K(Z) = (Z2, -Z1)/(2 pi |Z|^2). By (c), Omega(Y) = O(<Y>^(-1/3)); for fixed
X the kernel difference is O_X(|Y|^(-2)) for large |Y|, so the radial tail is bounded by C_X int_R^inf r^(-4/3) dr, and
the singularities at Y = 0 and Y = X are locally integrable: V converges absolutely. Smoothness: for X in a compact set,
split Omega into a compactly supported smooth part equal to Omega near that set and the origin, whose convolution may be
differentiated by moving derivatives onto it, and a distant part, against which every positive derivative of the
kernel difference is O(|Y|^(-2)) or smaller and absolutely integrable. The kernel is minus the counterclockwise rotated
gradient of log|Z|/(2 pi), so its distributional divergence is 0 and its scalar curl d1 K2 - d2 K1 is -delta_0; hence
div V = 0 and curl V = -Omega, and V(0) = 0. Growth: for R = |X| >= 2, the region |Y| > 2R contributes
C R int_(2R)^inf r^(-4/3) dr = O(R^(2/3)); on |Y| <= 2R the K(-Y) term is at most C int_0^(2R) <r>^(-1/3) dr = O(R^(2/3));
for the K(X - Y) term, on |X - Y| < R/2 one has |Y| >= R/2 and the contribution is at most C R^(-1/3) int_0^(R/2) dr, and
on the rest the kernel is at most C/R while int_(|Y| <= 2R) <Y>^(-1/3) dY = O(R^(5/3)); so |V(X)| <= C <X>^(2/3).
H := U - V is divergence-free and curl-free, so Delta H1 = d1 div H - d2 curl H = 0 and Delta H2 = d2 div H + d1 curl H = 0,
and |H| = O(<X>^(2/3)) by (c). The interior gradient estimate on B_R(X0) gives |grad H_i(X0)| <= C R^(-1) sup |H_i| =
O(R^(-1/3)) -> 0, so H is constant, and H(0) = U(0) - V(0) = 0 (U(0) = 0 by parity). This proves (d).

#### Step 8 (vertical axis)
At x = 0, (29.2) reads c |eta| E^(1/3) <= |y| <= C |eta| E^(1/3) with E = 1 + (eta/s)^6, so |y| -> inf iff |eta| -> inf
and, for |y| >= 1, |eta| is bounded below by a positive constant and E^(1/3) is comparable to max(1, (eta/s)^2); hence
|eta(0, y)| is comparable to |y|^(1/3) for |y| >= 1, and |Theta(0, y)| = |a0| |eta(0, y)| gives (e). (The two-sided rate
is a direct consequence of (29.2) added here; the source derivation states only unboundedness.)

#### Step 9 (the criterion for (H))
Outer part. Treat E as an independent variable at fixed eta and write L = E d_E. Then L t = l, L l = l2 and
L w = -w/3, with l = -(e^(alpha t) - 1)/(6 alpha) and l2 = e^(alpha t)(e^(alpha t) - 1)/(36 alpha); T(t) =
(1 - e^(-alpha t))/(1 - e^(-alpha)) inverts t(T). Put v = w^3, z = x^2/E, so z = 1 - T(t)^6 - v (since
x^2/E + (eta/s)^6/E + 1/E = 1). With H0 = P/3 + l P_t - w P_w/3, differentiation in x gives G_x = eta E^(1/3) J,
J = P + 2z H0. At fixed x, eta d_eta E = 6vE, eta d_eta z = -6zv, eta d_eta t = 6vl, eta d_eta w = 2w(1 - v), and
   A/E^(1/3) = (1 + 2v) J + eta d_eta J,
   eta d_eta J = 6vl P_t + 2w(1 - v) P_w - 12zv H0 + 2z eta d_eta H0,
   eta d_eta H0 = 6v [(l/3 + l2) P_t + l^2 P_tt - l w P_tw/3] + 2w(1 - v) [l P_tw - w P_ww/3].
Collecting the six derivatives of P gives (G_o)_(x eta) = E^(1/3) Q_o(t, w) with
   Q_o = C0 P + Cw P_w + Cww P_ww + Ct P_t + Ctw P_tw + Ctt P_tt,                                           (29.20)
   C0 = 1 + (2z + 6v)/3 - 8zv/3,   Cw = w (2 - 2z/3 - 2v + 8zv/3),   Cww = -(4/3) z (1 - v) w^2,
   Ct = (2z + 6v - 4zv) l + 12 zv l2,   Ctw = 4 z w l (1 - 2v),   Ctt = 12 zv l^2,
the scale s cancelling. Every (x, eta) maps into D (with t > 0), and conversely every (t, w) in D with t > 0 is attained
(E = T(t)^(-6), x = sqrt(zE), eta = s sqrt(w E^(1/3)), and reflections). So Q_o >= delta_o on D gives
(G_o)_(x eta) >= delta_o E^(1/3) on R^2.
Patches. For one patch put X2 = x^2, H2 = eta^2, z = X2/E, v3 = (eta/s)^6/E (so z, v3 >= 0, z + v3 <= 1), and for any
smooth K(X2, H2), using x d_x = 2 X2 d_X2 and eta d_eta = 2 H2 d_H2,
   (x eta E^(1/3) K)_(x eta)/E^(1/3) = C0' K + 2 H2 (1 + 2z/3) K_H2 + 2 X2 (1 + 2 v3) K_X2 + 4 X2 H2 K_X2H2,
   C0' = 1 + 2z/3 + 2 v3 - 8 z v3/3 = 1 + (2/3) z (1 - v3) + 2 v3 (1 - z), in [1, 3].
For K = exp(-(X2 + H2)/L^2) Q(xi, zeta), with X2 xi' = xi (1 - xi), H2 zeta' = zeta (1 - zeta), and
f0(r) = exp(-R^2 r/(L^2 (1 - r))), f1(r) = (R^2 r/(L^2 (1 - r))) f0(r), f2(r) = r (1 - r) f0(r) (all three extend
continuously to [0, 1] with value 0 at r = 1), so that X2 d_X2 [f0(xi) Q] = -f1(xi) Q + f2(xi) Q_xi and likewise in
H2, this gives
   (G_l)_(x eta)/E^(1/3) = Z_l = d0 Q + d1 Q_xi + d2 Q_zeta + d12 Q_(xi zeta),                              (29.22)
   d0 = C0' f0(xi) f0(zeta) - 2 (1 + 2z/3) f0(xi) f1(zeta) - 2 (1 + 2 v3) f1(xi) f0(zeta) + 4 f1(xi) f1(zeta),
   d1 = 2 (1 + 2 v3) f2(xi) f0(zeta) - 4 f2(xi) f1(zeta),   d2 = 2 (1 + 2z/3) f0(xi) f2(zeta) - 4 f1(xi) f2(zeta),
   d12 = 4 f2(xi) f2(zeta),
with 1 <= 1 + 2z/3 <= 5/3 and 1 <= 1 + 2 v3 <= 3. So Z_l is bounded by a finite B_l, and Q_o >= delta_o, sum B_l < delta_o
give A >= (delta_o - sum B_l) E^(1/3). Certificates: dyadic rectangles in (t, w) (a rectangle is discarded if a rational
lower bound of T(t_left)^6 + w_left^3 exceeds 1) or in (xi, zeta); on each leaf exact rational interval arithmetic with
tensor Bernstein bounds for the polynomial and its derivatives, a Taylor enclosure of exp with geometric remainder,
directed dyadic rounding, and for the patches the monotonicity of f0 and rigorous bounds that include the interior maxima
of f1 and f2, which occur at r = 1/(1 + a) and r = (a + 3 - sqrt((a + 3)^2 - 8))/4 with a = R^2/L^2 (f2 is not monotone;
for a = 1 both endpoint values vanish while f2(1/2) = e^(-1)/4 > 0), together
with corner bounds for z and v3 on interior leaves; on leaves meeting xi = 1 or zeta = 1 use 0 <= z, v3 and z + v3 <= 1. The f-factors vanish at those edges, so the resulting upper bounds tend to zero as edge leaves shrink. Interior bounds and certified input enclosures must also be refined to vanishing width. A single rational delta_o (or upper bound for B_l) is checked on every leaf of a
complete cover. This proves (f). QED

#### Remark (finite certificates)
Exact certificates of this kind exist for particular stored states of Section 6.9; for example, four stored states
satisfy (H) with delta = 1/100 (with a0 = 600). These are statements about the exact rational interpretation of the
stored coefficients; they supply no explicit perturbation radius (a strict margin is stable under sufficiently small
changes of the coefficients in a fixed finite basis, since A/E^(1/3) depends linearly on them through bounded basis
functions) and say nothing about (P1). The external audit did not verify these stored-state margins (their coefficient
and certificate files were not supplied to it); they rest on the independent verification.

#### Scope and dependencies
Uses: elementary differentiation, the implicit function theorem, the distributional fundamental solution of the
Laplacian on R^2, the interior gradient estimate for harmonic functions, and, for (f), finite polynomial identities and a
geometric Taylor remainder bound. Proposition 23(b) supplies the local formulas; Proposition 27 shows that (P1) fails.
Not covered: (P1); quadrature, inversion or fitting error bounds; leading or next-order asymptotics at infinity and
compatibility with the far-field theorems; constants; an explicit perturbation radius for (H).
