### A.30 Proposition 29 (vertical compression of a hydrostatic profile)

Report statement: see Proposition 29 in Section 3.

Proof. Fix lambda > 0 and write eta = lambda y. All base quantities (Psi, Theta, U, W, H, J, Q and their derivatives)
are evaluated at (x, eta).

#### Step 1 (fields)
d_y Psi_l = Psi_eta and d_x Psi_l = lambda^(-1) Psi_x, so U_l = (U1, lambda^(-1) U2) and, since beta y = lambda^(-1) beta eta,
W_l = (W1, lambda^(-1) W2). For smooth f and a constant p,
   W_l.grad_X [lambda^p f(x, lambda y)] = lambda^p (W1 f_x + lambda^(-1) W2 lambda f_eta) = lambda^p (W.grad f).          (30.1)
Also d_x^2 Psi_l = lambda^(-1) J and d_y^2 Psi_l = lambda Psi_(eta eta) = -lambda H, so Omega_l = lambda H - lambda^(-1) J and E = 0.

#### Step 2 (residuals and centre values)
By (30.1) and (HS), R_Theta = lambda (W.grad Theta - (beta - 2) Theta) = 0 and
   R_Omega = lambda (W.grad H + H - Theta_x) - lambda^(-1) (W.grad J + J) = -lambda^(-1) Q.
d_x d_y Psi_l(0) = Psi_(x eta)(0) = -2 and d_y Theta_l(0) = lambda^2 Theta_eta(0) = lambda^2 a0. This proves (a).

#### Step 3 (division by x y; centre value)
Psi is odd in x and in eta, so J, H are odd in both variables; W1 = beta x - Psi_eta is odd in x and even in eta, and
W2 = beta eta + Psi_x is even in x and odd in eta, so W.grad J, Q, Theta_x and every component of t, v, h, j are odd in
both variables. For smooth f odd in both variables, f(x, 0) = f(0, eta) = 0 and
   f(x, eta) = x eta int_0^1 int_0^1 f_(x eta)(s x, t eta) ds dt,
so f/(x eta) extends smoothly. Since x y = x eta/lambda, R_Omega/(x y) = -Q/(x eta) off the axes, and both sides extend.
With the stated jet, U = (2x - d1 x^3 - 3 d2 x eta^2, -2 eta + 3 d1 x^2 eta + d2 eta^3) + O(|.|^5), so the linear part of W is
((beta + 2) x, (beta - 2) eta), and ((beta + 2) x, (beta - 2) eta).grad(x eta) = 2 beta x eta exactly; hence W.grad(x eta) = 2 beta x eta + O(|.|^4)
(the cubic part of W contributes 2 d1 x^3 eta - 2 d2 x eta^3), J = 6 d1 x eta + O(|.|^4) and
Q = 6 (2 beta + 1) d1 x eta + O(|.|^4). Hence the extension of -Q/(x eta) equals -6 (2 beta + 1) d1 at 0. This proves (b).

#### Step 4 (normalizers)
d_x Omega_l = lambda H_x - lambda^(-1) J_x and d_y Omega_l = lambda^2 H_eta - J_eta. Hence
   W_l,1 d_x Omega_l = lambda W1 (H_x - lambda^(-2) J_x),   W_l,2 d_y Omega_l = lambda W2 (H_eta - lambda^(-2) J_eta),
   Omega_l = lambda (H - lambda^(-2) J),   d_x Theta_l = lambda Theta_x,
so N = lambda sum_i |t_i - lambda^(-2) v_i|. In the same way U_l,1 d_x Omega_l = lambda U1 (H_x - lambda^(-2) J_x),
U_l,2 d_y Omega_l = lambda U2 (H_eta - lambda^(-2) J_eta) and
   beta x d_x Omega_l + beta y d_y Omega_l + Omega_l = lambda (beta x H_x + beta eta H_eta + H) - lambda^(-1) (beta x J_x + beta eta J_eta + J),
so N2 = lambda sum_i |h_i - lambda^(-2) j_i|. Dividing |R_Omega| = lambda^(-1) |Q| gives the two ratio formulas of (c). By the
reverse triangle inequality sum_i |t_i - lambda^(-2) v_i| >= n - lambda^(-2) M >= n/2 on K when lambda^2 >= 2M/n, which also shows
that the denominator is positive there, gives the bound, and lambda^(-2) = |a0|/|a0_l|. The second ratio is treated in the
same way with n2 = inf_K ||h||_1 > 0 and M2 = sup_K ||j||_1; neither lower bound follows from (HS) (for Psi = -2 x eta,
Theta = a0 eta all of t, h vanish identically). On the axes N = N2 = R_Omega = 0. Off the axes the common factor |x eta|
cancels: at S_l z the first ratio equals lambda^(-2) |Q/(x eta)| / ||t/(x eta) - lambda^(-2) v/(x eta)||_1, whose right side is
continuous wherever its denominator is positive (Step 3; parity division alone does not make the divided denominator
positive or assign a value to 0/0, so positivity is a hypothesis); this defines the extension, and the bound holds with
nbar = inf_K ||t/(x eta)||_1 > 0, Mbar = sup_K ||v/(x eta)||_1 and sup_K |Q/(x eta)|, and likewise for (h, j). These are upper
bounds; under the lower bound, lambda^2 times the ratio tends to |Q|/||t||_1 uniformly on K, which is positive only where Q is.
This proves (c).

#### Step 5 (non-solution and canonical velocity)
Since S_l is invertible, R_Omega vanishes identically if and only if Q does, for every lambda. For the inverse fix lambda.
Since min(1, lambda) |X| <= |(x, lambda y)| <= max(1, lambda) |X|, the hypotheses give |Omega_l(X)| <= C_l (1 + |X|)^(-sigma) and
U_l = o(|X|). Replacing sigma by min(sigma, 1/2) we may assume 0 < sigma < 1. For |Y| > 2|X|, |K(X - Y) - K(-Y)| <= C |X| |Y|^(-2)
by the mean value theorem, so the canonical integral V of Omega_l converges absolutely; the kernel singularities at Y = 0 and
Y = X are locally integrable. Splitting into |Y| < |X|/2, |X|/2 <= |Y| <= 2|X| and |Y| > 2|X| gives |V(X)| <= C (1 + |X|)^(1 - sigma).
V is smooth with div V = 0, curl V = -Omega_l and V(0) = 0: on a compact set split Omega_l by a smooth cutoff; the compactly
supported part is smooth after moving derivatives onto it, and the remaining kernel is nonsingular there with absolutely
convergent differentiated tails. U_l satisfies div U_l = 0, curl U_l = Delta Psi_l = -Omega_l and U_l(0) = 0 (parity), so each
component of F = U_l - V is entire harmonic and o(|X|); the mean-value formula gives |d_i F_k(P)| <= (2/R) sup over the circle
of radius R about P of |F_k|, which tends to 0, so F is constant, and F(0) = 0.
Finally, under these hypotheses Q does not vanish identically. If it did, then J = 0: J is continuous and tends to 0 at
infinity, so if J were not identically zero, |J| would attain a positive maximum at a point where grad J = 0, and there
Q = J != 0. Then Psi_xx = 0 and oddness in x give Psi = x A(eta), so U1 = -x A'(eta); U = o(|X|) along x -> inf at fixed eta
forces A' = 0, contradicting Psi_(x eta)(0) = A'(0) = -2. Hence no member satisfies (P1). This proves (d). The argument
also gives sup |Q| >= max |J| > 0, and it uses neither (HS) nor beta > 2; its application to R_Omega uses (HS). The
hypotheses of (d) cannot be dropped: Psi = -2 x eta, Theta = a0 eta satisfies (HS) and has Q = 0 (and all of t, h zero),
while U1 = 2x is not o(|X|). QED

#### Remark (genuine scaling)
For Psi^mu(X) = mu^2 Psi(X/mu), Theta^mu(X) = mu Theta(X/mu) (Section 2.4), W^mu(X) = mu W(X/mu), so R_Omega^mu(mu Z) = R_Omega(Z),
N^mu(mu Z) = N(Z), N2^mu(mu Z) = N2(Z) and a0 is unchanged, while R_Omega^mu(mu Z)/((mu z1)(mu z2)) = mu^(-2) R_Omega(Z)/(z1 z2).
The divided absolute residual therefore depends on the spatial scale.

#### Scope and dependencies
Uses: elementary differentiation, parity division, the fundamental solution of the Laplacian on R^2 and the mean-value
gradient estimate for harmonic functions. No numerical data and no existence result for (HS) are used. Not covered:
existence of a nontrivial profile satisfying (HS) and the hypotheses of (d); families whose shape changes with lambda; inverse or
tail bounds uniform in lambda (the constants of Step 5 may depend on lambda); a two-sided rate without additional hypotheses
(a positive lower bound for |Q| on compact sets off the axes, or for |Q/(x eta)| on compact sets meeting them); membership
in the full admissible class A' (which would also need polynomial tail control of Theta and the required derivatives);
nonexistence in the full class A'. The upper bounds of (c) on fixed rescaled sets for large lambda and the exclusion in (d)
of every member of the fixed compressed family are proved.

### A.31 Proposition 30 (the free-exponent family near the centre for every beta > 2, and under a global chart bound)

Report statement: see Proposition 30 in Section 3.

Proof of (a), of the local part of (c) and of (d). Throughout Steps 1 to 8 beta is 5/2 or 8/3 (Step 8a extends them
to the other integer values of m, Step 8b to every beta > 2), a = beta + 2, b = beta - 2, p = 1/beta, m = beta/b, d = 1 - e^(-alpha) in (0, 1),
and the notation of the statement is used. The argument follows A.28; the differences are the exponents, which change
the constants of every case and require the residue-class arguments below. Primes denote derivatives in x. Orders of
meromorphic functions refer to the finite sums over the patches; cancellations between patches are allowed.

#### Step 1 (local chart and centre)
1 + (eta/s)^6 >= 1, so E = x^2 + (1 + (eta/s)^6)^(m/3) >= 1 is real analytic on R^2 and even in x and in eta; as in
A.28 Step 1, 1 - d E^(-p/2) >= e^(-alpha) > 0, and E^p, t, w, xi_l, zeta_l and the Gaussian factors are real analytic and
even in each variable. At the origin E = 1, t = 1, w = xi_l = zeta_l = 0, so G = h x eta + O((|x| + |eta|)^4) with
h = P(1, 0) + sum_l Q_l(0, 0) > 0. The analytic implicit function theorem gives the inverse eta(x, y) = y/h + O(|X|^3),
even in x and odd in y, and Proposition 23(b) applies near 0: (P2), (P3) and U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x) hold identically, and
the parities follow as in A.28 Step 1. Finally Psi = (beta + b - 2 beta) h x eta + O(4) = -2xy + O(|X|^4) and
Theta = (a0/h) y + O(|X|^3).

#### Step 2 (expansion in eta on the horizontal axis)
Fix real x near 0 and put u = 1 + x^2. Since (1 + (eta/s)^6)^(m/3) = 1 + O(eta^6), E = u + O(eta^6), E^p = u^p + O(eta^6),
t = t(u) + O(eta^6) with t(u) = -log(1 - d u^(-p/2))/alpha, and w = (eta/s)^2 u^(-1/m) + O(eta^8). Put P0(t) = P(t, 0)
and P1(t) = P_w(t, 0). As in (28.1), using p - 1/m = 3p - 1,
   G = eta g(x) + eta^3 k(x) + O(eta^5),
   g = x u^p f,  f = P0(t) + h_c(u),  k = x s^(-2) u^(3p - 1) P1(t) + x u^p j_c(u),                          (31.1)
with h_c, j_c the finite patch sums of (28.1) (meromorphic on C, poles only at the real points 1 - R_l^2, a pole at
u = 0 possible exactly when some R_l = 1) and an analytic remainder.

#### Step 3 (the coefficient of y in (P1))
Let A = g', so A(0) = h > 0 and G_x = eta A + eta^3 k' + O(eta^5); inversion gives eta = y/A - k' y^3/A^4 + O(y^5).
Since G_eta = g + 3 eta^2 k + O(eta^4) and 3b - 2 beta = beta - 6,
   Psi = eta (beta x A - a g) + eta^3 (beta x k' + (beta - 6) k) + O(eta^5),
and substitution of the inverse gives
   Psi = y H + y^3 K3 + O(y^5),   H = beta x - a g/A,   K3 = a g k'/A^4 + (beta - 6) k/A^3,                    (31.2)
the terms beta x k'/A^3 cancelling. Hence U1 = -H + O(y^2), U2 = y H' + O(y^3), Omega = y v + O(y^3) with
v = -H'' - 6 K3, Theta_x = -a0 y A'/A^2 + O(y^3), W1 = a g/A + O(y^2) and W2 = y (beta + H') + O(y^3), and the
coefficient of y in W.grad Omega + Omega - Theta_x is
   L_H[v] + a0 A'/A^2 = 0,   L_H[v] = a (g/A) v' + (beta + 1 + H') v,                                         (31.3)
which holds for real x in an interval (0, x0) if (P1) holds near 0. The highest power of 1/A in (31.3) is the sixth, so
A^6 (31.3) has no denominator A.

#### Step 4 (continuation)
Let S = {u : Im u > 0}, with u^p and u^(-p/2) defined by arg u in (0, pi), x = sqrt(u - 1) with arg(u - 1) in (0, pi)
(so x -> i as u -> 0), and d_x = 2x d_u. On S, arg u^(-p/2) is in (-p pi/2, 0), so 1 - d u^(-p/2) has positive imaginary
part and its logarithm is taken with argument in (0, pi). Then A^6 times the left side of (31.3) is holomorphic on S,
extends across the real interval 1 < u < 1 + x0^2, where it vanishes, and hence vanishes on S (identity theorem). Choose
eps > 0 with eps < d^(2 beta) (so that d u^(-p/2) > 1 for 0 < u < eps) and eps below every positive pole 1 - R_l^2. For
0 < u < eps, 1 - d u^(-p/2) < 0 is approached from positive imaginary part and its logarithm extends with argument near
pi; so the cleared identity extends across (0, eps) and vanishes there. In each case below A != 0 on a shorter interval
(0, eps'), so (31.3) itself holds there. From now on all limits are u -> 0+ along this boundary interval (not the
physical origin u = 1). Write Lu = log u and sigma = 1/Lu. For beta = 5/2 put N = 5, r = 1; for beta = 8/3 put N = 16,
r = 3; then p/2 = r/N, and with z = u^(1/N)
   t = Lu/(2 beta alpha) - (log d)/alpha - i pi/alpha - log(1 - z^r/d)/alpha,                                (31.4)
   Du := u d/du = (z/N) d_z - sigma^2 d_sigma,   d_x = (2x/u) Du.
If P0 has degree q0 >= 1 and leading coefficient c0, then P0(t) = Lu^(q0) B(z, sigma) with B holomorphic near (0, 0) and
B(z, 0) = c_P := c0/(2 beta alpha)^(q0) != 0; likewise for P1 when P1 != 0. Every non-zero meromorphic germ of u at 0
is an integer power of u times a holomorphic unit, and an analytic function of u is an analytic function of z. All
derivatives below are computed from such explicit factorizations by the operator Du; no unspecified O-term is
differentiated. When first exponents are compared, an identically zero contribution is omitted (given order +inf).

#### Step 5 (factored forms and the multiplier)
Put ell = p + Du f/f and B1 = u + 2(u - 1) ell. Since A = u^p f + (2x^2/u) Du(u^p f), wherever f != 0 and B1 != 0,
   A = u^(p - 1) f B1,   g/A = x u/B1,   H = beta x - a x u/B1.                                                (31.5)
If ell -> ell0 != 0 and Du ell -> 0 (true in each case below), then B1 -> -2 ell0, and, since x^2 -> -1,
   H' -> beta - a/ell0,   a (g/A)(2x/u) = 2a x^2/B1 -> a/ell0.                                               (31.6)
Hence, for any v = C u^rho Lu^q (1 + o(1)) with C != 0 obtained from explicit factorizations, so that Du v/v -> rho,
   L_H[v]/v -> lambda_ell0(rho) := 2 beta + 1 + a (rho - 1)/ell0.                                          (31.7)
Write k = k_1 + k_j with k_1 = x s^(-2) u^(3p - 1) P1(t) and k_j = x u^p j_c, and K3 = K3_1 + K3_j accordingly (K3 is
linear in k). For any factor k_* of the form x u^c times a unit times a power of Lu, (31.2) and (31.6) give
   K3_* = (k_*/A^3) [a (g/A)(2x/u) Du log k_* + beta - 6] = (k_*/A^3) [a c/ell0 + beta - 6 + o(1)].          (31.8)
Equation (31.3) reads L_H[-H''] + L_H[-6 K3_1] + L_H[-6 K3_j] + a0 A'/A^2 = 0. Three cases exhaust the possibilities.

#### Step 6 (case 1: P0 nonconstant, h_c holomorphic at 0)
Here f = Lu^(q0) B + h_c, ell = p + q0/Lu + O(Lu^(-2)) (with the same form for its Du derivatives), ell0 = p. Expanding the
unit 1/B1 about its value at ell = p, the leading non-analytic part of H is -a q0 x u/(2 p^2 Lu); applying d_x twice and
using x^2 -> -1, d_x^2 (x u/Lu) = 4x/(u Lu^2) (1 + o(1)), so
   -H'' = 2 a beta^2 q0 x/(u Lu^2) (1 + o(1)),                                                             (31.9)
while the analytic part of H contributes bounded terms. By (31.7) with rho = -1, lambda_p(-1) = 1 - 2 beta - 2 beta^2
!= 0, so L_H[-H''] has the non-zero leading term lambda_p(-1) times (31.9), of order u^(-1) Lu^(-2). The forcing is
a0 A'/A^2 = O(u^(-p) |Lu|^(-q0)), because A = u^(p-1) Lu^(q0) (-2p c_P + o(1)); the term K3_1 is O(u^2 |Lu|^q) for a
finite q by (31.8), and so is its image under L_H. If j_c = 0 these cannot cancel the leading term, a contradiction.
If j_c != 0, write j_c = u^mu J(u) with mu an integer and J(0) != 0. By (31.8) with c = p + mu and ell0 = p,
   K3_j = C_j u^(3 - 2p + mu) Lu^(-3 q0) (1 + o(1)),   C_j proportional to beta a mu + 2 beta - 4,
which is (45 mu + 4)/4 for beta = 5/2 and (112 mu + 12)/9 for beta = 8/3, never zero for an integer mu. Its multiplier is
lambda_p(3 - 2p + mu) = 2 beta^2 + 4 beta - 3 + beta a mu, that is (78 + 45 mu)/4 or (197 + 112 mu)/9, never zero for an
integer mu. The exponent 3 - 2p + mu is never -1 (2p = 4/5 or 3/4). If it is below -1, the j_c term is the unique leading
term: it dominates the term from (31.9), the forcing (whose exponent -p exceeds -1) and the K3_1 term. If it is above -1,
the term from (31.9) is the unique leading term. Either way (31.3) fails.

#### Step 7 (case 2: P0 constant)
Then f = P0 + h_c is meromorphic at 0 and not identically zero (otherwise g = 0 by continuation, contradicting A(0) > 0).
Write f = u^nu F(u) with nu an integer and F(0) != 0. Then ell -> ell0 = nu + p != 0, A = u^(nu + p - 1) a1(u) with a1
analytic and a1(0) = -2 (nu + p) F(0) != 0, and by (31.5) H and g/A are analytic at 0, g/A divisible by u. The forcing is
   a0 A'/A^2 = u^(-nu - p) c(u),   c analytic,   c(0) = 2 i a0 (nu + p - 1)/a1(0) != 0.                     (31.10)
The term F0 := L_H[-H''] is analytic. The term L_H[-6 K3_j] equals u^(3 - 2p - 3nu) F1(u) with F1 meromorphic (possibly
zero), by (31.8). Modulo 1, the exponents of F0 are 0, those of the j_c term are 1 - 2p (1/5 or 1/4) and those of the
forcing are 1 - p (3/5 or 5/8): three distinct classes. If P1 = 0, multiply (31.3) by a large power of z0 = u^(1/5)
(beta = 5/2) or z0 = u^(1/8) (beta = 8/3); it becomes a convergent power series identity in z0 in which the three terms
occupy disjoint residue classes of exponents, so the forcing must vanish, contradicting c(0) != 0.
If P1 != 0 has degree q, then by (31.8) with c = 3p - 1 and ell0 = nu + p,
   K3_1 = C1 u^(2 - 3nu) Lu^q (1 + o(1)),   C1 proportional to [-(beta - 2) + (beta - 6) nu]/(nu + p),
which vanishes only at nu = -1/7 (beta = 5/2) or nu = -1/5 (beta = 8/3), so C1 != 0. Its multiplier lambda_ell0(2 - 3nu)
has numerator -(beta + 5) nu + beta + 4 + p over nu + p, whose only zero lies strictly between 0 and 1, so it is not zero
at an integer nu. For nu >= 2 the exponent 2 - 3nu is a negative integer below the forcing exponent (their difference is
2nu - 2 - p > 0) and below every exponent of F0; it differs from every exponent of the j_c term (classes 0 and 1 - 2p).
The smaller of 2 - 3nu and the first exponent of the j_c term is attained by a single non-zero term, which no other term
reaches (the K3_1 contribution has the non-zero leading term C u^(2 - 3nu) Lu^q with a remainder of smaller modulus;
terms at the same u-exponent may have lower degree in Lu, and no term has a smaller u-exponent). For nu <= 1 the exponent of K3_1 exceeds the
forcing exponent by 2 + p - 2nu > 0, so every term of the K3_1 contribution lies above the forcing exponent, while among
F0, the j_c term and the forcing (distinct classes, forcing non-zero) the least exponent is attained by exactly one of
them. In both sub-cases (31.3) fails. (The expansion of the K3_1 contribution may contain exponents of other classes
through log(1 - z^r/d); the argument uses only its leading exponent.)

#### Step 8 (case 3: P0 nonconstant, h_c with a pole at 0)
Write h_c = u^(-k) b0(u) with k >= 1 an integer, b0 analytic and b0(0) = B != 0, and let q0 = deg P0 >= 1. Put
ell0 = p - k < 0 and eps_f = u^k Lu^(q0) B(z, sigma)/b0(u), so f = u^(-k) b0 (1 + eps_f). By the finite product rule, every
Du derivative falling on a unit tends to zero and differentiation of Lu lowers its degree, so for each fixed j >= 0
   Du^j eps_f = k^j (c_P/B) u^k Lu^(q0) (1 + o(1)).                                                           (31.11)
Let H_b and the coefficients of L_H be computed from f_b = h_c alone; they are analytic at 0. From (31.5),
   H - H_b = C_H u^(k + 1) Lu^(q0) (1 + o(1)),   C_H = -a i k c_P/(2 ell0^2 B) != 0,
   -H'' + H_b'' = 4 C_H k (k + 1) u^(k - 1) Lu^(q0) (1 + o(1)),                                             (31.12)
with the differentiated forms from (31.11). The coefficient differences of L_H are O(u^(k+1) |Lu|^(q0)) for a g/A and
O(u^k |Lu|^(q0)) for H'; multiplied by bounded base derivatives or by (31.12) they are smaller than u^(k-1) |Lu|^(q0).
Hence
   L_H[-H''] = F0(u) + C_* u^(k - 1) Lu^(q0) (1 + o(1)),   C_* = 4 C_H k (k + 1) lambda_ell0(k - 1),          (31.13)
with F0 analytic and lambda_ell0(k - 1) = [(beta - 1) k + 2 beta + 2 - p]/(k - p) > 0, so C_* != 0. The forcing is
O(u^(k - p)) and the K3_1 contribution is O(u^(2 + 3k) |Lu|^q), both smaller than the non-analytic term of (31.13). If
j_c = 0, either the first exponent of F0 is smaller than k - 1, and then F0 dominates the whole non-analytic part of
(31.13), which is O(u^(k-1) |Lu|^(q0)), or it is at least k - 1, and then the term C_* u^(k-1) Lu^(q0) is the leading term
(an analytic function contains no power of Lu); (31.3) fails. If j_c = u^mu J(u) != 0, (31.8) with c = p + mu gives the
bracket [2 - 4p + a mu + (6 - beta) k]/(p - k), whose numerator is (4 + 45 mu + 35 k)/10 for beta = 5/2 (non-zero modulo
5 after multiplication by 10) and (3 + 28 mu + 20 k)/6 for beta = 8/3 (odd after multiplication by 6); so
   K3_j = C_j u^rho (1 + o(1)),   C_j != 0,   rho = 3 - 2p + 3k + mu (not an integer).
rho != k - 1. If rho > k - 1, the j_c contribution is smaller than the term of (31.13), and the previous sub-case applies.
If rho < k - 1, its multiplier lambda_ell0(rho) is non-zero, because the only zero of lambda_ell0 is
rho_* = 1 - (2 beta + 1)(p - k)/a and rho_* - (k - 1) = 2 - (2 + p)/a + (beta - 1) k/a > 0; so the j_c contribution has
the non-zero leading term of order u^rho, with a non-integral exponent, while F0 has integral exponents. On the common
scale z = u^(1/N) the smaller of rho and the first exponent of F0 is attained by a single term, which dominates all the
others. So (31.3) fails in every case, which proves (a).

#### Step 8a (the other integer values of m)
Let now beta = 2m/(m - 1) with an integer m >= 2, m != 3, 4, 5 (beta = 4, 12/5, 7/3, 16/7, ...), and assume h > 0. Steps 1
to 8 extend to these parameters with the general values of the constants listed below and one modification in Step 7:
when m = 2 and nu = -1, the factorization of K3_1 and its lower bound on u-exponents given below replace the non-zero
leading coefficient C1. Here p = (m - 1)/(2m), so 2p = (m - 1)/m lies in (0, 1), 1 - 2p = 1/m, 1 - p = (m + 1)/(2m),
a = (4m - 2)/(m - 1), and beta (beta + 2) = 4m(2m - 1)/(m - 1)^2 > 8; also 2 < beta <= 4 and 1/4 <= p < 1/2 (at m = 2, 3p - 1 = -1/4 is
negative; its sign is not used).
 - Step 4: p/2 = (m - 1)/(4m) = r/N in lowest terms, N = 4m/g and r = (m - 1)/g with g = gcd(m - 1, 4) (N = 8, r = 1 for
   m = 2); the continuation threshold is u < d^(2 beta) as before.
 - Step 6: lambda_p(-1) = 1 - 2 beta - 2 beta^2 != 0. The factor beta a mu + 2 beta - 4 of C_j vanishes only at
   mu = -(m - 1)/(m(2m - 1)), which lies in (-1, 0); the multiplier lambda_p(3 - 2p + mu) = 2 beta^2 + 4 beta - 3 + beta a mu
   vanishes only at mu = -2 + 3/(beta (beta + 2)), which lies in (-2, -13/8); neither is an integer. 3 - 2p + mu != -1
   because 2p is not an integer.
 - Step 7: the three classes modulo 1 are 0, 1/m and (m + 1)/(2m), pairwise distinct for m >= 2; for P1 = 0 take
   z0 = u^(1/(2m)), in which they are the residues 0, 2 and m + 1 modulo 2m. c(0) != 0 because nu + p - 1 != 0 for an
   integer nu. C1 is proportional to -(beta - 2) + (beta - 6) nu, which vanishes only at nu = (beta - 2)/(beta - 6)
   = -1/(2m - 3); this is not an integer for m >= 3, and it is nu = -1 for m = 2. The proof of Step 7 uses C1 != 0 only in
   the sub-case nu >= 2. The sub-case nu <= 1 uses only that every term of the K3_1 contribution has u-exponent at least
   2 - 3 nu, and this holds whether or not C1 = 0: by (31.1), (31.2) and (31.5), K3_1 is u^(2 - 3 nu) Lu^q times a
   function holomorphic in (z, sigma) near (0, 0), and L_H, whose coefficients a (g/A)(2x/u) and beta + 1 + H' are
   analytic at 0 in this case, maps such a function to one of the same form. The only zero of the multiplier
   lambda_(nu + p)(2 - 3 nu), nu = (beta + 4 + p)/(beta + 5), lies in (0, 1).
 - Step 8: with m(m - 1)/2 times the numerator of the j_c bracket,
      (m(m - 1)/2) [2 - 4p + a mu + (6 - beta) k] = (m - 1) + m [(2m - 1) mu + (2m - 3) k],
   which is congruent to -1 modulo m, hence non-zero for all integers mu and k (for m = 5 and m = 4 the factor m(m - 1)/2 is
   the 10 and the 6 of Step 8). rho = 3 - 2p + 3k + mu is not an integer. The formulas for lambda_ell0(k - 1) > 0, rho_* and
   rho_* - (k - 1) > 0 in Step 8 hold for every beta > 2, and the common scale is z = u^(1/N) with N from Step 4.
The remaining analyticity, continuation, factorization and order-comparison arguments of Steps 1 to 8 apply to these
parameters; the bounds they use are 0 < p < 1/2, nu + p != 0 and nu + p - 1 != 0 for integers nu, and the inequalities
2 nu - 2 - p > 0 (nu >= 2), 2 + p - 2 nu > 0 (nu <= 1), (k - p) - (k - 1) = 1 - p > 0 and (2 + 3k) - (k - 1) = 3 + 2k > 0
(k >= 1), which hold for every p in (0, 1/2). Hence (31.3) fails in every case, and the conclusion of (a)
holds at these values of beta. The general constants above are rational functions of m; the identities were checked
symbolically in m by the authors, and the formulas reproduce the values of Steps 6 to 8 at m = 4 and 5.

#### Step 8b (every beta > 2)
Let now beta > 2 be arbitrary and assume h > 0. Then p = 1/beta lies in (0, 1/2), so p and 2p are not integers, and
1 - 2p = 1/m and p - 1/m = 3p - 1 hold as before. All limits and bounds below are for the fixed beta; no uniformity as
p tends to 0 is asserted. Steps 1 to 3 and the continuation of Step 4 use no other property of beta: every real power is
defined with the same logarithm on S, and the threshold u < d^(2 beta) and the boundary argument pi are unchanged. The
general constants listed in Step 8a are rational functions of beta, and the following non-vanishing statements there use
only beta > 2 and 0 < p < 1/2, so they hold for every beta > 2: lambda_p(-1) = 1 - 2 beta - 2 beta^2 < 0; the zeros
-(m - 1)/(m (2m - 1)) of the factor of C_j and -2 + 3/(beta (beta + 2)) of its multiplier in Step 6 lie in (-1, 0) and in
(-2, -13/8); 3 - 2p + mu != -1; c(0) != 0, since nu + p - 1 != 0 for an integer nu; the zero (beta + 4 + p)/(beta + 5) of
the multiplier lambda_(nu + p)(2 - 3 nu) of Step 7 lies in (0, 1); rho = 3 - 2p + 3k + mu is not an integer;
lambda_ell0(k - 1) > 0 and rho_* - (k - 1) > 0. So are the bounds listed at the end of Step 8a. Integrality of m is used
in Steps 4 to 8a only through the common scale z = u^(1/N), the argument with z0 for P1 = 0 in Step 7, the non-vanishing
of C1 in the sub-case nu >= 2 of Step 7 and the non-vanishing of the bracket of K3_j in Step 8. These are replaced as
follows.

(i) Differentiation without a common scale. Put w = u^(p/2) and sigma = 1/Lu. For Phi holomorphic near (0, 0, 0), along
the curve (w, u, sigma)
   Du Phi = (p/2) w Phi_w + u Phi_u - sigma^2 Phi_sigma,
so every Du derivative of Phi of fixed positive order tends to 0. Hence, if Phi(0, 0, 0) = C != 0, c is real and j is an
integer, F = u^c Lu^j Phi satisfies Du F/F -> c and Du^r F/(u^c Lu^j) -> c^r C for r >= 1, by repeated application of
the displayed operator and the product rule; denominators tending to non-zero limits are inverted with the corresponding
differentiated bounds. Where a factor to be inverted or a remainder contains u^k Lu^n (integers k >= 1, n) or u Lu, as in
the pole case of Step 8 (where A is u^(p - k - 1) times a unit in these variables) and in the divided analytic remainder
of (iii), these are adjoined as further variables varpi = u^k Lu^n and varpi1 = u Lu, with Du varpi = (k + n sigma) varpi and
Du varpi1 = varpi1 + u; for Phi holomorphic in (w, u, sigma, varpi, varpi1) near 0 the displayed operator acquires the terms
(k + n sigma) varpi Phi_varpi + (varpi1 + u) Phi_varpi1, and the conclusions are unchanged. In (31.4) put w in place of z^r:
t = (p/(2 alpha)) Lu + c_t(w) with c_t holomorphic near 0, so
P0(t) = Lu^(q0) B(w, sigma) and P1(t) = Lu^q B_P(w, sigma) with B, B_P holomorphic near (0, 0) and B(w, 0) = c_P. With
these factorizations (31.11) holds as before (eps_f and its Du derivatives of fixed order tend to 0, so (1 + eps_f)^(-1)
may be differentiated), and so do the differentiated remainders of Step 6; for instance the fractional remainder after
two x-derivatives is O(u^(-1 + p/2) |Lu|^(-1)), whose ratio to the leading u^(-1) Lu^(-2) is O(u^(p/2) |Lu|), which tends
to 0. Steps 6 to 8 then compare finitely many contributions, each given by a leading term of this form, by a function
analytic or meromorphic in u, or by an O-bound, through their real exponents and, at equal exponents, their degrees in
Lu. No common scale is needed: the sentences of Steps 7 and 8 that use z = u^(1/N) are replaced by this comparison (in
Step 8, the smaller of rho and the first exponent of F0, which differ because rho is not an integer, is attained by a
single term), and the argument with z0 by (ii). In Case 2, f is meromorphic at 0 and A = u^(nu + p - 1) a1(u) with a1
holomorphic and a1(0) != 0; g/A, H and the coefficients V = a (g/A)(2x/u) and beta + 1 + H' of L_H = V Du + beta + 1 + H'
are holomorphic at 0, and K3_1 is u^(2 - 3 nu) Lu^q times a function holomorphic in (w, u, sigma) near 0, which L_H maps
to a function of the same form; this is the factorization used in Step 8a for the sub-case nu <= 1.

(ii) Step 7 when P1 is constant. If P1 is a constant (zero or not), k_1 contains no t, so by (31.2) and (31.5) K3_1 is
u^(2 - 3 nu) times a function holomorphic at 0 (which may vanish at 0, or identically), and L_H maps it to a function of
the same form. Then (31.3) reads
   M0(u) + u^(-2p) M1(u) + u^(-p) M2(u) = 0   on (0, eps'),
with M0 = L_H[-H''] + L_H[-6 K3_1], u^(-2p) M1 = L_H[-6 K3_j] (so M1 = u^(3 - 3 nu) F1) and u^(-p) M2 the forcing (31.10),
M2 = u^(-nu) c(u). M0, M1 and M2 are meromorphic at 0, and M2 is not identically zero. Each non-zero contribution has a
least exponent, from the Laurent expansion of its meromorphic factor; these least exponents lie in the classes Z,
Z - 2p and Z - p, which are pairwise disjoint because p and 2p are not integers. Hence their minimum e* occurs in exactly
one contribution, and u^(-e*) times the left side tends to a non-zero limit, a contradiction. This replaces the argument
with z0 for P1 = 0 in Steps 7 and 8a and covers a non-zero constant P1 without using C1.

(iii) Step 7 when P1 has degree q >= 1 and nu >= 2. C1 is proportional to -(beta - 2) + (beta - 6) nu, which vanishes at
an integer nu >= 2 exactly when beta = 2(3 nu - 1)/(nu - 1) = 6 + 4/(nu - 1) (beta = 10, 8, 22/3, 7, ..., all in (6, 10]);
for beta < 6 its zero (beta - 2)/(beta - 6) is negative, and for beta = 6 it has none. Suppose C1 = 0. By (31.2),
K3_1 = (k_1/A^3) [V Du log k_1 + beta - 6] exactly, with V analytic at 0 and V(0) = a/ell0, ell0 = nu + p, and
Du log k_1 = 3p - 1 + Du log x + Du log P1(t), where Du log x = u/(2(u - 1)) and, from (31.4), Du t = (p/(2 alpha))/(1 - w/d),
so Du log P1(t) = q sigma (1 + O(w) + O(sigma)). Hence
   V Du log k_1 + beta - 6 = [V (3p - 1) + beta - 6] + V Du log x + V Du log P1(t)
                          = (a q/ell0) sigma + O(u) + O(w sigma) + O(sigma^2),
since the first bracket is analytic and vanishes at 0 (its value there is the bracket of (31.8) with c = 3p - 1, which is
zero when C1 = 0). As u = o(|sigma|) and w = o(1), the bracket is (a q/ell0) sigma (1 + o(1)), and its Du derivative is
O(u) + O(sigma^2), since w sigma = o(sigma^2). Therefore, with c_P1 = lc(P1)/(2 beta alpha)^q,
   K3_1 = C1' u^(2 - 3 nu) Lu^(q - 1) (1 + o(1)),   C1' = i s^(-2) c_P1 (a q/ell0)/a1(0)^3 != 0,
and Du K3_1/K3_1 -> 2 - 3 nu. Its multiplier lambda_ell0(2 - 3 nu) is not zero, as before (at this beta it equals
-(33 nu - 13)/(3 nu + 1)). The argument of Step 7 for nu >= 2 uses of the K3_1 contribution only that it has a non-zero
leading term at the integral exponent 2 - 3 nu, which lies below the forcing exponent (by 2 nu - 2 - p > 0) and below
every exponent of F0, and differs from every exponent of the j_c term; it applies with Lu^(q - 1) in place of Lu^q (for
q = 1 the logarithmic degree is 0).

(iv) Step 8 without the congruence. Let B3 = 2 - 4p + a mu + (6 - beta) k be the numerator of the bracket of K3_j in
Step 8 and D_(beta,k) = 4(beta + 1) + (3 beta - 2) k > 0. Direct algebra gives
   a (rho - (k - 1)) = B3 + D_(beta,k).
If rho < k - 1, then B3 < 0, so the bracket and C_j are non-zero and the sub-case rho < k - 1 of Step 8 applies as written.
If rho > k - 1, Step 8 uses of the j_c contribution only that it is smaller than the term of (31.13), and this holds
whether or not B3 = 0: the factorizations of Step 8 give K3_j = O(u^rho) and Du K3_j = O(u^rho), hence
L_H[-6 K3_j] = O(u^rho) = o(u^(k - 1) |Lu|^(q0)). rho = k - 1 is impossible because rho is not an integer. So the
non-vanishing of the bracket is needed only where it holds for every beta > 2, and the congruence modulo m of Step 8a is
not needed.

(v) Conclusion. With (i) to (iv), Steps 1 to 8 and the constants of Step 8a show that (31.3) fails for every beta > 2 and
every member with h > 0. This proves (d). The global assertion of (c) follows from (d) as stated there: A >= kappa makes
each map eta -> G_x(x, eta) strictly increasing and onto, so the chart is global, and the exclusion is independent of
Steps 10 and 11 and of Theorems 11 and 15; Step 9 is still needed for the other requirements of class A'.

Proof of (b) and (c). Let beta > 2 and assume A >= kappa E^p on R^2 for a constant kappa > 0. The notation of Steps 9 to 11 is local to them
(symbols introduced in Steps 2 to 8 do not carry over): b = beta - 2, p = 1/beta and m = beta/b as in the statement, so
m > 1, 0 < p < 1/2 and 2p + 1/m = 1 (in (b), m is in [7/3, 5] and p is in [2/7, 2/5]); rho = E^(1/2) >= 1; Z = 1 + (eta/s)^6, so E = x^2 + Z^(m/3);
K = Z^(m/3 - 1); <eta> = (1 + eta^2)^(1/2); C and c denote positive constants that depend on the member, on kappa and on
beta. A function f on R^2 has weight nu if |d_x^i d_eta^j f| <= C rho^(nu - i - j/m) on R^2 for i + j <= 2. Weights add
under products (Leibniz rule), and weight nu implies weight nu' for nu' >= nu since rho >= 1.

#### Step 9 (the fields under the chart bound)
(i) Powers of E. c <eta>^6 <= Z <= C <eta>^6. For |eta| >= s, Z^(m/3) = (|eta|/s)^(2m) (1 + (s/eta)^6)^(m/3) and
K = (|eta|/s)^(2m - 6) (1 + (s/eta)^6)^(m/3 - 1), where (1 + tau)^r is smooth for tau in [0, 1]; differentiating, and using
continuity on |eta| <= s, |d_eta^j Z^(m/3)| <= C <eta>^(2m - j) for j <= 2 and |d_eta^j K| <= C <eta>^(2m - 6 - j) for
j <= 1. Since E >= Z^(m/3) >= c <eta>^(2m), one has <eta> <= C rho^(1/m), |eta| <= C rho^(1/m) and
|d_eta E|/E <= C <eta>^(-1); as 2m - j > 0 for j <= 2, <eta>^(2m - j) <= C rho^(2 - j/m). Hence E has weight 2
(|x| <= rho), x has weight 1, eta has weight 1/m, and by the chain rule E^r has weight 2r for every real r.
(ii) The variables t and w. T := E^(-p/2) lies in (0, 1] and has weight -p. Since 1 - dT >= e^(-alpha), t lies in (0, 1],
and t and l_E := E d_E t (at fixed eta) = -(e^(alpha t) - 1)/(2 beta alpha) are T times functions of T that extend smoothly to [0, 1];
so t and l_E have weight -p, and every function of T that extends smoothly to [0, 1] has weight 0. Next, w = (eta/s)^2 E^(-1/m) lies in [0, 1]
(E^(1/m) >= Z^(1/3) >= (eta/s)^2) and has weight 2/m - 2/m = 0. Hence P and each of its partial derivatives, evaluated
at (t, w), have weight 0. Moreover d_eta t = (l_E/E) d_eta E and d_eta w = 2 eta s^(-2) E^(-1/m) - (w/m) (d_eta E)/E,
with |eta| E^(-1/m) <= |eta| Z^(-1/3) <= C <eta>^(-1), so |d_eta t| + |d_eta w| <= C <eta>^(-1).
(iii) Patches. Each G_l = x eta E^p exp(-(x^2 + eta^2)/L_l^2) Q_l(xi_l, zeta_l) has all partial derivatives of order
at most 3 bounded by C_N rho^(-N) for every N: they are finite sums of products of factors bounded by a polynomial in
|x| + |eta|, times the Gaussian, and rho <= C (1 + |x| + |eta|)^m (as in A.29 Step 2).
(iv) Orders of G. G_o := x eta E^p P(t, w) has weight 1 + 1/m + 2p = 2. With (iii), |A| <= C rho^(2 - 1 - 1/m) = C E^p
and |B0| = |G_xx| <= C on R^2.
(v) Chart and radius. A >= kappa and G_x(x, 0) = 0 make eta -> G_x(x, eta) strictly increasing with
|G_x(x, eta)| >= kappa |eta|, so (x, eta) -> (x, G_x) is a diffeomorphism of R^2 (implicit function theorem) and
|eta| <= |y|/kappa. For eta > 0 and eta/2 <= r <= eta one has 1 + (r/s)^6 >= Z/64, hence E(x, r) >= 64^(-m/3) E(x, eta);
integrating A over [eta/2, eta] for the lower bound, and using A <= C E^p with E increasing in |eta| for the upper
bound (and oddness in eta),
   c |eta| E^p <= |y| <= C |eta| E^p.                                                                          (31.14)
With |eta| <= C rho^(1/m) and 2p + 1/m = 1 this gives |y| <= C rho, so <X> <= C rho. Conversely, if rho is large then
x^2 >= rho^2/2 or Z^(m/3) >= rho^2/2; in the second case Z >= 2 once rho is large, so (eta/s)^6 >= Z/2,
|eta| >= c rho^(1/m) and |y| >= c rho by (31.14). Hence c rho <= <X> <= C rho on R^2.
(vi) Parities, centre and transport. G is odd in x and in eta and E, t, w and the patch factors are even in each, so,
as in A.29 Step 5, eta(x, y) is even in x and odd in y and all fields have the A1 parities. G is real analytic on R^2
(E >= 1 and 1 - dT >= e^(-alpha) > 0), so the analytic implicit function theorem at each point makes eta(x, y) and all
fields real analytic on R^2. The
computation of Step 1, which uses only h > 0 and holds for every beta > 2, gives h = A(0, 0) >= kappa (E(0, 0) = 1),
Psi = -2xy + O(|X|^4) and Theta_y(0) = a0/h != 0. By Proposition 23(b), div U = 0, (P2) and (P3) hold identically.
(vii) Cancellation in the stream function. Put Lambda = beta x d_x + b eta d_eta, so Psi = Lambda G - 2 beta G.
Since beta/m = b and p beta = 1, direct computation gives Lambda E = 2 beta (E - K), Lambda E^p = 2 E^p (1 - K/E),
Lambda (x eta) = (2 beta - 2) x eta, Lambda t = 2 beta l_E (1 - K/E) and Lambda w = 2 b w K/E. Hence
   Psi_o := Lambda G_o - 2 beta G_o = Psi_1 + Psi_2,   Psi_1 = 2 beta x eta E^p l_E P_t,
   Psi_2 = x eta E^(p - 1) K Pi,   Pi = 2 (b w P_w - P) - 2 beta l_E P_t,                                         (31.15)
with P and its derivatives evaluated at (t, w).
(viii) Velocity. Psi_1 has weight 1 + 1/m + 2p - p = 2 - p, so |d_x Psi_1| <= C rho^(1 - p) and
|d_eta Psi_1| <= C rho^(1 + p). For Psi_2, (i) and (ii) give |Pi| <= C, |d_x Pi| <= C rho^(-1), |d_eta Pi| <= C <eta>^(-1),
|d_x E^(p - 1)| <= C rho^(2p - 3) and |d_eta E^(p - 1)| <= C rho^(2p - 2) <eta>^(-1); with |x| <= rho, |eta| <= <eta>
and the bounds for K and d_eta K this gives
   |d_x Psi_2| <= C rho^(2p - 2) <eta>^(2m - 5),   |d_eta Psi_2| <= C rho^(2p - 1) <eta>^(2m - 6).
Using <eta> <= C rho^(1/m) when the exponent of <eta> is positive and <eta> >= 1 otherwise, and 1/m = 1 - 2p (so
2p - 5/m = 12p - 5 and -1 + 2 - 6/m = 12p - 5), one gets |d_x Psi_2| <= C rho^e and rho^(-2p) |d_eta Psi_2| <= C rho^e
with e := max(12p - 5, -1): |d_x Psi_2| <= C rho^(12p - 5) if 2m >= 5, and <= C rho^(2p - 2) <= C rho^(-1) otherwise;
rho^(-2p) |d_eta Psi_2| <= C rho^(-2p) rho^(2p - 1 + 2 - 6/m) = C rho^(12p - 5) if 2m >= 6, and <= C rho^(-1) otherwise. The patch part of Psi,
Lambda G_l - 2 beta G_l, has first derivatives bounded by C rho^(-N) for every N by (iii). Since U = (-Dy Psi, Dx Psi),
U1 = -Psi_eta/A, U2 = Psi_x - (B0/A) Psi_eta, A >= kappa rho^(2p) and |B0| <= C, one has
|U| <= C (|Psi_x| + rho^(-2p) |Psi_eta|), and the three parts contribute at most C rho^(1 - p) (using
rho^(-2p) rho^(1 + p) = rho^(1 - p)), C rho^e and C rho^(-1). Since p < 1/2, 12p - 5 < 1, and 12p - 5 <= 1 - p
exactly when p <= 6/13, that is beta >= 13/6 (on [5/2, 7/2], 12p - 5 <= -1/5). By (v),
   |U(X)| <= C <X>^q   on R^2,   q := max(1 - p, 12p - 5) < 1,   q = 1 - p for beta >= 13/6,               (31.16)
so U = o(|X|) uniformly.
(ix) Polynomial bounds and canonical velocity. Every partial derivative of G is bounded on R^2 by a polynomial in
|x| + |eta| (finite formulas in x, eta, powers of E >= 1 whose derivatives are polynomially bounded, functions of
T in (0, 1] that extend smoothly to [0, 1], smooth functions of w in [0, 1], and Gaussian factors). Since A >= kappa, every composition of the physical derivatives
Dx = d_x - (B0/A) d_eta and Dy = (1/A) d_eta applied to Psi or to eta is a polynomial with constant coefficients in x, eta,
finitely many partial derivatives of G and 1/A (by induction, since d(A^(-q)) = -q A^(-q-1) dA), hence polynomially
bounded in (x, eta), as 1/A <= 1/kappa; and |x| <= |X|, |eta| <= |y|/kappa. So Theta = a0 eta, Omega = -(Dx^2 + Dy^2) Psi and
their gradients are polynomially bounded on R^2. U is divergence-free with curl U = -Omega, U = o(|X|) uniformly and
U(0) = 0 by parity, so U is the canonical velocity of Omega (Section 2.3). Thus, under the chart bound, the fields
satisfy every requirement of class A' except possibly (P1), with physical slope a0/h != 0. Step 9 also gives
|Theta| <= C <X>^(1/m) and |grad Theta| = |a0| |(-B0/A, 1/A)| <= C <X>^(-2p). (The argument needs no decay estimate
for Omega and no absolute convergence of the subtracted kernel integral of Section 2.3; the conditional construction
of the independent verification, which this step replaces, also proves such bounds.)

#### Step 10 (the integer-m condition)
Assume in addition that (P1) holds on R^2. By Step 9 the hypotheses of Theorem 11 hold; the exponents called
delta and gamma there are 1/beta = p and 1 - 2p = 1/m. By Theorem 11(b), |X|^(-1/m) Theta(X) -> F(phi) uniformly in the polar angle phi as
|X| -> inf, and by Theorem 15(a), F is C^infinity.
(i) Sign of P(0, 0). On eta = 0 one has E = 1 + x^2 and w = 0, and as x -> +inf, T, t and l_E tend to 0 and the patch
terms and their derivatives, divided by E^p, tend to 0 faster than any power. For the unpatched term,
   (G_o)_x = eta E^p [P + 2 (x^2/E) (p P + l_E P_t - (w/m) P_w)],   G_x = (G_o)_x + sum_(l=1)^n (G_l)_x,           (31.17)
so A(x, 0)/E(x, 0)^p -> (1 + 2p) P(0, 0), and the chart bound gives c0 := P(0, 0) >= kappa/(1 + 2p) > 0.
(ii) The scaled chart. For r > 0 and real chi put Y_r(chi) = G_x(r, r^(1/m) chi)/r. At x = r, eta = r^(1/m) chi one has
E/r^2 = 1 + (r^(-6/m) + (chi/s)^6)^(m/3) -> B(chi) := 1 + (|chi|/s)^(2m), x^2/E -> 1/B,
w = (chi/s)^2 (E/r^2)^(-1/m) -> w0(chi) := (chi/s)^2 B(chi)^(-1/m), and t, l_E -> 0, locally uniformly in chi. By (31.17),
2p + 1/m = 1 and (iii) of Step 9,
   Y_r(chi) -> Y_0(chi) := chi B^p [P(0, w0) + 2 B^(-1) (p P(0, w0) - (w0/m) P_w(0, w0))]                     (31.18)
locally uniformly in chi. Moreover Y_r'(chi) = r^(1/m - 1) A(r, r^(1/m) chi) >= kappa r^(1/m - 1) E^p >= kappa (E >= r^2),
so Y_r(chi2) - Y_r(chi1) >= kappa (chi2 - chi1) for chi2 > chi1, and in the limit the same holds for Y_0. Y_0 is odd and
continuous, hence a homeomorphism of R; let chi_0 be its inverse.
(iii) Rays. Fix tau in R. The point X = (r, r tau) has mixed coordinate eta = r^(1/m) chi_r(tau), where chi_r(tau) is the
unique solution of Y_r(chi) = tau, so Theta(r, r tau) = a0 r^(1/m) chi_r(tau). Since
kappa |chi_r(tau) - chi_0(tau)| <= |Y_r(chi_r(tau)) - Y_r(chi_0(tau))| = |Y_0(chi_0(tau)) - Y_r(chi_0(tau))| -> 0,
r^(-1/m) Theta(r, r tau) -> a0 chi_0(tau). On the other hand |X| = r (1 + tau^2)^(1/2) and the angle of X is arctan tau,
so the far-field limit gives r^(-1/m) Theta(r, r tau) -> (1 + tau^2)^(1/(2m)) F(arctan tau). Therefore
   a0 chi_0(tau) = (1 + tau^2)^(1/(2m)) F(arctan tau)   for every real tau,
and, since a0 != 0, chi_0 is C^infinity on R.
(iv) Expansion of Y_0. Write P(0, w) = sum_(k=0)^J c_k w^k, where J is the degree of P(0, .) (so c_0 = c0 > 0), and h_k = p - k/m. Substituting
w0^k = (chi/s)^(2k) B^(-k/m) in (31.18),
   Y_0(chi) = sum_k c_k s^(-2k) chi^(2k+1) g_(h_k)(v),   v = (|chi|/s)^(2m),   g_h(v) = (1 + v)^h + 2h (1 + v)^(h - 1).
Each g_h is analytic for |v| < 1, with g_h(0) = 1 + 2h and g_h'(0) = h + 2h(h - 1) = h (2h - 1). Hence
Y_0(chi) = (1 + 2p) c0 chi + O(|chi|^3) near 0, so Y_0'(0) = (1 + 2p) c0 > 0, and, as chi -> 0+,
   Y_0(chi) = Q(chi) + c* chi^(2m+1) + O(chi^(2m+3) + chi^(4m+1)),   c* = c0 p (2p - 1) s^(-2m),                 (31.19)
where Q(chi) = sum_k c_k s^(-2k) (1 + 2h_k) chi^(2k+1) is an odd polynomial. c* != 0, since c0 > 0 and 0 < p < 1/2.
(v) Conclusion. Since Y_0 is differentiable at 0 with Y_0'(0) > 0, its inverse chi_0 has chi_0'(0) = 1/Y_0'(0) != 0;
as chi_0 is C^infinity by (iii), the inverse function theorem makes Y_0 C^infinity on a neighbourhood of 0. Suppose
that m is not an integer. Let N be the least integer >= 2m + 1 and T_N the Taylor polynomial of degree N of Y_0 at 0;
T_N is odd, since Y_0 is. By (31.19), as chi -> 0+,
   (T_N - Q)(chi) + O(chi^(N+1)) = c* chi^(2m+1) + o(chi^(2m+1)).
Let j be the least degree of a non-zero term of the odd polynomial T_N - Q (j = +inf if T_N = Q). If j < 2m + 1, the
left side has exact order chi^j while the right side is O(chi^(2m+1)); if j > 2m + 1, the left side is o(chi^(2m+1))
(N + 1 > 2m + 1) while the right side has exact order chi^(2m+1). Both are impossible. Finally j = 2m + 1 is impossible:
if 2m + 1 is not an integer this is clear, and if it is an integer then 2m is an odd integer (m is not an integer), so
2m + 1 is even and the odd polynomial T_N - Q has no term of that degree. Hence m is an integer.

#### Step 11 (conclusion of (b) and (c))
By Step 10, m = 1 + 2/(beta - 2) is an integer, m >= 2 since m > 1, and beta = 2m/(m - 1); h >= kappa > 0 by Step 9. If m = 3, then beta = 3, b = 1, p = 1/3 and E = 1 + x^2 + (eta/s)^6, so G,
t, w and the fields are those of Proposition 27 with the same polynomials, patches and a0 (the number of patches, called m in
Proposition 27, is the present n; the present exponent is m = 3), and Proposition 27 shows
that (P1) fails on every neighbourhood of 0. For m = 4 and 5 (beta = 8/3 and 5/2), part (a) shows the same, and for
every other integer m >= 2 (beta = 4 and beta = 2m/(m - 1) with m >= 6), Step 8a does. In every case (P1) does not hold on
R^2, a contradiction. This proves the global assertion of (c); its local assertion was proved in Step 8a. (By Step 8b the global
assertion also follows from (d) without Steps 10 and 11, as stated in Proposition 30(d).) For beta in [5/2, 7/2], m lies in [7/3, 5], so only m = 3, 4 and 5 occur and
Step 8a is not needed; this is (b). QED

#### Scope and dependencies
Uses: for (a), the local part of (c) and (d), as in A.28 (analytic implicit function theorem, finite Taylor expansion in eta, the one-variable identity
theorem, explicit asymptotics on one boundary branch, Proposition 23(b)); for (b) and (c), in addition elementary weighted bounds for the finite formulas (Step 9), the uniqueness definition of the
canonical velocity (Section 2.3), Proposition 23(b), Theorems 11(b) and 15(a), the smooth and the real analytic implicit
and inverse function theorems, Proposition 27 and (a). In (a), (c) and (d) the hypothesis h > 0 is used only for the local inverse
and to exclude g = 0; no global positivity is used. In (b) and (c) the chart bound gives the global chart, the velocity bound (31.16) and P(0, 0) > 0, and is
essential to the argument. Not covered: limits of increasing degree; estimates uniform in beta; other maps or exponents; general analytic or smooth G;
residual lower bounds; Setting A1 in general.
