### A.32 Proposition 31 (conditional obstructions for large-beta asymptotic families)

Step 1 (rescaled equations). In polar coordinates U_r = -r^(-1) Psi_phi = -r psi_phi and
U_phi = Psi_r = r (2 psi + eps psi_s), since r d_r = eps d_s on functions of (s, phi). Hence
W.grad = (beta r + U_r) d_r + r^(-1) U_phi d_phi = (1 - eps psi_phi) d_s + (2 psi + eps psi_s) d_phi on functions of
(s, phi). (P2) for Theta = r theta, with W.grad r = beta r - r psi_phi, gives
r [(beta - psi_phi) theta + (1 - eps psi_phi) theta_s + (2 psi + eps psi_s) theta_phi] = (beta - 2) r theta, which is
(T). Theta_x = cos phi Theta_r - r^(-1) sin phi Theta_phi = cos phi (theta + eps theta_s) - sin phi theta_phi, so (P1)
is (V). Delta f = r^(-2) [(r d_r)^2 + d_phi^2] f and (r d_r)(r^2 psi) = r^2 (r d_r + 2) psi give
Delta(r^2 psi) = (eps d_s + 2)^2 psi + psi_phiphi, so (P3) is (E). The pure strain satisfies (T), (V), (E): for
theta = a0 sin phi and psi = -sin 2phi, 2 psi theta_phi - psi_phi theta = a0 C(-sin 2phi) = -2 a0 sin phi cancels
2 theta, B sin phi = 0 and 4 psi + psi_phiphi = 0. The identities used here and below are
   C g := 2 g cos phi - g_phi sin phi = -sin^3 phi (g/sin^2 phi)_phi,   C (sin 2phi) = 2 sin phi,
   B f = -sin^2 phi (f/sin phi)_phi,   B sin phi = 0,   (B f)_phi = -sin phi (f + f_phiphi).
The limits of p_beta: Psi/r^2 -> -sin 2phi as r -> 0 by the centre jet; if sup_(|X| >= R) |U|/|X| -> 0 as R -> oo,
then |Psi(X)| <= int_0^r |grad Psi| = o(r^2) since Psi(0) = 0, so psi -> 0 uniformly as s -> +oo. Under the scaling,
psi_lambda(s, phi) = psi(s - (ln lambda)/beta, phi). If U = o(|X|) uniformly, the continuous function p_beta therefore
takes the value -1/2, and a scaling moves such a point to s = 0.

Step 2 (notation for (a)). On T use ||f||_(L^2)^2 = pi^(-1) int_0^(2 pi) f^2 and
||f||_(H^1)^2 = ||f||_(L^2)^2 + ||f_phi||_(L^2)^2. P1 is the projection on sin phi and Q1 = I - P1; both are orthogonal
in L^2 and in H^1. On the span of sin 2m phi let K sin 2phi = 0 and K sin 2m phi = sin 2m phi/(4 (m^2 - 1)), m >= 2;
then ||K w||_(H^2) <= (17/12) ||w||_(L^2) (for n = 2m >= 4, (1 + n^2)/(n^2 - 4) <= 17/12), hence
||C K w||_(H^1) <= C0 ||w||_(L^2) and ||B v||_(L^2) <= sqrt(2) ||v||_(H^1). For an equation f_s + b f_phi + c f = F with f
of class C^2 and periodic b, c of class C^1, integration by parts gives
   (1/2) d/ds ||f||_(H^1)^2 = pi^(-1) int [ (b_phi/2 - c) f^2 + (-b_phi/2 - c) f_phi^2 - c_phi f f_phi ] + <f, F>_(H^1),
so |(1/2) d/ds ||f||_(H^1)^2| <= C(b, c) ||f||_(H^1)^2 + ||f||_(H^1) ||F||_(H^1), and the analogous L^2 inequality
holds. If f = Q1 f and the equation is projected by Q1, the same inequality holds, because <f, Q1 h>_(H^1) = <f,
h>_(H^1). Inserting the expansions into (T), (V), (E) and using that products and the displayed derivatives preserve
o(eps) in C^0(J x T), the coefficients of eps^0 and eps^1 vanish. Fix S0 < s1 < S and work on I = [S0, S]; all
coefficients are bounded on I x T with the derivatives used (at most two in total, so C^2 suffices). Each energy Z
below satisfies |Z'| <= C Z on I with Z(s1) = 0, hence Z = 0 on I by Gronwall's inequality applied forward and backward
from s1; S0 and S are arbitrary.

Step 3 (order 0 for the given p). By (E) at order 0, omega_0 = -(4 + d_phi^2) psi_0, so omega_0 has no sin 2phi
component and psi_0 = p sin 2phi + K omega_0 with p the sin 2phi coefficient of psi_0. Let
a = a* exp(-2 int_(s1)^s (1 + p)), so that a' = -2 (1 + p) a, a(s1) = a*. For v0 = theta_0 - a sin phi and w0 = omega_0
the order-0 parts of (T) and (V) are exactly
   v0_s + 2 psi_0 v0_phi + (2 - psi_0,phi) v0 = -a C K w0,      w0_s + 2 psi_0 w0_phi + w0 = B v0,
since a' sin phi + 2 a sin phi + a C (p sin 2phi) = (a' + 2 (1 + p) a) sin phi = 0 and B (a sin phi) = 0. The first
equation is estimated in H^1 and the second in L^2; C K gains one derivative and B loses one, so
Z0 = ||v0||_(H^1)^2 + ||w0||_(L^2)^2 satisfies |Z0'| <= C Z0. The data give Z0(s1) = 0 (omega_0(s1) = 0 already follows
from psi_0(s1) by (E)). Hence theta_0 = a sin phi, omega_0 = 0 and psi_0 = p sin 2phi on I. No equation for p has been
used yet.

Step 4 (order 1 determines p). Let v = Q1 theta_1, w = omega_1, and w_1 the sin 2phi coefficient of w. (E) at order 1
is omega_1 = -(4 + d_phi^2) psi_1 - 4 p' sin 2phi, so w_1 = -4 p' and psi_1 = K w + q sin 2phi with q the kernel
coefficient. With L_p f := 2 f + 2 p sin 2phi f_phi - 2 p cos 2phi f one has L_p sin phi = 2 (1 + p) sin phi, and
q sin 2phi contributes to the order-1 part of (T) only a C (q sin 2phi) = 2 a q sin phi; the sin phi component of
theta_1 is annihilated by B. Hence the order-1 equations projected by Q1 in (T) are exactly
   v_s + Q1 L_p v + a Q1 C K w = Q1 [ -a p' sin 2phi cos phi + 2 p a' cos 2phi sin phi ],
   w_s + 2 p sin 2phi w_phi + w = B v + (a'/2) sin 2phi,
   p' = -w_1/4,   a' = -2 (1 + p) a,
with no finite Fourier truncation. Put d = p + 1 and e = a - a*. Then |p'| <= ||w||_(L^2)/4 and |a'| <= 2 |a| |d|, the
H^1 norm of the forcing of the first equation is at most C (||w||_(L^2) + |d|), and the L^2 norm of the forcing of
the second is at most C (||v||_(H^1) + |d|). With Z1 = ||v||_(H^1)^2 + ||w||_(L^2)^2 + d^2 + e^2 the estimates of
Step 2 give |Z1'| <= C Z1, and the data give Z1(s1) = 0. So p == -1, a == a*, Q1 theta_1 = 0 and omega_1 = 0 on I;
then psi_1 = q sin 2phi, theta_1 = t sin phi, and the remaining sin phi projection of (T) at order 1 is
t' + 2 a* q = 0. Since S0 and S are arbitrary this holds on R, and p_beta = p + O(eps) gives the last assertion of (a).
(Remark: if all orders exist with remainders O(eps^(N+1)) in C^2 and pure data through order N at s1, the same
estimates applied successively to the orders n + 1 in the unknowns (h_n, b_n, Q1 theta_(n+1), omega_(n+1)), where
theta_n = b_n sin phi, psi_n = h_n sin 2phi and b_n' = -2 a* h_n, show that all orders below N are pure strain on
R; a product of two order-n coefficients enters order n + 1 only for n = 1, as 2 b_1 h_1 sin phi, which Q1
removes. The top pair theta_N = t_N sin phi, psi_N = q_N sin 2phi with t_N' + 2 a* q_N = 0 is not determined. This is
not used.)

Step 5 ((b) and (c): hydrostatic leading order). Put M = a0(beta); under (b) or (c), |M| -> oo. (T) is linear in
theta, so eta satisfies (T). Divide (V) by M:
   B eta + eps cos phi eta_s = M^(-1) [omega_s + omega + 2 psi omega_phi + eps (psi_s omega_phi - psi_phi omega_s)],
whose right side is O(1/|M|) in C^0(J x T) because psi and omega are bounded in C^1. Letting beta -> oo gives
B eta_0 = 0, so (eta_0/sin phi)_phi = 0 on 0 < phi < pi and, by parity, eta_0 = alpha(s) sin phi with alpha of class
C^2. Passing to the limit in (T) for eta gives eta_0,s + 2 eta_0 + 2 psi_0 eta_0,phi - psi_0,phi eta_0 = 0, that is
(alpha' + 2 alpha) sin phi + alpha C psi_0 = 0. Let I0 be a component of the open set {alpha != 0}; it is non-empty
because eta_0 is not identically zero. On I0, (psi_0/sin^2 phi)_phi = kappa/sin^2 phi with kappa = alpha'/alpha + 2, so
psi_0 = -kappa sin phi cos phi + K(s) sin^2 phi on 0 < phi < pi; psi_0 is odd under phi -> pi - phi, sin phi cos phi
is odd and sin^2 phi is even, so K = 0 (on pi < phi < 2 pi the same holds by oddness under phi -> -phi) and
psi_0 = p sin 2phi with p = -kappa/2, that is alpha' = -2 (1 + p) alpha. The limit of (E), in which eps^2 psi_ss -> 0
since psi is bounded in C^2, gives omega_0 = -(4 psi_0 + psi_0,phiphi) = 0 on I0 x T.

Step 6 ((b): the exact axis identity). Assume (b) and let J be a compact subinterval of I0. Let L be the left side of
(V). Its phi-derivative
   L_phi = omega_(s phi) + omega_phi + 2 psi_phi omega_phi + 2 psi omega_phiphi
           + eps (psi_(s phi) omega_phi + psi_s omega_phiphi - psi_phiphi omega_s - psi_phi omega_(s phi))
contains derivatives of total order at most 2; since omega -> omega_0 = 0 in C^2(J x T) by Step 5 and psi is bounded
in C^2(J x T), L_phi -> 0 uniformly on J x T. On the right side of (V), (B theta)_phi = -sin phi (theta + theta_phiphi)
and (eps cos phi theta_s)_phi = eps (cos phi theta_(s phi) - sin phi theta_s). At phi = 0 the phi-derivative of (V) is
therefore exactly L_phi(s, 0) = eps M eta_(s phi)(s, 0), that is
   eta_(s phi)(s, 0) = (beta/M) L_phi(s, 0).
By hypothesis |beta/M| is bounded for large beta, so the right side tends to 0 uniformly on J, while
eta_(s phi)(s, 0) -> eta_0,(s phi)(s, 0) = alpha'(s). Hence alpha' = 0 on J, and so on I0. No expansion beyond the
limits is used.

Step 7 ((c): psi - psi_0 = O(eps) away from the x-axis). Assume (c) and let J be a compact subinterval of I0, so
|alpha| >= c > 0 on J. Put D = eta - eta_0, which is O(eps) in C^2(J x T), and v = psi - psi_0. Subtracting the limit
equation of Step 5 from (T) for eta gives
   alpha C v = -[ D_s + 2 D + 2 psi D_phi - psi_phi D + eps (psi_s eta_phi - psi_phi eta_s) ] =: alpha R,
and R = O(eps) in C^1(J x T) since psi and eta are bounded in C^2. As psi and psi_0 vanish at phi = pi/2 (oddness
under phi -> pi - phi), C v = R integrates to v(s, phi) = sin^2 phi int_phi^(pi/2) R(s, u) sin^(-3) u du. Fix
0 < phi1 < pi/2. With I(s, phi) = int_phi^(pi/2) R(s, u) sin^(-3) u du this gives v = sin^2 phi I,
v_phi = 2 sin phi cos phi I - R/sin phi and v_phiphi = 2 cos 2phi I - (cos phi/sin^2 phi) R - R_phi/sin phi, all
O(eps) on J x [phi1, pi - phi1]. Since 4 psi_0 + psi_0,phiphi = 0, (E) gives
omega = -(4 v + v_phiphi) - 4 eps psi_s - eps^2 psi_ss = O(eps) on J x [phi1, pi - phi1].

Step 8 ((c): the next order of (V), weakly). Let chi be smooth with compact support in the interior of
J x [phi1, pi - phi1]. Integrating by parts in s and phi,
   int [omega_s + omega + 2 psi omega_phi + eps (psi_s omega_phi - psi_phi omega_s)] chi
      = int omega [chi - chi_s - (2 psi chi)_phi] + eps int (psi_s omega_phi - psi_phi omega_s) chi = O(eps),
using Step 7 and the boundedness of psi and omega in C^1. The right side of (V) is
M (B eta + eps cos phi eta_s) = M eps (B eta_1 + cos phi eta_0,s) + o(M eps) in C^0, because B eta_0 = 0,
eta - eta_0 - eps eta_1 = o(eps) in C^1 and eta_s - eta_0,s = O(eps) in C^0. Dividing by M eps,
int (B eta_1 + cos phi eta_0,s) chi = O(1/|M|) + o(1), which tends to 0. As chi is arbitrary and the integrand is
continuous, B eta_1 = -alpha' sin phi cos phi on J x [phi1, pi - phi1], and, phi1 being arbitrary, on J x (0, pi).
Hence (eta_1/sin phi)_phi = alpha' cos phi/sin phi there, and
   eta_1 = alpha' sin phi ln(sin phi) + C(s) sin phi   on J x (0, pi).
Its phi-derivative alpha' (cos phi ln(sin phi) + cos phi) + C cos phi is unbounded as phi -> 0+ unless alpha' = 0,
while eta_1 is C^1 on T. So alpha' = 0 on J, hence on I0.

Step 9 ((b) and (c): conclusion). On I0, alpha is a non-zero constant; if I0 had a finite end point s_e, continuity
would give alpha(s_e) = that constant != 0, so s_e would lie in {alpha != 0}, contradicting maximality. Hence I0 = R,
alpha is a non-zero constant, alpha' = -2 (1 + p) alpha gives p == -1, so psi_0 = -sin 2phi and omega_0 = 0 on R x T,
and p_beta = p + o(1) locally uniformly, since |p_beta(s) - p(s)| <= (4/pi) sup_phi |psi(s, phi) - psi_0(s, phi)|.
(The hypotheses do not identify alpha with 1.) In (b) the bound on beta/|a0| is used only in Step 6; in (c) only
|a0| -> oo is used, in Steps 5 and 8. For bounded a0 the bound O(1/|M|) in Step 8 is not small, and neither argument
applies.

Step 10 (the normalized scale and the sufficient condition). In the normalized scale p_beta(0) = -1/2, which
contradicts p_beta(0) -> -1 in (a), (b) and (c) when their hypotheses hold for the normalized fields. For the sufficient
condition: dividing the remainders by r, r^2 and 1 gives |theta - a0 sin phi|, |psi + sin 2phi|, |omega| <= C
(r/rho_beta)^2 <= C e^(2 beta (s - s_*)) for s <= s_*, and d_s = beta r d_r gives the same bounds times beta^j for (s,
phi)-derivatives of order (j, l). At the fixed s1 < s_* (both independent of beta) these are at most
C beta^j e^(-2 beta (s_* - s1)), smaller than every power of eps, so the coefficients of the expansions of (a) at s1
are those of the pure strain: theta_0 = a0 sin phi, psi_0 = -sin 2phi, omega_0 = 0,
theta_1 = psi_1 = omega_1 = 0. The condition supplies only these data; the expansions on every compact s-interval
remain hypotheses.

Step 11 ((d): finite beta by compactness). Suppose that (d) fails for some Lambda >= 1. Then there are beta_n -> oo and
smooth solutions of (P) with the A1 parity, a0 = a0,n != 0 and p_(beta_n)(0) = -1/2 satisfying (d1) to (d3). The
derivatives of order at most 2 of eta, psi, omega are bounded and equicontinuous on Q by (d2), so by the Arzela-Ascoli
theorem, and the fundamental theorem of calculus to identify the limits of the derivatives, a subsequence converges in
C^2(Q) to limits eta_0, psi_0, omega_0 of class C^2 with the A1 parities (each parity is preserved under uniform
convergence). Then max over [-1, 1] x T of |eta_0| >= 1/Lambda, and the sin 2phi coefficient p of psi_0 satisfies
p(0) = -1/2, since |p_(beta_n)(s) - p(s)| <= (4/pi) sup over phi of |psi_n(s, phi) - psi_0(s, phi)|. Moreover
|a0,n| >= beta_n/Lambda -> oo and |beta_n/a0,n| <= Lambda. Steps 5 and 6 use only these facts, the C^2 convergence on
J x T for compact intervals J and the C^2 bounds on psi and omega there; they therefore hold with R replaced by
(-2, 2): eta_0 = alpha sin phi with alpha of class C^2, and on every component I0 of {s in (-2, 2): alpha(s) != 0} one
has psi_0 = p sin 2phi, omega_0 = 0, alpha' = -2 (1 + p) alpha and alpha' = 0. Choose s0 in [-1, 1] with
|alpha(s0)| >= 1/Lambda and let I0 be the component containing s0. Then alpha is the non-zero constant alpha(s0) on I0;
an end point of I0 inside (-2, 2) would carry the same non-zero value by continuity, contrary to maximality, so
I0 = (-2, 2) and p = -1 there; in particular p(0) = -1, a contradiction. No far-field information and no quantitative
centre estimate enter this step.

Uses: Section 2.4 (centre strain -2), Proposition 26 (cited in the scope remark only). Checks: the rescaled equations
(T), (V), (E), the identities for B and C and the order-0 and order-1 projections were checked symbolically by the
authors (exact rewriting, Fourier projections by Laurent-polynomial algebra); the logarithmic solution of
B f = -alpha' sin phi cos phi, the hydrostatic expansion of (c) and the x-axis identities obtained by differentiating
(T) and (V) in phi at phi = 0 were checked symbolically by the authors. The independent verification wrote
its own complete proofs of (a) in the present two-sided C^2 form, of (b) and of (c), checked their algebra
symbolically (136, 40 and 50 finite identity records), and confirmed the arguments of Steps 1 to 10; the corrections it
required in the records of Appendix B were made before installation.
The independent verification checked Step 11 with its own standalone proof (the exact polar and axis equations, the
relation d_s = beta r d_r and the annulus e^(-2 beta) <= r <= e^(2 beta), the C^2 compactness from the C^3 bounds, the
persistence of the lower bound (d3) in the limit, and the argument of Steps 5 and 6 on (-2, 2)); it also proved that
eta(s, pi/2) > 0 for every s for each smooth A1 profile with beta > 2, so the exception in the remark after (d) does
not occur and each single profile satisfies (d1) to (d3) for some Lambda depending on it.

### A.33 Proposition 32 (rough separated modes at the pure strain; linear level)

Statement: Section 3, after Proposition 31. Notation of A.32: eps = 1/beta, s = (ln r)/beta, the operators
L_p f = 2f + 2p sin 2phi f_phi - 2p cos 2phi f, C h = 2 cos phi h - sin phi h_phi and B u = cos phi u - sin phi u_phi,
the projection Q1 removing the sin phi coefficient and the inverse K of -(d^2/dphi^2 + 4) on the span of sin 2m phi,
m >= 2. Throughout a = a* > 0 and S = sqrt(9 + 4a*). The scalar unknown F' below is called b, to distinguish it from
the operator B.

Step 1 (the linearization). Insert v = e^(lam s) f, w = e^(lam s) g, psi_1 = e^(lam s) h, p = -1 + P e^(lam s) and
a = a* + A e^(lam s) into the closed order-1 system of A.32 Step 4 and keep the terms linear in (f, g, h, P, A). The
equation a' = -2 (1 + p) a gives lam A = -2 a* P. With J = -a* lam P sin 2phi cos phi + 4 a* P cos 2phi sin phi
(the linearized forcing of the first equation; a' = -2 a* P e^(lam s) at this order), the equations for v, w and the
order-1 part of (E) become
  (L1)  lam f + L_(-1) f + a* C h = J   up to a multiple of sin phi,
  (L2)  lam g - 2 sin 2phi g_phi + g = B f - a* P sin 2phi,
  (L3)  h_phiphi + 4h + g + 4 lam P sin 2phi = 0.
The closed system keeps only Q1 (L1), with h = K g + q sin 2phi; C (sin 2phi) = 2 sin phi, so q affects only the
sin phi coefficient. The sin 2phi coefficient of (L3) is g_1 = -4 lam P, the linearization of p' = -w_1/4. The
unprojected lift also imposes the sin phi coefficient of (L1), for the full temperature coefficient f + t sin phi.

Step 2 (reduction). Write D = z(1 - z) and f = sin phi F(z), g = sin 2phi G(z), h = sin 2phi H(z), z = sin^2 phi, and
put b = F', R = H'. These representations satisfy all reflection parities of A1 automatically (f odd in phi and even
under phi -> pi - phi; g and h odd under both); regularity at the axes is the only remaining condition. Direct
substitution gives L_(-1) f/sin phi = -8D F', C h/sin phi = 2H - 4D H', (B f)/sin 2phi = -z F' and
J/sin phi = a P [(4 - 2 lam) + (2 lam - 8) z]. Hence (L2) and (L3), divided by sin 2phi, are equations (2) and (3)
below, and the residual of (L1) divided by sin phi is
   T(z) = lam F - 8D b + a (2H - 4D R) - a P [(4 - 2 lam) + (2 lam - 8) z],
whose derivative is T' = (left side of (1)) - a (left side of (3)). The system (*) for Y = (b, G, R, P) is
   (1) -8D b' + (lam - 8 + 16z) b + a G + 4a (1 - z) R + 2a (lam + 4) P = 0,
   (2) -8D G' + (lam - 3 + 8z) G + z b + a P = 0,
   (3)  4D R' + 6 (1 - 2z) R + G + 4 lam P = 0,
   P' = 0.
So (*) is equivalent to (L2), (L3) and the statement that the residual of (L1) is a constant multiple of sin phi
(the first integral (I1): T is constant along (*)). Its solution space on (0, 1) is 4-dimensional and its only
singular points are the regular singular points 0, 1 and oo.

Step 3 (integral identity). For every solution of (3), since D' = 1 - 2z,
   (I2) [D^(3/2) R]' = D^(1/2) [D R' + (3/2)(1 - 2z) R] = -(1/4) D^(1/2) (G + 4 lam P).
With g_1 = (1/pi) int_0^(2 pi) g sin 2phi dphi = (8/pi) int_0^1 D^(1/2) G dz and int_0^1 D^(1/2) dz = pi/8,
integration of (I2) over (0, 1) with D^(3/2) R -> 0 at both ends gives int_0^1 D^(1/2) G dz = -(pi/2) lam P, that is
g_1 = -4 lam P. The vanishing of the end fluxes holds for every admissible solution (Step 5), so the compatibility
condition of the closed system holds for them; the differential identity alone is not that condition.

Step 4 (exponents). Write (*) as Y' = M(z) Y. The residue z M at z = 0 has the eigenvalues
   0,   rho_b = (lam - 8)/8,   rho_G = (lam - 3)/8,   -3/2,
and the residue -(1 - z) M at z = 1, for differentiation in xi = 1 - z, has the eigenvalues
   0,   rho_+ = -lam/8 - 13/16 + S/16,   rho_- = -lam/8 - 13/16 - S/16,   -3/2.
The angular behaviour of the branches, after subtraction of analytic parts and of the constants of the primitives
F and H (an integration constant can add a lower-order smooth term to f or h, so these are the rough contributions
and not necessarily the leading terms of f and h), is as follows.
 - z = 0, branch rho_b: b ~ c z^(rho_b), G ~ (c/3) z^(rho_b + 1), R ~ -2c/(3 (lam + 12)) z^(rho_b + 1); hence f and g
   carry the power phi |phi|^(2 rho_b + 2) = phi |phi|^(lam/4) (signed power (lam + 4)/4) and h the power two
   higher.
 - z = 0, branch rho_G: g ~ phi |phi|^(2 rho_G), the signed power (lam + 1)/4, and f, h carry the power two
   higher.
 - z = 1, branch rho_+, with t = pi/2 - phi: g carries the signed power 2 rho_+ + 1 = (S - 2 lam - 5)/8, f the even
   power one higher and h the signed power two higher.
 - The exponent 0 contributes analytic terms when its Frobenius recurrence is unobstructed; at resonances it can
   contain logarithms. For example, at a* = 600, lam = 8 and P = 1 every locally admissible solution at z = 0 has
   G -> -120, R -> 44/3 and b = -2800 log z + O(1), which gives phi^3 log|phi| terms in f and g, of class C^2.
 - The branches -3/2 give H ~ z^(-1/2) (or xi^(-1/2)), so h has opposite non-zero one-sided limits at the axis,
   which no integration constant removes.
 - For a > 0 and lam > 0, rho_- < -1, and the G component of its branch is non-zero, so g ~ sign(t) |t|^(2 rho_- + 1),
   which is not in L^2.
   At a collision rho_- = -3/2 (for example a* = 10, lam = 2) the ordinary eigenvector is the R direction, with
   G = 0, which gives the jump of h, and the generalized vector has a G component not in L^2 (or an R log term); no
   further admissible direction appears.

Step 5 (admissibility). A signed power sign(x) |x|^m (or an even power |x|^m) with m not an integer of the right
parity is C^k at 0 exactly when m > k, and a term |x|^m times a fixed polynomial in log|x| is C^k when m > k; with the
strict inequalities below, logarithmic factors are harmless. Two classes are used.
 (C^k) f, g in C^k(T) and h in C^(k+2)(T); the last follows from (L3) once g is in C^k. The following strict
   inequalities are sufficient for admissibility of the respective branches, also in the presence of logarithms (they
   are not asserted to classify exceptional branches outside these intervals; an integral power of the right parity
   can be smooth). At z = 0: lam > 4k - 4 (branch rho_b) and lam > 4k - 1 (branch rho_G). At z = 1:
   2 rho_+ + 1 > k, that is lam < lam_c(k) := (S - 8k - 5)/2.
 (E) f in H^1, g in L^2 and h in H^2. At z = 0 every branch except -3/2 qualifies for lam > 0. At z = 1 the branch
   rho_+ qualifies if and only if 2 rho_+ + 1 > -1/2, that is lam < lam_E := (S - 1)/2 (its G coefficient is non-zero,
   and logarithms cannot improve borderline integrability).
In both classes and in the stated intervals of lam, every admissible exponent at an end has larger real part than every
excluded exponent there: at z = 0 the excluded exponent is -3/2 < -1 and the admissible ones are 0, rho_b, rho_G > -1;
at z = 1 the excluded ones are -3/2 and rho_- < -1 and the admissible ones are 0 and rho_+ > -3/4. The admissible
solutions near an end are therefore exactly the solutions with |Y| = O(x^mu) (x = z or xi) for any mu strictly between
the two groups of exponents. By the Frobenius theory of linear systems with a regular singular point (convergent
expansions in powers times polynomials in log x, with the resonant coefficient recurrence; G. Teschl, Ordinary
Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, Section 4.4), this space has dimension equal to the number of admissible
exponents counted with multiplicity: logarithms couple an exponent only to equal or larger exponents differing by an
integer, which are again admissible, and the inequalities are strict. So the admissible space has dimension 3 at
z = 0 and 2 at z = 1, also at resonances (for example lam = 8, where rho_b = 0, or rho_+ = 0, which occurs for
a* = (lam + 8)(lam + 5) inside the energy interval). For admissible solutions the R exponents are 0, lam/8 and
rho_G > -3/8 at z = 0 and 0 and rho_+ > -3/4 at z = 1, all above -3/2, so D^(3/2) R -> 0 at both ends (Step 3).

Step 6 (existence; the dimension is at least 1). The admissible spaces at the two ends continue to subspaces of the
4-dimensional solution space on (0, 1), of dimensions 3 and 2, so their intersection has dimension at least
3 + 2 - 4 = 1. The interval of (ii) is non-empty if and only if S > 16k + 3, that is a* > 64k^2 + 24k (k = 2:
a* > 304); the interval of (i) is non-empty for every a* > 0. An element of the intersection is admissible on the
whole circle: the representation of Step 2 is regular for 0 < z < 1 and the end behaviour is that of Step 5.

Step 7 (P != 0; the dimension is exactly 1). Suppose a non-zero admissible solution has P = 0. Then (b, G, R) solves
the homogeneous three-dimensional system, whose residue at z = 1 has the eigenvalues rho_+, rho_- and -3/2. Only
rho_+ is admissible; it is simple and strictly larger than the other two, so the solution is a multiple of its
Frobenius branch (also when rho_+ = 0 in the four-dimensional system). The leading vector of this branch in the
coordinates (b, G, R), normalized by G = 1, is ((3 - S)/2, 1, 1/(4 rho_+ + 6)); since S > 3 and
rho_+ > -3/2, the functions m := -b, G and R are strictly positive for small xi > 0 (after choosing the sign of the
multiple). In xi = 1 - z the homogeneous equations read
   8D m_xi = -(lam - 8 + 16z) m + a G + 4a (1 - z) R,
   8D G_xi = z m - (lam - 3 + 8z) G,
   4D R_xi = G + 6 (1 - 2z) R.
Every off-diagonal coefficient is non-negative on 0 < z < 1, and the non-zero ones a/(8D), a/(2z), z/(8D) and 1/(4D)
are strictly positive. With scalar integrating factors on each compact subinterval, the integral form of a cooperative
linear system keeps all three components strictly positive (a first component to reach zero would contradict its
integral formula), starting from a small xi > 0 where all three are positive; no argument is applied at a singular end.
Hence G > 0 on (0, 1). But (I2) with P = 0 and the vanishing end fluxes of Step 5 give int_0^1 D^(1/2) G dz = 0, a
contradiction. So Y -> P is injective on the admissible space, its dimension is exactly 1, and every non-zero
admissible solution has P != 0. This proves (i) and (ii).

Step 8 ((iii): no smooth reduced mode). Suppose f, g, h are C^oo with the parities. At either axis g and h are odd
and sin 2phi has a simple zero, so g/sin 2phi and h/sin 2phi are smooth and even in the local angular coordinate; at
phi = 0 the same holds for f/sin phi, and at phi = pi/2 sin phi is non-zero and f is even. A smooth even function is a
smooth function of the square of the coordinate, and z (or 1 - z) is a smooth invertible function of that square; so
F, G, H, and hence Y, are C^oo functions of z at both ends.
A C^oo solution on [0, x0) of a linear system x Y' = A(x) Y with A analytic at x = 0 is analytic there. Write
A = sum_(j >= 0) A_j x^j with radius of convergence R0, fix 0 < r < R0, put M = sum_(j >= 1) ||A_j|| r^j and choose an
integer N > 2M with ||(n I - A_0)^(-1)|| <= 2/n for all n >= N. The Taylor coefficients y_n of Y at 0 satisfy
   (n I - A_0) y_n = sum_(j=1)^n A_j y_(n-j),
so c_n = ||y_n|| r^n satisfies c_n <= (2/n) sum_(j=1)^n ||A_j|| r^j c_(n-j) for n >= N, and induction gives
c_n <= C0 := max_(n < N) c_n for all n, since (2/n) M C0 <= C0. So the Taylor series of Y converges for |x| < r and
defines an analytic solution, and the difference Z of Y and this solution is a solution on (0, r) that is flat at 0.
There |Z'| <= C |Z|/x, and Gronwall's inequality gives
   |Z(x0)| <= |Z(x)| (x0/x)^C   for 0 < x < x0 < r,
whose right side tends to 0 as x -> 0 by flatness; so Z = 0 and Y is analytic at 0. The same holds at 1, for every real
lam and also at resonances. Hence Y continues analytically along every path in the plane punctured at 0 and 1, with
trivial monodromy around each puncture, to a single-valued entire function. Since M(z) = O(1/z) as z -> oo,
Gronwall's inequality along rays from the circle |z| = 2 gives polynomial growth, and Cauchy's estimates make Y a
polynomial. Let n be the largest degree among b, G, R, with top coefficients b_n, g_n, r_n. The coefficients of
z^(n+1) in (3), (1) and (2) are
   -4 (n + 3) r_n = 0,   (8n + 16) b_n - 4a r_n = 0,   (8n + 8) g_n + b_n = 0,
so r_n = b_n = g_n = 0, a contradiction; hence b = G = R = 0, and (2) gives a P = 0. This proves (iii); lam > 0 is not
used. It excludes non-zero reduced solutions only, not the smooth fundamental and kernel directions invisible in Y.

Step 9 ((iv): the lift). Choose the constant of the primitive F so that Q1 f = f. The end behaviour gives global
reconstructions in the stated classes; in the energy class h and h_phi are continuous across the axes and h_phiphi is in
L^2, so (L3) holds in the sense of distributions on the whole circle. The compatibility g_1 = -4 lam P (Step 3) gives
h = K g + q sin 2phi for some q (the difference lies in the kernel of d^2/dphi^2 + 4, and the parities exclude
cos 2phi). With h0 = K g, the first integral (I1) gives
   lam f + L_(-1) f + a* C h0 - J = c0 sin phi
with a constant c0, computed with q = 0. If the full temperature coefficient is f + t sin phi, the remaining sin phi
equation is lam t + 2 a* q + c0 = 0, which has no obstruction: with t = 0 and q = -c0/(2 a*) the unprojected equations
(L1) to (L3) hold exactly; alternatively q is free and t is solved for. Finally A = -2 a* P/lam, non-zero with P. The
projected equations and the equations for P and A are the separated linearization of A.32 Step 4; for energy solutions
the transport equations hold in the sense of distributions, for C^k solutions classically, and h is in C^(k+2) when g is
in C^k. The decay as s -> -oo and the non-vanishing at finite s follow from lam > 0 and Y != 0. QED.

Uses: A.32 Steps 1 to 4 (the closed order-1 system), the Frobenius theory of regular singular points (Teschl, Section
4.4), Gronwall's inequality. Checks: the reduction of Step 2, the identities (I1) and (I2), the residues and the
top-degree coefficients were checked symbolically by the authors; these are consistency checks, not part of the proof.
Numerical consistency checks by the authors (not part of the proof and not reproduced independently): with Frobenius
series of 40 terms at x = 0.05 from each end and numerical integration to z = 1/2, the 4 x 5 matching matrix of the
admissible branches has four non-zero singular values (a one-dimensional kernel) and the glued solution has P != 0 for
a* = 600, lam = 9.5 (class C^2, interval (7, 14.0408); smallest of the four singular values 2.4e-4, normalized
P = 3.4e-3), a* = 10,
lam = 1 (class E, lam_E = 3; 0.12, 0.094) and a* = 10, lam = 2.5 (class E; 0.088, 0.11); the homogeneous branch at z = 1
with P = 0 has min G = 1.9e-3, 0.89 and 0.85 on [0.05, 0.95] in these three cases.
The independent verification checked Proposition 32 with its own complete proof (independent derivation of the angular
reduction and the residue matrices, strict end integrability, grouped exponent dimensions, the cooperative positivity
and the polynomial exclusion, with the convergent-majorant and Gronwall argument of Step 8, and the normalized lift;
20 exact symbolic checks); it did not reproduce the numerical matching values, which the proof does not use.

### A.34 Proposition 33 (vorticity slope on the horizontal axis)

Statement: Section 3, after Proposition 32. Notation: a = beta + 2, delta = 1/beta, gamma = 1 - 2 delta, W = beta X +
U, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), DW(0) = diag(a, beta - 2), V(x) = W1(x, 0), tau(x) = Theta_y(x, 0), w(x) = Omega_y(x, 0); F
and A are the angular profiles of Theorem 11(b).

Standing facts. By the parities, on the axis y = 0: Theta = Theta_x = 0, Omega = Omega_x = 0, W2 = 0 and d_y W1 = 0
(U1 = -Psi_y is even in y); V is odd and smooth, tau and V' are even, and w is odd. Since div W = 2 beta, d_y W2(x, 0)
= 2 beta - V'(x). From DW(0) = diag(a, b), V'(0) = a, so V(x) = a x + O(x^3) and V'(x) - a = O(x^2) as x -> 0. By
Proposition 25(a), V tau' = (V' - a) tau on R and tau(0) = a0. Theorem 11(a) gives |U| = O(r^(1 - delta)) and Theorem
15(a) gives |DU| = O(r^(-delta)) as r -> inf, so V(x) = beta x + O(x^(1 - delta)) and V'(x) = beta + O(x^(-delta)) as
x -> inf; in particular V' is bounded on [0, inf). By hypothesis and V'(0) = a > 0, V > 0 on (0, inf).

(a) Write V(u) = u v(u) with v smooth, even, v(0) = a and v > 0 on [0, inf). Then a/V(u) - 1/u = (a - v(u))/(u v(u)),
and a - v(u) = O(u^2) is smooth and even, so the integrand is smooth on [0, inf) and O(u) at 0. Hence xi is smooth and
positive on (0, inf), xi(x) = x (1 + O(x^2)) at 0 and xi'/xi = 1/x + a/V - 1/x = a/V. For u >= 1, a/V(u) - (1 + 2
delta)/u = a/V(u) - a/(beta u) = -a U1(u, 0)/(beta u V(u)) = O(u^(-1 - delta)), since a/beta = 1 + 2 delta and V(u) >=
beta u/2 for large u. Therefore
   ln xi(x) - (1 + 2 delta) ln x = int_0^1 (a/V - 1/u) du + int_1^x (a/V(u) - (1 + 2 delta)/u) du
converges as x -> inf, which gives xi(x) = C_xi x^(1 + 2 delta) (1 + o(1)) with C_xi > 0. On (0, inf), (tau xi/V)' =
(xi/V^2) (V tau' - (V' - a) tau) = 0 (using xi' = a xi/V), so tau xi/V is constant there; as x -> 0+, xi/V -> 1/a and
tau -> a0, so tau = a0 V/(a xi), and tau' = (a0/a)(V'/xi - V xi'/xi^2) = (a0/a)(V' - a)/xi. Finally x^(2 delta) tau =
(a0/a) (V/x) (x^(1 + 2 delta)/xi) -> (a0/a) beta/C_xi. By Theorem 11(b), r^(2 delta) grad Theta -> gamma F e_r + F'
e_phi uniformly in phi; at phi = 0, e_phi = e_y and F(0) = 0 (Theta is odd in y), so x^(2 delta) tau(x) -> F'(0).

(b) Differentiate (P1), W1 Omega_x + W2 Omega_y + Omega = Theta_x, in y and put y = 0. With the standing facts, (d_y
W1) Omega_x = 0, W1 Omega_xy = V w', (d_y W2) Omega_y = (2 beta - V') w, W2 Omega_yy = 0 and Theta_xy(x, 0) = tau'(x),
so V w' + (1 + 2 beta - V') w = tau' on R. On (0, inf), E > 0 and E'/E = ((1 + 2 beta)/a)(a/V) - V'/V = (1 + 2 beta -
V')/V, hence (E w)' = (E/V)(V w' + (1 + 2 beta - V') w) = E tau'/V. As x -> 0+, E(x) = x^((1 + 2 beta)/a - 1) (1 +
O(x^2))/a = x^((beta - 1)/a) (1 + O(x^2))/a -> 0 because beta > 1, and w = O(x) near 0 (w is smooth and odd), so E w =
O(x^(1 + (beta - 1)/a)) -> 0. The integrand satisfies E tau'/V = (a0/a) xi^((beta - 1)/a) (V' - a)/V^2 = O(x^((beta -
1)/a)) near 0 (V' - a = O(x^2), V^2 ~ a^2 x^2), so it is integrable at 0; integrating (E w)' from epsilon to x and
letting epsilon -> 0+ gives E(x) w(x) = int_0^x E tau'/V du, with no integration constant (a nonzero multiple of 1/E
would be unbounded like x^(-(beta - 1)/a)).

(c) As x -> inf, xi^((1 + 2 beta)/a) = C_xi^((1 + 2 beta)/a) x^((1 + 2 delta)(1 + 2 beta)/a) (1 + o(1)) and (1 + 2
delta)(1 + 2 beta)/a = (1 + 2 beta)/beta = 2 + delta, so E(x) x^(-1 - delta) = xi^((1 + 2 beta)/a) x^(-2 - delta)
(x/V) -> C_xi^((1 + 2 beta)/a)/beta = c_E > 0. For large x the integrand of (b) is (a0/a) xi^((beta - 1)/a) (V' -
a)/V^2 = O(x^((1 + 2 delta)(beta - 1)/a - 2)) = O(x^(-1 - delta)), because (1 + 2 delta)(beta - 1)/a = (beta - 1)/beta
= 1 - delta and V' - a is bounded; so the integral over (0, inf) converges absolutely and
   x^(1 + delta) w(x) = (x^(1 + delta)/E(x)) int_0^x E tau'/V du -> (1/c_E) int_0^inf E tau'/V du
   = (a0/(a c_E)) int_0^inf xi^((beta - 1)/a) (V' - a) V^(-2) dx.
Identification of the limit. By Theorem 15(b) with k = 1, f_R(X) = R^delta Omega(R X) converges in C^1(1 <= |X| <= 2)
to f(X) = |X|^(-delta) A(arg X). At X = (1, 0), d_y f_R = R^(1 + delta) Omega_y(R, 0) = R^(1 + delta) w(R), and d_y
f(1, 0) = A'(0) because d_y |X|^(-delta) = -delta y |X|^(-delta - 2) = 0 and d_y arg X = x/|X|^2 = 1 at (1, 0). Hence
R^(1 + delta) w(R) -> A'(0), and A'(0) equals the limit above. Finally V' - a = beta + U1_x(x, 0) - (beta + 2) and
U1_x(0, 0) = V'(0) - beta = 2.

(d) The weight xi^((beta - 1)/a) V^(-2) is positive on (0, inf). If V' - a <= 0 there, V' - a is not identically zero
on (0, inf) (otherwise V = a x, against V = beta x + o(x)), and it is continuous, so the integral in (c) is negative
and sign A'(0) = -sign a0. In particular A is not identically zero, which is branch (i) of Theorem 12. Equivalences:
by (a), tau' has the sign of a0 (V' - a), so tau is monotone on [0, inf) exactly when V' - a has one sign there; since
V(x) - a x = -2 x + o(x), V' - a is negative somewhere, so this means V' - a <= 0, that is a0 tau' <= 0 (tau is
nonincreasing if a0 > 0 and nondecreasing if a0 < 0). If V(x)/x is nonincreasing then x V' - V <= 0, so V' <= V/x <=
lim_{u -> 0+} V(u)/u = a. Sector: put s = sign a0, so s A'(0) < 0. A is smooth (Theorem 15(a)) with A(0) = 0 (Omega is
odd in y); choose 0 < phi0 < pi/2 with s A'(phi) <= s A'(0)/2 for 0 <= phi <= phi0. By Theorem 15(b) with k = 1
restricted to |X| = 1, d_phi (r^delta Omega(r, phi)) -> A'(phi) uniformly in phi as r -> inf, so there is R0 with s
d_phi (r^delta Omega(r, phi)) <= s A'(0)/4 for r > R0 and 0 <= phi <= phi0. Since Omega(r, 0) = 0, integration in phi
gives s r^delta Omega(r, phi) <= (s A'(0)/4) phi < 0 for 0 < phi <= phi0, that is a0 Omega < 0 on the sector.

(e) In branch (ii), A = 0 identically, so A'(0) = 0 and, as a0 != 0, the integral in (c) vanishes. By the argument of
(d) it is negative if V' - a <= 0 on (0, inf); hence V' - a > 0 somewhere (neither this sign change nor A'(0) = 0 is
claimed to be sufficient for branch (ii)), and it is negative somewhere since V(x) - a x = -2 x + o(x). By (a), tau'
has the sign of a0 (V' - a), so tau' takes both signs and tau is not monotone.

Consistency check with Theorem 12(ii) (not needed for the proof). In branch (ii) the vanishing of the integral gives
w(x) = -E(x)^(-1) int_x^inf E tau'/V du. Using only V' - a -> -2 (Theorem 15(a)) and the asymptotics of xi, V and E in
(a) and (c), the integrand is -(2 a0/a) C_xi^((beta - 1)/a) beta^(-2) x^(-1 - delta) (1 + o(1)), so x^(1 + 2 delta)
w(x) -> (2 a0/a) C_xi^((beta - 1)/a - (1 + 2 beta)/a) = 2 a0/(a C_xi) = 2 delta F'(0) by (a). On the other hand, by
Theorem 15(c) with A = 0, r^(2 delta) Omega(r, .) -> B in C^1(S^1), and on the axis d_y = r^(-1) d_phi, so x^(1 + 2
delta) w(x) -> B'(0) = F'(0) - gamma F'(0) = 2 delta F'(0) for B = sin(phi) F' - gamma cos(phi) F. The two values
agree.

Hypotheses actually used: smoothness, the A1 parities, (P1), (P2), div U = 0, DW(0) = diag(a, b), V > 0 on (0, inf),
the far-field bounds of Theorem 11(a) and Theorem 15(a), the angular limit of grad Theta in Theorem 11(b) (for F'(0)
in (a)) and the C^1 convergence of Theorem 15(b) (for A'(0) in (c) and the sector in (d)); Theorem 12 supplies the
branch terminology and Theorem 15(c) is used only in the consistency check. (P3) and the canonical-velocity condition
enter only through Theorems 11, 12 and 15, whose hypotheses class A' supplies. The proposition is a direct corollary
of the differentiated equation (P1) on the axis and these results; Proposition 25(a) gives tau in terms of V,
Proposition 25 does not use (P1), and Theorem 16 leaves A and F undetermined without a formula for A'(0).

Remark (the axis equations alone do not decide the branch; an example of the independent verification). For beta > 2
put rho = 3/a, nu = 2/a (so 0 < nu < rho < 1), H0(z) = (1 + z^2)^(nu/2), p(t) = t^2 exp(-t^2) and H(z) = H0(z) - k
p(z/eps). With
   J0 = int_0^inf z^(-rho) H0'(z) dz = (nu/2) B(1 - rho/2, (rho - nu)/2),
   Jb = int_0^inf z^(-rho) (d/dz) p(z/eps) dz = (rho/2) eps^(-rho) Gamma(1 - rho/2)
(the first by t = z^2, the second by parts), choose eps so small that k = J0/Jb < 1/2. Then H is smooth and even, H(0)
= 1, H >= 1 - k > 1/2 and H(z) ~ z^nu as z -> inf. Put x(z) = int_0^z dt/H(t), an odd diffeomorphism of R onto R (nu <
1), and V(x(z)) = a z/H(z), tau(x(z)) = a0/H(z), w(x(z)) = -(a0/(a H(z) z^(1 - rho))) int_0^z t^(-rho) H'(t) dt for z
> 0, extended oddly. These functions are smooth, V is odd with V'(0) = a and V > 0 on (0, inf), V = beta x + O(1) and
V' = beta + o(1) as x -> inf, xi = z, and both axis equations V tau' = (V' - a) tau and (b) hold. Since V' - a = -a z
H'(z)/H(z) and dx = dz/H, the integral in (c) equals -(1/a) int_0^inf z^(-rho) H'(z) dz = -(J0 - k Jb)/a = 0, so x^(1
+ delta) w -> 0, while x^(1 + 2 delta) w -> 2 a0/(a C_xi) as in the consistency check, and V' - a takes both signs.
These are axis data only: no extension to a solution of (P) in the plane and no canonical inverse is claimed. The
example shows that the axis identities, the centre data and the sublinear tails do not by themselves exclude branch
(ii). (Constructed and proved by the independent verification; the authors rechecked the two integrals and the
reduction of the integral in (c).)

Numerical consistency checks by the authors (finite-radius checks of the algebra for prescribed axis velocities, not
profiles; not part of the proof and not rerun independently). Integrating the two axis equations for V = beta x + 2 x
(1 + x^2)^(-delta/2), with and without an added term k x^3 exp(-x^2) (k = 3), at beta = 2.5, 3 and 5, the value of
x^(1 + delta) w at x = 4.3e15 differs from a finite-radius proxy of the formula of (c) (the integral accumulated up to
that radius and the constant C_xi estimated there, not the exact value of A'(0)) by the relative amounts 4.1e-6
(beta = 3), 4.1e-7 to 4.5e-7 (beta = 2.5) and 3.0e-4 (beta = 5), each below x^(-delta) at that radius (6.1e-6, 5.6e-7
and 7.5e-4). This comparison is empirical: for the exact solutions of these models x^(1 + delta) w approaches its
limit at the upper rate O(x^(-delta)) with an unspecified constant (independent verification, below), which bounds no
difference at a given radius. For the branch (ii) check the base velocity is changed to V = beta x + 2 x
(1 + x^2)^(-delta) + k x^3 exp(-x^2), so that U1 = O(x^(1 - 2 delta)), and the amplitude is numerically tuned at
beta = 3: k = 9.5571359 is a numerical root of the integral of (c) accumulated up to the final radius, including its
contribution near the origin, plus a leading-order tail term, not a certified zero. Then x^(1 + 2 delta) w at
x = 4.9e8, 2.0e11, 2.9e13 and 4.3e15 is 2.7341044, 2.7341130, 2.7341124 and 2.7341086, against 2 delta x^(2 delta)
tau = 2.7341133 at the largest radius; the variation among the four values has no identified cause. An earlier version
of the tuned computation started the accumulated integral at 0 at x0 = exp(-14), omitting a contribution of about
2.3e-9, and drifted to 2.7374826 at 4.3e15; the external audit identified the omission, which is consistent at leading
order with the drift; neither a nonzero A'(0) at that amplitude nor a complete decomposition of the error is
certified. The branch (ii) limit rests on the analytic argument above, not on these computations.
The independent verification checked Proposition 33 with its own proof (the two axis identities, the integrating-factor
formula and its absolute convergence, the identification of the limit with A'(0), the sign and the sector, and part
(e)) and constructed the example of the remark above with an analytic proof; its finite diagnostics (6 symbolic
identities, 96 ODE and 18 tail samples) are its own; it did not execute the authors' model checks.
A later installation check (closed 2026-10-21 at 21:25Z; Appendix B) proved that for the exact solutions of the model
systems of the preceding paragraph x^(1 + delta) w approaches its limit at the upper rate O(x^(-delta)), with no
explicit constant, and found that the printed relative differences and tuned values round as quoted.

### A.35 Proposition 34 (vorticity slope on the vertical axis)

Statement: Section 3, after Proposition 33. Notation: a = beta + 2, b = beta - 2, delta = 1/beta, gamma = 1 - 2 delta,
W = beta X + U, U = (-Psi_y, Psi_x), DW(0) = diag(a, b), D = 2 (beta + 2)(2 beta + 1); Y(y) = W2(0, y) = beta
y + U2(0, y), T(y) = Theta(0, y), s(y) = Theta_xx(0, y), z(y) = Omega_x(0, y); F, A and H are the angular profiles of
Theorem 11(b).

Standing facts. On x = 0 the parities give Theta_x = Theta_xxx = 0, Omega = Omega_y = Omega_xx = 0, W1 = W1_xx = 0
(U1 = -Psi_y is odd in x) and W2_x = 0 (U2 = Psi_x is even in x). Since div U = 0, W1_x(0, y) = 2 beta - Y'(y). Y, T,
s and z are smooth and odd, Y'(0) = b and T'(0) = a0, so Y(y) = y v(y) with v smooth, even and v(0) = b. By Theorem
1(b), Y > 0 on (0, inf), so v > 0 on [0, inf). Theorem 11(a) and Theorem 15(a) give, for r >= 1, |U| <= C
r^(1 - delta), |DU| <= C r^(-delta) and |D^2 Theta| <= C r^(gamma - 2); hence Y = beta y + O(y^(1 - delta)),
Y' = beta + O(y^(-delta)) and s = O(y^(gamma - 2)) as y -> inf.

(a) (P2) at x = 0 is Y T' = b T. Apply d_x^2 to (P2), W1 Theta_x + W2 Theta_y = b Theta, and put x = 0. The terms
W1_xx Theta_x, W1 Theta_xxx and 2 W2_x Theta_xy vanish, leaving 2 W1_x Theta_xx + W2_xx Theta_y + W2 Theta_xxy = b
Theta_xx, that is Y s' + (2 (2 beta - Y') - b) s = -W2_xx(0, y) T', and 4 beta - b = 3 beta + 2. Differentiating (P3)
in x gives Psi_xxx = -Omega_x - Psi_xyy; at x = 0, Psi_xyy(0, y) = (d/dy)^2 Psi_x(0, y) = (d/dy)^2 U2(0, y) = Y''(y),
and W2_xx = U2_xx = Psi_xxx, so -W2_xx(0, y) = -U2_xx(0, y) = z + Y''. Apply d_x to (P1), W1 Omega_x + W2
Omega_y + Omega = Theta_x, at x = 0: W1_x Omega_x + W1 Omega_xx + W2_x Omega_y + W2 Omega_xy + Omega_x = Theta_xx
gives (2 beta - Y') z + Y z' + z = s. For the sign of T': b/Y(u) - 1/u = (b - v(u))/(u v(u)) is smooth on [0, inf)
(b - v is smooth, even and O(u^2)), so eta is smooth and positive on (0, inf), eta(y) = y (1 + O(y^2)) and eta' = b
eta/Y. On (0, inf), (T/eta)' = (Y T' - b T)/(Y eta) = 0 and T/eta -> a0 as y -> 0+, so T = a0 eta and T' = a0 b eta/Y,
which has the sign of a0; T'(0) = a0.

(b) Insert the finite Taylor expansions (odd powers only) into the two equations of (a); no analyticity is used. With
Y' = b + 3 Y3 y^2 + ..., Y'' = 6 Y3 y + ... and T' = a0 + O(y^2), the coefficients of y give (b + 3 beta + 2 - 2 b)
s1 = (2 beta + 4) s1 = a0 z1 + 6 a0 Y3 and (b + 1 + 2 beta - b) z1 = (2 beta + 1) z1 = s1. Eliminating s1,
((2 beta + 4)(2 beta + 1) - a0) z1 = 6 a0 Y3, and (2 beta + 4)(2 beta + 1) = D. At the coefficient of y^(2n-1), Y s'
contributes (2n - 1) b s_(2n-1) and (3 beta + 2 - 2 Y') s contributes (3 beta + 2 - 2 b) s_(2n-1) = (beta + 6)
s_(2n-1), plus terms with lower coefficients of s; T' (z + Y'') contributes a0 z_(2n-1) plus lower coefficients of z
and the coefficients of Y'' through y^(2n-1) (that is, of Y through y^(2n+1)), with T' determined by a0 and Y through
Y T' = b T (at degree 2j + 1 the new coefficient of T has the multiplier 2jb, non-zero for j >= 1). Since (2n - 1)
b + beta + 6 = 2nb + 8 and (2n - 1) b + 1 + 2 beta - b = 2nb + 5, the matrix is as stated, with determinant
(2nb + 8)(2nb + 5) - a0. At a singular block a solution still satisfies the system, but compatibility of arbitrary
right sides and uniqueness are not asserted. The distinction from Proposition 17 is visible at n = 1: the axis
determinant vanishes at a0 = D, whereas kappa_1 = (2 - a0/D)/8 vanishes at a0 = 2D and is positive at a0 = D.
Consistency with the report: in the notation of Section 2.4 (Theta = a0 y + b1 x^2 y + b2 y^3 + ..., Psi = -2 x y + d1
x^3 y + d2 x y^3 + ..., Omega = g x y + ...) one has s1 = 2 b1, z1 = g and Y3 = d2, so s1 = (2 beta + 1) z1 is (T3),
and the second relation follows from (T1), (T3) and g = -6 (d1 + d2).

(c) For u >= 1, b/Y(u) - (1 - 2 delta)/u = b/Y(u) - b/(beta u) = -b U2(0, u)/(beta u Y(u)) = O(u^(-1 - delta)), since
1 - 2 delta = b/beta and Y(u) >= beta u/2 for large u; so ln eta(y) - (1 - 2 delta) ln y converges as y -> inf, which
gives eta = C_eta y^(1 - 2 delta) (1 + o(1)) with C_eta > 0. Then eta^((1 + 2 beta)/b) = C_eta^((1 + 2 beta)/b)
y^(2 + delta) (1 + o(1)) because (1 - 2 delta)(1 + 2 beta)/b = (1 + 2 beta)/beta = 2 + delta, and Y = beta y
(1 + o(1)), so E_v = c_v y^(1 + delta)(1 + o(1)). On (0, inf), E_v'/E_v = ((1 + 2 beta)/b)(b/Y) - Y'/Y =
(1 + 2 beta - Y')/Y, so by (a) (E_v z)' = (E_v/Y)(Y z' + (1 + 2 beta - Y') z) = E_v s/Y. As y -> 0+,
E_v(y) = y^((1 + 2 beta)/b - 1) (1 + O(y^2))/b = y^((beta + 3)/b) (1 + O(y^2))/b -> 0, and z is bounded near 0, so E_v
z -> 0; the integrand E_v s/Y = O(y^((beta + 3)/b)) is integrable at 0. Hence E_v(y) z(y) = int_0^y E_v s/Y du. As
y -> inf the integrand is O(y^(1 + delta) y^(gamma - 2) y^(-1)) = O(y^(-1 - delta)), so the integral over (0, inf)
converges absolutely, and
   y^(1 + delta) z(y) = (y^(1 + delta)/E_v(y)) int_0^y E_v s/Y du -> (1/c_v) int_0^inf E_v s/Y du.
Identification of the limit. By Theorem 15(b) with k = 1, f_R(X) = R^delta Omega(R X) converges in C^1(1 <= |X| <= 2)
to f(X) = |X|^(-delta) A(arg X). At X = (0, 1), d_x f_R = R^(1 + delta) Omega_x(0, R) = R^(1 + delta) z(R), while
d_x |X|^(-delta) = -delta x |X|^(-delta - 2) = 0 and d_x arg X = -y/|X|^2 = -1 there, so d_x f(0, 1) = -A'(pi/2).
Hence R^(1 + delta) z(R) -> -A'(pi/2), which gives the formula.

(d) If s = 0 on (0, inf), then E_v z = 0 by (c), so z = 0, and the s equation gives T' Y'' = 0, hence Y'' = 0 on
(0, inf) (T' != 0 by (a)). With Y(0) = 0 and Y'(0) = b this means Y = b y, that is U2(0, y) = -2 y, against
U = o(|X|). So s is not identically zero. Now let a0 s >= 0 on (0, inf). Then a0 E_v z = int_0^y a0 E_v s/Y du >= 0;
for y > y_s the continuous function a0 s is nonnegative and not identically zero on (0, y), so this integral is
positive, and a0 z > 0 on (y_s, inf). By (c), a0 A'(pi/2) = -(1/c_v) int_0^inf a0 E_v s/Y dy < 0. In particular A is
not identically zero, which is branch (i) of Theorem 12. Sector: A is smooth (Theorem 15(a)) and A(pi/2) = 0
(Omega is odd in x). Put sigma = sign a0 and choose 0 < phi0 < pi/2 with sigma A'(phi) <= sigma A'(pi/2)/2
for |phi - pi/2| <= phi0. By Theorem 15(b) with k = 1 restricted to |X| = 1, d_phi (r^delta Omega(r, phi)) -> A'(phi)
uniformly as r -> inf, so there is R0 with sigma d_phi (r^delta Omega(r, phi)) <= sigma A'(pi/2)/4 < 0 for r > R0
and |phi - pi/2| <= phi0. Since Omega(r, pi/2) = 0, for pi/2 - phi0 <= phi < pi/2, sigma r^delta Omega(r, phi) =
-int_phi^(pi/2) sigma d_phi (r^delta Omega) dphi' >= -(pi/2 - phi) sigma A'(pi/2)/4 > 0.

(e) Time change. tau(y) = int_1^y du/Y(u) is a smooth increasing bijection of (0, inf) onto R: 1/Y(u) - 1/(b u) =
(b - v(u))/(b u v(u)) is smooth and O(u) near 0, so tau(y) = (ln y)/b + C0 + O(y^2) as y -> 0+, and Y <= 2 beta u for
large u, so tau -> inf as y -> inf. Hence y(tau) <= C e^(b tau) for tau <= 0. With u = (s, z) as functions of tau and
d/dtau = Y d/dy, (a) reads
   du/dtau = M(tau) u + f(tau),  M = [[-(3 beta + 2 - 2 Y'), T'], [1, -(1 + 2 beta - Y')]],  f = (T' Y'', 0),
or, keeping z + Y'' together, ds/dtau = -alpha s + T' q with alpha = 3 beta + 2 - 2 Y' and q = z + Y''.
(H2): here q = -U2_xx(0, y) >= 0 on (0, inf). For tau0 < tau,
   s(tau) = exp(-int_tau0^tau alpha) s(tau0) + int_tau0^tau exp(-int_sigma^tau alpha) T'(sigma) q(sigma) dsigma.
As tau -> -inf, alpha -> 3 beta + 2 - 2 b = beta + 6, so there is tau1 with alpha >= beta + 5 on (-inf, tau1]. For
tau <= tau1, as tau0 -> -inf the first term is at most exp(-(beta + 5)(tau - tau0)) |s(tau0)| -> 0
(s is bounded near y = 0), and the integrand is at most exp(-(beta + 5)(tau - sigma)) |T' q| with T' q bounded near
y = 0. Hence
   s(tau) = int_-inf^tau exp(-int_sigma^tau alpha) T'(sigma) q(sigma) dsigma      (*)
for tau <= tau1. For tau > tau1, the formula with tau0 = tau1 and (*) at tau1 give (*) at tau; the kernel
exp(-int_sigma^tau alpha) is positive whatever the sign of alpha on [tau1, tau]. Since a0 T' > 0 and q >= 0, a0
s >= 0.
(H1): here a0 > 0, so T' > 0 by (a), and M(tau) has nonnegative off-diagonal entries T' and 1 (a Metzler matrix).
Positivity of the propagator: let sigma <= tau and choose c >= max(0, sup(-M11), sup(-M22)), the suprema taken over
[sigma, tau]. Then M + c I >= 0 entrywise on [sigma, tau], Phi(rho, sigma) = exp(-c (rho - sigma)) Psi(rho) with
Psi' = (M + c I) Psi, Psi(sigma) = I, and the Picard iterates Psi_(k+1)(rho) = I + int_sigma^rho (M + c I) Psi_k are
entrywise nonnegative, so Phi(tau, sigma) >= 0 entrywise. This holds for all sigma <= tau.
Behaviour at tau = -inf: Y' - b and T' - a0 are O(y^2), Y'' = O(y) and (s, z) = O(y) near y = 0, so
M(tau) = M0 + O(e^(2 b tau)), f(tau) = O(e^(b tau)) and u(tau) = O(e^(b tau)) for tau <= 0, where
   M0 = [[-(beta + 6), a0], [1, -(beta + 3)]].
With q0 = sqrt(9 + 4 a0), the eigenvalues of M0 are mu_+- = (-(2 beta + 9) +- q0)/2, with eigenvectors ((q0 - 3)/2, 1)
and (-(q0 + 3)/2, 1); let P have these columns (det P = q0 >= 3) and L = diag(mu_+, mu_-). For sigma <= tau <= 0,
G(tau) = exp(-mu_+ (tau - sigma)) P^(-1) Phi(tau, sigma) P satisfies
   G(tau) = exp((L - mu_+)(tau - sigma)) + int_sigma^tau exp((L - mu_+)(tau - rho)) N(rho) G(rho) drho,
   N = P^(-1) (M - M0) P,
with |N(rho)| <= C' e^(2 b rho) and |exp((L - mu_+) t)| <= 1 for t >= 0 (matrix norm induced by the maximum norm), so
by Gronwall |G| <= exp(C' int_-inf^0 e^(2 b rho) drho) and |Phi(tau, sigma)| <= K exp(mu_+ (tau - sigma)) for
sigma <= tau <= 0. Now mu_+ < b if and only if q0 < 4 beta + 5, that is 4 a0 < (4 beta + 2)(4 beta + 8) = 4 D, that is
a0 < D. For tau <= 0 the variation-of-constants formula u(tau) = Phi(tau, tau0) u(tau0) + int_tau0^tau Phi(tau, sigma)
f(sigma) dsigma has |Phi(tau, tau0) u(tau0)| <= K C e^(mu_+ tau) e^((b - mu_+) tau0) -> 0 as tau0 -> -inf and an
integrand bounded by K C e^(mu_+ tau) e^((b - mu_+) sigma), integrable on (-inf, tau]. Hence u(tau) = int_-inf^tau
Phi(tau, sigma) f(sigma) dsigma for tau <= 0, and for tau > 0
   u(tau) = Phi(tau, 0) int_-inf^0 Phi(0, sigma) f(sigma) dsigma + int_0^tau Phi(tau, sigma) f(sigma) dsigma
          = int_-inf^tau Phi(tau, sigma) f(sigma) dsigma
by Phi(tau, 0) Phi(0, sigma) = Phi(tau, sigma). If U2_yy(0, y) = Y''(y) >= 0 for y > 0, then f >= 0, and therefore
s >= 0 and z >= 0 on (0, inf); with a0 > 0, a0 s >= 0.

(f) If a0 > 0 and (H1) or (H2) holds, (d) and (e) give z(y1) > 0 for some y1 > 0; since Omega(0, y1) = 0,
Omega(x, y1) = x z(y1) + o(x) > 0 for small x > 0, so Omega <= 0 on Q1 is impossible, and Proposition 6 excludes
Omega >= 0 on Q1. Under the hypotheses of Proposition 33(d) (V > 0 gives its no-positive-zero assumption, V' <= a its
monotonicity assumption), sign A'(0) = -sign a0, and by (d) sign A'(pi/2) = -sign a0. With A(0) = A(pi/2) = 0 this
gives sigma A < 0 on (0, epsilon) and sigma A > 0 on (pi/2 - epsilon, pi/2) for some epsilon > 0, and the two sectors
of Proposition 33(d) and of (d) above give the last assertion with R1 the larger of their radii.

Remarks (not used in the proof).
 1. Threshold. The resonance mu_+ = (2n - 1) b is equivalent to q0 = 4nb + 13, that is a0 = (2nb + 5)(2nb + 8), the
    determinant zeros of (b); at n = 1 this is a0 = D. The bound a0 < D ensures that the origin condition removes the
    homogeneous contribution in the representation used in (e). If a smooth profile has a0 > D and Y3 > 0, then s1,
    z1 < 0 by (b), so the positivity conclusion fails near the origin. This is a conditional local obstruction to
    extending the criterion with the convexity condition of (H1) to a0 > D; existence of such profiles and sharpness
    within class A' are not established (at the level of the axis system, Y = b y near 0 with convexity acquired later
    gives u = 0 near 0 and no obstruction). At a0 = D, the order-one compatibility condition is Y3 = 0.
 2. Far-field compatibility of the hypotheses. By Theorem 11(b) and the C^2 convergence of Theorem 15(b), as y -> inf
       U2(0, y) = -H'(pi/2) y^(1 - delta) + o(y^(1 - delta)),
       U2_yy(0, y) = delta (1 - delta) H'(pi/2) y^(-1 - delta) + o(y^(-1 - delta)),
       s(y) = (gamma F + F'')(pi/2) y^(gamma - 2) + o(y^(gamma - 2)).
    So U2_yy(0, y) >= 0 for all large y requires H'(pi/2) >= 0, and a0 s >= 0 for all large y requires a0
    (gamma F + F'')(pi/2) >= 0; equality gives no eventual sign by itself. These are necessary conditions, not
    sufficient, on leading data not determined by the far-field recursion of Theorems 11 and 16.
 3. The stored state 62df5606 (beta = 3, a0 = 600/h with |h - 1| < 2e-14, so a0 > D = 70). It satisfies (P2) and (P3)
    exactly but not (P1), so it is not a profile and (a) to (f) do not apply to it; the following concerns its own
    centre coefficients. In the independent verification of this proposition (Appendix B), rational interval
    arithmetic on its 5706 stored coefficients gives, in the notation of Section 2.4 and rounded to nearest at the
    printed digits, d1 = 0.7455968624338064, Y3 = d2 = 5.645233466987034, z1 = g = -6 (d1 + d2) = -38.34498197652504,
    s1 = 2 b1 = -268.41487047617072 and, for q = -U2_xx(0, y) = z + Y'', q1 = z1 + 6 d2 = -6 d1 = -4.473581174602838.
    Since a0 > D, (H1) fails; since q1 < 0, (H2) fails on some interval (0, epsilon); since s1 < 0 < a0, a0 s < 0 on
    some interval (0, epsilon). No radius epsilon is certified. The relations of (b), which hold for profiles, fail
    for this state: D0 = 7 z1 - s1 = -3.3595045728699587e-6 (rounded to nearest), the coefficient of x y in its (P1)
    residual, is rigorously nonzero, and (D - a0) z1 - 6 a0 Y3 = 10 D0, about -3.36e-5 (equivalently, (D - a0)(-d1) -
    D d2 = (10/6) D0). These are statements about the stored function, not about a profile.

Model checks of the algebra (by the authors; not a proof and not profiles; the model axis equations do not construct
an angular profile A). A symbolic computation confirms the block matrices of (b) for n = 1, ..., 5 and the order-1
relations. The axis system was integrated for the prescribed convex Y = beta y - 2 y (1 + y^2)^(-delta/2), with
Y'' = 2 delta y (1 + y^2)^(-delta/2 - 2) (3 + (1 - delta) y^2) > 0 and Y3 = delta, at beta = 2.5, 3, 5 and a0 = 0.1 D,
0.5 D, 0.95 D, from series data at y = 1e-2. These are finite-radius observations. At the sampled points of [1e-2,
4.3e15], s > 0 and z > 0; z/y at y = 2e-2 agrees with 6 a0 Y3/(D - a0) to within 1.1e-3 relative (the O(y^2)
correction). At y = 4.311e15, y^(1 + delta) z and I/c, where I is the integral of E_v s/Y accumulated from the
starting radius and c is the value of c_v estimated at the final radius, agree to 4.1e-6 relative
(beta = 3, a0 = 0.5 D) and 3.0e-4 (beta = 5, a0 = 0.5 D). For the exact solutions of these model systems y^(1 + delta)
z approaches its limit at the upper rate O(y^(-delta)) with an unspecified constant (proved in the independent
verification, below); this bounds neither the numerical error at the final radius nor the relative speed of approach
at different beta. Since E_v z equals that integral on every finite interval up to the omitted term E_v(y0) z(y0),
this agreement is an integrating-factor consistency check, not an error bound for the limit. A start from zero data at
y = 1e-6 gives the same y^(1 + delta) z at 4.311e15 to all ten printed digits (beta = 2.5, 3; a0 = 0.5 D) and to below
8e-8 relative (beta = 5), as the representation of (e) predicts for a0 < D. At beta = 3 with a0 = 100 and 140
(both > D) the same Y gives z/y near the origin equal to 6 a0 Y3/(D - a0) < 0 (-6.67 and -4.00), so s, z < 0 near the
origin; y^(1 + delta) z at 4.311e15 is -1.3169e4 (a0 = 100) and +9.8006e4 (a0 = 140; there z changes sign on the
sampled axis). These runs were not executed independently.

Hypotheses actually used: smoothness, the A1 parities, (P1), (P2), (P3) (through Psi_xxx = -Omega_x - Psi_xyy), div
U = 0, DW(0) = diag(a, b), Theorem 1(b) (Y > 0), the bounds of Theorem 11(a) and Theorem 15(a) (k <= 2), U = o(|X|),
and the C^1 convergence of Theorem 15(b); in (f) also Proposition 6 and Proposition 33(d).
The independent verification checked Proposition 34 with its own proof (the three axis equations, the block matrices
and the threshold D of (b), the integrating-factor formula of (c) and its absolute convergence at both ends, the sign
in the identification with -A'(pi/2), the strict sign and the far sector of (d), both sufficient conditions of (e),
with the propagator near the origin controlled by a weighted energy estimate in place of the eigenbasis argument
above, and (f)), and computed the centre values of Remark 3 for 62df5606 by rational interval arithmetic on the stored
coefficients. Its finite diagnostics (12 symbolic identities, 18 axis integrations for its own model Y = beta y - 2
asinh(y), 54 comparisons with the integrating-factor formula and 558 exact coefficient checks) are its own; it read
the printed records of the authors' model checks and checked their printed comparisons, without executing the authors'
runs. It also proved, for every beta > 2 and every positive C^2 axis velocity Y on a half-line y >= y0 > 0 with
Y = beta y + O(y^(1 - delta)), Y' = beta + O(y^(-delta)) and Y'' = O(y^(-1 - delta)), that every solution of the three
axis equations of (a) with finite data at y0 has finite limits of y^(1 + 2 delta) s and y^(1 + delta) z, each
approached at the upper rate O(y^(-delta)); both model velocities satisfy these conditions. No sharp rate and no
finite-radius error constant is asserted.

### A.36 Proposition 35 (nonpositive vorticity on the first quadrant)

Statement: Section 3, after Proposition 34. Notation: as in the statement, A.34 and A.35; c_v and C_eta are the
constants of Proposition 34(c).

Throughout, beta > 2 (Corollary 4), so b > 0, 0 < delta < 1/2, gamma = b/beta and 3/2 < d < 2.
Step 1 (the identity (a)). By Proposition 34(a), Y s' + (3 beta + 2 - 2 Y') s = -T' C and Y z' + (1 + 2 beta - Y')
z = s, with T = a0 eta and eta'/eta = b/Y (Proposition 34(c)), so T' = a0 b eta/Y. Put I_s = eta^((3 beta + 2)/b)
Y^(-2); since E_v = eta^((1 + 2 beta)/b) Y^(-1),
   (I_s s)' = (I_s/Y) (Y s' + (3 beta + 2 - 2 Y') s) = -a0 b P C,   (E_v z)' = E_v s/Y = eta^(-h) I_s s,
using (3 beta + 2)/b + 1 = 4 beta/b and (3 beta + 2)/b - h = (1 + 2 beta)/b. As y -> 0+, Y = b y + O(y^3) and eta = y
(1 + O(y^2)), so I_s ~ b^(-2) y^((3 beta + 2)/b - 2) and E_v ~ b^(-1) y^((1 + 2 beta)/b - 1), and since s, z = O(y),
I_s s = O(y^(2 + 8/b)) and E_v z = O(y^(2 + 5/b)) tend to 0. Integrating twice and exchanging the order of integration
(absolutely integrable on the triangle: P C = O(u^(1 + 8/b)), so eta(t)^(-h) int_0^t |P C| du = O(t^(1 + 5/b)) near 0;
at infinity see below),
   E_v(y) z(y) = int_0^y eta(t)^(-h) (int_0^t (-a0 b) P(u) C(u) du) dt = -a0 b int_0^y K_y(u) C(u) du.
Near 0, P(u) ~ b^(-4) u^(8/b), int_u^1 eta^(-h) ~ (b/3) u^(-3/b) (h - 1 = 3/b), so K_y(u) = O(u^(5/b)) and
C(u) = O(u). As u -> inf, eta(u) ~ C_eta u^gamma (Proposition 34(c)) and Y ~ beta u, so P tends to a positive limit,
eta^(-h) ~ C_eta^(-h) u^(-gamma h) = C_eta^(-h) u^(-1 - delta) (gamma h = (beta + 1)/beta), K_inf(u) ~ k_inf
u^(-delta) with a constant k_inf > 0, and C(u) = O(u^(-1 - delta)) by Theorem 15(a); so K_inf C is absolutely
integrable on (0, inf). Since 0 < K_y <= K_inf and K_y -> K_inf pointwise, dominated convergence gives
E_v(y) z(y) -> -a0 b J_inf. By Proposition 34(c), y^(1 + delta) z(y) -> -A'(pi/2) and E_v(y) = c_v y^(1 + delta)
(1 + o(1)), so -c_v A'(pi/2) = -a0 b J_inf.
For the second identity, differentiate (P1) in y and restrict to y = 0. There Omega = Omega_x = 0 and W2 = 0 by the
parities, and d_y W2(x, 0) = 2 beta - V'(x) since div W = 2 beta (A.34, standing facts, which do not use the
hypothesis on V), so V w' + (1 + 2 beta - V') w = tau' on R, with tau(x) = Theta_y(x, 0). Integrating over (0, R) and
using V(0) = 0 gives int_0^R (1 + 2 beta - 2 V') w dx = tau(R) - tau(0) - V(R) w(R). By Theorems 11(a) and 15(a),
V(R) = O(R), V' = O(1), w = O(R^(-1 - delta)) and tau(R) = O(R^(-2 delta)), so the integral converges absolutely and
V(R) w(R) and tau(R) tend to 0; tau(0) = a0, and 1 + 2 beta - 2 V' = 1 - 2 U1_x(x, 0) since V = beta x + U1(x, 0).
Step 2 (the stream function, (b)). Psi is odd in x and in y, so Psi = 0 on both axes,
and |grad Psi| = |U| = O(r^(1 - delta)) (Theorem 11(a)) gives, by integration along rays from 0, |Psi| <= M
(1 + r)^(2 - delta) with a constant M. On Q1, Lap Psi = -Omega >= 0. Fix k with 2 - delta < k < 2 and put
g(r, phi) = r^k cos(k (phi - pi/4)), harmonic on Q1, with g >= cos(k pi/4) r^k > 0 on the closed quadrant without the
origin (k pi/4 < pi/2). For eps > 0 the subharmonic function Psi - eps g is <= 0 on the axes and on the arc r = R of
Q1 for all R >= R(eps); by the maximum principle on Q1 intersected with {r < R}, Psi <= eps g there; letting R -> inf
and then eps -> 0 gives Psi <= 0 on Q1. Psi is not identically zero on Q1, since Psi_xy(0) = -2. By the strong maximum
principle Psi < 0 on Q1, and by the Hopf lemma at the boundary points (x, 0), x > 0, and (0, y), y > 0 (flat boundary,
Psi smooth up to it, Psi = 0 there), -Psi_y(x, 0) > 0 and -Psi_x(0, y) > 0. Hence U1(x, 0) = -Psi_y(x, 0) > 0 and
U2(0, y) = Psi_x(0, y) < 0, that is, V(x) > beta x and Y(y) < beta y; Y > 0 by Proposition 34(a).
Step 3 (the far field, (c)). By Theorem 11(b), r^delta Omega -> A uniformly, so A <= 0 on [0, pi/2]; A is smooth
(Theorem 15(a)) and vanishes at 0 and pi/2 by parity, so A'(0) <= 0 <= A'(pi/2). If A were identically zero on [0,
pi/2], then by parity on [0, 2 pi], branch (ii) of Theorem 12 would hold, in which Omega takes both signs on Q1 for
a0 > 0; so A is not identically zero. Since Omega(x, 0) = 0 and Omega <= 0 on Q1, w(x) = Omega_y(x, 0) <= 0 for x > 0.
By (b) Proposition 33 applies; by its part (b), E(x) w(x) = I(x) := int_0^x E(u) tau'(u)/V(u) du with tau' = (a0/a)
(V' - a)/xi, and V' - a = U1_x(x, 0) - 2 -> -2 as x -> inf (Theorem 15(a)), so the integrand is negative for u >= u0.
By Proposition 33(c), I(inf) is absolutely convergent and A'(0) = I(inf)/c_E. If I(inf) = 0, then
E(x) w(x) = -int_x^inf E tau'/V du > 0 for x >= u0, against w <= 0. Hence I(inf) < 0 and A'(0) < 0. Finally
q = -w >= 0, q = O(x^(-1 - delta)) is integrable, and x^(1 + delta) q(x) -> -A'(0) > 0, so q is not identically zero;
the second identity of (a) reads int_0^inf (1 - 2 U1_x(x, 0)) q dx = a0, which gives the stated mean.
Step 4 ((d) and (e)). Since Omega(0, y) = 0 and Omega <= 0 on Q1, z(y) = Omega_x(0, y) <= 0, so J_y >= 0 by (a), and
J_inf >= 0 by the limit in Step 1. If z were identically zero on (0, inf), the third equation of Proposition 34(a)
would give s = 0 on (0, inf), against Proposition 34(d); so z(y0) < 0 for some y0 and J_y0 > 0. If s >= 0 on (0, inf),
Proposition 34(d) gives z > 0 on (y_s, inf), against z <= 0; so s(y) < 0 for some y. At such a y, z(y) < 0: if
z(y) = 0, then y is a maximum of z on (0, inf), so z'(y) = 0, and the third equation gives s(y) = 0. Since J_y0 > 0
and K_y0 > 0, C = U2_xx(0, .) is positive somewhere on (0, y0).
Step 5 ((f)). By Theorem 11(b), U = r^(1 - delta) (V_inf + o(1)) with V_inf = -H' e_r + d H e_phi (the angular field
called V in Theorems 11 and 15; here V denotes W1(x, 0)) and -H'' - d^2 H = A; by parity H vanishes at 0 and pi/2.
Multiplying by sin(d t) and integrating over [0, L] gives
   H'(L) sin(d L) = int_0^L sin(d t) (-A(t)) dt,
and sin(d t) > 0 on (0, L] since 0 < d L < pi; with A <= 0 and A not identically zero on [0, L], H'(L) > 0. At
phi = L, e_r = e_y, so U2(0, y) = -H'(L) y^(1 - delta) + o(y^(1 - delta)), and by the C^k convergence of Theorem
15(b), U2_yy(0, y) = -H'(L) (1 - delta)(-delta) y^(-1 - delta) + o(y^(-1 - delta)) = delta (1 - delta) H'(L)
y^(-1 - delta) + o(y^(-1 - delta)) > 0 for large y. The centre relation (D - a0) z1 = 6 a0 Y3 of Proposition 34(b) and
z1 <= 0 (z = z1 y + O(y^3) <= 0) give the signs of Y3. If 0 < a0 < D and U2_yy(0, .) >= 0 on (0, inf), Proposition
34(e)(H1) and (d) give z > 0 somewhere, against z <= 0; so U2_yy(0, y) < 0 for some y.
Step 6 ((g)). Put alpha = A'(pi/2) >= 0 and m = delta (1 - delta) H'(pi/2) > 0. By Proposition 34(c), z = -alpha
y^(-1 - delta) + o(y^(-1 - delta)), and by Step 5, C = -z - Y'' = (alpha - m) y^(-1 - delta) + o(y^(-1 - delta)); if
alpha < m, C is negative for large y and, by (e), changes sign. If alpha > 0, z < 0 for large y. Let alpha = 0 and put
S = I_s s, Z = E_v z, so Z <= 0, Z(y) -> -c_v alpha = 0 and C < 0 for y >= y2. Then S' = -a0 b P C > 0 on [y2, inf),
and S has a finite limit S_inf since P C is absolutely integrable. If S_inf <= 0, then S < 0 on [y2, inf) and
Z(y) = -int_y^inf eta^(-h) S dt > 0, against Z <= 0; so S_inf > 0, s > 0 for large y, and Z(y) = -int_y^inf eta^(-h) S
dt < 0 for large y. In both cases z < 0, hence J_y > 0, for large y. By Theorem 15(b) (C^2 convergence of R^(-gamma)
Theta(R X)) and Lap (r^gamma F) = r^(gamma - 2)(gamma^2 F + F''), at x = 0 y^(1 + 2 delta) s(y) -> F''(pi/2) + gamma
F(pi/2); with I_s = c_s y^(1 + 2 delta) (1 + o(1)), c_s > 0, this limit equals S_inf/c_s > 0 when alpha = 0. For the
limit of z in that case, Z(y) = -int_y^inf eta^(-h) S dt with S -> c_s sigma and eta^(-h) = C_eta^(-h) t^(-1 - delta)
(1 + o(1)), so Z(y) = -(c_s sigma/(delta C_eta^h)) y^(-delta) (1 + o(1)) and y^(1 + 2 delta) z(y) tends to -c_s
sigma/(delta C_eta^h c_v), which equals -sigma since c_s = C_eta^((3 beta + 2)/b)/beta^2, c_v =
C_eta^((1 + 2 beta)/b)/beta and (3 beta + 2)/b - h = (1 + 2 beta)/b. For a fixed large y with s(y) > 0,
Theta_x(0, y) = 0 by parity and Theta_xx(0, y) = s(y) is positive, so Theta_x(x, y) > 0 for small x > 0; since
Theta(0, y) = T(y) > 0 and, by Theorem 11(a) and Theta(x, 0) = 0, |Theta(x, y)| <= y sup over 0 <= t <= y
of |Theta_y(x, t)| = O_y(x^(-2 delta)) -> 0 as x -> inf, Theta_x(x, y) < 0 for some x > 0.
Step 7 ((h)). Theta and Psi are smooth (class A'), so Omega, Theta and Psi have Taylor expansions at 0; by the
parities Psi and Omega contain only monomials x^i y^j with i and j odd, and Theta only monomials with i even and j
odd. Write Psi = -2 x y + Psi_4 + Psi_6 + O(|X|^8), Omega = g x y + Omega_4 + O(|X|^6) and
Theta = a0 y + Theta_3 + Theta_5 + O(|X|^7) with homogeneous parts of the indicated degrees, so that
W = ((beta + 2) x, b y) + O(|X|^3). On a monomial x^i y^j the linear part of (P1) acts as multiplication by
(beta + 2) i + b j + 1, and that of (P2) by (beta + 2) i + b j - b. Let g = 0 and write Theta_3 = t21 x^2 y + t03 y^3
and Psi_4 = p31 x^3 y + p13 x y^3. The degree-2 part of (P1) gives (2 beta + 1) g = 2 t21, so t21 = 0; the degree-2
part of (P3) gives -6 (p31 + p13) = g = 0; the degree-3 part of (P2), whose only nonlinear term is a0 d_x Psi_4, gives
2 (beta + 2) t21 + 3 a0 p31 = 0 and 2 b t03 + a0 p13 = 0. Since a0 != 0, p31 = p13 = 0 and t03 = 0, so Theta_3 = 0 and
Psi_4 = 0. Write Omega_4 = G1 x^3 y + G2 x y^3, Theta_5 = u41 x^4 y + u23 x^2 y^3 + u05 y^5 and
Psi_6 = h51 x^5 y + h33 x^3 y^3 + h15 x y^5. The nonlinear terms of degree 4 in (P1) involve Psi_4 and g x y, and
those of degree 5 in (P2) other than a0 d_x Psi_6 involve Psi_4 and Theta_3, so all of them vanish, and (P1), (P2)
give (4 beta + 5) G1 = 4 u41, (4 beta - 3) G2 = 2 u23, 4 (beta + 2) u41 + 5 a0 h51 = 0 and 4 beta u23 + 3 a0 h33 = 0,
hence
   G1 = -5 a0 h51/((beta + 2)(4 beta + 5)),   G2 = -3 a0 h33/(2 beta (4 beta - 3)),
while (P3) gives G1 = -20 h51 - 6 h33 and G2 = -6 h33 - 20 h15. On the ray of angle phi in Q1,
r^(-4) Omega -> cos(phi) sin(phi) (G1 cos(phi)^2 + G2 sin(phi)^2) as r -> 0, so Omega <= 0 on Q1 gives G1 <= 0 and
G2 <= 0, hence h51 >= 0 and h33 >= 0 (a0 > 0, 4 beta - 3 > 0). If h51 = 0, then G1 = 0, so h33 = 0 and G2 = 0. If
h51 > 0, equating the two expressions for G1 gives
   a0 = 4 (beta + 2)(4 beta + 5) + (6/5) (beta + 2)(4 beta + 5) h33/h51 >= 4 (beta + 2)(4 beta + 5).
A symbolic computation of the full equations through these degrees (by the authors) reproduces these relations; it is
not part of the proof.
Remark 1 (the vertical-axis relations do not exclude Omega_x(0, y) < 0 at a0 = D). For every beta > 2 there are smooth
odd functions Y, T, s, z on R satisfying the three equations of Proposition 34(a) with C = -z - Y'', a0 = D,
0 < Y < beta y and Y'' >= 0 on (0, inf), T, T' > 0, s, z < 0 on (0, inf), and the far behaviour
Y = beta y - C_Y y^(1 - delta) + O(1), T ~ C_T y^gamma, s ~ -C_s y^(-1 - 2 delta), z ~ -C_z y^(-1 - delta) with
positive constants. Construction: take smooth f >= 0 vanishing on [0, 1], equal to c y^(-1 - delta) for y >= 2, with
int_0^inf f = 2; put Y = b y + int_0^y (y - t) f(t) dt and T = D eta. Then Y'' = f, b <= Y' < beta, and Y = beta y - c
(delta (1 - delta))^(-1) y^(1 - delta) + O(1). On (0, 1], z = -M y and s = -(2 beta + 1) M y solve the equations
exactly (Y = b y, T' = D, C = M y, using 3 beta + 2 - 2b + b = 2 beta + 4 and D = 2 (beta + 2)(2 beta + 1)); continue
them by the linear equations. In the variables S = I_s s, Z = E_v z the equations on [1, inf) read S' = D b (P/E_v)
Z + D b P f, Z' = eta^(-h) S, with nonnegative coefficients and forcing that are O(y^(-1 - delta)), hence integrable.
The homogeneous solution q_h with q_h(1) = ((2 beta + 1)/b^2, 1/b) has components >= their initial values and bounded
(Gronwall), the forced solution q_f with q_f(1) = 0 is >= 0 and bounded, and (S, Z) = -M q_h + q_f; for M large both
components are negative and bounded away from 0, with finite negative limits, which with I_s ~ c_s y^(1 + 2 delta) and
E_v ~ c_v y^(1 + delta) gives the stated far behaviour. These are axis data only: no extension to a solution in the
plane, and no consistency with the full centre jet, is asserted. The criterion (H1) of Proposition 34(e) therefore
cannot be extended to a0 = D by the vertical-axis relations alone.
Remark 2 (leading far-field data compatible with Omega <= 0). For every beta > 2 and kappa > delta put
   A(phi) = -sin(2 phi) cos(phi)^2,   F(phi) = sin(phi) (1 + kappa cos(phi)^2),
   H(phi) = -sin(2 phi)/(2 (4 - d^2)) - sin(4 phi)/(4 (16 - d^2)).
These smooth functions have the parities of Theorem 11 (A and H odd about 0 and about pi/2, F odd about 0 and even
about pi/2), -H'' - d^2 H = A, A < 0 on (0, pi/2), A'(0) = -2, A'(pi/2) = 0, F(pi/2) = 1, F'(0) = 1 + kappa > 0,
H'(pi/2) = 1/(4 - d^2) - 1/(16 - d^2) > 0, H'(0) < 0, H = -(sin(2 phi)/2)(1/(4 - d^2) + cos(2 phi)/(16 - d^2)) < 0 on
(0, pi/2) and F''(pi/2) + gamma F(pi/2) = 2 (kappa - delta) > 0, so they satisfy the angular sign conditions just
displayed; no axis integral, centre or profile condition is tested. With V_inf = -H' e_r + d H e_phi and
B = -delta V_r A + V_phi A' - gamma cos(phi) F + sin(phi) F' as in Theorem 15(c) (V_r, V_phi the components of V_inf),
B is odd about 0 and about pi/2, B(pi/2 - t) = -2 (kappa - delta) t + O(t^3) and A(pi/2 - t) = -2 t^3 + O(t^5); with
A(phi) = -2 phi + O(phi^3) and B = O(phi) near 0 and A bounded away from 0 on compact subintervals of (0, pi/2),
A + epsilon B < 0 on (0, pi/2) for all small epsilon > 0. Hence the two-term far-field vorticity r^(-delta)
(A + r^(-delta) B) of Theorem 15(c) is negative on Q1 for all large r. These are angular data only: no profile, no
finite-radius data, no matching with the centre and no higher far-field order is asserted. Symbolic checks of the
displayed identities: by the authors, not part of the proof.
The independent verification checked Proposition 35 with its own proof in two steps. For the second draft (parts (a)
to (g) and Remark 1) it rederived the axis identities and the vanishing integration constants at the origin and at
infinity, gave a direct proof of Y > 0 for either sign of a0, justified the maximum principle on Q1 with a harmonic
barrier of degree strictly between 2 - delta and 2, checked the Hopf signs on each open axis, used the C^2 convergence
on annuli of Theorem 15(b) to differentiate the vertical velocity asymptotics, and proved the construction of Remark 1
from the integrability of the coefficients and the Gronwall bound (no planar extension and no centre jet). For the
additions it proved the second identity of (a) without dividing by the horizontal transport speed, the strict mean of
(c), the limits of (g) and the sign changes of Theta_x on high horizontal lines, the threshold of (h) (the relevant
determinant is 72 a0 b) and the sign of the two-term vorticity of Remark 2, with the neighbourhoods of the two axes
and the compact interval between them treated separately. Its finite diagnostics are its own (20 symbolic records, 54
finite kernel integrals, 5 angular Green identities and 3 axis integrations for the second draft; 37 exact symbolic
identities, 9 finite polynomial jets that satisfy only the specified orders, and 3 jets below the threshold of (h)
with a positive quartic ray for the additions); the authors' scripts were read as data and not executed. No profile,
no realization of the angular data or of the jets, and no exclusion of the class is asserted.

### A.37 Proposition 36 (nonpositive vorticity on the first quadrant with a0 < 0)

Statement: Section 3, after Proposition 35. Notation: as in the statement and in A.34 to A.36.

Throughout, beta > 2, a0 < 0 and Omega <= 0 on Q1, so b > 0, 0 < delta < 1/2, 0 < gamma < 1 and -a0 b > 0.
Step 1 ((a)). Step 2 of A.36 does not use the sign of a0: the Phragmen-Lindelof comparison on Q1, the strong maximum
principle and the Hopf lemma give Psi < 0 on Q1, -Psi_y(x, 0) > 0 and -Psi_x(0, y) > 0, that is, V(x) > beta x and
Y(y) < beta y; Y > 0 by Proposition 34(a). By Proposition 34(c), T = a0 eta with eta > 0, so T < 0 on (0, inf), and a0
T' > 0 (Proposition 34(a)) gives T' < 0. By Theorem 11(b), r^delta Omega -> A uniformly, so A <= 0 on [0, pi/2]; A is
smooth and vanishes at 0 and pi/2 by parity, so A'(0) <= 0 <= A'(pi/2).
Step 2 ((b)). By (a), Proposition 33 applies. Since Omega(x, 0) = 0 and Omega <= 0 on Q1, w(x) = Omega_y(x, 0) <= 0
for x > 0; by Proposition 33(b), E w = I with E > 0, so I <= 0 on (0, inf). By Proposition 33(a),
tau' = (a0/a)(V' - a)/xi, and V' - a = U1_x(x, 0) - 2 -> -2 as x -> inf (Theorem 15(a)); since a0 < 0,
tau'(x) = Theta_xy(x, 0) > 0 on [u0, inf) for some u0 > 0. If U1_x(x, 0) <= 2 for all x > 0, then tau' >= 0 on
(0, inf), so I(x) >= I(x) - I(u0) > 0 for x > u0, against I <= 0; hence U1_x(x, 0) > 2 for some x > 0. On [u0, inf)
the function I is strictly increasing, with the finite limit I(inf) <= 0 (Proposition 33(c)); so I < 0 and w < 0 on
[u0, inf). By Proposition 33(a), E(x) = c_E x^(1 + delta) (1 + o(1)), so x^(1 + delta) w(x) -> I(inf)/c_E, which is
A'(0) by Proposition 33(c). If A'(0) = 0: in B = -delta V_r A + V_phi A' - gamma cos(phi) F + sin(phi) F' (Theorem
15(c)) one has A(0) = A'(0) = 0, F(0) = 0 and V_phi(0) = 0 (V_phi = d H with H odd about 0), so B'(0) = (1 - gamma)
F'(0) = 2 delta F'(0). On the horizontal axis d_y = r^(-1) d_phi, so the C^1(S^1) estimate of Theorem 15(c) gives
w(x) = A'(0) x^(-1 - delta) + B'(0) x^(-1 - 2 delta) + o(x^(-1 - 2 delta)); when A'(0) = 0, x^(1 + 2 delta)
w(x) -> B'(0) = 2 delta F'(0), and F'(0) = a0 beta/(a C_xi) < 0 by Proposition 33(a). Finally q = -w >= 0,
q = O(x^(-1 - delta)) by Theorem 15(a), and q > 0 on [u0, inf); the second identity of Proposition 35(a) reads
int_0^inf (1 - 2 U1_x(x, 0)) q dx = a0, which gives the stated mean.
Step 3 ((c)). By Proposition 35(a), E_v(y) z(y) = -a0 b J_y with E_v > 0 and -a0 b > 0. Since Omega(0, y) = 0 and
Omega <= 0 on Q1, z(y) = Omega_x(0, y) <= 0, so J_y <= 0, and J_inf <= 0 by the limit in Step 1 of A.36. If z were
identically zero on (0, inf), the third equation of Proposition 34(a) would give s = 0 on (0, inf), against
Proposition 34(d); so z(y0) < 0 and J_y0 < 0 for some y0, and since K_y0 > 0 on (0, y0), C < 0 somewhere on (0, y0).
With S = I_s s and Z = E_v z as in Step 1 of A.36, Z' = eta^(-h) S and Z(y) -> 0 as y -> 0+; since Z(y0) < 0, Z' < 0
somewhere on (0, y0), and s < 0 there. If s(y) < 0 and z(y) = 0, then y is a maximum of z on (0, inf), so z'(y) = 0,
and the third equation of Proposition 34(a) gives s(y) = 0; hence z(y) < 0 wherever s(y) < 0. Let A'(pi/2) = 0. By
Proposition 34(c), Z(y) -> -c_v A'(pi/2) = 0 as y -> inf, so int_0^inf eta^(-h) S dt = 0, an absolutely convergent
integral since eta^(-h) S = E_v s/Y = O(y^(-1 - delta)) (Theorem 15(a) and Proposition 34(c)). Since S < 0 where s < 0
and eta^(-h) > 0, S > 0 and s > 0 somewhere. By Step 1 of A.36, S' = -a0 b P C with -a0 b P > 0 and S(y) -> 0
as y -> 0+; S > 0 somewhere gives S' > 0, hence C > 0, somewhere, and C < 0 somewhere was shown above. The limit of s
is that of Step 6 of A.36 (Theorem 15(b), sign-independent): y^(1 + 2 delta) s(y) -> F''(pi/2) + gamma
F(pi/2) = sigma. For z, A(L) = A'(L) = 0, F'(L) = 0 and V_phi(L) = d H(L) = 0 by parity, so B'(L) = F''(L) + gamma
F(L) = sigma; on the vertical axis d_x = -r^(-1) d_phi, so Theorem 15(c) gives z(y) = -A'(L) y^(-1 - delta) - B'(L)
y^(-1 - 2 delta) + o(y^(-1 - 2 delta)) and y^(1 + 2 delta) z(y) -> -sigma. Since z <= 0, sigma >= 0.
Step 4 ((d)). On Q1, r^(-2) Omega -> g cos(phi) sin(phi) as r -> 0 along each ray, so g <= 0. Write
Theta = a0 y + t21 x^2 y + t03 y^3 + O(|X|^5) and Psi = -2 x y + d1 x^3 y + d2 x y^3 + O(|X|^6). As in Step 7 of A.36
(whose coefficient identities do not use the sign of a0 or of g; only its final sign argument uses a0 > 0), the
